rows.name: Anhui Guild Hall
rows.summary: Regarded as the largest of Beijing's old provincial guild halls, it was built in 1871 with money from Li Hongzhang and other officers of the Huai Army. Its opera stage saw the Anhui troupes that helped create Peking opera, and in the 1890s it housed the reformers' Self-Strengthening Society. The restored core, with its timber theatre, shrine building and Bilinglong Hall, has displays on the hall's history and on Peking opera.

rows.name: Asbury Church (Chongwenmen Church)
rows.summary: Founded in 1870 by American Methodist Episcopal missionaries, Asbury Church is usually described as the oldest Protestant church in Beijing; the present grey-brick building in an eclectic style was rebuilt in 1902–04 after the earlier church was burnt in 1900. Used as a school hall from 1958, it reopened for worship in 1982 as Chongwenmen Church and is still an active congregation.

rows.name: Badachu
rows.summary: Badachu, the 'Eight Great Sites', is a hillside park in the Western Hills linking eight Buddhist temples and nunneries founded between the Sui and Qing dynasties on three hills. The best known is Lingguang Temple, an active monastery where a Buddha tooth relic found in the ruins of an older pagoda is kept in a pagoda built in 1964. Old trees, including white-bark pines and ginkgos more than 600 years old, shade the paths between the temples.

rows.name: Baili Shanshui Gallery
rows.summary: A 371-square-kilometre scenic area covering the whole of Qianjiadian town in the hills of north-eastern Yanqing, matching the Qianjiadian area of the Yanqing Geopark and strung along a riverside road loop of about 56 km. Its main stops are a geopark of fossilised (silicified) tree trunks, the Wulong Gorge, the Dishuihu waterfall and the old Chaoyang Temple, Dragon King Temple and Guandi Temple, with village guesthouses along the way.

rows.name: Bailin Temple
rows.summary: Founded in 1347 and rebuilt in the Ming, Bailin Temple was given a major overhaul in 1713 by Prince Yinzhen, the future Yongzheng Emperor, for his father the Kangxi Emperor's 60th birthday, and was counted among the eight great temples inside the old city. Its main halls survive along a central axis of five courtyards, with Qianlong-era steles and a bronze bell cast in 1707, and for two centuries it stored the woodblocks of the Qing imperial edition of the Buddhist canon.

rows.name: Baoguo Temple
rows.summary: A large temple of the southern city, rebuilt in 1466 as Ciren Temple and renamed in 1754, where the scholar Gu Yanwu lodged in 1668 and a shrine to him was added in the 1840s; it was the city's best-known book market in the late Ming and early Qing. After use as a factory and offices it was restored and from 1997 to 2020 housed a famous collectors' market, and it is now the Baoguo Temple Cultural Park, which holds second-hand book fairs and cultural events in its courtyards.

rows.name: Baqi Cave
rows.summary: A large limestone cave in the hills near Tanzhe Temple, hollowed out by an underground river, with a visitor route of about 1.35 km through big chambers and narrow passages. Its name, 'Eight Wonders', refers to eight featured sights, above all a huge figure-of-eight fold in the rock; the cave also has a 410 m underground slide and films projected onto a cave wall, and it stays at about 16°C all year.

rows.name: Beigong National Forest Park
rows.summary: A forest park in the low hills of western Fengtai, established in 2002 and approved as a national forest park in 2005. Paths climb through planted woods, flower gardens and stream valleys, and in autumn its maples and other coloured trees make it one of Beijing's popular red-leaf spots.

rows.name: Beijing Ancient Observatory
rows.summary: Built in 1442 on a stretch of the old city wall, the Ancient Observatory was the imperial observatory of the Ming and Qing dynasties. On its 14 m brick platform stand eight large Qing bronze instruments, six of them designed by the Flemish Jesuit Ferdinand Verbiest and finished in 1674, while the courtyard below keeps the Ziwei Hall, replicas of Ming instruments and exhibitions on traditional Chinese astronomy.

rows.name: Beijing Aquarium
rows.summary: A large indoor aquarium opened in 1999 in the northern part of Beijing Zoo, run as a commercial attraction separate from the zoo. Its halls hold tanks of fish and other aquatic animals, and staged marine-animal shows are part of the programme, which makes it mainly a family outing.

rows.name: Beijing Auto Museum
rows.summary: A museum of the motor car opened in 2011 on the South 4th Ring Road, with some 80 vehicles across 13 exhibition areas covering the history, technology and future of the car. Exhibits range from a replica of Benz's 1886 Patent-Motorwagen to Hongqi state cars and Beijing-built jeeps, alongside interactive displays.

rows.name: Beijing Dongyue Temple
rows.summary: A Taoist temple of the Zhengyi school founded in 1319 outside the old Chaoyang Gate and dedicated to the god of Mount Tai, the Great Deity of the Eastern Peak, then rebuilt and enlarged under the Ming and Qing. Around its main courtyard, rows of small rooms hold plaster figures of the 'seventy-six departments' of the Taoist pantheon, and many old steles survive. It also houses the Beijing Folk Customs Museum, which holds a large temple fair at Spring Festival.

rows.name: Beijing Garden Expo Park
rows.summary: The site of the 2013 China International Garden Expo on the west bank of the Yongding River, built over a former construction-waste landfill and kept as a public park. It holds 69 exhibition gardens in regional, modern and international styles, a sunken flower valley made from an old waste pit, and the 69.7-metre Yongding Tower, a new pagoda in Liao–Jin style with views over the river.

rows.name: Beijing Horticultural Expo Park
rows.summary: The 503-hectare site of the 2019 International Horticultural Exposition at Yanqing, kept open and renamed Beijing Horticultural Expo Park in 2020. Its main buildings are the China Pavilion, the flower-shaped International Pavilion and the Plant Pavilion, a large greenhouse of tropical and rare plants, set among the gardens left by Chinese provinces and foreign countries.

rows.name: Beijing International Flower Port
rows.summary: A large flower park in Yangzhen, Shunyi District, best known as the venue of the Beijing Tulip Festival each April and early May. During the festival the grounds are filled with mass plantings of tulips and other spring bulbs, many of them imported, with costumed parades and stage shows, and areas are set aside for camping.

rows.name: Beijing Lu Xun Museum
rows.summary: The small courtyard house that the writer Lu Xun remodelled and lived in from 1924 to 1926, where he wrote Wild Grass and other works, kept with its furnishings including the tiny room he lived and wrote in, known as the 'tiger's tail'. Beside it a museum opened in 1956 tells the story of his life, drawing on his manuscripts, letters and books and the prints and stele rubbings he collected.

rows.name: Beijing Planetarium
rows.summary: China's first large planetarium, opened in 1957 opposite Beijing Zoo, with a domed star theatre in the original building and a glass-walled second building added in 2004. The two buildings hold dome and 3D/4D theatres, astronomy exhibition halls and small observatories, making it a good indoor stop with children.

rows.name: Beijing Shijingshan Amusement Park
rows.summary: Opened in 1986 as one of Beijing's first amusement parks, this district-owned park mixes Chinese garden scenery with a fairy-tale castle. It has six roller coasters, family rides and a converted Boeing 747 airliner, plus seasonal events such as a Spring Festival temple fair and summer water-splashing days, and it suits families with children.

rows.name: Beijing Wildlife Park
rows.summary: A large forested safari park near Yufa in southern Daxing, opened in 2001, with a self-drive route through the big-animal and predator areas and walk-through zones for smaller species. Themed areas include red-panda and capybara exhibits, a gibbon area and a Madagascar forest, and the park keeps sizeable groups of chimpanzees, jaguars and African elephants.

rows.name: Beijing World Park
rows.summary: A theme park opened in 1993 in south-western Fengtai District, laid out by continent with more than 100 scale models of famous buildings and monuments, most of them at one-tenth size. A walk takes you past miniatures of the Eiffel Tower, the Egyptian pyramids, Angkor Wat and the Sydney Opera House, and it suits families with children.

rows.name: Beijing Zoo
rows.summary: Regarded as China's oldest public zoo, it grew out of the Qing government's agricultural experimental farm founded in 1906 and first opened to visitors in 1908. Besides the giant pandas and other animal houses, the wooded grounds keep buildings of the old farm, among them the brick gateway and Changguanlou, a Baroque-style two-storey villa built in 1908 as a stopping place for Empress Dowager Cixi on her boat trips to the Summer Palace.

rows.name: Beijing railway station
rows.summary: Opened in 1959 as one of the Ten Great Buildings marking the tenth anniversary of the People's Republic, Beijing railway station was then the largest station in the country. Designed under the architects Yang Tingbao and Chen Deng'ao, it pairs a broad central hall with two 34 m clock towers and glazed-tile Chinese-style roofs on a monumental, Soviet-influenced plan. It is still a working main-line station, the only one inside the old walled city.

rows.name: Big Bell Temple
rows.summary: Built in 1733 as the imperial Juesheng Temple, this Qing monastery took its popular name after the Yongle Bell, a huge bronze bell cast under the Ming Yongle Emperor, was moved here in 1743. Since 1985 it has been the Big Bell Temple Ancient Bell Museum, showing more than 400 Chinese and foreign bells, with the Yongle Bell hanging in its two-storey bell tower.

rows.name: Capital Museum
rows.summary: Beijing's municipal museum, founded in 1981 in the Confucius Temple and moved in 2006 to a large modern building on Chang'an Avenue designed by Cui Kai with Jean-Marie Duthilleul. Its galleries cover the history of Beijing alongside collections of porcelain, bronzes, jade, calligraphy, painting and Buddhist sculpture, much of it excavated in and around the city, and it hosts major touring exhibitions.

rows.name: Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception (Nantang)
rows.summary: Beijing's oldest Catholic church site, begun in 1605 as a chapel at the residence of the Jesuit Matteo Ricci and rebuilt as a church under Adam Schall von Bell in 1650. The present Baroque-style building dates from 1904; it was closed for renovation from 2018 and reopened in 2022 as a working parish church.

rows.name: Central Radio & TV Tower
rows.summary: A 405-metre broadcasting and observation tower on Beijing's West Third Ring Road, completed in 1992 and opened to sightseers in 1994; it was the city's tallest structure until 2018. Lifts climb to an observation deck at 238 m and a revolving restaurant a little lower down, with views across Yuyuantan Park and the city.

rows.name: Changchun Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple founded in 1592 by order of the Wanli Emperor's mother and once among the most prosperous in the capital, later used as housing before its restoration in the early 2000s. Since 2005 its courtyards have housed the Xuannan Culture Museum, which covers the history of the old southern city's scholars, guild halls, opera and trade.

rows.name: Changxindian February 7th Strike Sites
rows.name_zh: 长辛店二七大罢工旧址
rows.summary: A group of sites in the old railway town of Changxindian linked to the strike of 7 February 1923 on the Beijing–Hankou railway, a workers' movement led by the early Chinese Communist Party. The February 7th Memorial Hall, opened in 1986 around four courtyards, displays documents and objects from the strike, and nearby stand the former workers' club, the preparatory school for work-study in France founded in 1918, and buildings of the old locomotive works, now a creative park.

rows.name: Chaoyang Park
rows.summary: Regarded as the largest park inside Beijing's 4th Ring Road, Chaoyang Park was developed from 1984 on the east side of the city. Lakes, lawns and woods share the grounds with play areas, the former beach-volleyball venue of the 2008 Olympics and seasonal music festivals, and a long walking loop runs through the park.

rows.name: Chateau Changyu AFIP
rows.summary: A wine estate of the Changyu wine company in Jugezhuang town, built around a European-style castle with vineyards, a large underground cellar, a European-style village of shops and restaurants and a museum of Changyu's history since its founding in 1892. Visitors can tour the cellar, taste wine, pick table grapes in season and stay at the estate.

rows.name: Cheng'en Temple
rows.summary: Built in 1510–1513 for the Ming eunuch Wen Xiang on Moshikou's old caravan road, Cheng'en Temple keeps Ming halls, bell and drum towers flanking the Hall of Heavenly Kings with its murals, and four stone watchtowers at the corners of the compound. Used as a school from the 1950s and later restored, it now houses the Yanjing Bajue Museum of traditional Beijing crafts, and its old ginkgo draws visitors in autumn.

rows.name: China National Botanical Garden
rows.summary: Formed in 2022 by joining the Beijing Botanical Garden with the Chinese Academy of Sciences' garden, the China National Botanical Garden has a planned area of nearly 600 hectares at the foot of the Western Hills, between Fragrant Hills and Jade Spring Hill. The north garden has themed collections such as the peach, peony, lilac and rose gardens, a tropical conservatory, Cherry Valley (Yingtaogou) and a memorial hall to the novelist Cao Xueqin. It also takes in Wofo Temple (Shifang Pujue Temple), whose Hall of the Reclining Buddha holds a large bronze Buddha cast in 1321.

rows.name: China Red Sandalwood Museum
rows.summary: A private museum opened in 1999 by the entrepreneur Chen Lihua and devoted to zitan, a dense dark-red hardwood long used for fine Chinese furniture. Its five-storey building in Ming–Qing style shows a large collection of classical furniture and carving, and its zitan carving craft was listed as national intangible cultural heritage in 2011.

rows.name: Church of the Saviour (Beitang)
rows.summary: Beijing's Catholic cathedral, founded in 1703 on land given by the Kangxi Emperor near the palace and moved here in 1887 when the Guangxu court wanted the old site, with its grey-stone Gothic façade completed in 1890. The church was besieged during the Boxer uprising of 1900, and after restoration in 2018 it is again the cathedral of the Archdiocese of Beijing.

rows.name: Cross Temple
rows.summary: The ruins of a hillside temple that was Buddhist for most of its history but was used by Christians of the Church of the East during the Yuan dynasty, one of very few such places of worship known in China. Foundations, column bases, two old ginkgo trees and two marble steles remain, a Liao text recut in the Ming and a Yuan stele topped by a cross; two stones carved with crosses and a Syriac psalm verse, found here in the early 20th century, are now in the Nanjing Museum.

rows.name: Dagaoxuan Hall
rows.summary: A Ming and Qing imperial Taoist temple just north-west of the Forbidden City, where emperors worshipped the Three Pure Ones and the Jade Emperor. Used by military units from 1950, it was handed back to the Palace Museum in 2010 and restored from 2015, and in 2025 its halls opened as a digital gallery of the Palace Museum's collection.

rows.name: Dajue Temple
rows.summary: A temple at the foot of Yangtai Mountain in the Western Hills, founded in 1068 under the Liao as Qingshui Yuan and given its present name when it was rebuilt in 1428. It faces east towards the rising sun, reflecting a Khitan custom of the Liao period, and is known for spring water channelled through its courtyards, a ginkgo about 1,000 years old and 300-year-old magnolias that flower in April. It is run as a museum by the Beijing cultural heritage bureau.

rows.name: Deshengmen Arrow Tower
rows.summary: The archery tower of Deshengmen, the western of the two northern gates of the Ming inner city, added in 1436–39, its tall front pierced by rows of arrow slits. The gatehouse and barbican were pulled down between 1915 and 1955 and the wall in the 1960s, leaving the tower and a stretch of barbican wall as one of the few surviving gates of old Beijing.

rows.name: Early Buildings of Tsinghua University
rows.summary: Twenty buildings from before 1935 survive in the western part of Tsinghua University's campus, alongside the Qing-era Tsinghua Garden whose Gongzi Ting hall predates the university. They range from the European-style Tsinghua Xuetang and Second Gate of 1909–1912 to the 'Four Great Buildings' of the American architect Henry Murphy's 1914 plan: the Grand Auditorium, library, gymnasium and science building.

rows.name: Fahai Temple
rows.summary: Built between 1439 and 1443 with funds raised by a Ming court eunuch, Fahai Temple is known for the murals in its main hall, painted in the 1440s by court and local artists and among the oldest and best-preserved wall paintings in Beijing. The hall is kept dark and visitor numbers are strictly limited to protect them, so the nearby digital Fahai Temple Mural Art Museum reproduces the murals at full size on high-resolution screens.

rows.name: Fayuan Temple
rows.summary: Regarded as the oldest surviving Buddhist temple in Beijing's old city, it was founded in the Tang dynasty in memory of soldiers killed in the Korean campaigns of the 640s and rebuilt many times since. Its courtyards climb gently north past halls with Ming bronze Buddhas, old steles and a large Qing stone basin on a Yuan base, and the temple houses the China Buddhist Academy and is known for its lilacs in spring.

rows.name: Fenghuangling
rows.summary: A scenic area of about 9.7 km² of rocky hills in north-west Haidian, named after a huge 'Fenghuangling' inscription carved on a cliff and nicknamed the 'Little Huangshan of western Beijing'. Three hiking routes follow the valleys past cave shrines carved in the Liao and Jin periods, the Daoist Taoyuan Temple, a 53-step 'Heavenly Ladder' cut almost vertically into the rock, and Longquan Temple, an active Buddhist monastery at the foot of the hills.

rows.name: Former National Library of Peiping
rows.summary: The library building opened in 1931 for the National Library of Peiping, paid for with returned Boxer Indemnity funds and designed by V. Leth-Moller, with a Chinese palace-style exterior over an interior fitted with the most modern equipment of its day. Marble columns and stone lions brought from the ruined Old Summer Palace stand in its forecourt, and until 1987 it was the main building of the national library, which later used it as its Ancient Books branch.

rows.name: Former National Mongolian and Tibetan School
rows.summary: A Qing nobleman's mansion near Xidan that became a school for Mongolian and Tibetan students in 1913, where Li Dazhao and others carried out political work in the 1920s and, in 1924, Mongolian students including Ulanhu formed the Communist Party's first branch among an ethnic minority. After decades as a clothing market it was restored and reopened in 2023 as an exhibition hall on China's ethnic groups and national unity.

rows.name: Former Residence of Li Dazhao
rows.summary: The small courtyard house where Li Dazhao, a co-founder of the Chinese Communist Party, lived with his family from 1920 to 1924, the years in which he set up a Marxist study society and the early Communist group in Beijing. Restored and opened in 2007, it shows the family's rooms furnished as they were and an exhibition on his activities in those years.

rows.name: Former Residence of Soong Ching-ling
rows.summary: The Beijing home from 1963 until her death in 1981 of Soong Ching-ling, widow of Sun Yat-sen and later Honorary President of the PRC, set in the former garden of Prince Chun's Mansion, the estate where the last emperor Puyi was born. Her two-storey house, kept with its original furnishings, and a hall with an exhibition on her life stand beside a garden lake ringed by artificial hills, covered walkways and pavilions.

rows.name: Grand Canal Scenic Area, Tongzhou
rows.summary: Tongzhou marks the northern end of the Grand Canal, and this scenic area follows about 12 km of the North Canal from the confluence of five rivers south to Gantang Bridge, with parks along both banks. At its northern end stand the 'three temples and a pagoda': a Confucian temple, the Daoist Ziqing Palace and the Buddhist Yousheng Temple, grouped around the 56-metre, 13-storey Randeng Pagoda that once told boatmen they were nearing Tongzhou. Further south are Canal Park and the large Grand Canal Forest Park, and sightseeing boats run on the canal.

rows.name: Guangji Temple
rows.summary: A working Buddhist temple and headquarters of the Buddhist Association of China since 1953, rebuilt in the 1450s on a Jin-dynasty site and named Hongci Guangji Temple in 1466. Its Ming-plan courtyards hold a white-marble ordination platform of 1698, a bronze incense tripod from 1793 and halls of Ming statues, with a large Qing finger painting behind the main altar.

rows.name: Guo Moruo Residence
rows.summary: The courtyard home where the writer, historian and senior cultural official Guo Moruo lived from 1963 until his death in 1978, on a site that once belonged to Prince Gong's Mansion and later served as the Mongolian embassy and as a residence of Soong Ching-ling. His study, reception room and bedroom are kept as they were, and the side halls hold exhibitions on his literary and historical work, with a large ginkgo tree in the front yard.

rows.name: Gushan Village
rows.summary: A mountain village in Miaofengshan town turned into a farming-culture park, with displays of old farm tools and machinery, a small farm, children's play areas and hands-on craft workshops. Pear and apple orchards surround it, with white pear blossom in spring, and it suits families with children.

rows.name: Guyaju Caves
rows.summary: A group of 117 cave dwellings with some 350 rooms cut into the cliffs of a side valley west of Yanqing, found in 1984 and still of uncertain age and origin; the most common view links them to the Xi people of the Tang to Five Dynasties period. Stone steps lead up to rooms carved with beds, stoves, flues, window openings and lamp niches, cut at several levels so that parts of the cliff look like a many-storeyed building.

rows.name: Han Meilin Art Museum
rows.summary: A museum devoted to Han Meilin, the artist best known for designing the Fuwa mascots of the 2008 Beijing Olympics, opened in 2008 in Liyuan, Tongzhou. Its galleries show his paintings, calligraphy, sculpture, ceramics and folk-craft designs, and it suits anyone interested in contemporary Chinese art and design.

rows.name: Haotian Pagoda
rows.summary: A five-storey octagonal brick pagoda in pavilion style on a low hill on the east side of Liangxiang, the only pagoda of this type in Beijing. First built in the Sui dynasty and rebuilt in 1068 under the Liao, it is hollow, with corridors and stairs inside; the Buddha figures in the niches of its doorways were smashed in 1901 during the Eight-Nation Alliance occupation.

rows.name: Happy Valley Beijing
rows.summary: An amusement park opened in 2006 by the OCT group on the south-eastern side of the city, with dozens of rides, from big roller coasters and drop towers to gentle children's rides, spread over themed zones such as a Mayan jungle, an Aegean harbour and a Shangri-La area. Live shows and parades run through the day, and it suits families and thrill-seekers.

rows.name: Heilongtan (Black Dragon Pool), Miyun
rows.summary: A narrow gorge about 4 km long north of Lupiguan in Shicheng town, where a stream drops through a chain of named pools and several waterfalls. Paths, steps and bridges follow the water up the cliff-lined valley.

rows.name: Holy Saviour's Cathedral
rows.summary: The former Anglican cathedral of North China, built in 1907 on a cross-shaped plan that mixes a European church layout with grey brick walls, Chinese tiled roofs and pavilion-like towers. Worship ended after 1949 and the building was used as a warehouse and offices, and after restoration it reopened in 2019 as a branch of the Mofan bookshop.

rows.name: Hongluo Temple
rows.summary: A large Buddhist temple at the southern foot of Hongluo Mountain, by tradition founded in 338 and rebuilt many times, which became a leading centre of Pure Land Buddhism in northern China under the Qing masters Jixing and Yinguang. Its halls are laid out in several courtyards on the hillside, surrounded by an old pine forest, with Hongluo Lake to the south.

rows.name: Huanghuacheng Lakeside Great Wall
rows.summary: A section of the Ming Great Wall at Xishuiyu in Jiuduhe town, where the wall runs down the hillsides into a reservoir so that parts of it lie under water, hence the name 'Lakeside' or 'Water' Great Wall. The walls guarded the Huanghuacheng garrison and its pass, built in the Yongle, Zhengde and Jiajing reigns; it is usually quieter than Mutianyu or Badaling, and a steep climb leads to watchtowers with views over the lake.

rows.name: Huguang Guild Hall
rows.summary: A guild hall for officials from Hunan and Hubei, built in 1807 and given its galleried opera theatre in 1830, where Sun Yat-sen spoke at the founding meeting of the Kuomintang in August 1912. The richly painted theatre still stages Peking opera, and the complex has housed a small museum of Peking opera history; it reopened in January 2024 after renovation.

rows.name: Imperial Ancestral Temple
rows.summary: Built in 1420 together with the Forbidden City, the Imperial Ancestral Temple is where Ming and Qing emperors honoured their ancestors, in three great halls set one behind the other within triple walls. The main hall, built largely of the prized hardwood nanmu, stands on a three-tier white-marble terrace among centuries-old cypresses and reopened with exhibitions in 2024 after restoration. Opened as a park in 1924 and run as the Working People's Cultural Palace since 1950, the temple is part of the Beijing Central Axis World Heritage Site.

rows.name: Imperial Historical Archives (Huangshicheng)
rows.summary: Built in 1534–36, the Huangshicheng was the imperial archive of the Ming and Qing dynasties, where the court kept its official chronicles, imperial instructions and the genealogies of the imperial clan. The fireproof main hall uses no wooden beams, with brick walls about 5 m thick and carved white-marble details, and inside, on a marble plinth, stand 152 gilded, bronze-clad camphorwood chests that once held the records; the complex was restored by the First Historical Archives of China in 2020–21.

rows.name: Jiaozhuanghu Tunnel Warfare Site
rows.summary: During the Second Sino-Japanese War the villagers of Jiaozhuanghu dug tunnels linking houses and neighbouring villages into a network some 23 li (about 11.5 km) long, with traps, firing holes hidden in millstones and pigsties, and secret entrances in kitchen stoves and wells. The memorial museum, founded in 1964, has an exhibition hall, restored wartime village houses and about 830 m of tunnel that visitors can walk through.

rows.name: Jietai Temple
rows.summary: A large Buddhist temple on the slopes of Ma'an Mountain in the Western Hills, known for its ordination altar, counted among the three great ordination platforms of Chinese Buddhism. The altar hall was first built under the Liao in 1069 and houses a three-tiered stone altar of the Ming; the courtyards are famous for old pines with names such as the 'Moving Pine', and Prince Gong lived here for about ten years after he was dismissed from office in 1884.

rows.name: Jin Dynasty Imperial Tombs
rows.summary: The burial ground of the Jin dynasty emperors, laid out below Jiulong Mountain after the Jurchen court moved its capital to Zhongdu (Beijing) in the 1150s, and the earliest imperial cemetery in the Beijing area. Archaeologists excavated the tomb of the dynasty's founder, Aguda, in 2001–2003; no halls stand today, and the remains are building foundations, a stone stairway on the Sacred Way and broken steles on the hillside.

rows.name: Jin Zhongdu Water Gate Site
rows.summary: The excavated foundations of a water gate that let a river pass under the southern wall of Zhongdu, the Jin dynasty capital that stood in what is now south-western Beijing. Found during building work in 1990, the 43-metre timber-and-stone base is displayed where it lies beneath a museum, now a branch of the Beijing Archaeological Site Museum, whose upper galleries cover the city's history up to the Liao and Jin periods and a collection of stone carvings.

rows.name: Jingdong Grand Canyon
rows.summary: A narrow, steep-walled canyon near Yuzishan village in northern Pinggu, with a waterfall, a chain of pools and walkways fixed to the cliffs, ending at a small lake where boats can be hired. A second area climbs to the flat top of Jingtai Mountain for views, and a cliffside walkway includes a glass-floored stretch.

rows.name: Jingshan Park
rows.summary: The former imperial garden directly north of the Forbidden City, centred on an artificial hill piled up in the early Ming from earth dug out for the palace moat and canals. Five pavilions stand on its five peaks, and the central Wanchun Pavilion on the city's north–south axis gives the classic view over the palace roofs; the last Ming emperor, Chongzhen, hanged himself on the hill's eastern slope in 1644. Opened to the public in 1928, the park is part of the Beijing Central Axis World Heritage site inscribed in 2024.

rows.name: Jinhai Lake
rows.summary: A large reservoir in the hills of eastern Pinggu, formed by the Haizi dam built in 1959–1960 and enlarged until 1983, with hills on three sides. It hosted the rowing and canoeing events of the 1990 Asian Games, and today boats, speedboats and other water sports run from the shore, with a pagoda and viewpoints on the surrounding hills.

rows.name: Juyong Pass
rows.summary: A Ming fortress pass in the Guangou valley north-west of Beijing, one of the 'three inner passes' that guarded the capital, where a walled garrison town with gated barbicans at both ends closes the valley and the Great Wall climbs steeply up the slopes on either side. Inside the pass stands the Cloud Platform, a white-marble base built in 1342–1345 for three Tibetan-style stupas, whose archway is carved with the Four Heavenly Kings and with Buddhist texts in six scripts: Sanskrit, Tibetan, Phags-pa, Uyghur, Tangut and Chinese.

rows.name: Leduogang Holiday Plaza
rows.summary: A modern leisure complex on the south-west edge of Changping town, combining a shopping and dining centre (now Leduogang Wanda Plaza), a Marriott resort hotel with a large hot-spring complex, and Karle Planet, a space-themed amusement park opened in 2022 on the site of an earlier theme park. It suits families looking for rides, shopping and a hot-spring break rather than sightseeing.

rows.name: Lingyue Temple
rows.summary: A remote Buddhist temple on Baitie Mountain above Zhaitang, first built in the Tang dynasty and rebuilt on a large scale under the Yuan; its main hall keeps a Yuan-period roof frame and bracket sets, rare in the Beijing area. Restored from 2005 and long kept closed, it reopened in late 2025, with a gate, Heavenly King Hall, main hall and side halls, an old locust tree before the gate and steles of 1293 and 1683.

rows.name: Liulihe Bridge
rows.summary: A Ming stone arch bridge over the Liuli River on the old main road south from Beijing, ordered by the Yongle Emperor in 1418 and rebuilt in 1539–1546. Among Beijing's old stone bridges only the Marco Polo Bridge is larger; its eleven arches carry carved beast heads and long rows of stone balustrades, and it has carried no traffic since a new road bridge opened beside it in 1999.

rows.name: Liulihe Yan Capital Site
rows.summary: The site of the capital of Yan, a vassal state of the Western Zhou dynasty, founded about 3,000 years ago and the earliest known city in the Beijing area. Excavations since the 1960s have found stretches of rammed-earth wall, dwellings and a cemetery of nobles whose inscribed bronzes record the granting of Yan to the family of the Duke of Shao; a site museum opened here in 1995, and new finds were named among China's top ten archaeological discoveries of 2024.

rows.name: Longtan Park
rows.summary: A city park laid out around the eastern of the three Longtan lakes, dug in 1952 to drain marshy ground in south-east Beijing, and opened as Longtan Park in 1984. Its islands, bridges and pavilions are themed on the dragon, with spots such as a Dragon Gate and a Dragon Pavilion, and the grounds also hold a shrine to the late-Ming general Yuan Chonghuan. It is an everyday neighbourhood park rather than a historic site, handy for a stroll after the Temple of Heaven next door.

rows.name: Luanzhou Uprising Memorial Park
rows.summary: A memorial built in 1936–37 by the general Feng Yuxiang for those killed in the Luanzhou Uprising of January 1912, a failed revolt against the Qing in which he took part. Its monuments stand in a line up Xianlong Hill: a granite memorial arch, a stele, an octagonal cenotaph pillar naming 14 of the dead, a cliff inscription in Feng's calligraphy and a 12-metre white stone pagoda at the top.

rows.name: Mei Lanfang Memorial Museum
rows.summary: The courtyard house where Mei Lanfang, the Peking opera star often credited with first taking the art abroad, with tours to Japan and in 1930 to North America, spent his last decade from 1951 to 1961. Opened as a memorial in 1986, it keeps his reception room, study and bedroom as they were and shows his stage costumes, programmes and paintings.

rows.name: Ming City Wall Relics Park
rows.summary: The longest surviving stretch of Beijing's Ming-dynasty inner city wall, about 1.5 km of rampart running east from Chongwenmen, ends at the Southeast Corner Tower, completed in 1439 and described as the largest and oldest city-wall corner tower surviving in China. The double-roofed tower, pierced by 144 arrow windows, was badly damaged in 1900 and dismantled and rebuilt in 1981–83; you can climb up to it and onto a section of the wall top, while lawns and trees line the foot of the wall as an open park.

rows.name: Museum of Chinese Gardens and Landscape Architecture
rows.summary: China's first national museum devoted to gardens, opened in 2013 at the foot of Yingshan hill beside the Garden Expo Park, with galleries on the history, techniques and culture of Chinese garden-making. Indoor courts hold rebuilds of famous small gardens, among them Suzhou's Chang Yuan, Guangzhou's Yuyin Shanfang and Yangzhou's Pianshi Shanfang, and the outdoor gardens include a partial rebuild of Beijing's lost Banmu Yuan.

rows.name: Nangong Scenic Area
rows.summary: A resort area in Wangzuo town, south-western Fengtai, built around the geothermal water of Nangong village. It groups hot-spring bathing centres and a hot-spring water park with a plant and parrot park and children's play areas, and suits families and anyone after a hot-spring soak close to the city.

rows.name: Niujie Mosque
rows.summary: Regarded as Beijing's oldest and largest mosque, it is the centre of the Muslim neighbourhood along Niujie (Ox Street); it is said to have been founded in 996 under the Liao, was rebuilt in 1443 and enlarged in 1696. Its timber halls look like a Chinese temple from outside but are decorated inside with Arabic calligraphy, and the street around it is known for halal food shops.

rows.name: Pagoda of Cishou Temple
rows.summary: A 13-storey octagonal brick pagoda about 50 m tall, built in 1576 by the Wanli Emperor for his mother, Empress Dowager Cisheng; the temple around it burned down in the late Qing, leaving the pagoda standing alone. Its base is carved with flying apsaras, Buddhas and musical instruments, more than 3,000 iron bells hang from its eaves, and since 1989 it has been the centrepiece of the small Linglong Park.

rows.name: Pagoda of Monk Wansong
rows.summary: A slender nine-tier brick pagoda at the mouth of Zhuanta Hutong, first built as the Yuan-era tomb pagoda of the Chan master Wansong Xingxiu (1166–1246) and raised from seven to nine tiers in 1753. It is the only brick pagoda left in the old inner city and gave Zhuanta (Brick Pagoda) Hutong its name; in 2014 its small courtyard was opened as a public reading room run with a local bookshop.

rows.name: Pagoda of Tianning Temple
rows.summary: A solid octagonal brick pagoda of thirteen tiers from the Liao dynasty, dated to 1119 by a stele found in its top during repairs in 1992, which confirmed the earlier dating by the architectural historians Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin. Its base and first storey carry carved doors, windows, guardian figures and dragons, and it stands in the grounds of the working Tianning Temple.

rows.name: Peking Legation Quarter (Dongjiaominxiang)
rows.summary: From 1861 foreign legations clustered along this lane east of Tiananmen Square, and after the siege of 1900 it became a walled, foreign-run Legation Quarter with its own banks, barracks and churches. A group of early 20th-century European-style buildings survives, among them the former legations of Japan, France and Italy, the old Yokohama Specie Bank and Citibank buildings and St Michael's Church of 1904. Most are offices seen from the street, so the quarter is best explored on foot as a walk through Beijing's colonial-era history.

rows.name: Pudu Temple
rows.summary: Raised on a high brick terrace in the lanes east of the Forbidden City, Pudu Temple stands on the site of the mansion of Dorgon, the Manchu prince-regent of the early Qing, which was turned into a temple to the Tibetan Buddhist protector deity Mahakala in 1694. Its main hall, with features of early Manchu palace building, sits on a Ming-era carved stone base, and since its restoration in 2001–03 the temple grounds have served as a small public garden.

rows.name: Purple Bamboo Park
rows.summary: Laid out from 1953 and named after the small Fuyin Zizhu Yuan temple inside it, Purple Bamboo Park covers about 47 hectares, a third of it water, with the Changhe River flowing through. Over ten thousand bamboo plants line its lakes, islands and bridges, making it a quiet place for a walk in north-west Beijing.

rows.name: Qinglong Gorge
rows.summary: A wooded gorge north of Huairou town, dammed to form the Dashuiyu Reservoir, with Ming Great Wall watchtowers on the ridges above. Boats run on the lake behind the dam and adventure activities have been offered on its banks, and in wet summers water spills over the dam as a broad waterfall.

rows.name: Qinglongqiao Station, Jingzhang Railway
rows.summary: The historic station at the heart of the protected Nankou–Badaling section of the Beijing–Zhangjiakou (Jingzhang) railway, the first major line designed and built by Chinese engineers (1905–1909), under Zhan Tianyou. Here a zigzag switchback lets trains climb the steep Guangou valley; the 1908 station building keeps its original style, with a statue of Zhan Tianyou and his tomb beside it, and suburban Line S2 trains still reverse on the switchback.

rows.name: Red Building of Peking University
rows.summary: Completed in 1918 as the main building of Peking University, this red-brick block was a centre of the New Culture and May Fourth movements: Li Dazhao ran the university library here, and the young Mao Zedong worked in it as a library assistant in 1918–19. It now houses the New Culture Movement Memorial of Beijing, part of the Beijing Lu Xun Museum, with restored rooms such as Li Dazhao's office and a newspaper reading room, and exhibitions on the period and on early Communist activity in Beijing.

rows.name: Ritan Park (Altar of the Sun)
rows.summary: The altar where Ming and Qing emperors made offerings to the sun at the spring equinox, built in 1530 when the Jiajing Emperor gave the sun and moon separate altars. The square white-stone altar inside its round enclosing wall survives with several ancillary buildings, set in a public park of gardens and a small lake among the embassies of the Jianguomen area.

rows.name: Shangzhai Culture Museum
rows.summary: A site museum for the Shangzhai culture, a Neolithic culture of about 7,500 to 6,000 years ago excavated at Shangzhai village in 1985–1987 and the earliest Neolithic culture found in the Beijing area with signs of early farming. Opened in 1989 in a building shaped like a prehistoric hut, it displays stone axes, grinding slabs, pottery jars and bowls and small carved animal figures from the site.

rows.name: Shenglian Mountain
rows.summary: A steep limestone mountain in the upper Dashi River valley, part of the Fangshan UNESCO Global Geopark, with karst peaks, arches, caves and springs. Taoist and Buddhist temples are spread over the slopes, among them a Quanzhen Taoist Zhenwu Temple rebuilt in 2004, and a 57 m statue of a seated Laozi, a pagoda on the summit area and a large Buddha carved into the cliff stand out on the walk up.

rows.name: Shidu
rows.summary: A long valley where the Juma River has cut through the northern end of the Taihang Mountains, leaving limestone peaks and cliffs above the water; it is one of the largest karst landscapes in northern China and part of the Fangshan UNESCO Global Geopark. The name, 'Tenth Ferry', comes from the river crossings along the old road, and today the valley is a busy weekend resort with rafting, boating and other outdoor activities, while the river attracts wintering birds.

rows.name: Shihua Cave
rows.summary: A large limestone show cave on the Dashi River, the core of the Shihuadong National Geopark and part of the Fangshan UNESCO Global Geopark. Eight levels have been explored, and the four upper levels, about 2.5 km of passages, are open to visitors, with stalagmites, columns, flowstone curtains and the delicate helictites and 'stone flowers' (anthodites) that give the cave its name. A Ming monk found it in 1446 and had a statue of the bodhisattva Ksitigarbha carved inside; it opened to the public in 1987.

rows.name: Shilin Gorge
rows.summary: A gorge in the hills of north-eastern Pinggu, named after the groups of rock pinnacles that rise from its slopes, with clear pools, huge boulders and a waterfall that drops in several tiers. The path follows the valley floor, which narrows to a few metres in places, beneath cliffs where cypresses grow straight out of the rock.

rows.name: Shuiguan Great Wall (Badaling)
rows.summary: A Ming-dynasty section on the eastern part of the Badaling wall, which climbs in a steep V up both sides of the Guangou valley where it was cut by the Beijing–Zhangjiakou railway. Its name, 'Water Pass', is said to come from an arrow tower on the valley floor that also served as a water gate, and the wall here is known for its steep gradients.

rows.name: Shunyi Olympic Rowing-Canoeing Park
rows.name_zh: 顺义奥林匹克水上公园
rows.summary: Built beside the Chaobai River for the rowing, canoeing and marathon swimming events of the 2008 Olympics, this venue is now a water-sports and leisure park. Visitors can try rowing and kayaking on the still-water course, go rafting on the slalom channel in summer, or use the waterside walking routes, camping lawn and children's play areas, and it suits active families.

rows.name: St. Joseph's Church, Beijing
rows.summary: Known as the East Church (Dongtang), this Catholic parish was founded in 1653 by the Jesuit missionaries Lodovico Buglio and Gabriel de Magalhães on land granted by the Shunzhi Emperor, and the present Romanesque Revival building dates from 1904. Still an active church, its grey-brick façade with three towers faces a square laid out on Wangfujing's shopping street in 2000.

rows.name: Taoranting Park
rows.summary: A large lake park laid out in 1952 on old kiln land in the south of the city, named after the Taoran Pavilion, a hall built in 1695 by the kiln supervisor Jiang Zao inside the older Cibei Nunnery and a favourite gathering place of Qing scholars. Pavilions are scattered around three lakes and their islands, and the grounds also hold the graves of the lovers Gao Junyu and Shi Pingmei, whose story was retold in a book and a film.

rows.name: Temple of Agriculture
rows.summary: The altar complex where Ming and Qing emperors worshipped the god of agriculture and ploughed a ceremonial field each spring, founded in 1420 opposite the Temple of Heaven on the city's southern axis. Its surviving halls, including the great Taisui Hall and the emperors' viewing terrace, house the Beijing Museum of Ancient Architecture, and the site is part of the Beijing Central Axis World Heritage site inscribed in 2024.

rows.name: Temple of Ancient Monarchs
rows.summary: The temple where Ming and Qing emperors offered sacrifices to China's legendary sage-kings and earlier rulers, built in 1530–31 under the Jiajing Emperor and later enlarged by the Qing until 188 rulers were honoured. Its main hall, Jingde Chongsheng Hall, was re-roofed in imperial yellow tiles during a rebuilding of 1762–64, and the honoured rulers, who included Xianbei, Khitan, Jurchen and Mongol emperors, were chosen to present an unbroken line of legitimate dynasties.

rows.name: Temple of Earth
rows.summary: Built in 1530, the Temple of Earth is where Ming and Qing emperors made offerings to the earth at the summer solstice, the northern counterpart of the Temple of Heaven. Its centrepiece, the Square Water Altar, is a two-tier square platform ringed by a water channel, the square form standing for the earth, and the cypress-planted grounds around it became a public park in the 20th century, with a Spring Festival temple fair held here since the 1980s.

rows.name: Temple of the Moon
rows.summary: The altar where Ming and Qing emperors made offerings to the moon at the autumn equinox, built in 1530 as the western counterpart of the Temple of the Sun. The altar platform itself was demolished in the 1960s and a television transmitter tower still stands on its site, but the bell tower, gates and robing hall survive in Yuetan Park, whose southern half is a garden of moon-themed pavilions laid out in 1983.

rows.name: Tuancheng Fortress
rows.summary: Built in the late 1740s for the Qianlong Emperor's Jianrui Brigade, an elite unit trained to storm stone watchtowers like those it met in the Jinchuan campaigns, this is the only Qing military review ground left in Beijing. It comprises the oval walled Tuancheng with gate towers, the review hall where the emperor watched drills, a tall gate used for scaling-ladder practice and a stele pavilion, and it holds an exhibition on the brigade's history.

rows.name: Wanfotang and Kongshui Cave
rows.summary: A Buddhist site above a karst spring cave, founded as a temple in the Tang dynasty: a Ming-rebuilt brick hall stands on a platform over the mouth of the Kongshui Cave, and inside it is a long Tang marble relief of Manjushri and Samantabhadra with a host of bodhisattvas. Buddha niches and carved sutras from the Sui to the Jin line the cave walls, and on the slope stand a Liao 'flower pagoda', one of only two in Beijing, and a Yuan pagoda with dense eaves.

rows.name: Wanshou Temple
rows.summary: Founded in 1577 under the Wanli Emperor to store Buddhist scriptures, Wanshou Temple became an imperial temple and was enlarged under the Qing into a complex of temple halls, a travelling palace and gardens. A museum since 1987, it reopened in 2022 after a five-year restoration and in July 2026 was renamed the Wanshou Temple Museum (formerly the Beijing Art Museum), with displays on the temple's history, Buddhist statues, auspicious objects and traditional furniture.

rows.name: Wen Tianxiang Temple
rows.summary: A small shrine to Wen Tianxiang, the Southern Song chief minister who was captured by the Yuan, held in Dadu (today's Beijing) and executed in 1283 after refusing to serve the new dynasty. First built in 1376 near the site of the prison where he was held and moved to its present site in the Wanli reign, it has two courtyards: the front hall holds an exhibition on his life, and the rear hall a modern seated statue with Ming and Qing steles. A stone carving of his Song of Righteousness, after the calligraphy of Wen Zhengming, stands in the front courtyard, and an old jujube tree in the rear courtyard, said to have been planted by Wen himself, leans south.

rows.name: White Cloud Temple
rows.summary: The leading monastery of the Quanzhen school of Taoism, founded in the Tang dynasty and rebuilt around the tomb of the Quanzhen patriarch Qiu Chuji, who travelled to meet Genghis Khan in 1222. It remains an active Taoist temple and the seat of the China Taoist Association, with courtyards of halls and shrines leading to a rear garden, and its Spring Festival temple fair draws large crowds.

rows.name: White Dagoba of Miaoying Temple
rows.summary: A huge whitewashed Tibetan-style stupa built between 1271 and 1279 for Kublai Khan under the Nepalese craftsman Araniko, regarded as the oldest and largest of its kind in China. The temple around it, rebuilt and renamed Miaoying Temple in the Ming, is now a museum whose halls display Buddhist statues and relics found in the stupa's top during repairs in 1978; the stupa was last restored in 2013–15.

rows.name: World Flower Garden
rows.summary: A flower park and botanical garden just north of the South 4th Ring Road, with tropical and ornamental plants in large greenhouses and a series of themed outdoor gardens and plazas, some laid out in foreign styles such as a formal garden modelled on Versailles. The greenhouses host seasonal flower shows, such as a winter orchid show, and it makes an easy half-day for plant lovers inside the city.

rows.name: Xianju Valley
rows.summary: A wooded valley by the Andamu River in Taishitun town, entered past a small mountain lake, with streams, pools and waterfalls along two trails: a gentler one past three linked falls and a steeper, rougher route to caves, a rock gate and a cherry-blossom valley. Wild cherry, peach and azalea flower on the slopes in spring, and a small Taoist temple, the Sanqing Gong, stands among old cypresses.

rows.name: Xiaotangshan Agricultural Science Park
rows.name_zh: 小汤山现代农业科技示范园
rows.summary: A large modern-agriculture demonstration park in the Xiaotangshan area of Changping, showing greenhouse growing, seedling breeding and flower and fruit production, and run partly as a family day out. Visitors walk through glasshouses of flowers, orchids and fruit trees and pick strawberries, vegetables and fruit in season.

rows.name: Xihuang Temple
rows.summary: A Tibetan Buddhist temple built in the early 1650s to house the Fifth Dalai Lama on his visit to the Qing court, and since 1987 the seat of the High-Level Tibetan Buddhist College of China. Its centrepiece is the Qingjing Huacheng Pagoda, a white diamond-throne stupa completed in 1782 as a memorial to the Sixth Panchen Lama, who died at the temple in 1780. Part of the complex opened as the Xihuang Temple Museum in 2018, with displays on the pagoda, the Panchen Lamas and Tibetan Buddhist art.

rows.name: Xijiaominxiang Historic Bank Buildings
rows.name_zh: 西交民巷近代银行建筑群
rows.summary: A row of late Qing and Republican-era bank buildings on the lane west of Tiananmen Square, once Beijing's banking street, including the former Hubu (Da Qing) Bank, the classical-columned Baoshang Bank and the domed clock tower of the Continental Bank of 1924. The former Baoshang Bank and its neighbour now house the China Numismatic Museum of the central bank, which displays Chinese coins and paper money from ancient times to the modern era.

rows.name: Yaji Mountain
rows.summary: A hill in Liujiadian town named after its two rocky summits, which resemble a girl's twin hair buns, and long a Taoist pilgrimage site whose temple fairs drew crowds from the capital and visits from Qing emperors. Its temple buildings were restored or rebuilt from the 2000s, and a stepped path climbs past steles and halls to the Bixia Yuanjun shrine and the Jade Emperor Pavilion on the two peaks.

rows.name: Yanqi Lake
rows.summary: A reservoir in the hills north of Huairou town, built in 1959–1962, whose shores were developed into the conference area that hosted the 2014 APEC leaders' meeting and the first two Belt and Road Forums. A renovation removed the old lakeside amusement rides, and the lake is now an open waterfront park with boardwalks along the shore, stepped grass slopes and a large lawn on the east side used for events.

rows.name: Yanyuan Campus of Peking University
rows.summary: Built in the 1920s for Yenching University on former Qing princely gardens, to a plan by the American architect Henry Murphy, this has been Peking University's main campus since 1952. Its buildings have Chinese palace-style exteriors with what were then modern interiors, and the classic walk runs from the West Gate past the old administration building to Weiming Lake and the Boya Pagoda, modelled on Tongzhou's Randeng Pagoda.

rows.name: Yao Guangxiao's Tomb Pagoda
rows.summary: The tomb pagoda of Yao Guangxiao (1335–1418), the Buddhist monk who advised the future Yongle Emperor during his seizure of the throne and later helped compile the Yongle Encyclopedia. Built between 1418 and 1426, it is an octagonal brick pagoda with nine tiers of dense eaves and an iron gourd finial, and in front of it a large stele under a pavilion carries an inscription composed by the Yongle Emperor.

rows.name: Yeya Lake National Wetland Park
rows.summary: A national wetland park of reservoir shallows, rivers, reed beds and marsh on the south-western edge of Yanqing, the largest wetland in the Beijing area and part of a municipal nature reserve. Migrating and wintering water birds, among them cranes, storks and swans, make it a noted birdwatching site, named one of Beijing's ten best in 2015, and a wetland museum explains the ecosystem.

rows.name: Yinshan Pagoda Forest
rows.summary: A group of eighteen Buddhist pagodas in the hills of Yanshou town, the tomb pagodas of monks from temples that flourished below the dark cliffs of 'Iron Wall, Silver Mountain' from the Jin dynasty onwards. Five Jin brick pagodas with dense eaves stand together on the site of Fahua Temple, which Japanese troops destroyed in 1941, with a Yuan pagoda nearby and smaller Yuan and Ming stupas scattered on the slopes.

rows.name: Yuan Dadu City Wall Ruins Park
rows.summary: A narrow park about 9 km long that follows the surviving earth ramparts of the western and northern walls of Dadu, the Yuan dynasty capital built between 1267 and 1276, known locally as Tucheng ('earth wall'). Paths run along the grassed-over wall and the Xiaoyue River at its foot, past large sculpture groups including a statue of Kublai Khan, a crabapple grove and the Qianlong Emperor's 'Jimen Yanshu' stele of 1750.

rows.name: Yunju Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple at the foot of Shijing Shan ('Stone Sutra Mountain'), famous for the Buddhist scriptures that monks carved on thousands of stone slabs from the Sui dynasty to the Ming, begun by the monk Jingwan to protect the texts from destruction. The slabs were stored in nine caves on the mountain and in a vault below the temple; the halls were bombed in the 1940s and rebuilt from the 1980s, but several Tang and Liao pagodas survive, among them the Liao North Pagoda.

rows.name: Yuyuantan Park
rows.summary: The largest park inside Beijing's Third Ring Road, covering about 137 hectares, 61 of them water, between the ring road and the Diaoyutai State Guesthouse. The lake was created under the Qianlong Emperor in 1773 and revived as a public park from 1960, and its 25-hectare cherry garden is the focus of a cherry-blossom festival each spring.

rows.name: Zhalan Cemetery (Tomb of Matteo Ricci)
rows.name_zh: 利玛窦和外国传教士墓地
rows.pinyin: Lì Mǎdòu Hé Wàiguó Chuánjiàoshì Mùdì
rows.summary: Regarded as the oldest Christian cemetery in China, it was granted by the Wanli Emperor in 1610–11 for the burial of the Italian Jesuit Matteo Ricci, and later Jesuit scholars of the imperial court were also laid to rest here. Ricci's tombstone, inscribed in Chinese and Latin, stands between those of Adam Schall von Bell and Ferdinand Verbiest, near the tombstones of dozens of other missionaries, all set up again after desecration during the Boxer uprising and the Cultural Revolution.

rows.name: Zhengang Pagoda
rows.summary: A solid brick 'flower pagoda' about 18 metres tall on a hillock east of Yungang village, thought from its style to date from the Jin dynasty. Above an octagonal base with carved brackets and relief figures, its upper part is covered in seven tiers of small niches holding seated Buddhas, which give it the bunched look of a flower. Its tip was destroyed during the war with Japan, and it has been repaired several times since.

rows.name: Zhenjue Temple
rows.summary: Better known as the Five Pagoda Temple, Zhenjue Temple keeps one of China's earliest surviving 'diamond throne' stupas, completed in 1473 and inspired by the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya: a 7.7-metre stone platform carved with rows of Buddhas, with a chamber and stairs inside and five small pagodas on top. The temple's other buildings were lost to a late-Qing fire and a sale in 1927, and the grounds now house the Beijing Stone Carving Art Museum.

rows.name: Zhihua Temple
rows.summary: Founded in 1443 by the powerful eunuch Wang Zhen, Zhihua Temple keeps one of the most complete groups of Ming-dynasty wooden buildings in central Beijing, roofed in unusual black glazed tiles. Its halls hold Ming Buddhist statues and murals and a two-storey hall whose upper floor is the Ten Thousand Buddha Pavilion, and the temple, home to the Beijing Cultural Exchange Museum since 1992, is known for Jing music, a centuries-old Buddhist ritual music still performed by its musicians.

rows.name: Zhizhu Temple
rows.summary: A Tibetan Buddhist temple of the Qianlong era, Zhizhu Temple stands beside the larger Songzhu Temple in the lanes east of Jingshan Park. Its halls served as factory workshops and storerooms from the 1950s and were restored with private investment in 2007–12, keeping their weathered paintwork and timbers. The temple no longer has a religious use: the courtyards now hold an art space, a restaurant and a café.

rows.name: Zhongshan Park
rows.summary: Just west of Tian'anmen, Zhongshan Park grew out of the Altar of Land and Grain (Shejitan), where Ming and Qing emperors made offerings to the gods of soil and harvest; its square marble altar is still spread with earth in five colours for the five directions. Opened to the public in 1914, the grounds were renamed in 1928 after Sun Yat-sen, whose coffin lay in the altar's hall in 1925, and also hold ancient cypresses, pavilions and a stone archway first raised for the German envoy Clemens von Ketteler, killed in 1900.

rows.name: Beijing Medicinal Plant Garden
rows.summary: The living plant collection of the Institute of Medicinal Plant Development, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, in Malianwa, north-west Haidian. It grows plants used in Chinese and other traditional medicine for research and teaching, with an open season for visitors. It was listed in 2018 as a TCM health-tourism demonstration base.

rows.name: Ancient Culture Street (Guwenhua Jie)
rows.summary: Ancient Culture Street is a pedestrian street of Ming-and-Qing-style shop-houses on the west bank of the Hai River, opened in 1986 on the old streets that ran either side of the Tianhou Palace. It runs from Tongbei Road south to Shuige Street, and its shops sell antiques, old books and folk crafts such as Yangliuqing New Year prints and Clay Figure Zhang figurines. The Tianhou Palace and the Yuhuang Pavilion stand along it, which makes it a convenient first stop for a taste of old Tianjin.

rows.name: Astor House Hotel
rows.summary: Astor House was founded in 1863 by the British missionary John Innocent on the Hai River embankment and was the first foreign-funded hotel in Tianjin; the present building dates from an enlargement in 1886 and a further wing added in 1924. Sun Yat-sen and Herbert Hoover are among the guests recorded there, and treaties and consular business were handled in its rooms in the 19th century. It is still a working hotel, and its museum on the building's history is open to the public.

rows.name: Binhai Aircraft Carrier Park
rows.summary: A military-themed park in the Sino-Singapore Tianjin Eco-city built around the Kiev, a Soviet-built aircraft carrier that left Russian service in 1993 and arrived in Tianjin in 2000. The carrier, moored on the coast, is the main sight and visitors can go aboard; a linked tour also takes in two other warships, including a retired Chinese destroyer. The park also puts on shows, including a sea-battle show and Russian-style song and dance, and fireworks on summer weekends.

rows.name: Changlu Sea Salt Cultural Tourism Area
rows.summary: A tourism area on the Hangu saltworks in the north of Binhai New Area, a working saltworks whose history is traced to the year 925. Visitors can walk on the heaps of harvested salt beside the salt pans, and children can try traditional salt-making. It was rated a national 4A scenic area in 2024.

rows.name: Dagu Dockyard Site (Beiyang Fleet Dockyard)
rows.name_zh: 北洋水师大沽船坞遗址
rows.summary: The remains of a shipyard founded in 1880 during the Self-Strengthening Movement, the third modern shipyard in China after Mawei and Shanghai's Jiangnan Arsenal and the earliest shipyard in the north. It is the only surviving Self-Strengthening site in Tianjin, was listed as national heritage in 2013 and was added to China's industrial heritage list in 2018. A memorial hall to the Beiyang Fleet dockyard has been set up on the site.

rows.name: Dule Temple
rows.summary: Dule Temple, in the old town of Jizhou, keeps two Liao-dynasty timber buildings from 984, the mountain gate and the Guanyin Pavilion, which are among the oldest surviving wooden buildings in China. The pavilion holds a clay statue of the eleven-headed Guanyin about 16 metres tall, and its walls carry Yuan-dynasty murals. A Qing imperial lodge built in 1753 stands in the east of the compound, and the architectural historian Liang Sicheng's survey of the temple in the 1930s brought it wide attention.

rows.name: Former French Municipal Board, Tianjin
rows.summary: Built in 1929–31 as the headquarters of the administration of Tianjin's French concession, this neoclassical building has a granite-faced base, a three-storey centre block with an Ionic colonnade and symmetrical two-storey wings. The square in front of it was the site of the October 1945 ceremony at which Japanese forces in Tianjin surrendered, when the building was the US military headquarters. It has since served as a library and an art museum, and since 2023 it has housed the Tianjin Digital Art Museum.

rows.name: Former Huanghai Society for Chemical Industry Research
rows.name_zh: 黄海化学工业研究社旧址
rows.summary: A two-storey grey brick-and-concrete villa on a site of about 440 square metres, built in 1922 for the Huanghai Society for Chemical Industry Research, China's first privately funded chemical research institute, which the industrialist Fan Xudong set up on the laboratory of the Jiuda refined-salt company. The society worked on salt brines, potash and iodine, and in 1935 made the first sample of metallic aluminium produced in China. The building is a national heritage site and a Tianjin historic building under special protection.

rows.name: Former Nankai School (Nankai High School)
rows.summary: Nankai School was founded in 1904 by the educators Yan Xiu and Zhang Boling and grew into Nankai High School, whose campus keeps its listed buildings: the Bailing Building (built 1906–07 and rebuilt to its original design after the 1976 earthquake), the North Building, the Fansun Building of 1930 and the Ruiting Auditorium of 1934. Zhou Enlai studied here, and the school's history display in the Bailing Building includes a classroom recreated as it was in his student days.

rows.name: Former Qianxiangyi Silk Store
rows.summary: A silk and cloth store built in 1913–17 on Guyi Street in the old city for the Meng family of Zhangqiu, Shandong, one of the old 'Eight Xiang' shops of Tianjin. The building is a three-courtyard brick-and-timber structure in a mixed Chinese and Western style, with carved doors and a verandah gallery. When Guyi Street was rebuilt in 2000 it was the only listed building kept, and since its restoration in 2002 it has housed a tea house that stages crosstalk and other storytelling performances.

rows.name: Former Site of the Juewu Society (Awakening Society)
rows.summary: A small courtyard of seven single-storey rooms where the Awakening Society (Juewushe), a student group led by Zhou Enlai, was founded in September 1919 in the May Fourth period. It has been a memorial hall since 1984, with one room restored as the society's meeting room and a second showing about ninety documents, photographs and models of its history.

rows.name: Former Tanggu Railway Station (Tanggu South)
rows.summary: A railway station at Yujiapu near the Hai River, first built in 1888 when a line was laid to carry Kaiping coal to the coast; its main building was rebuilt in 1907–08 and the station extended in 1937. Passenger service ended in 2004, and freight stopped in 2024 when the branch line was removed. It was named in a 2007 public selection as one of Tianjin's ten notable immovable relics, and the city heritage bureau approved a conservation design for the buildings in 2024.

rows.name: Former Tianjin College of Industry and Commerce Main Building
rows.name_zh: 天津工商学院主楼旧址
rows.summary: The main building of the former Tianjin College of Industry and Commerce was built by French Jesuits in the 1920s to a design by the French firm Yonghe, and is a three-storey brick building with a mansard roof, rusticated stonework and large clock faces on its front and back gables. Its west wing holds a small chapel, and the entrance hall has portraits of Matteo Ricci and Ferdinand Verbiest and a large world map by Verbiest. The site passed to a foreign-languages institute in 1970, now Tianjin Foreign Studies University, and the building is still the university's main building.

rows.name: Former Yien Yieh Commercial Bank, Tianjin
rows.summary: Built in 1925–28 as the head office of the Yien Yieh (Salt Industry) Commercial Bank, this red-brick Roman-revival building was designed by the Chinese architect Shen Liyuan, with a portico of tall Ionic columns under a pediment. Inside, an octagonal banking hall is ringed by Corinthian columns and has a gilded ceiling and Belgian coloured glass picturing salt pans.

rows.name: Guangdong Guild Hall (Tianjin Museum of Theatre)
rows.summary: Built in 1903–07 with money raised by Cantonese merchants in Tianjin, this guild hall is one of the largest and best-preserved Qing guild-hall complexes in China, with a courtyard house, an apprenticeship hall and a classical opera theatre whose pillarless stage has a domed ceiling that carries sound. Sun Yat-sen spoke here twice in 1912. It now houses the Tianjin Museum of Theatre, with exhibitions on the history of Chinese opera and Peking opera and on opera costume and characters.

rows.name: Guanghegu Resort
rows.summary: Guanghegu, 'Photosynthesis Valley', is a resort and agri-tourism park of about 4,500 mu (300 hectares) on the east side of Tuanbo new town, planned in four zones: youth culture, hot-spring hotels, a wetland park and facility agriculture. It has a reed-filled artificial wetland park, a children's zoo with some 30 kinds of animals such as alpacas and kangaroos, and about twenty greenhouses where visitors pick vegetables and fruit, so it suits families.

rows.name: Guanhu Castle Hot Spring Resort
rows.summary: A hot-spring resort in the Dongli Lake holiday area, across the street from Happy Valley, with indoor and outdoor hot-spring pools, spa treatments, dining and leisure facilities. It suits a restful stay or a visit combined with the theme park.

rows.name: Guojiagou Village
rows.summary: Guojiagou is a small hill village of about 50 households beside a reservoir in northern Jizhou, rebuilt from 2012 as a tourist village of blue-brick courtyards and farmstay guesthouses, and in 2022 became Tianjin's first village-type 4A scenic area. Besides the guesthouses it has added flower fields, a petting zoo, a forest light-and-shadow park and a dinosaur-themed valley, so it suits families wanting a short country break.

rows.name: Hoangho Paiho Museum (Beijiang Museum)
rows.summary: Founded in 1914 by the French Jesuit naturalist Émile Licent and housed in purpose-built premises from the 1920s, the Hoangho Paiho Museum is the forerunner of Tianjin Natural History Museum, and Pierre Teilhard de Chardin worked there. Xinhua describes it as the only early Chinese museum whose site, buildings, collections and display cases all survive in their original form, with more than 200,000 items, from animal, plant, fossil and rock specimens to historical and folk relics. It reopened to the public in 2016 after restoration.

rows.name: Huangyaguan Great Wall
rows.summary: Huangyaguan is a section of the Great Wall in the mountains of northern Jizhou, first built in the Northern Qi dynasty and rebuilt in brick and stone under General Qi Jiguang in the Ming. The fortified pass, water gate and square and round watchtowers climb the ridge, and the complex includes an eight-trigram maze town and a Great Wall museum, with a large statue of Qi Jiguang on the hillside.

rows.name: Italian Style Town (Marco Polo Square)
rows.summary: The former Italian concession, laid out from 1902: a district of about 28 hectares with 137 historic buildings designed by Italian architects, restored from 2002 and now given over to restaurants, shops and hotels. Its centre is Marco Polo Square, where a column topped by a peace figure stands among six Italian-style villas built between 1908 and 1916; the square and its buildings are a national heritage unit. Liang Qichao's former home is also in the district.

rows.name: Jingwumen Wulin Garden (Huo Yuanjia Memorial Park)
rows.summary: A memorial park for the martial artist Huo Yuanjia, built on the site of his former home and grave in Jingwu town, where he was born; he was one of the founders of the Jingwu sports association in Shanghai. The east side has his mausoleum with a memorial hall, a martial-arts spirit way and his tomb, and the west side a square with his statue and a memorial hall showing his life, relics and films. The grounds are large and open.

rows.name: Jinjie Pedestrian Street
rows.summary: Jinjie, the 'Golden Street', is the pedestrian stretch of Heping Road in central Tianjin, about 1.2 kilometres between Fu'an Street and Chifeng Road. The road dates from 1902, when the French concession built its first section, with a Japanese-concession section following in 1908; it became the city's main shopping street in the 1920s, and many of its stores and bank buildings date from the early 20th century, including the Quanyechang department store.

rows.name: Jizhou Karst Cave
rows.summary: Jizhou Karst Cave is a cave about 1,500 metres long in the Yanshan hills of northern Jizhou, in ancient dolomite rock, and is billed as the only cave attraction in Tianjin. It formed along large tectonic cracks rather than by dissolving water, which left a forest of tall stone columns. A farmer found it in 1998 while chasing a badger and it opened to visitors in 2006; the grounds around it now also have a hotel and outdoor rides.

rows.name: Jizhou White Pagoda
rows.summary: The Jizhou White Pagoda is an octagonal brick tower 30.6 metres high, rebuilt in 1058 in the Liao style on a structure that radiocarbon dating of its timbers places in the Sui dynasty. Its lower part has tiered eaves and its upper part ends in an upturned-bowl dome with a bronze finial, an unusual form among Liao pagodas. It was once part of the Dule Temple layout, and Liang Sicheng noted in 1932 that the Guanyin statue in Dule's pavilion looks out toward it.

rows.name: Li Chun Ancestral Hall (Zhuangwangfu)
rows.summary: Completed in 1923 for the family of the warlord Li Chun, this hall complex was assembled from timbers, tiles and stone carried from the Qing-dynasty Prince Zhuang's mansion in Beijing, and is described by the Tianjin government as the largest surviving group of historic buildings in the city's urban area. Courtyards of halls with glazed-tile roofs and colonnades lie behind a stone archway and bridge. After decades as the Nankai People's Cultural Palace it was restored, and it reopened on a trial basis in 2026 as the Zhuangwangfu cultural venue, with courtyard performances, craft displays and long-established Tianjin food brands.

rows.name: Liang Qichao's Former Residence (Yinbingshi)
rows.summary: The Italian-style house where the reformist scholar Liang Qichao lived from 1914; his 1924 study, the Yinbingshi, designed by an Italian architect, stands beside it. Together they form a memorial museum with twelve rooms on his life and times, and the study is arranged as it was when he wrote there. It stands in the former Italian concession.

rows.name: Limutai Scenic Area
rows.summary: Limutai is a forest and gorge area in the northernmost hills of Tianjin, covering more than 1,000 hectares of quartzite crags, pools, streams and waterfalls. It is part of a national geopark and a national forest park, and lies in the same hills as the Huangyaguan section of the Great Wall. A pear-blossom festival is held there each spring, with peach, apricot and azalea flowering after it.

rows.name: Memorial Hall of the Boxer Uprising (Lüzutang)
rows.name_zh: 义和团吕祖堂坛口遗址
rows.summary: A former Taoist temple, the Lüzutang, built as a village shrine in 1433 and made a Taoist temple in 1719, which became the main Boxer altar in Tianjin during the uprising of 1900. It is now the Tianjin Boxer Uprising Memorial Hall, with a restored altar, a reconstructed meeting hall for the movement's leaders and exhibitions on the uprising and its course in Tianjin.

rows.name: Memorial to Zhou Enlai and Deng Yingchao
rows.summary: A memorial museum opened in 1998, the centenary of Zhou Enlai's birth, beside Tianjin Water Park, with exhibitions on the lives of Zhou Enlai and of Deng Yingchao, whose part in the women's movement has its own display. It also holds a full-size replica of Xihua Hall in Zhongnanhai, Beijing, with its fittings restored, and an Ilyushin Il-14 aircraft presented by the Soviet government for his use, now classed as a national second-grade cultural relic.

rows.name: Milifang Water Park
rows.summary: An indoor water park in Xiaozhan town built around a building shaped like a grain of Xiaozhan rice, with a wave pool, a drifting river that runs through a cave and past a waterfall, a slide complex, a children's area and a hot-spring spa, all kept warm throughout the year. It suits families and groups looking for water play in any season.

rows.name: Mount Pan (Panshan)
rows.summary: Panshan is a mountain scenic area of about 106 square kilometres in northern Jizhou, long called the 'first mountain east of the capital'. Its five main peaks, odd-shaped boulders and pines drew emperors for centuries: the Qianlong Emperor climbed it 32 times and wrote about 1,700 poems on it, and the area once held 72 temples, 13 pagodas and the imperial retreat of Jingji Shanzhuang. The Tianjin government's description lists five visitor zones and more than 300 sights, including temple sites and stone inscriptions left by visiting rulers.

rows.name: Nanhu Green Expo Park, Wuqing
rows.summary: A lakeside park in Wuqing with a lake about 5.2 kilometres round and 136 hectares of water, and a northern garden-exhibition area of 862 mu (about 57 hectares) in which provinces and other bodies built 48 gardens under six themes, from Jiangnan-style gardens to folk-custom and landscape designs. Other zones around the lake include a water-street shopping area, a family sports and recreation area and a wetland area.

rows.name: National Maritime Museum of China
rows.summary: China's national maritime museum, opened for trial operation on 1 May 2019 and run jointly by the Ministry of Natural Resources and the Tianjin government. Its exhibitions cover the geological history of the oceans, marine life, ships and maritime culture, and it keeps a preserved Type 037IG missile boat. The building was designed by the Australian architect Philip Cox.

rows.name: Old Tianjin West Station Building
rows.summary: The 1910 waiting hall of the original Tianjin West station, a two-storey brick building in German neoclassical style with a red tiled roof, dormer windows and stone trim carved with crane and dragon motifs. In 2009–10 it was moved 175 m (135 m south, then 40 m east) to its present site during the station's rebuilding.

rows.name: Our Lady of Victory Church (Wanghailou)
rows.summary: A Gothic-style Catholic church beside the Sanchakou confluence, first built in 1869 and rebuilt in 1897 and 1904 after being burned in the Tianjin Incident of 1870 and in the fighting of 1900. The brick church has three towers on its front and a basilica-style interior with pointed arches and coloured glass. It is still used by the city's Catholic community and was listed as national heritage in 1988.

rows.name: Pingjin Campaign Front Headquarters Site, Mengjialou
rows.name_zh: 平津战役前线司令部旧址
rows.summary: In December 1948 the headquarters of the People's Liberation Army's Northeast Field Army moved into this ordinary farmhouse in Mengjialou village and directed the Pingjin (Beiping–Tianjin) Campaign from it. The single-storey brick-and-timber house has a through-hall and east and west wings, the west wing serving as the operations room. An exhibition hall in the village shows historical photographs and relics of the campaign, including a telegram draft addressed to the Central Military Commission.

rows.name: Pingjin Campaign Memorial Hall
rows.summary: A national first-grade museum beside the Ziya River, opened in July 1997, on the Pingjin (Beiping–Tianjin) Campaign of 1948–49 in the Chinese civil war. Its galleries cover the campaign's decisions, its execution, civilian support and the people who fought, and the grounds hold a bayonet-shaped Victory Monument and a garden of retired military aircraft, a patrol boat and a missile.

rows.name: Quanyechang Department Store
rows.summary: Quanyechang is a department store at the corner of Heping Road and Binjiang Dao, opened in December 1928 in the former French concession to a design by the French architect Paul Muller. The eclectic building has a corner tower, a galleried atrium and a rooftop entertainment garden, and the Tianjin Daily calls it the only department store in China on the national heritage list. Its restoration began in October 2024, and in August 2026 the Tianjin Daily reported that the building was expected to reopen before the end of the year.

rows.name: Renai Tuanbo Lake Leisure Expo Park
rows.name_zh: 仁爱团泊湖国际休闲博览园
rows.summary: Renai Tuanbo Lake Leisure Expo Park is a leisure and resort district on the eastern shore of Tuanbo Lake, in the lakeside new town of Tuanbo, planned from 2009 to combine eco-leisure, conference and exhibition space, hot-spring resorts and housing.
