The Lincheng Xingyao Museum, a national second-grade museum on the white porcelain once made in this area, stands inside the scenic area.

rows.name: Nanhe Agricultural Carnival
rows.summary: A modern-agriculture leisure park in the north of Nanhe District, built around large greenhouse halls. The Xingtai agriculture bureau lists a visitor-service area, a creative themed hall, a rose garden, a high-tech farming demonstration area and an agriculture-themed amusement park, and its greenhouses host flower displays. It is a commercial attraction that suits families looking for a short outing from Xingtai.

rows.name: Nanjia Village Stone Pagoda
rows.summary: A lone stone pagoda standing in the countryside just south of Nanjia village, in Nanshimen town in the hills west of Xingtai. It is the only structure recorded at the site, and it was added to the national heritage list in 2013 (seventh batch), which dates it to the Tang dynasty. It is a rural monument rather than a developed attraction, so it suits those who enjoy seeking out out-of-the-way pagodas.

rows.name: Nikeng Liquor Culture Park
rows.name_zh: 泥坑酒文化旅游产业园
rows.summary: A liquor-culture tourism park in Ningjin built around Nikeng baijiu, a strong grain spirit that traces back to a distillery founded in 1916. Its mud-pit solid-state fermentation craft is a Hebei provincial intangible-heritage item, and the old brewing pits and workshops were listed as provincial industrial heritage in 2025. It was added to Hebei's 4A list in December 2025 and suits visitors interested in how baijiu is made rather than in historic sites.

rows.name: Pingxiang Confucian Temple
rows.summary: The main hall of the Confucian temple of Pingxiang County, first built between 1008 and 1016 under the Northern Song and repaired seven times between the Song and the Qing. The surviving Dacheng Hall is listed as a Yuan-to-Ming timber building, and it was used as a grain store from the 1960s until 1993. It is a small county-town monument for those interested in Confucian temples and old timber architecture.

rows.name: Puli Temple Pagoda
rows.summary: A square, eight-storey brick pagoda 33 m high, built in 1052 under the Northern Song in imitation of timber construction, with closely spaced eaves. It is described as the only pagoda of this square, dense-eaved brick type from the Northern Song to survive in China. The temple it belonged to, founded in the Northern Dynasties, fell into ruin in modern times, leaving the pagoda standing in the middle of Lincheng town.

rows.name: Putong Pagoda
rows.summary: A Ming-dynasty pagoda in the rebuilt Putong Temple on the western side of Nangong, added to the national heritage list in 2013. Local tradition dates the temple to AD 67, a year before Luoyang's White Horse Temple, but the original temple has gone and the present one is a modern reconstruction. It is a small stop for pagoda enthusiasts rather than a major sight.

rows.name: Qiannanyu
rows.summary: A wooded valley in the Taihang Mountains that was the headquarters of the Anti-Japanese Military and Political University (known as Kangda) from November 1940, the school the Chinese Communist Party ran to train military and political cadres. The village is described as holding the largest and best-preserved group of Kangda sites, including a monument, leaders' former residences, a stele forest and the medical station, together with a national second-grade exhibition hall on the school's history. The surrounding forest park, which the provincial tourism department puts at about 38 square km, gives the visit a woodland setting.

rows.name: Qingfeng Tower, Xingtai
rows.summary: A two-storey, double-eaved timber tower on a brick platform about six metres high, with a vaulted passage running through its base. Built in the Chenghua era (1465–87) of the Ming dynasty on the site of a predecessor said to go back to the Tang, it has served as a library and an exhibition hall and is one of Xingtai's traditional 'eight views'. The Tao Te Ching Pillar stands in the garden behind it.

rows.name: Qinghe Cashmere Town
rows.summary: A purpose-built cashmere trading and tourism town in Qinghe, with a planned area of about 3.2 sq km, grown from the Qinghe Cashmere Products Market, which began operating in September 2008. It is a place to browse and buy cashmere knitwear along its shopping streets, and the county has been building an e-commerce park and upgrading a riverside park nearby. It suits visitors interested in a Chinese specialist-industry town rather than in historic sites.

rows.name: Qishan Lake
rows.summary: A large reservoir on the Zhi River in Lincheng County, officially the Lincheng Reservoir and first called the Sanqi Reservoir, built in 1958–60 and later also called Qishan Lake. It is run as a lakeside scenic area in the Taihang foothills a few kilometres west of Kongshan Baiyun Cave, so the two can be visited together.

rows.name: Song Jing Stele
rows.summary: A Tang-dynasty memorial stele for the chancellor Song Jing (died 737), standing at Donghu village in Shahe. Song Jing was buried in the family cemetery at Shahe in 738, and the stele was set up in 772 in front of his tomb, with the text composed by the calligrapher Yan Zhenqing and a revised passage cut on its left side in 778. It is a stop for lovers of Tang epigraphy and calligraphy rather than a developed visitor site.

rows.name: Tang Ancestors Mausoleum, Longyao
rows.summary: Two joined tombs, the Jianchu and Qiyun mausolea, mark the burial place of two ancestors of Li Yuan, founder of the Tang dynasty, to whom he gave imperial titles after taking the throne in 618. They stand near Wangyin village south of Longyao, which presents itself as the ancestral home of the Tang imperial Li family, a descent that historians have debated. Li-clan gatherings held in Longyao each October have included visits to the tombs.

rows.name: Tao Te Ching Pillar, Xingtai
rows.summary: An eight-sided stone pillar 6.89 metres tall, carved with the text of the Tao Te Ching and the Tang emperor Xuanzong's commentary on it. It was set up in 739 by the prefect of Xingzhou at the Longxing Daoist temple, was blown apart during the Cultural Revolution, and was raised again in 1990 with a newly carved middle section. It now stands in Qingfeng Garden behind Qingfeng Tower.

rows.name: Tianhe Mountain, Xingtai
rows.summary: A scenic mountain area of about 30 square km on the Hebei–Shanxi border, with ravines, streams and waterfalls below a high meadow and a main peak of 1,780 m. Local tradition places the Cowherd and Weaver Girl legend here, and the mountain is marketed as the 'Love Mountain' and a centre of Qixi (Double Seventh) culture. It suits visitors after mountain scenery with a romantic theme.

rows.name: Tianning Temple, Xingtai
rows.summary: Tianning Temple, known locally as the West Temple, was founded in the Tang dynasty and rebuilt under the Yuan, and only its Yuan-era front hall survived the Cultural Revolution, when the work units that had taken the site over pulled down the other buildings. Kublai Khan is recorded as staying here twice and the adviser Liu Bingzhong became a monk here. The city has been restoring the temple since 2011 and opened it in 2025 as the Tianning Temple Cultural Park, with a rebuilt middle hall and a Liu Bingzhong memorial, and the temple and Kaiyuan Temple face each other across the old city.

rows.name: Tiantai Mountain, Lincheng
rows.summary: A mountain scenic area in the Taihang foothills north-west of Lincheng, in the same hills as Kongshan Baiyun Cave and Qishan Lake. The Hebei culture and tourism department lists more than thirty natural sights, among them a lotus-seed lake, a red-cliff waterfall, a cliff plank walk and a gorge, along with the Tang-founded Ciyun'an temple, where worship continues. Its layered red sandstone cliffs are of the Zhangshiyan landform type.

rows.name: Tianti Mountain, Xingtai
rows.summary: A hill scenic area in Xindu District, the nearest of the district's mountain 4A sites to Xingtai, known for the red autumn foliage of wild smoke trees growing on its cliffs. It has a cave, viewing platforms and walking paths, and the foliage is at its best from late October. It suits a short autumn outing from the city.

rows.name: Xingtai Grand Canyon
rows.summary: A cluster of 24 sandstone canyons in the Taihang Mountains at Luluo town, near the Shanxi border, eight of them more than a kilometre long; it is a national key scenic area and a national geopark. The main gorge, Huangchao Gorge, runs for about 4 km between cliffs well over 100 m high, narrowing to a metre or two in places, and waterfalls drop through the canyons. Five of the canyons have been opened for walking.

rows.name: Xingyao Kiln Site
rows.summary: The site museum in Neiqiu county town protects 11 kiln furnaces uncovered in 2012 in a dig named one of China's ten major archaeological discoveries of that year, and visitors look down on them from an elevated walkway. Beside it stand the Xingyao Museum, which shows the white porcelain fired here from the late Northern Dynasties onwards, and a ceramics studio where visitors can try the craft. Xingyao ware, one of the cradles of Chinese white porcelain, was fired at about two dozen main kiln sites, mostly in Neiqiu and Lincheng, which are protected together as a national unit.

rows.name: Yunmeng Mountain, Xingtai
rows.summary: A mountain gorge area on the Hebei–Shanxi border in Xindu District, laid out in four tiers called the 'pot-heaven' levels, with a main peak of about 1,300 m and a clear stream running through it. Its best-known sights are the Qiying waterfall, which drops about 105 m, and a large cave known as the lecture cave of Guiguzi, the legendary Warring States sage the mountain is traditionally linked with. It suits a day among the hills north-west of Xingtai.

rows.name: Zijin Mountain, Xingtai
rows.summary: A high mountain area in Baian township, Xindu District, averaging more than 1,300 m above sea level, with Motianling as its highest peak at about 1,750 m. It is described as a cool summer retreat and as the site of the ruins of the Yuan-dynasty Zijinshan Academy, where the astronomer Guo Shoujing is said to have studied under the adviser Liu Bingzhong. It suits hikers and anyone interested in Guo Shoujing's early life.

rows.name: Anjiagou Ecological Tourism Area
rows.summary: A scenic valley on the northern edge of Zhangjiakou, a gully about 4.6 km long with a dozen side gullies, run as an ecological tourism area for day visitors from the city. Visitors walk beside a stream between rocky gully walls, with a suspension footbridge and rafting among the activities. It suits a short outing for families.

rows.name: Bailin Temple, Xuanhua
rows.summary: A small Buddhist temple in a mountain hollow about 1 km south-west of Bailinsi village in Guocun township, south of Xuanhua, with Ming and Qing buildings. Local tradition dates its founding to the Northern Wei, and the compound includes a main hall, a Duobao ('Many Treasures') pagoda and grotto niches cut into the rock. It is a quiet rural temple rather than a developed attraction.

rows.name: Changping Granary, Yuxian
rows.summary: A Ming government granary standing west of the Drum Tower inside Yuxian's old town, one of the 'ever-normal' storehouses that stocked grain to steady prices. It has been a provincial heritage site since 1993 and a national one since 2006. It lies a short walk from Lingyan Temple.

rows.name: Chicheng Hot Spring Resort
rows.summary: A hot-spring valley west of Chicheng town, where mineral springs rise on the south bank of the Tangquan River and now supply hotels and sanatoria. The springs were already recorded in the Shuijing Zhu of the Northern Wei, and the county describes them as a former imperial spring. It suits visitors who want to soak in a quiet mountain setting rather than see sights.

rows.name: Chongguang Pagoda, Longguan
rows.summary: A Ming brick pagoda rising over the houses of Longguan town, an old frontier market town in Chicheng County. It began as the pagoda of Puji Temple, which the county's own history credits to the frontier general Yang Hong, and is now known as the Chongguang ('light restored') Pagoda. It was a provincial heritage site before joining the national list in 2013.

rows.name: Chongtai Temple, Yuxian
rows.summary: A large Buddhist temple on a hillock by Yanjiazhai village, laid out along a north–south axis from an opera stage and gate hall through several halls to a rear building dedicated to the Three Teachings, with a group of pagodas to one side. Its buildings date from the Ming and Qing, and it was listed as a provincial site in 1993 and nationally in 2013.

rows.name: Cuiyunshan Forest Scenic Area
rows.summary: A forested mountain area at Chongli with peaks above 2,000 m, developed as a mountain resort around the Galaxy ski area. In summer a cable car and slides run on the ski slopes, with mountain biking, archery, hiking and an artificial lake with pedal boats and lakeside events. It suits a day trip or a night in one of the resort hotels at its base.

rows.name: Dajingmen
rows.summary: A gate in the Great Wall on the northern edge of Zhangjiakou, built in 1644, through which the road to Mongolia once passed; the trade market that grew up outside it made Zhangjiakou a major caravan town. The gateway is about 12 m high and carries a 1927 inscription reading 'Magnificent Rivers and Mountains', with a stretch of wall running up the hills to the west. It is often counted with Shanhaiguan, Jiayuguan and Juyongguan as one of the Great Wall's four great passes.

rows.name: Daqingshan Mountain Resort, Shangyi
rows.name_zh: 大青山国际旅游度假区
rows.summary: A mountain tourist resort in Shangyi County beside the Grassland Sky Road, a scenic highway that passes through the Daqingshan forest hills. Its best-known feature is the Jingguang Glass Bridge, a transparent suspension footbridge about 640 m long that spans a valley between two peaks, so a visit is mostly about views over the hills and the road beyond.

rows.name: Former Chahar Democratic Government (Xuanhua Museum)
rows.summary: A courtyard compound beside Xuanhua's Catholic cathedral, built in 1930 as the Joseph General Seminary in a mix of Chinese and Western styles, with three courtyards and a two-storey central block under a Gothic-style roof. Communist forces took Xuanhua in September 1945 and set up a Chahar provincial government in the building, which withdrew about a year later. It is now the Xuanhua Museum, whose permanent displays cover the town's history from prehistory to the present and the short-lived Chahar government, and which holds finds from the nearby Liao tombs.

rows.name: Former Chahar Military Governor's Office
rows.summary: The only reasonably complete Qing government compound left in Zhangjiakou, built in 1762 for the military governor who oversaw the Chahar Mongol banners, one of only three posts of this kind in the Qing empire. Four courtyards and some 70 halls and rooms survive along a central axis, from the gate and ceremonial hall to the residence at the rear. In the Republican period it housed the Chahar regional government, and in 1941 the Mongol prince Demchugdongrub (Prince De), who headed the Japanese-backed Mengjiang regime, made it his residence, which is why it is also called the Prince De Mansion.

rows.name: Fozhen Sheli Pagoda
rows.summary: A Liao-dynasty (916–1125) brick relic pagoda with tightly stacked eaves, standing in Taer ('Pagoda') village west of Xuanhua. Its long name combines the Buddhist terms for a relic and a dharani, and it was added to the national heritage list in 2013. It is a village monument with a protection tablet, mainly seen from outside.

rows.name: Fulong Four Seasons Town
rows.summary: A resort town on the edge of Chongli's main town, built around the Fulong ski area, with a shopping street of 19 European-style buildings, a large indoor children's play centre and hotels. In winter it is a ski base; in summer it runs a bicycle pump-track park, mountain-bike downhill trails and a set of activities for children. It is mainly a family and active-break destination rather than a sightseeing stop.

rows.name: Genting Snow Park
rows.time_needed: Half a day to a full day
rows.summary: The ski park of the Genting Secret Garden resort in Taizicheng village, Chongli, which hosted the Olympic freestyle skiing and snowboarding events of the 2022 Winter Games (apart from big air, held in Beijing) and the Paralympic snowboarding. Since the Games it has redesigned three of its six Olympic courses to suit recreational skiers, has around 45 trails in all and keeps staging international competitions, including FIS World Cup halfpipe events. A resort hotel and Taizicheng high-speed station are close by, so it works as a winter day trip from Beijing.

rows.name: Guandi Temple, Yuxian
rows.summary: A small temple to Guan Yu, the deified general of the Three Kingdoms, whose four surviving buildings are in Ming style and stand on one north–south axis: an opera stage, an offering hall, the Guandi hall with wall paintings of Guan Yu's story, and a rear hall known as the Sanyi Hall. The original gate, bell and drum towers and side rooms are gone. It stands just outside the south gate of Yuxian's old town, next to Shijia Temple.

rows.name: Guanting Reservoir National Wetland Park
rows.name_zh: 官厅水库国家湿地公园
rows.summary: A very large wetland park on the shores of Guanting Reservoir, a 1950s reservoir on the Yongding River that straddles the Hebei–Beijing border. The park covers about 13,500 hectares of river, floodplain, reservoir, fish-pond and rice-paddy wetland, with a boardwalk out into the wetland and a wetland museum. It is a quiet outdoor stop for open water views rather than a monument.

rows.name: Gucheng Temple, Yuxian
rows.summary: A Ming Buddhist temple founded in 1507 on the site of an older Liao-period town, which gives it its name; it is also called Xinfo ('Heart Buddha') Temple and Dongda ('East Great') Temple. A Maitreya palace stands behind the Buddha hall, an arrangement that is rare. The temple lies in farmland north-east of Dagucheng village and was added to the national list in 2013.

rows.name: Huangdi City Ruins (Zhuolu Old City)
rows.summary: The remains of a rammed-earth walled town at Sanbao village, Fanshan town, which local tradition calls Huangdi City after the legendary Yellow Emperor. Archaeologists who excavated in 2014 found it was probably not built before the Warring States period, and the national heritage authority has said its nature still needs study. The tourist area around it has a lake, a spring, and a hall and ceremonial altar linked to the Yellow Emperor tradition, so it suits visitors interested in Chinese origin legends.

rows.name: Huanglong Mountain Resort
rows.summary: A wooded mountain resort and scenic area in the Yan Mountains north-west of Huailai town, with streams and springs, forest walks and a cool summer climate. The county holds a climbing festival here, and the fifth, in May 2024, drew more than 300 hikers. It suits walkers and day-trippers from the Beijing–Zhangjiakou corridor.

rows.name: Huayan Temple, Nuanquan
rows.summary: A Ming Buddhist temple in the south-east of Nuanquan town, also called the Great Temple, whose front hall keeps a large set of water-and-land (shuilu) wall paintings of the Buddhist realms of existence, with the ten Wisdom Kings on the north wall. The five-bay main hall behind it has a carved brick ridge of peonies and sunflowers and painted beams with dragons, qilin and lions. In front lies a round stone pool called the Buddha's Mirror, which may have given Nuanquan, 'warm spring', its name.

rows.name: Jiming Mountain
rows.summary: An isolated peak of about 1,100 m on the east side of Xiahuayuan, nicknamed the 'flying peak' because it stands alone above the Yang River valley, within a scenic area of about 17.5 sq km. A stepped path climbs past rebuilt Buddhist and folk temples, including the 33 m Linji Light Pagoda and the Liao-founded Yongning Temple, to the summit, where a 20 m stone footbridge across a cliff is a provincial heritage site. Its temple fair in the fourth lunar month draws worshippers and visitors.

rows.name: Jimingyi Post Station
rows.summary: A walled Ming post station covering about 22 hectares, described as the largest surviving courier station in China, built in 1420 as a station on the Ming post road to the Xuanfu frontier and still lived in by villagers. Brick-faced earth walls about 11 m high, with corner platforms and 26 bastions, enclose a grid of lanes with the old station office, granary and horse-yard areas and seven small temples. Empress Dowager Cixi spent a night here in 1900 on her flight from Beijing, and the station was named twice, in 2004 and 2006, on the World Monuments Fund's watch list of endangered sites.

rows.name: Kulun Nur Resort
rows.summary: A lake and holiday resort on the Bashang grassland just north of Guyuan town. The county government lists boat trips on the lake, a wetland flower field with boardwalks that blooms from June to October, horse riding, a Mongolian-style yurt camp with meals and evening bonfire parties, and staged outdoor shows. It suits a summer day or overnight trip for families and groups from Beijing and Zhangjiakou.

rows.name: Laojun Temple, Shazipo
rows.summary: A Ming-to-Qing Daoist temple, named for Laojun (the deified Laozi), on a mound at the north end of Nuanquan old town, with an opera stage, a mountain gate, a front hall and a rear hall. It is one of several nationally listed sites around Nuanquan, with Xigu Fortress and Huayan Temple, and joined the national list in 2013.

rows.name: Lingyan Temple, Yuxian
rows.summary: A Ming Buddhist temple rebuilt in 1441 and probably founded with imperial approval by the eunuch Wang Zhen; its ceilings, caissons and screens resemble those of Zhihua Temple in Beijing. The Tianwang (Dizang) Hall, Daxiong Hall and side halls survive, and the compound was used by the county's food company until restoration began in 2008. Since the old-town scenic area opened in 2016 it has been a visitor attraction, with an exhibition on Yuxian's grain-farming culture and an underground chamber to see.

rows.name: Luanhe Shenyun Scenic Area
rows.summary: A wetland and grassland viewing area on Zhuanfo Hill beside the Shandian River in northern Guyuan County, where the river winds in loops across the open grassland, with boardwalks and pavilions up the hill. The Zhangjiakou tourism bureau says a Neolithic altar and a Liao–Jin–Yuan-era general's review platform also stand here. It is a summer scenery and photography stop, close to the wetland park's bird-watching garden.

rows.name: Nan'an Temple Pagoda
rows.summary: A Liao-dynasty brick pagoda with thirteen close-set eaves on an octagonal plan, solid inside, standing just inside the south gate of Yuxian's walled old town. It is all that survives of an older Nan'an Temple, which was pulled down in the early Ming, around the time the town wall was rebuilt in brick. The small temple beside it dates from 1706 and has a Guanyin hall and three Qing stone tablets recording repairs.

rows.name: Nihewan Archaeological Park
rows.summary: A basin in the Sanggan River valley where more than 80 early-human sites have been found, among them some of the oldest known traces of people in East Asia, with stone tools more than 1.5 million years old. The national archaeological park is centred on the Xiaochangliang site and has a research centre, protective sheds over key excavations such as Majuangou, and a visitor centre. The setting is eroded lake-bed cliffs and farmland rather than a monument, so it suits visitors with a particular interest in human origins.

rows.name: Sanggan River Grand Canyon and Feibu Gorge
rows.summary: A gorge scenic area on the Sanggan River in the far south-west of Xuanhua District, whose main sight, the Feibu ('flying waterfall') Gorge, is a narrow stretch of canyon about 5 km long with many small waterfalls and spray. It lies close to the borders with Yangyuan and Zhuolu counties, in hill country well away from the city. The attraction is natural scenery rather than a historic site, and it suits a short outdoor visit from Zhangjiakou.

rows.name: Shacheng Liquor Culture Expo Park
rows.summary: A visitor area at the Shacheng Laojiao baijiu distillery in Shacheng town, rated a national 4A scenic area in December 2025. It has a liquor-history hall, hands-on blending and labelling workshops, vintage tastings and a dress-up 'imperial wine' sealing ceremony, while the production areas stay closed to the public. According to the operator, visitors book online and tour in guided groups.

rows.name: Shien Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in the old town of Xuanhua whose main hall, completed in 1470 under the Ming dynasty, is the city's oldest surviving timber building and its only one with a hip roof. The hall has five bays under a single-eaved roof and a Qing-era porch at the front, while the gate, side halls and monks' quarters around it were rebuilt between 2005 and 2014 after the rest of the temple had disappeared. It is an active temple, a short walk west of the Zhenshuo (drum) Tower.

rows.name: Shijia Temple, Yuxian
rows.summary: The largest Buddhist temple of old Yuxian, known locally as the Great Temple, with front, middle and rear halls in a walled courtyard just outside the south gate. The middle hall, usually taken as the main hall, is the oldest and largest, with Yuan and Ming features and painted caisson ceilings. It served as the county museum from 1998 until the museum moved to a new building, and has been an old-town attraction since 2016.

rows.name: Shujiu Temple Pagoda
rows.summary: A brick-and-earth pagoda on Jiufeng Ridge in the hills south of Xiaoyanchang village, listed nationally as Jin to Yuan in date although local tradition traces the temple back to the Tang. The top of the pagoda was shaken off in the 1989 Cetian earthquake, and only the pagoda survived into modern times. The temple, also called Jiufeng Temple, was reopened for worship in 2004 and has since been rebuilt with donations, so the pagoda now stands inside a working temple.

rows.name: Shuzhuanglou Yuan Tombs
rows.summary: A Mongol-era tomb group on the grassland east of Guyuan, named for its best-preserved tomb: a square brick tower about 9 m tall with a domed interior, long wrongly said to be the dressing tower of the Liao empress dowager Xiao. Excavation in 1999 showed it is a Yuan-dynasty burial chamber holding three coffins, and surveys later found 26 Yuan tombs and two stele pavilions in all; who lies in the main tomb is still debated. It is a stop for those interested in Mongol-Yuan history.

rows.name: Taizicheng Site (Jin Dynasty Palace)
rows.summary: The site of a Jin-dynasty imperial summer palace, identified as the Taihe Palace of Emperor Zhangzong and occupied for about two decades from around 1190, excavated from 2017 when the 2022 Winter Olympic village was planned beside it; the Games plans were changed so that the site could be kept. The walled enclosure measures about 417 by 343 m, with a central axis of gate, main hall and courtyards. The archaeological park shows that axis outdoors, and a covered hall of 4,600 sq m shows the excavated west courtyard in place beside finds such as bowls stamped for the imperial kitchen.

rows.name: Thaiwoo Ski Town
rows.summary: A ski resort town at Chongli built in the style of a European alpine village, 2 km from Taizicheng, where the Zhangjiakou events of the 2022 Winter Olympics were held. It has around 30 ski runs, and in summer its cable car to a viewpoint, hiking trails, mountain-bike descents and go-karts stay open. Hotels, restaurants, an ice rink and hot-spring pools make it a base for a family or active break rather than a sightseeing stop.

rows.name: Tianbao Nasutu Grassland Resort
rows.summary: A grassland holiday resort on the western edge of Zhangbei, laid out around a lake and a large flower meadow, with a Mongol-Yuan themed area and a hot-spring and water-play zone. The provincial tourism department lists a sightseeing mini-train that crosses the lake, a hillside path to a stone gate, and views of wind turbines across the grassland. It is mainly a summer outing for families and groups.

rows.name: Tianqi Temple, Yuxian
rows.summary: A Daoist temple to the Emperor of the Eastern Peak, built in 1599 and repaired in the Jiaqing reign, outside the east gate of Yuxian's old town. Of a once large complex only the offering hall and the main hall survive, joined under linked roofs and surrounded by ordinary houses; the main hall has a hip roof of yellow glazed tiles trimmed in green and imperial-style painted beams. The temple was put to other uses after 1949 and returned to the heritage authorities in 2001.

rows.name: Wanlong Ski Resort
rows.time_needed: Half a day to a full day
rows.summary: One of the large ski resorts in Chongli, the Olympic ski district of Zhangjiakou, with more than 30 runs, some of them certified by the International Ski Federation (FIS), a long gentle beginners' run and night skiing. It is a purpose-built mountain resort, so visits are mainly in the winter snow season, and it suits advanced skiers as well as first-timers.

rows.name: Wanquan Right Guard City
rows.summary: A Ming garrison town founded as an earth fort in 1393 and given a brick facing in 1438, whose square circuit of walls, about 880 m on each side, still stands with a south gate (Ying'en) and a north gate (Desheng). The town inside is still lived in and has been used as a filming location for period dramas. It served as a defence base on the Ming Xuanfu frontier and, from 1693, as the seat of Wanquan county.

rows.name: Xiabali Liao Tombs
rows.summary: A cemetery of Liao-dynasty (916–1125) brick tombs in Xiabali village, north-west of Xuanhua, mostly the family graves of the Han Chinese Zhang clan, with more than ten tombs found since 1972. Several chambers have walls and ceilings painted with scenes of processions, musicians, tea-making and board games, and the tomb of the official Zhang Shiqing (built in 1116) has a ceiling star map that combines the Chinese 28 lunar mansions with the western zodiac. The murals show how Khitan and Han customs mixed in the Liao period, and finds from the tombs, including a bottle of Liao-era grape wine, are held in the Xuanhua Museum.

rows.name: Xiaowutai Huichuan Scenic Area
rows.summary: A mountain-valley scenic area on the southern side of the Xiaowutai range, at Huichuan village in Yuxian's Baishu township, on Hebei's list of 4A scenic areas. Tour operators sell it for a hiking route past a series of waterfalls and pools. It suits walkers with a day to spare, and is a separate visit from the Jinhekou valley on the north side of the same mountains.

rows.name: Xiaowutai Jinhe Scenic Area
rows.time_needed: Half a day to a full day
rows.summary: A forested river valley below the Xiaowutai peaks, whose East Terrace, at 2,882 m, is the highest point in Hebei. Part of the Jinhekou area belongs to the mountain's protected wildlife zone, home to species such as the black stork and the brown eared pheasant, and the valley holds the Jinhe Temple and Xuankong'an pagoda groups, nationally listed clusters of Yuan-to-Ming pagodas. It is a place for walking and nature-watching rather than sightseeing.

rows.name: Xigu Fortress, Nuanquan
rows.summary: A walled fort village of the Ming and Qing in Nuanquan town, one of more than 400 fortified villages in Yuxian, which keeps its old courtyard houses, temples, lanes and an opera stage in fairly intact condition. Some of the houses now serve as guesthouses where visitors can try Yuxian paper-cutting. Nuanquan is a nationally designated historic town and the home of 'dashuhua', a show of molten-iron sparks staged at weekends and festivals.

rows.name: Ximalin City Wall
rows.summary: The walls of Ximalin, a fortified town in Wanquan District built in 1435 under the Ming and repaired in 1741 under the Qing, and a national heritage unit since 2013. The remains stand around the present-day village, which also has the nationally listed Yuhuang Pavilion. It is a rural heritage stop.

rows.name: Ximalin Yuhuang Pavilion
rows.summary: A Jade Emperor (Yuhuang) pavilion built in 1575 on a 7 m brick platform in Ximalin village and repaired in 1861, which the heritage listing describes as a concentrated example of Ming timber architecture. The main hall has a three-eaved hip-and-gable roof and rises more than 20 m, with side rooms on either flank. The pavilion also keeps a store of scriptures in 15 chests.

rows.name: Xuanhua Ancient City
rows.summary: The old walled city of Xuanhua, a Ming frontier stronghold known as the 'first prefecture west of Beijing', which has kept its Ming street layout and main monuments. The core is the Qingyuan Tower (bell tower, 1482) and the Zhenshuo Tower (drum tower, 1440), two multi-storey timber towers on brick platforms pierced by arched passages along the main street, with the Gongji Tower on the old south gate and long stretches of brick-faced city wall. The wall was enlarged in 1394, ran about 11 km round, and has been restored in sections since the mid-2000s.

rows.name: Yuan Zhongdu (Middle Capital of the Yuan)
rows.summary: The earthen remains of Yuan Zhongdu, the 'Middle Capital' that Emperor Wuzong began building on the grassland north of Zhangbei in 1307; work was halted in 1311 and the palace was burned in 1358 during the Red Turban uprising. Three nested walled enclosures can be traced on the ground as earthen walls and banks, with the foundations of the palace city's south gate, the I-shaped platform of the main hall and an excavated corner-tower platform. The Yuan Zhongdu Museum, in Zhangbei town about 15 km away, shows the finds and the story of the excavations.

rows.name: Yuquan Temple, Bubeibao
rows.summary: A temple built in 1439 as the family temple of the powerful Ming eunuch Wang Zhen, who came from Yuxian, standing by the gate of the old fort at Bubeibao village. Its main hall has an uncommon hip roof and, inside, wall paintings of figures in three tiers. The hall was in poor repair in 2016, when part of its roof and a wall had collapsed.

rows.name: Yuzhou Museum
rows.summary: Yuxian's county museum, ranked a national second-grade museum, which moved in 2016 from Shijia Temple into a purpose-built building of about 13,000 sq m. Its main exhibition, 'Daiwei Changge' ('A Long Song of Dai and Yu'), follows the area from prehistory through the ancient state of Dai, the Sui–Tang and Liao–Yuan periods and the Ming–Qing fortified villages, and was named one of China's ten best museum exhibitions of 2016. A second exhibition is devoted to Yuxian paper-cutting, a nationally listed intangible heritage craft, and the collection of about 11,000 items includes a Western Han painted bronze goose-and-fish lamp.

rows.name: Yuzhou Old Town and City Wall
rows.summary: The walled old town of Yuxian, first walled in 580 and rebuilt under the Ming in 1377, with a chessboard of streets and courtyard houses inside a wall circuit of 3.8 km. Landmarks include the Drum Tower, the tallest building in the old city, the Ming–Qing prefectural yamen in the south-west corner and the Yuhuang Pavilion on the north wall, while temples and halls within the walls, such as the Nan'an Temple pagoda, are nationally listed in their own right. Only part of the wall survives, mainly on the north and north-west sides, but the old town is still lived in, with street stalls selling local snacks and a tradition of Yuxian paper-cutting.

rows.name: Yuzhou Yuhuang Pavilion
rows.summary: A Ming gate-tower on the middle of Yuxian's north wall, completed in 1377 as the Jingbian ('border-pacifying') Tower and later used as a Jade Emperor temple. Its two courtyards climb about 3 m from the gate hall to the main hall, a two-storey building with three tiers of eaves and a green-glazed tile roof, where Daoist murals show the Jade Emperor with 41 attendants and 36 thunder generals. Stone tablets under the hall's eaves record Ming and Qing repairs, and the pavilion is one of the locations seen in the 2024 video game Black Myth: Wukong.

rows.name: Zhangjiakou Fort (Zhangjiakoubu)
rows.summary: The old Ming fort of Zhangjiakou, built in 1429 as a garrison post on the Great Wall defences, which grew into a major trading town on the caravan road to Mongolia and Russia. Its streets still hold several hundred Ming- and Qing-period courtyard houses, along with the Wenchang Pavilion, the Yuhuang Pavilion and an old academy, many of them restored in recent years. It is a lived-in old quarter rather than a closed attraction, and a protection regulation for it took effect in 2023.

rows.name: Zhaohua Temple
rows.summary: A Ming-dynasty Buddhist temple in the old town of Huai'ancheng, founded in the late 14th century and rebuilt in the 1430s and 1440s, and a national heritage unit since 2001. Its main hall holds 47 water-and-land ritual murals painted in 1562, showing Buddhist and Daoist deities. The compound also keeps its heavenly kings' hall, a stele and side halls, and is of interest mainly for the Ming murals.

rows.name: Zhenwu Temple, Yuxian
rows.summary: A Ming temple to Zhenwu, the Daoist Perfected Warrior whom the Ming court promoted as protector of the realm, standing in a small walled compound at the foot of the north-west city wall inside Yuxian's old town. Listed as a provincial site in 1993 and nationally in 2006, it was repaired in 2008 together with Lingyan Temple. It lies beside the stretch of town wall that survives on the north-west side.

rows.name: Zhongdu Grassland Resort
rows.summary: A grassland holiday resort on the Bashang plateau north of Zhangbei, built around a camp of Mongolian-style yurts that includes a very large domed yurt used as a restaurant and venue. In past summer seasons it has put on staged Mongolian song-and-dance and horse shows, an evening bonfire party and a stage play about the Yuan capital. It suits families and groups on a short summer break from Beijing or Zhangjiakou.

rows.name: Xiantaishan Forest Park
rows.summary: Xiantaishan is a national forest park and provincial nature reserve of about 6,900 ha in Xinzhuang township, in the Taihang foothills west of Shijiazhuang. It is a wooded mountain area for walking and sightseeing, and it is one of the first national forest-wellness bases named in 2020.

rows.name: Xinyi Qixiu Hotel, Langfang
rows.summary: A hotel in Han-Tang style in Langfang's economic and technological development zone, with a TCM spa among its leisure facilities. It is run as accommodation rather than as a sight, and was listed in 2018 as a TCM health-tourism base.

rows.name: Baofeng Temple, Tunliu
rows.summary: A temple in Jicun village, Lucun township, Tunliu District, now reduced to a single courtyard of about 960 square metres, where it once had three. The Water-and-Land Hall at the front is a Ming building with about 17 square metres of surviving murals, and the Five Buddhas Hall behind it is a Yuan structure with a glazed ridge. An inscription records a repair in 1469, and the temple was listed as a national key site in 2006.

rows.name: Baolingshan Scenic Area
rows.summary: A religious and forest-leisure scenic area at the foot of Longhu Mountain in Qinyuan County, built since 2002 by a local coal and coke group. It has more than 40 temple buildings in traditional style, including Lingtong Chan Temple, the Daoist Baotong Temple and Tianqi Temple; the Tianqi Temple customs and the Lingtong Temple fair are listed as provincial intangible heritage. It suits visitors interested in newly built Buddhist, Daoist and Confucian complexes and the temple fairs held here.

rows.name: Beihe Yandi Temple
rows.summary: A small temple to the legendary Emperor Yan (Yandi, also known as Shennong) in Beihe village, Beicheng township. Only its main hall, a Yuan-dynasty building three bays wide, is old; the other buildings are Qing, and a stele records a repair in 1846. It was listed as a provincial protected site in 1996 and as a national one in 2013, and stands among farmland on the plain south-west of Changzhi.

rows.name: Biyun Temple, Xiaozhang
rows.summary: A temple of three courtyards in Xiaozhang village whose main hall is a Song-dynasty building, three bays wide, with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, deep eaves and widely spaced brackets. Scholars differ on whether its bracket sets are Five Dynasties or Northern Song in style. Painted ceiling panels inside the hall are also of interest.

rows.name: Bucun Yuhuang Temple
rows.summary: A Jade Emperor temple in Bucun village, Zhangzi County, with a front hall, an offering hall, a middle hall and a rear hall, and halls dating from the Song to the Qing. The front hall shows Tang-style construction and was badly damaged before its restoration; the murals and statues no longer survive, and the compound served as a grain depot in the 1960s. It became a county-level protected site in 2006 and a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Changning Great Temple
rows.summary: Changning Great Temple, also known as Lingyuan Shengjing Temple (Sacred Well Temple), is a village temple in Changning village with a one-axis, two-courtyard layout. From south to north it has a brick screen wall, an entrance building with a stage facing into the courtyard, an offering hall, the main hall and a rear hall. The main hall is of the Yuan dynasty, with a glazed ridge and roof beams of naturally curved timber, and the other buildings are Ming and Qing.

rows.name: Chongjiao Temple, Machang
rows.summary: A temple in Guyi village, Machang town, in Luzhou District north of central Changzhi, with buildings from the Yuan to the Qing. It became a provincial protected site in 1986 and a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Chongqing Temple, Zhangzi
rows.summary: Chongqing Temple is a small Buddhist temple on the slope of Ziyun Mountain, with hills on three sides and a tributary of the Zhuozhang River to the south. Its Thousand Buddha Hall is Song-dynasty, and the side hall holds Song painted sculptures of Guanyin, Manjushri and Samantabhadra, dated by an inscription to 1079, with eighteen luohan figures on either side. Since 2024 it has drawn larger crowds as one of the Shanxi locations recreated in the video game Black Myth: Wukong.

rows.name: Chunhua Temple, Pingshun
rows.summary: Only the Jin-dynasty main hall of this temple survives, standing in Yanggao village where the cleared temple grounds now form the village square. The hall is three bays wide with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof and wide, upturned eaves, and in front of it stand two Song-dynasty stone sutra pillars dated 960 and 970. A county gazetteer of 1693 dates the temple's foundation to the Northern Qi, as a branch of Longmen Temple.

rows.name: Cuifujun Temple, Zhangzi
rows.summary: The main hall of a temple to Cui Fujun, a judge-of-the-underworld deity widely worshipped in northern China, whom tradition places as a seventh-century magistrate of Zhangzi. Only the Jin-dynasty hall survives, five bays wide with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof and five-puzuo double-ang brackets, with a pair of Ming stone lions in front. It stands in Zhangzi county town, in Tongfu village of Danzhu town, and was added to the national list in 2013.

rows.name: Danquan Town, Licheng
rows.summary: A mountain-valley leisure resort developed since 2021 around Yuanquan village in Xijing town, Licheng County, beside the Taihang Number One scenic road. The village is named for a spring that wells out of a cave beneath a hill the locals call Wugen ('rootless') Mountain and feeds a long pond; beside it stand a Yuhuang temple rebuilt in 2018 and a memorial pavilion put up by an Eighth Route Army chemical works for nine workers who died on duty. The resort adds camping and RV pitches, glass-walled 'Linglong' cabins, hillside guesthouses and a cave hotel, with nature-study and local-history programmes, so it suits families wanting a quiet rural stay.

rows.name: Dayun Temple, Pingshun
rows.summary: A hill temple founded in 938 under the Later Jin, whose Buddha hall and small stone Qibao Pagoda are Five Dynasties work and among the very few buildings of that period left in China. The hall has deep, gently sloping eaves and keeps about 29 sq m of Five Dynasties murals on its east wall and central screen, including a Vimalakirti scene; the other buildings are Qing. The pagoda, six metres high, was built in 954 and has five of its original seven storeys.

rows.name: Dayun Temple, Qin County
rows.summary: A small temple in Guocun village, of Song origin, where a stele of 1212 gives the name Dayun Chanyuan. Only the Qing-dynasty gate and the main hall survive; the hall is a Song-Jin structure three bays wide with a single-eave overhanging gable roof, and about 50 sq m of Ming wall paintings remain on its side walls. The compound covers about 770 sq m.

rows.name: Dayun Temple, Wuxiang
rows.summary: A temple on a terrace in Gucheng town, on the site of the Eastern Han county seat of Nieshi, renamed Dayun Temple in 1064 under the Northern Song. The compound covers 7,900 sq m, with a Guanyin hall, the main hall and side halls. The five-bay main hall keeps its original Jin-dynasty frame, and the other buildings are Ming or Qing.

rows.name: Dongyi Dragon King Temple
rows.summary: A Dragon King temple in Dongyi village covering about 1,570 sq m in two courtyards, with a gate, a two-storey opera stage, a main hall and side halls. The main hall is Jin-dynasty work, three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eave overhanging gable roof and a front porch; the other buildings are Qing.

rows.name: Eighth Route Army Cultural Park
rows.summary: A themed park between Phoenix Hill and the Mamu River in Wuxiang, built to recreate the wartime life and campaigns of the Eighth Route Army through hands-on, high-technology displays. Its seven parts include a front plaza, a visitor centre, Victory Avenue, a live-action theatre and a village area. It is a staged, family-oriented introduction to the subject rather than an archive, beside the Taihang memorial museum.

rows.name: Eighth Route Army Headquarters Sites
rows.time_needed: Half a day to a day
rows.summary: Three former headquarters of the Eighth Route Army in the Taihang Mountains: Beicun in Lucheng District, used from October 1938 to July 1939, and Zhuanbi and Wangjiayu in Wuxiang, used between 1939 and 1942. Each is a set of farmhouse or temple courtyards kept as the commanders' offices and residences, with displays of photographs and relics. Zhuanbi, a temple group and farmhouse courtyard, is where the Hundred Regiments Offensive of 1940 was directed.

rows.name: Faxing Temple, Zhangzi
rows.summary: Faxing Temple rises in steps up the slope of Cuiyun Mountain, from the gate through a Tang stone pagoda to the Song-dynasty Yuanjue Hall. The temple was moved here between 1984 and 1996 from its original site on Cilin Mountain, where coal mining had caused the ground to subside. It is known for three treasures: the sandstone pagoda of the Tang, built on a double-walled square plan, a Tang stone lamp stand dated 773, and the Song painted sculptures inside Yuanjue Hall.

rows.name: Former Taiyue Military Region Headquarters
rows.summary: A group of ten cave dwellings in three connected courtyards, covering about 1,800 sq m, at Yanzhai village. The headquarters of the Taiyue Military Region and the area's Party and government bodies were based here from 1940 until October 1942, and the central courtyard served as the office of Bo Yibo and Chen Geng. A display room holds photographs and relics of the period.

rows.name: Fotou Temple
rows.summary: A small temple in Chedang village, Yanggao township, named for the hill behind it, whose outline resembles a Buddha's head. Only its hall survives, a three-bay building with a glazed-tile ridge that the national list dates to the Song and Changzhi Daily to the Jin. Its walls carry murals of the Twenty-four Devas, the guardian deities, which Changzhi Daily dates to the Ming.

rows.name: Fuxi Temple, Zhongzhang
rows.summary: A small village temple to Fuxi, the legendary culture hero, standing on a hilltop south-east of Zhongzhang village. The one-courtyard compound keeps a Yuan-dynasty main hall and a Ming offering pavilion, with Qing side halls and wing rooms, and the hall's eave columns are stone. Steles in the temple record repairs in the Ming and Qing dynasties.

rows.name: Fuyuan Temple, Wuxiang
rows.summary: A village temple in Beilianghou village whose main building is a two-storey Ming hall, three bays wide with an overhanging gable roof. The west side hall is Yuan, with a glazed ridge ornament inscribed in 1324, and the east side hall is early Qing; a stele records a repair in 1725. Stone Buddha figures in the northern-dynasty style stand within the temple.

rows.name: Guancun Yandi Temple
rows.summary: A temple to the legendary Emperor Yan (Yandi, also known as Shennong) in Guancun village in the Laodingshan subdistrict of Changzhi, covering about 1,400 sq m. The main hall is a Yuan-dynasty building three bays wide, and about 40 sq m of wall paintings survive on its east and west gable walls, which Changzhi Daily notes are rare among the Yandi temples of Changzhi because they show episodes from the Yandi story; the other buildings are mostly Qing. It was added to the national list in 2013 and stands inside the village's dense housing.

rows.name: Guanyin Hall, Changzhi
rows.summary: Guanyin Hall is a Ming-dynasty temple in the western suburbs of Changzhi, begun in 1582 and repaired in the Qing, with two courtyards leading through a gate hall and an offering pavilion to the main hall. The main hall is original Ming work under yellow and green glazed tiles, and more than 500 painted and gilded hanging sculptures cover its walls, roof frame, doors and windows, with Buddhist, Daoist and Confucian figures and Shakyamuni in the centre between Laozi and Confucius. The temple is also one of the real-world reference locations for the video game Black Myth: Wukong.

rows.name: Happy Taihang Valley
rows.summary: A large leisure complex in Huguan County, east of Changzhi, that combines an amusement park, a water park (Jingwei Water World), an aquarium, a children's area, a hot-spring hotel and a farm. Its evening programme of light shows and performances is built around a 'Taihang myth' theme. It is a commercial venue for families rather than a historic or natural site.

rows.name: Hongji Temple, Wuxiang
rows.summary: A two-courtyard temple in Dongliang village with an opera stage, bell and drum towers, a Ming south hall and a main hall, and a side courtyard with a Guandi hall. The five-bay main hall stands on a stone base 1.5 m high and has Jin-style features, and its walls carry Qing and early Republican Buddhist murals. A sandstone thousand-Buddha pagoda about 2 m high stands beside the main hall, and a traditional temple fair falls on the 23rd day of the sixth lunar month.

rows.name: Hongjiao Temple, Nannieshui
rows.summary: A village temple in Nannieshui village on two courtyards covering about 1,500 sq m. Its main hall, the Daxiong Hall at the back, is a Yuan-dynasty building three bays wide with an overhanging gable roof; the Heavenly Kings Hall in front is Ming, the Second Buddha Hall behind it is Qing, and the side halls are Ming or Qing. Steles record repairs in 1271 and between 1701 and 1717, and an old cypress stands in the courtyard.

rows.name: Huangyadong Arms Factory Site
rows.summary: A gorge in the northern Taihang Mountains where the Eighth Route Army built an arms factory in the early 1940s, which Changzhi Daily calls its earliest and largest; the name comes from a natural cave in the cliff, about 30 m above the valley floor, that was used for storing weapons. More than a hundred remains survive, including workshops, barracks, trenches and a martyrs' cemetery with a memorial tower for the defenders of the November 1941 battle, and a narrow gorge passage of about 500 m. It combines a revolutionary site with steep red-sandstone cliff scenery.

rows.name: Huguo Lingkuangwang Temple, Xiahuo
rows.summary: A temple to Houyi, the mythical archer who shot down nine suns and was enfeoffed Lingkuang King by the Song emperor Huizong as a rain-bringing god; it was founded in 1122 on White Cloud Hill, among farmland. The main hall is Jin work with a glazed ridge, six-puzuo brackets and donor inscriptions of 1184 and 1194, and holds statues of Houyi and Chang'e and murals of the king bringing rain. A Qing offering hall in front, which hides the main hall's full view, has reliefs of Houyi shooting the suns and Chang'e flying to the moon.

rows.name: Huilong Temple, Pingshun
rows.summary: A small temple beside the Zhuozhang River in Houbi village, of which only the main hall survives. The hall is a Jin-dynasty building three bays wide, with a single-eave overhanging gable roof and plain, early-style brackets. Qing-dynasty murals of about 54 square metres cover its side walls and show figures from Journey to the West and the Four Heavenly Kings.

rows.name: Huixian Daoist Temple
rows.summary: A Daoist temple in Jianzhang village, founded in 1229 under the Jin and covering 2,263 sq m. Along its axis stand a gate, a Guandi hall, a Jade Emperor hall and the Three Pure Ones hall, with bell and drum towers and side rooms. The five-bay Three Pure Ones hall is original Jin work and the Jade Emperor hall is Yuan; the remaining buildings are Ming or Qing.

rows.name: Jindeng Temple
rows.summary: A temple of seven courtyards built along a cliff in the Taihang Mountains on the Henan border, with 16 caves carved mainly between 1504 and 1565, which the Changzhi government calls the largest surviving group of Ming-dynasty grottoes in China. The central Shuilu Hall is a cave with a spring-fed pool crossed by a stone bridge and 69 painted scenes of Buddhist, Daoist and Confucian figures on its walls. North of the temple stands a forest of 46 monks' pagodas, the tallest the seven-storey Thousand Buddha Pagoda, 10.3 m high.

rows.name: Jiutian Shengmu Temple
rows.summary: A hilltop temple of the Holy Mother of the Nine Heavens in Hedong village, Beishe township, founded under the Tang and rebuilt in the Northern Song. A flight of 53 white-marble steps climbs from the lower courtyard to the gate, with eight stone cave-dwellings of Qing date, topped by painted galleries, on either side. The Holy Mother Hall at the back is Song work from 1101, the offering pavilion is Yuan in form, and the gate, which doubles as an opera stage, was rebuilt in the Qing with carved dragon-shaped brackets.

rows.name: Liaohetou Guandi Temple
rows.summary: A temple to Guan Yu (Guandi) in Liaohetou village, Huangniuti township, in a single courtyard of about 460 square metres. The main hall is of the Yuan dynasty, three bays wide, and the other buildings are Qing; the gate building doubles as an opera stage on its upper floor. It was added to the national list in 2019.

rows.name: Licheng City God Temple
rows.summary: A City God temple in the centre of Licheng, moved to this site in 1025 with the county town and rebuilt in 1369 after a fire. Its triple-eave gate tower, about 20 m high and roofed in glazed tile, keeps a Ming-dynasty character despite later repairs; behind it stand a Qing main hall of five bays and a gallery of old stelae, including Northern Wei and Sui examples. It suits visitors interested in temple architecture in a county town.

rows.name: Lingzewang Temple, Taiping
rows.summary: A village temple in Taiping village, where an inscription on a front-eave column records its founding in 1210 under the Jin. The Lingzewang Hall at the back is the Jin building: three bays wide, with a single-eave overhanging gable roof, double-ang bracket sets and four front stone columns that carry Jin dates. The opera stage and the other buildings of the compound are Qing.

rows.name: Lizhuang Confucian Temple
rows.summary: A village Confucian temple: a small compound facing south, with a Jin-dynasty main hall (Dacheng Hall) and a middle hall and side halls of the Qing period. Steles in the temple record its founding in 1221 and a repair in 1263, and the hall is three bays wide with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof. The village's Martial Temple stands about 250 m away.

rows.name: Lizhuang Martial Temple
rows.summary: Lizhuang Martial Temple is a temple to Guan Yu (Guandi), the deified Three Kingdoms general, in a two-courtyard compound that faces west. The main hall is of the Yuan dynasty, the music pavilion in front of it of the Ming and the remaining buildings of the Qing, and the entrance building combines a gate with a stage facing into the courtyard. Steles dated 1849 and 1902 record repairs to the Guandi hall.

rows.name: Longmen Temple, Pingshun
rows.summary: A hillside temple of about 5,070 sq m at the foot of Longmen Mountain, also called Huiri Yuan, that keeps timber buildings from every period from the Five Dynasties to the Qing. The west side hall dates from about 925 under the Later Tang, the main hall from 1098 under the Song, the gate hall from the Jin, the rear Randeng Buddha hall from the Yuan and the east side hall from the Ming. About 34 sq m of Ming and Qing murals survive in the main hall, and a Later Han stone sutra pillar of 950 stands in the courtyard.

rows.name: Lu Xun Art School Site at Xiabeizhang
rows.name_zh: 鲁迅艺术学校下北漳旧址
rows.summary: A wartime site in Xiabeizhang village, where teachers and students of the Lu Xun Art School's front-line branch and other wartime cultural groups worked in 1940. The scenic area includes the former school, the Jindongnan branch of the Sino-Soviet Cultural Association, the former home of Li Bozhao and an exhibition on the Communist Party and wartime culture. It is one of the sites in the Wangjiayu revolutionary-relics cluster and has been listed as a provincial protected site since 2021.

rows.name: Lu'an Prefectural Office (Shangdang Gate)
rows.summary: The surviving gate complex of the government office of Lu'an Prefecture, whose Shangdang Gate stands on a high platform flanked by a bell tower and a drum tower. The gate dates from the Sui dynasty and was rebuilt in 1370, with the towers added in 1398 and 1471; the gate, the two towers, the second hall, an office courtyard and a west garden survive. It is regarded as the symbol of Changzhi.

rows.name: Lu'an Prefecture City God Temple
rows.summary: A City God temple founded in 1285 under the Yuan dynasty, laid out in three courtyards along a north-south axis in central Changzhi and covering more than 7,000 sq m. The main hall is Yuan work, the gate and the rear sleeping hall are Ming, and the other buildings are Ming or Qing, many with roofs in coloured glazed tile; repairs are recorded in 1488 and 1834. The Changzhi culture and tourism bureau describes it as the largest and best-preserved surviving prefectural City God temple in China, and a temple fair is held on the 15th day of the fourth lunar month.

rows.name: Nannieshui Stone Carving Museum
rows.summary: A county museum on Erlang Hill beside the west source of the Zhuozhang River, showing more than 1,100 stone carvings from a hoard unearthed at Nannieshui village, dated from the Northern Wei to the Northern Song. The galleries cover about 3,000 sq m and also hold Jin-dynasty brick carvings of the Twenty-four Filial Exemplars from a Qin County tomb found in 1999. It is a third-grade national museum, and its collection is listed nationally as the Nannieshui stone carvings.

rows.name: Pagoda of Master Minghui
rows.summary: A six-metre stone pagoda in Hongni village, the burial pagoda of Master Minghui, abbot of the long-vanished Haihui Temple, who was killed in 877. A tablet on the pagoda is dated 932, under the Later Tang, and the square pagoda has a base, a body and a finial. The village around it stands on a cliff edge above a waterfall and is built largely of stone.

rows.name: Penglai Palace, Shishi
rows.summary: Penglai Palace is a group of Ming and Qing buildings just east of Shishi village in Lucun township, Tunliu District. It was listed as a national key site in 2013.

rows.name: Puzhao Temple, Qin County
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Kaicun village which the Qianlong-era Qinzhou gazetteer records as founded in 488 under the Northern Wei and repaired under the Jin, Ming and Qing. Only the Great Buddha Hall survives, a Jin-dynasty building on a low stone base, three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof; the whole site covers about 210 sq m. A stele inside records a repair in 1820, and the temple was listed nationally in 2006.

rows.name: Sanjiao Hall, Yihe
rows.summary: Yihe Sanjiao Hall is a village temple whose name means Three Teachings Hall; Changzhi Daily describes it as a folk-deity temple that brings Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism together. The main hall dates to the Jin dynasty and the middle hall to the Yuan, with Qing side halls, and Qing murals survive on a gable wall. It is a small one-courtyard compound of about 20 m by 35 m.

rows.name: Sanzong Temple, Beishe
rows.summary: A Sanzong temple in Beishe village, Beishe township, Pingshun County, one of many across south-east Shanxi that honour Hou Yi, the legendary archer. Its single courtyard of about 860 square metres has a three-bay main hall of the Yuan dynasty, while the offering hall, the gate building with an opera stage above and the side halls are Qing, with repairs recorded in 1845 and 1892. It became a provincial protected site in 2004 and a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Sanzong Temple, Dazhonghan
rows.summary: A Sanzong temple in Dazhonghan village, Changzhang township, Zhangzi County, one of many across south-east Shanxi that honour Hou Yi, the legendary archer. An inscription records its founding in 1291; the main hall is of the Yuan dynasty, three bays wide, with stone eave columns and about 80 square metres of Qing murals, and the other buildings, including an opera stage at the entrance, are Qing. It was listed as a national key site in 2013.

rows.name: Sanzong Temple, Nanyanghu
rows.summary: A Sanzong temple in Nanyanghu village, Huangshan township, one of the many in south-east Shanxi that honour Hou Yi, the legendary archer. Inscriptions record a title granted to the temple in 1103 and a rebuilding in 1175 under the Jin, with repairs under the Yuan and Ming. It stands in a single courtyard of about 1,170 square metres; the three-bay main hall is Jin original work and the offering hall, bell and drum towers and side halls are Qing.

rows.name: Sarira Pagoda of Monk Xianshi
rows.summary: A Tang-dynasty nine-storey pagoda of dense eaves, built for the relics of a monk named Xianshi, stands at Jinchan Temple on the western peak of Laoye Mountain, anciently Sanzong Mountain, in Tunliu District. Its body is pitted with bullet holes from the fighting of September 1945, when the mountain was a main battlefield of the Shangdang Campaign, and the battle site is a provincially protected monument. Local legend sets Hou Yi's shooting of the extra suns on the mountain's east peak.

rows.name: Shengmu Temple, Beiganquan
rows.summary: A temple to the Holy Mother in Beiganquan village, Miaozhuang town, Pingshun County, in a single courtyard of about 1,100 square metres. The three-bay main hall is of the Yuan dynasty, and the other buildings, among them a two-storey gate building with an opera stage above, are Qing. It became a provincial protected site in 2004 and a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Shengshou Temple, Lingkongshan
rows.summary: A small temple among old pines in the Lingkongshan forest reserve, founded under the Tang and laid out in five courtyards. From west to east these are the Luohan, Yaolou (cave-building), central, Guandi and monks' courtyards, and the five-bay main hall of the central courtyard has a flush-gable glazed-tile roof. Steles of 1514 and 1575 survive, and the surrounding pines include trees about 500 years old.

rows.name: Taihang Dragon Cave
rows.summary: A karst cave in Shiquan village in Panlong town, east of Wuxiang, with four levels and more than 2,000 m of passages, of which three levels are open. The route passes more than 70 named sights among stalactites, stalagmites, flowstone curtains and 'stone waterfall' formations. It suits a short visit combined with the Eighth Route Army headquarters site at Zhuanbi, which is in the same town.

rows.name: Taihang Memorial Museum of the Eighth Route Army
rows.summary: A national first-class museum on the Eighth Route Army's war of resistance against Japan, opened in 1988 at the foot of Phoenix Hill in Wuxiang and enlarged in 2005. The main exhibition runs for 1,450 m and shows more than 1,000 items and over 600 photographs and charts; the grounds also hold a panorama hall on the Hundred Regiments Offensive, a stele park and a 19.37 m monument on the hilltop. It suits visitors interested in the wartime Taihang base area, and it adjoins the Eighth Route Army Cultural Park.

rows.name: Taihang Water Town (Chibi Xuanliu Gorge)
rows.summary: A 12 km stretch of the Zhuozhang River gorge in the Taihang foothills of Pingshun County, named after 'Chibi Xuanliu' (red cliffs and hanging streams), one of the old 'eight sights' of the Taihang. Red rock walls rise from green water, a broad waterfall about 118 m wide and 22 m high crosses the river bed, and a 4.5 km boardwalk runs through the red cliffs. The Commentary on the Waterways Classic, written in the early sixth century, already praised the blue-green cliffs and red walls like dawn cloud here, and today the gorge suits a half-day walk.

rows.name: Tangwang Temple, Qianwanhu
rows.summary: A village temple in Qianwanhu village, named for King Tang (Tangwang). Its main hall dates from the Yuan dynasty and keeps its Yuan brackets and wall paintings.

rows.name: Temple of Yu the Great, Beishe
rows.summary: A temple to Yu the Great, the legendary tamer of floods, in Beishe village, Pingshun County, in a single courtyard of about 990 square metres. The three-bay main hall is of the Yuan dynasty and keeps traces of painted decoration on its brackets and beams, while the other buildings, including a gate building with an opera stage above, are Qing; a repair of 1803 is recorded. It stands in the same village as the Beishe Sanzong Temple, and both were listed as provincial sites in 2004 and national ones in 2013.

rows.name: Temple of Yu the Great, Xiqingbei
rows.summary: A temple to Yu the Great, the legendary tamer of floods, in Xiqingbei village, Beishe township, Pingshun County, with Ming and Qing buildings. It became a provincial protected site in 2004 and a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Tianji Mountain
rows.summary: A mountain scenic area in the Taihang Mountains of eastern Pingshun County, near Yanglaoyan village in Dongsitou township, which borders Henan, with streams, pools and waterfalls running in its valleys through the year. A cliffside plank walkway looks down on a drop of more than 300 m, and its highest fall, the Tianji Longpu, is promoted as dropping 346 m. A geopark of the same name, the Pingshun Tianjishan Geopark, holds national geopark qualification.

rows.name: Tianqiwang Temple, Xincun
rows.summary: Tianqiwang Temple stands at the eastern edge of Xin village in Dongyangguan town. It was founded in 1341 according to a Yuan stele; the main hall, five bays wide with an overhanging gable roof, is a Yuan building, and the entrance doubles as a two-storey opera stage. Changning Great Temple, another national-level village temple, is about 1 km to the east.

rows.name: Tiantai An, Pingshun
rows.summary: A small hall on high ground in Wangqu village that was long counted among China's four surviving Tang timber buildings, until repairs in 2014 turned up ink inscriptions dating it to the Later Tang (Five Dynasties) period, about 929–933. It is three bays wide, about 7 m square, on a stone platform about 1 m high, with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, very plain brackets and a simple early roof frame. Only the hall and a worn Tang stele remain of the temple.

rows.name: Tianwang Temple, Zhangzi
rows.summary: Tianwang Temple (Heavenly King Temple) stands in Zhangzi county town, where only its middle hall and rear hall survive, both of the Jin dynasty. The middle hall, three bays wide with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof and five-layer bracket sets, is described by Changzhi Daily as a typical Jin building. The county gazetteer dates the founding to the Tang, and the temple grew out of the Tang and Song cult of the war deity Vaishravana (Pishamen Tianwang).

rows.name: Tianxian Temple, Zhuangtou
rows.summary: A village temple in Zhuangtou village, Jinzhuang town, Huguan County, in a single courtyard of about 1,550 square metres. Inscriptions record a Song-dynasty founding and repairs in 1629 and 1671; the main hall is of the Yuan dynasty, three bays wide with a glazed ridge, and the other buildings, among them bell and drum towers, are Qing. It became a provincial protected site in 2004 and a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Tongtian Gorge
rows.summary: A gorge scenic area of about 65 sq km in south-eastern Pingshun County, in Hongtiguan and Dongsitou townships, which is also a national geopark. The main gorge runs about 26 km, with Tongtian Lake and its small island of macaques, a cliff more than 170 m high known as Shiping ('Screen') Mountain, the three-step Sandie waterfall and, in winter, a long natural ice curtain. The ancient Hongti Pass and the Minghui Master Pagoda lie nearby.

rows.name: Weigong Temple, Xishe
rows.summary: A village temple to Li Jing, the Tang general enfeoffed as Duke of Wei, begun under the Yuan in Xishe village. A gate building with a two-storey stage, an offering hall and the main hall survive; the main hall is Yuan-dynasty work, three bays wide with a flush-gable roof and about 8 sq m of surviving murals, and the offering hall has a rounded, ridgeless roof. It was added to the national list in 2019.

rows.name: Western Zhou Tombs of the Marquises of Li
rows.summary: The cemetery of the marquises of Li, a small Zhou-period state in the Licheng area, lies beside Tapo Reservoir at Xiguan village; the national list dates the tombs from the Western Zhou to the Spring and Autumn period. On the ground there is a modern memorial park on a promontory over the reservoir, with a large gate inscribed Lihou Wangling (Tomb of the Marquis of Li), a paved plaza and rows of pillars.

rows.name: Wulong Temple, Xiangyuan
rows.summary: Wulong (Five Dragons) Temple is a small compound on the northern edge of Xiangyuan county town, of which only the main hall survives. Changzhi Daily describes the hall as a Yuan-dynasty building five bays wide with a single-eave overhanging gable roof and large bracket sets, with diagonal brackets between the columns. A rebuilding of 1350 is recorded, and the temple was later used as a store and a blacksmith's workshop.

rows.name: Xi'er River Scenic Area
rows.summary: A mountain and river-valley scenic area of about 30 sq km in the Taihang Mountains of northern Licheng County, rising to Wuzhi Mountain at about 1,500 m. Local accounts place two legendary hermits here, Xu You and Chaofu, the source of the idiom xi'er gongting ('to listen respectfully'), and the stream is known for its clear spring water. After an upgrade it reopened in August 2026 with a water-play street, rock climbing, a jungle-adventure course, go-karts and mountain guesthouses.

rows.name: Xiangyuan Confucian Temple
rows.summary: Xiangyuan Confucian Temple is the surviving core of the county's old temple of Confucius, which was founded in the Jin dynasty and repaired in 1296 under the Yuan. Its Dacheng Hall, five bays wide with a single-eave overhanging gable roof, keeps about 40 sq m of old wall paintings on its interior side walls, and a library tower also stands in the compound. The compound is small, about 23 m by 15 m, and stands about 600 m south of Wulong Temple.

rows.name: Xiantang Mountain
rows.summary: Xiantang Mountain is a scenic area in the hills north-east of Xiangyuan, centred on Xiantang Temple, a Buddhist temple traced to the Eastern Jin whose group of Ming and Qing buildings has been a provincial-level protected monument since 1996. Caves including the Nuwa Palace, Guanyin Cave and Black Dragon Cave lie among the peaks, and the slopes turn red with smoke-tree and maple foliage between mid-October and the end of November.

rows.name: Xiayu Shrine, Pingshun
rows.summary: A shrine to Yu the Great, the mythical tamer of floods, built in 1336 under the Yuan on the highest ground of Houbi village and repaired in the Ming and Qing. Its single courtyard has a gate building with an opera stage on the upper floor, a Yuan-dynasty main hall and side halls, and a projecting terrace in front of the hall carved in relief on three sides. The hall keeps a Ming stone tablet set into its wall, two Qing ones and three Ming stone offering tables.

rows.name: Xiyan Temple Pagoda, Shangdang
rows.summary: A Tang-dynasty brick pagoda in Sangzi village, Yincheng town, also known as the Zhangba Temple Pagoda. It is a square, six-storey pagoda with closely spaced eaves, about 16 m high in its surviving form, and it was repaired in 1705 under the Kangxi emperor.

rows.name: Yaowang Temple, Hanfang
rows.summary: A village temple whose name means Temple of King Yao, with a Jin-dynasty main hall and a Qing-dynasty stage in a one-courtyard compound. The hall is three bays wide with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, stone columns and five-layer bracket sets, and steles record repairs in 1218 and 1278.

rows.name: Yonghui Bridge, Xiangyuan
rows.summary: Yonghui Bridge is a single-arch stone bridge over the Gan River moat outside the north gate of Xiangyuan's old town. The county gazetteer dates it to the Jin dynasty (the 1123–1137 era), with a repair in 1471, and Changzhi Daily calls it the oldest surviving stone arch bridge in Changzhi. The balustrade slabs are carved with figures, flowers, birds and animals, and the posts are topped with stone lions and other figures.

rows.name: Yuanqi Temple
rows.summary: Yuanqi Temple is a small hilltop temple on Phoenix Hill, above the west bank of the Zhuozhang River near Xin'an village. Its main hall and a seven-storey octagonal brick pagoda, about 17 m high and dated 1087, are Song-dynasty work, while the other buildings are Ming and Qing. It belongs to a group of early timber temples in the Zhuozhang valley, which also includes Tiantai'an and Dayunyuan in neighbouring Pingshun County.

rows.name: Yuhuang Temple, Changchun
rows.summary: A Jade Emperor temple in Changchun village, Yincheng town, on two courtyards covering about 2,800 sq m. The main hall is a Song-dynasty building and the Great Buddha Hall behind it is Ming; the opera stage, gate, bell and drum towers and the other buildings are Qing, so the compound shows how local building fashions changed over the centuries. Steles record repairs in 1473, 1712 and 1770, and it became a provincial protected site in 2016 and a national one in 2019.

rows.name: Yuhuang Temple, Nansong
rows.summary: This temple to the Jade Emperor in Nansong village has a single courtyard on a south-facing axis, with a gate tower, an offering pavilion and the main hall at the back, and the gate tower and the east side hall date from the Yuan while the rest is Ming and Qing. The gate tower, the Wufeng (Five Phoenix) Tower, rises five storeys to about 29 m and is climbed by a steep inner stair cut from a single mulberry trunk. The main hall, Lingxiao Hall, has eleven oversized nine-tier bracket sets under its front eaves.

rows.name: Zhangze Lake Wetland Park
rows.name_zh: 漳泽湖国家城市湿地公园
rows.summary: A landscaped wetland park on the edge of Zhangze Reservoir, which Changzhi promotes as the 'Taihang Heavenly Pond', on the north-western side of the city. The reservoir, a large one on the south branch of the Zhuozhang River, was completed in 1960; the park has waterways, woodland, walking paths, boat rides and Chinese-garden pavilions, and is known for its summer lotus. It makes an easy outing from the city for a walk by the water.

rows.name: Zhangzi Confucian Temple
rows.summary: Zhangzi Confucian Temple is the county's old temple of Confucius, laid out in two courtyards along an axis of gate, Dacheng Hall and Minglun Hall. The Dacheng Hall, of the Yuan dynasty, is five bays wide with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, widely spaced bracket sets and glazed ridge ornaments added in the Ming. The compound stands in the grounds of the Zhangzi County Museum, and the entrance building in front is a recent copy in the old style.

rows.name: Zhaozewang Temple, Guozhuang
rows.summary: A village temple to Zhaoze King, a Tang-dynasty swordsman of Xiangyuan surnamed Jiao who was later titled king and worshipped as a spirit with power over rain. An inscription on the hall's front stone columns records its founding in 1187 under the Jin, and the Zhaoze King Hall at the back is original Jin work, three bays wide with a single-eave overhanging gable roof and glazed-tile ridges. The gate, side buildings and other halls are Qing, and the stage and the bell and drum towers survive only as foundations.

rows.name: Zhaozewang Temple, Xiangyuan
rows.summary: A temple in the south of Xiangyuan county town, also called Longdong Temple, on a single courtyard of about 170 sq m. Two buildings survive: the five-bay main hall, a Yuan-dynasty structure with a single-eave overhanging gable roof and double-ang bracket sets, and an offering hall in front of it that dates from the Ming, and a stele records a rebuilding in 1607. It is a different temple from the nationally listed Zhaoze King temple at Guozhuang village, also in Xiangyuan.

rows.name: Zhaozewang Temple, Xixiazhuang
rows.summary: A village temple at Xixiazhuang, north-west of Licheng county town, with buildings dated from the Yuan to the Qing dynasties. It was listed as a provincial protected monument in 2016 and as a national one in 2019.

rows.name: Zhengjue Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Kansi village, founded in the Tang dynasty (827–835) and rebuilt in 1070 under the Song. The five-bay rear hall, with an overhanging gable roof, deep eaves and square stone columns, is a Song survival, while the middle hall and side halls are Yuan or Ming work; a Ming stele of 1623 records village rules protecting the temple. It suits visitors interested in early timber architecture.

rows.name: Zhenru Temple, Wuxiang
rows.summary: A village temple in Tuhe village, Hanbei township, whose inscriptions record its founding in 1323 under the Yuan and repairs in 1534 and 1738. The five-bay main hall is Yuan work with an overhanging gable roof and double-ang bracket sets, and the south hall in front of it is Qing; three old pines stand in the courtyard. It became a national heritage unit in 2013.

rows.name: Zhenxing Town, Shangdang
rows.summary: A rural-tourism complex built around Zhenxing village in Shangdang District, mixing family attractions with local folk culture. It has an agricultural science-and-technology park with themed indoor gardens (a 'suspended rainforest', an insect world, a pet area), a VR 'metaverse' hall, a patriotic-education area with relief carvings of wartime episodes such as the Hundred Regiments Offensive, an adventure area with zip lines and climbing, and a night-time pedestrian street in modern 'national-trend' style.
