Holiday programmes include folk shows such as sedan-chair processions and dragon dances, and the place suits families and school groups.

rows.name: Zhenze Erxian Palace
rows.summary: This large temple complex in Shenjiao village honours the two Yue sisters, known for their filial devotion and venerated as the Two Immortals, a cult that is popular around Huguan. Founded in the Tang, it moved to its present site in 1574 and covers about 17,000 square metres, with five courtyards along a south-facing axis: a wooden memorial arch, the gate, the Dangyang Hall, a rear sleeping hall and the Holy Mother hall, flanked by side halls, bell and drum towers and a dressing tower. The Dangyang Hall is Yuan work with about 76 square metres of murals inside, and the other buildings are Ming and Qing.

rows.name: Chanfang Temple Pagoda
rows.summary: A Liao-dynasty brick pagoda of seven tiers and eight sides on the summit of Ta'er Mountain (Zhangren Peak) south-west of Datong, beside the site of the Tang-founded Chanfang Temple. It is a solid, close-eaved pagoda about 12 m high before its restoration in 2005–07, standing on a tall carved base in the Xumi-throne style typical of Liao brickwork. The temple was already abandoned by the early nineteenth century, and only the pagoda survived.

rows.name: Chehe Organic Community
rows.summary: A rural community in the hills of Hongshileng township, set up in 2013 around the villages of Upper and Lower Chehe and run as a showcase for organic farming. It has organic fields, a produce exhibition hall, a new village-style housing area, a fishing area and a valley eco-tourism zone, with oil-peony fields that flower in late spring. An international organic-agriculture forum has been held here twelve times, and the place suits visitors who want a quiet countryside stay.

rows.name: Ciyun Temple, Tianzhen
rows.summary: A Ming-dynasty Buddhist temple in the middle of Tianzhen, laid out in three courtyards on about 5,600 m², which took its present name when the Xuande emperor (1426–35) granted it. The Piluzhen Hall is the most imposing building and holds two Ming wooden cabinet-pavilions, the main hall has Ming wall paintings, and the bell and drum towers have rounded domed roofs, a form the county government calls rare in China. It draws large crowds at the Spring Festival.

rows.name: Daquanshan Ecological Tourism Area
rows.summary: A loess-hill area south of Yanggao that was once bare, gullied slopes and is now about 69% forest, held up as a national model of soil and water conservation. In 1955 Mao Zedong gave an article on the village's conservation work a new title and added a note of his own, and the scenic area has exhibition halls on that note and on soil conservation. Forest trails, the Daquanshan reservoir and Xiaolongmen are the main natural sights, and there is a visitor centre.

rows.name: Datong Drum Tower
rows.summary: A three-storey timber tower with triple eaves, standing on a stone base on Yongtai Street in the middle of Datong's old city. It was built in the Ming dynasty and repaired several times under the Qing; a drum once hung in the top storey to mark the hours at night. It has been open to visitors since 2012, and stone tablets recording the Qing repairs are kept under the lower eaves.

rows.name: Datong Mass Grave Memorial
rows.summary: A memorial museum at Meiyukou, south-west of Datong, built where the remains of miners were found in two natural caves; it records the forced labour used in the Datong coal mines during the Japanese occupation of 1937–1945. The memorial complex, which opened in its present form in 2010, covers about 337,000 square metres, and a black granite wall is inscribed with the figures for coal taken (14 million tonnes) and lives lost (60,000). The exhibition also traces the history of coal mining around Datong.

rows.name: Datong Volcanic Group
rows.summary: A field of more than 30 volcanic cones on the loess plateau in Yunzhou District, formed in the Quaternary period; the best known are Heishan, Jinshan, Langwoshan, Gelaoshan and Haotianshan. The national geological park covers 129.9 square kilometres, and the scenic area has a visitor service centre, a car park and wooden boardwalks. It suits travellers who want open, quiet scenery rather than monuments.

rows.name: Dayun Temple, Jingzhuang
rows.summary: The surviving main hall of Dayun Temple, which the 1763 county gazetteer records as a Northern Wei foundation, in the village of Jingzhuang south-west of Hunyuan. The three-bay hall dates from the Jin dynasty and stands about 8 m high under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; it was repaired under the Yuan, Ming and Qing, and its interior walls carry murals.

rows.name: Fantawild Adventure, Datong
rows.summary: A theme park on the eastern edge of Datong, one of the Fantawild chain, which opened in 2016. The Datong government's 2026 description counts more than 30 themed rides and attractions, and the park adds parades, evening shows with fireworks and seasonal events such as a summer water-splashing festival. It is aimed mainly at families with children.

rows.name: Former Shanxi Provincial Third Middle School
rows.name_zh: 山西省立第三中学旧址
rows.summary: A school campus built between 1918 and 1921 on the Shili River west of Datong, in a blend of Chinese and Western styles, and used for schools until recently. The buildings stand on a north–south axis: a gate and office building, a large auditorium shaped like a reclining elephant, twelve identical classrooms arranged in a square, and a library and laboratory at the back. Most of the original structures survive.

rows.name: Guandi Temple, Datong
rows.summary: A temple to the war god Guan Yu in the old city of Datong. Its main hall is the only Yuan-dynasty timber building in the city, with a Qing-dynasty porch added at the front. The gate, the hall of passage, the Spring and Autumn Pavilion and the side halls were rebuilt in 2008, and the opera stage in front was moved here from another site in the city.

rows.name: Guanyin Hall, Datong
rows.summary: A small Buddhist temple on a low hill west of Datong, first founded under the Liao dynasty and rebuilt in 1651 under the Qing. What survives is a screen wall, an opera stage, the main Guanyin Hall and the Sanzhen Hall. It stands just north of the road to Yungang, so it can be added to a trip to the grottoes.

rows.name: Guchengbao Han Tombs
rows.summary: A cemetery of 58 Han-dynasty mounds scattered over about 19 km² around Gucheng town in Yanggao County, the mounds about 4–6 m high and still well preserved. Japanese archaeologists dug six of the tombs in 1941 and found bronze, pottery and lacquer objects, and the burials date from the early Western Han.

rows.name: Huayan Temple, Datong
rows.summary: A large Buddhist temple in the west of Datong's old city, founded in 1038 as a royal temple of the Liao dynasty and divided into an upper and a lower temple under the Ming. The upper temple's main hall, rebuilt in 1140 under the Jin, is among the largest surviving ancient Buddhist halls in China, and the lower temple's Bhagavan Hall still holds 29 Liao-dynasty painted statues. Among them is a smiling bodhisattva with clasped hands, nicknamed the 'Oriental Venus'.

rows.name: Hunyuan Confucian Temple
rows.summary: The county's Confucian temple, founded before the Liao and Jin and rebuilt on a large scale in 1472, set on a north–south axis over about 15,580 m² in the old town of Hunyuan. The standing buildings are Ming, and the main hall, the five-bay Dacheng Hall, has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof covered in yellow and green glazed tiles.

rows.name: Jinhuagong National Mining Park
rows.summary: A former coal mine west of Datong, now a national mining park of about 36 hectares and one of the first 28 in China. Visitors can go underground into part of the old workings, and the park also has the Datong Coal Museum and an area of surface mine remains. It stands across the river from the Yungang Grottoes, so it combines easily with a visit there.

rows.name: Jueshan Temple
rows.summary: A temple founded in 483 as a Northern Wei imperial temple and rebuilt in the 1880s, whose Liao-dynasty brick pagoda survived the 1626 earthquake that brought down the rest of the compound. The thirteen-tier octagonal pagoda is 44.23 m high, with carved brick bases and a ground-floor chamber holding Liao murals, and the temple climbs the hillside in courtyards, with a cave shrine on the cliff above and a small brick pagoda on the hill to the south-west.

rows.name: Li'erkou Great Wall
rows.summary: A stretch of Ming-dynasty Great Wall built of rammed earth in the 16th century, in the hills of Tianzhen County in the far north of Shanxi. Two sections of the wall meet here in a T-shape, and the stretch is on the national list of important Great Wall sections. Li'erkou village at its foot has been restored as a small tourist village.

rows.name: Lülüshen Temple, Hunyuan
rows.summary: A shrine of the rain-bringing Lülü deity, worshipped as the Water Mother and her husband, in Shenxi village, inside the Shenxi National Wetland Park north-west of Hunyuan. It was founded under the Northern Wei, and its surviving main structures are mostly Yuan. The village around it has a Guandi temple, an old opera stage, Fengshan Academy and Ming–Qing houses.

rows.name: Mount Heng (Beiyue Hengshan)
rows.summary: Mount Heng is the northern one of China's Five Great Mountains, rising to 2,016.1 m at Tianfengling just south of Hunyuan; it took over the title of Northern Peak from a mountain in Hebei in the early Qing. Its temples, halls and pavilions are built against cliffs and in caves, and the Beiyue Temple stands high on the main peak, the only one of the five mountains' main temples built there. A cable car and walking routes serve the temple area, and the Hanging Temple on neighbouring Cuiping Peak is a separate sight.

rows.name: Nine-Dragon Wall, Datong
rows.summary: A glazed-tile screen wall decorated with nine dragons, built between 1392 and 1396 in front of the palace of Zhu Gui, the Prince of Dai and thirteenth son of the first Ming emperor. It is about 45 metres long, 8 metres high and 2 metres thick, and Chinese sources describe it as the oldest and largest surviving nine-dragon wall in the country. The dragons have four claws rather than the five reserved for the emperor, and the palace behind the wall was destroyed in the wars at the end of the Ming.

rows.name: Pingcheng Site (Northern Wei capital)
rows.summary: Pingcheng was the capital of the Northern Wei dynasty from 398 to 494, and almost all of it now lies under modern Datong. The main place to see it is the Mingtang site in a park on the south-eastern side of the city, where the rammed-earth foundations and the circular moat of a ceremonial hall are shown in a museum with a model of the Wei capital. It makes a good companion to the Yungang Grottoes, which were begun while Pingcheng was the capital.

rows.name: Pingxingguan Battle Site
rows.summary: The memorial site for the Battle of Pingxingguan of 25 September 1937, when the Eighth Route Army's 115th Division ambushed a Japanese column in the Qiaogou gully, an engagement that Chinese accounts treat as the first major Chinese victory after the full-scale war began. The site has a memorial museum with a main exhibition hall and a panorama gallery, a plaza with ten bronze statues of the commanders, and a memorial monument on a ridge about 1 km to the east; the Qiaogou gully, about 4 km long, lies nearby. The Pingxingguan pass itself, a Great Wall gate, is about 10 km away by road.

rows.name: Quhui Temple Stone Sculptures
rows.summary: A mound-like heap of stone blocks beside the ruined Quhui Temple, carved with Buddha figures in the style of the late Tang and partly covered by sand and gravel, in the village of Quhuisi on the Duyu river. The carved faces of the blocks can be seen on the outside of the heap, and the old temple itself survives only as foundations.

rows.name: Shaliangpo Han Tombs
rows.summary: A cemetery of Han-dynasty frontier garrison soldiers on the slopes south of Tianzhen, known locally as Huangliangdui. About forty earth mounds survive across roughly 70 hectares, and excavations in 1991–92 recovered bronze mirrors, ring-pommel swords and pottery jars. The mounds are the visible remains, scattered over the hillside.

rows.name: Shanhua Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple just inside the south gate of Datong's old city, popularly known as the South Temple, which keeps buildings from both the Liao and Jin dynasties. Its Daxiongbao Hall dates from the Liao and is one of the largest surviving halls of its type in China; it holds Jin-dynasty clay statues of the Five Tathagatas and the Twenty-four Devas. The gate building and the Sansheng Hall are of the Jin, and a glazed five-dragon screen wall moved here in 1980 from the former Xingguo Temple stands in front of the gate.

rows.name: Shuishen Temple, Guangling
rows.summary: A temple complex on a small hill beside the Huquan spring in the middle of Guangling, whose name covers a water-god shrine and a Buddhist hall, Dashi'an. The standing buildings are Ming and Qing and cover about 7,600 m². They include the seven-storey, six-sided Lingying Pagoda of the Qianlong period, the Holy Mother Hall built over the spring, a Wenchang Pavilion, bell and drum towers and a Laojun Hall.

rows.name: Tomb of Li Yumei
rows.summary: The walled tomb park of Li Yumei (1778–1840), a Hunyuan-born Qing river-control official remembered for his brick-dam method of flood protection, built by imperial order after his death. From the front gate a path leads past a white marble archway and ornamental columns, a stele pavilion with an inscription by Lin Zexu, and a spirit way lined with stone figures and animals to the grave mound.

rows.name: Weidu Water World, Datong
rows.summary: A large leisure complex of about 600 mu (40 hectares) on the southern edge of Datong, developed from 2015 around a water park with slides, a wave pool and a lazy river. The Datong government lists hot-spring bathing, hotel rooms, restaurants, an outdoor amusement area, a year-round ice rink and fishing among its facilities. It suits families and anyone looking for a leisure day out from the city.

rows.name: Xingguo Temple, Pingcheng
rows.summary: A former Buddhist temple in the southern part of central Datong, founded in 1619 under the Ming and repaired in 1667 and 1765. Only the main hall survives, a two-storey building with three brick-vaulted cave rooms below and a timber hall of three bays with a hip-and-gable roof above, fronted by a five-bay timber porch. The temple's glazed five-dragon screen wall was moved to Shanhua Temple in 1980.

rows.name: Yong'an Temple, Hunyuan
rows.summary: A Yuan-dynasty temple compound in the old town of Hunyuan, begun under the Jin, burned down and rebuilt in the early Yuan, with extensions and repairs under the Ming and Qing. Its main hall, the Chuanfa Zhengzong Hall, dates from 1315 and has a hip roof covered in yellow glazed tiles, and its interior walls carry large murals of the Buddhist water-and-land ritual and the ten Wisdom Kings.

rows.name: Yonggu Mausoleum
rows.summary: The tomb of Empress Dowager Feng (Wenming), the Northern Wei regent who died in 490, begun in 481 on the southern part of the Fangshan hill north of Datong. A large earth mound still covers the tomb, and the 2 km² site also preserves remains of her memorial hall, the empty 'Wannian' tomb prepared for Emperor Xiaowen, gate foundations and a Buddhist pagoda. The Datong government describes it as the only confirmed imperial cemetery of the Northern Wei's Pingcheng period.

rows.name: Yuanjue Temple Pagoda, Hunyuan
rows.summary: A nine-storey octagonal brick pagoda of 1158, over 30 m high, in the old town of Hunyuan, known locally as the Little Temple Pagoda. Its base is carved with lions, lotus petals and rows of musicians and dancers, and the upper tiers imitate timber brackets and eaves. The iron phoenix on top still turns with the wind, a rare surviving ancient wind-direction indicator.

rows.name: Yunlin Temple, Yanggao
rows.summary: A Ming-dynasty temple built by imperial decree in the south-west of Yanggao old town, locally called the West Temple, of which the main hall, the Heavenly Kings Hall and side halls survive. The five-bay main hall has twelve carved lattice doors across its front, 25 Ming clay figures and 123 groups of wall paintings on three walls.

rows.name: Baiyu Palace
rows.summary: A temple at Jiaodi village, laid out in three courtyards along a south-facing axis about 100 m long, entered through a stage building that serves as the gate. The oldest hall is Jin-dynasty, three bays wide with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, and inscriptions record repairs in 1212, 1544 and the Republican period; the other buildings are Ming and Qing.

rows.name: Beima Yuhuang Temple
rows.summary: A village temple to the Jade Emperor in Beima village, Fucheng town, in a single courtyard of about 860 sq m. The main hall is Jin-dynasty, five bays wide with an overhanging gable roof; the county government notes that its size and the number of bracket projections are rare in Lingchuan. The gate and the other buildings are Ming and Qing, and the temple became a national monument in 2013.

rows.name: Beiyicheng Yuhuang Temple
rows.summary: A village temple to the Jade Emperor whose main hall is an original Song-dynasty building, renovated in 1110. The offering hall, side halls, stage building and rooms around the courtyard are mostly of later date. The main hall is three bays wide and deep, with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof and simple bracket sets under the eaves.

rows.name: Biluo Temple
rows.summary: Biluo Temple is a Buddhist temple built into the hillside at the foot of Biluo Mountain, founded in the Northern Qi and laid out in east, middle and west courtyards. Surviving remains include a Northern Qi grotto, two Tang-dynasty grottoes, more than ten Tang and Wu Zhou niches, two Ming stone bridges and over a hundred inscriptions and steles. It was once ranked first of the four great old temples of Zezhou, and its view of clouds on the mountain is first among Zezhou's eight views.

rows.name: Chong'an Temple, Lingchuan
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in the middle of Lingchuan county town, given its present name by imperial order in the 970s. A two-storey gate tower with triple eaves, a five-bay through-hall and the five-bay main hall stand on the main axis, with a two-storey side tower to the west, all Yuan to Qing in date. The temple keeps many stelae from the Tang to the Qing dynasty that record its history.

rows.name: Chongming Temple, Gaoping
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in a hill valley, laid out in two courtyards, whose central hall was begun in 971 in the early Northern Song. The hall has deep eaves on large seven-tier bracket sets and no interior columns, and its main beams are each made of two equal short timbers joined end to end, a construction rare among surviving Chinese timber buildings. The rear hall, repaired in 1591, has stone column bases at its front carved with mounted warriors.

rows.name: Chongshou Temple, Zezhou
rows.summary: Chongshou Temple is a Buddhist temple in Xigao village, Bagong township, recorded as a Northern Song-dynasty building. It has been a provincial monument since 1986 and a national one since 2019, and the national register dates its buildings from the Northern Song to the Qing.

rows.name: Chuandi Buddhist Hall
rows.summary: Chuandi Buddhist Hall is a tiny one-courtyard temple of about 233 sq m in Chuandi village, with a main hall, a gate and two side rooms. The three-bay main hall keeps many Jin-dynasty timber members, with Yuan-style bracket sets under the eaves of its single-eave hip-and-gable roof, and a stele of 1332 records a Yuan repair.

rows.name: Cuifujun Temple, Lingchuan
rows.summary: Cuifujun Temple, also called Xianying Wang Temple, is a two-courtyard temple on a raised platform in Liyi town, dedicated to Cui Fujun (Cui Jue), a Tang-dynasty magistrate whom local people worshipped. Its axis runs from a double-eave gate building through an opera stage and an offering hall to the Fujun Hall; the gate is of the Song–Jin period and the other buildings are Ming and Qing. It was repaired in 1184 and again in 1369 and the late Qing.

rows.name: Dayang Ancient Town
rows.summary: The old town of Dayang, famous in the Ming and Qing for hand-made needles and a national historic and cultural town since 2008. It has many official and merchant houses, towers, bridges and temples, and the scenic area adds folk performances such as yangge dancing, iron-flower displays and paper-cutting, with an evening market and light shows.

rows.name: Dazhou Village Temples
rows.summary: A group of six buildings spread through Dazhou village, dating from the Song to the Qing and listed as a national heritage unit in 2013: Zisheng Temple, Tangwang (King Tang) Temple, Yuandi (Zhenwu) Pavilion, Wuhu Temple, Baizi Bridge and a brick pagoda. The middle hall of Zisheng Temple is a Song building with deep eaves and a gently sloping hip-and-gable roof, and the main hall of Tangwang Temple, five bays wide, is Yuan.

rows.name: Diji Fortress
rows.summary: Diji Fortress is a walled settlement begun in 1638 on a rise in the Qin River, oval in plan and about 2.4 hectares in area, with a water gate to the river on the north and a land gate on the south. Its walls are built of brick and stone together with discarded iron-smelting crucibles, and carry watchtowers, gun ports and troop shelters. Inside are lanes, courtyard houses of two or three storeys, temples and a garden, and it is now run as a scenic area with folk performances in holiday periods.

rows.name: Dinglin Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple halfway up a wooded hillside, with a two-storey gate pavilion, Leiyin Hall and Qifo Hall on its main axis. Leiyin Hall was rebuilt in 1317 and the gate pavilion has an octagonal caisson ceiling hung with thirteen carved lotus posts, while Dizang Hall keeps Ming murals of the ten kings of hell dated 1525. Two old tree peonies in the east courtyard flower in spring, around April.

rows.name: Douzhuang Fortified Village
rows.summary: Douzhuang is a village on a bend of the Qin River that was fortified in the Tianqi era (1621–27) by Zhang Wudian, a Ming minister of war, and people still live in it. An old quarter of about 4 ha survives, mostly intact, with some 500 m of wall, a south gate and a small north gate, courtyard houses, temples, ancestral halls, a drill ground, a courtroom and prison cells; the oldest hall belongs to a Yuan-dynasty Buddhist temple.

rows.name: Erlang Temple, Wangbao
rows.summary: A temple to the god Erlang on a hillock north of Wangbao village, with a stage, an offering hall and a main hall in one courtyard. The small square stage at the front, built over the entrance, was put up in 1183 according to an inscription on its stone base, and is regarded as the oldest surviving opera stage in China. Its roof rests directly on bracket sets without beams, while the offering hall and main hall behind it are Ming and Qing.

rows.name: Fucheng Guandi Temple
rows.summary: A temple to Guan Yu (Guandi), the god of war and loyalty, in Fucheng village, founded in 1633 and repaired several times in the Qianlong era; it was listed as a national heritage unit in 2013 and is now laid out as a small park with a filial-piety gallery. It is known for its stone pillars: four tall pillars wound with openwork dragons stand before the main hall, and the pillars of the rear hall are carved with hundreds of figures from history and myth.

rows.name: Fucheng Yuhuang Temple
rows.summary: The Yuhuang (Jade Emperor) Temple at Fucheng is a Taoist temple of four courtyards climbing a hillside, founded in 1076 and rebuilt mainly in the Yuan dynasty, with halls from the Song to the Qing. It holds more than 260 painted clay figures of the Taoist pantheon, best known for the Yuan-dynasty Twenty-Eight Mansions, the star deities shown as human figures with animal features, and it is run as a museum.

rows.name: Fushan Village
rows.summary: Fushan, in Sizhuang town, is a village restored for tourism around old Qing-dynasty courtyards, a Confucian temple and a reservoir with boats and a floating bridge. Newer additions include a park of old pear trees, a coin museum and a pedestrian shopping street built in the style of 1978, so it suits a relaxed half-day rather than a monument visit.

rows.name: Gaodu Jingde Temple
rows.summary: Jingde Temple is a two-courtyard Buddhist temple of about 3,400 sq m in Nanjie village, founded in 572 and long counted among the four great old temples of Zezhou. Its rear hall (the Fatang), first built in 1087 and repaired in 1205, keeps four of its six octagonal front columns from the Song, with a timber frame in Jin manner and a roof edged with Ming green-glazed ridge ornaments. The village is part of Gaodu old town, a historic town with Ming and Qing courtyard houses.

rows.name: Guobi Old Fortified Village
rows.summary: Guobi is an old market village on the west bank of the Qin River, with Ming and Qing courtyard houses (some 3,400 rooms), cave dwellings, seven temples, towers and ancestral halls, including eleven residences of jinshi graduates. It also keeps a stretch of rammed-earth wall that local people describe as the only one left among Jincheng's castle-villages.

rows.name: Guoyu Walled Town
rows.summary: A walled Ming-era market village a short walk from Huangcheng Xiangfu, enclosed by a wall about 1.4 km round and 12 m high on average, begun in 1635, with cave-like chambers built into it. Inside are about forty Ming and Qing courtyard houses, the seven-storey Yu Tower, 33 m high, and a Tangdi temple with a nine-bay main hall.

rows.name: Guzhong Temple
rows.summary: A temple to the legendary farmer-god Emperor Yan (Yandi, Shennong), once called the Shennong Crown Prince Shrine, in Zhongmiao village. Its Taizi Hall of 1361 is a one-bay Yuan building with no roof beams, hence its local name, the beamless hall, and its octagonal caisson ceiling is built up from bracket sets like an open umbrella or lotus. The other halls are Qing, and an opera stage and viewing galleries stand outside the main gate.

rows.name: Haihui Temple and Academy
rows.summary: Haihui Temple, at the foot of Dongfan Mountain, is known for its pair of brick pagodas: an early-10th-century pagoda that leans to the west and a Ming pagoda of 1565 with a glazed-tile balcony on its tenth level. Around them are the temple halls, springs and pools, among them the 'Haihui Longqiu' water view, and the site of Haihui Academy, where 68 of the 123 jinshi graduates recorded for Yangcheng studied in Ming and Qing times. The temple has been a national heritage site since 2006.

rows.name: Hedi Chengtang Temple
rows.summary: Hedi Chengtang Temple is a one-courtyard temple to Chengtang, King Tang of the Shang, built up the slope in rising terraces at the edge of Hedi village. Its main hall dates from 1108, the year inscribed on its stone door frame and columns, and a Song stele records a rebuilding between 1107 and 1120; the stone terrace walls on the west and south sides preserve Tang-style work. Ming and Qing steles record later repairs.

rows.name: Huaitan Guild Hall
rows.summary: A merchants' guild hall built in 1793–1802 by traders from three prefectures of northern Henan (Zhangde, Weihui and Huaiqing) who dealt in flour and cloth in the prefecture of Zezhou, now central Jincheng. Only the offering hall, main hall, flanking halls and side halls survive, the offering hall being a square building with a hip-and-gable roof and fine carving; the rest was lost after the site was damaged in the Cultural Revolution and turned into a factory.

rows.name: Ji Family House, Zhongzhuang
rows.summary: A single small house in Zhongzhuang village, built in 1294 under the Yuan dynasty and dated by an inscription. It is three bays wide with a single-eave gable roof, on a plot of about 98 square metres. Gaoping's government describes it as the earliest dwelling found in China with an exact date, which makes it a reference point for dating Chinese houses.

rows.name: Jiaxiang Temple, Gaoping
rows.summary: Jiaxiang Temple is a two-courtyard Buddhist temple about 50 m west of Chixiang village, with a Jin-dynasty front hall, a Yuan-dynasty middle hall (the Vairocana Hall) and later side buildings. The middle hall's walls carry Ming water-and-land ritual paintings, and two bluestone sutra pillars stand in front of it, one of them inscribed with a date of 953 in the Later Zhou. It has been a national monument since 2013.

rows.name: Jidu Temple, Jiannan
rows.summary: Jidu Temple at Jiannan stands on the top of Cuiping Mountain, a three-courtyard temple to the god of the Ji River with a gate, an offering hall, a middle hall and a rear hall, bell and drum towers and side halls. The middle and rear halls are Yuan, both five bays wide, and large murals survive on the back wall of the middle hall; the other buildings are Ming and Qing. A Jin-style stone base survives at the second gate.

rows.name: Jidu Temple, Xidun
rows.summary: Jidu Temple at Xidun is a one-courtyard temple to the god of the Ji River, one of the four great rivers of old Chinese tradition with the Yangtze, Yellow and Huai. Inscriptions show that work began in 1122 under the Song and was completed only in 1188 under the Jin, after a gap caused by war; the main hall has octagonal stone front columns and a single-eave overhanging-gable roof. A local enthusiast found it in 2009, and in 2011 it was named one of the 100 new discoveries of the third national survey of cultural relics.

rows.name: Jincheng Erxian Temple
rows.summary: A Song-dynasty temple to the two Yue sisters, local deities of south-east Shanxi, laid out in two courtyards in Xiaonan village. A stele of 1117 records that building began in 1097, and the main hall is the only Northern Song building left in the complex. Inside stand sixteen Song painted clay figures and a finely made miniature timber shrine with pavilions and a rainbow bridge.

rows.name: Kaifu Temple, Yangcheng
rows.summary: Kaifu Temple is an old Buddhist temple in Yangcheng county town, where a Jin-style scripture pavilion, a Yuan-style main hall and a Ming-style stage survive. In 1938–39 it was the headquarters of the Eighth Route Army's Jin-Yu border guerrilla detachment, and Zhu De and Peng Dehuai stayed there on journeys through Yangcheng. The county lists it on its red-tourism routes.

rows.name: Kaihua Temple, Gaoping
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple on the wooded slope of Sheli Mountain, whose main hall (Daxiong Hall) was begun in 1073. Its east, west and north walls are covered with Northern Song murals painted between 1092 and 1096, showing scenes from Buddhist sutras alongside everyday life of the period, and the beams and brackets still carry Song painted decoration. A Jin-dynasty Guanyin pavilion and Yuan side halls stand in the compound.

rows.name: Lianghu Ancient Village
rows.summary: Lianghu is a Taihang village of Ming and Qing courtyard houses in the Dan River valley, a China Historic and Cultural Village since 2007, now run as a heritage site with a guesthouse in restored courtyards. The sights include the Shilang (vice-minister's) Mansion, home of the official Tian Fengji, with its screen wall and carved brick, stone and wood, and Yuxu Temple, a Taoist temple with Yuan-dynasty halls that is a national heritage site.

rows.name: Lishan, Qinshui
rows.summary: The Qinshui side of the Lishan range in the Zhongtiao Mountains, a national nature reserve and forest park of about 204 square kilometres with forest, cave systems, alpine meadow and canyon scenery. Its main peak, Shunwangping, rises to 2,358 m and is named for the sage-king Shun, whom Chinese tradition places farming on Mount Li.

rows.name: Liu Family Houses, Xiwenxing
rows.summary: A hillside village of courtyard houses where the Liu clan, who trace their descent to the Tang writer Liu Zongyuan, have lived for centuries. Most of the surviving buildings are Qing, built on the clan's salt and pawnbroking wealth, and the best preserved, Sima Di, is a two-courtyard house with a two-storey main hall and two Ming stone memorial archways in its yard. The village is a national historic and cultural village.

rows.name: Longyan Temple, Lingchuan
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Liangquan village, laid out in an upper and a lower courtyard on a plot of about 1,900 sq m. The through-hall was built in 1129 under the Jin dynasty and is three bays square with a single-eave overhanging gable roof, while the main hall, side halls and other buildings are Ming. It began as Longquan Temple, a place where villagers prayed for rain, and took its present name in 1162.

rows.name: Mang River Scenic Area
rows.summary: A forested gorge area on the Shanxi–Henan border, set up as a national nature reserve and forest park mainly to protect rhesus macaques and subtropical plants, and nicknamed the 'little Guilin of the north'. Streams run through the gorges as waterfalls, pools and rapids beside the walking paths, and the wild macaques, which are often seen along the paths, are the main draw.

rows.name: Mount Jue
rows.summary: A steep twin-peaked hill on the south bank of the Dan River, climbed by a long flight of stone steps through successive gates to temple halls near the summit, built from the Song dynasty onwards. The scenic area also runs a river sports centre on the Dan with speedboats, bamboo rafts and similar rides. Qinglian Temple, with Tang-dynasty clay figures, lies at the foot of the mountain and is usually visited with it.

rows.name: Nanshentou Erxian Temple
rows.summary: A small temple to the two Yue sisters in a fold of the hills south of Shigeluan village in Lingchuan County, built as a single courtyard. The main hall, on a stone platform, is a Jin-dynasty building with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, and about 20 square metres of Qing wall paintings survive on its side walls, partly flaked. The stage at the front is now only a foundation, and the other buildings are later.

rows.name: Nanzhao Confucian Temple
rows.summary: A Confucian temple in Nanzhao village, built in a single courtyard of about 900 sq m. The five-bay main hall, on a stone platform, is Yuan-dynasty work with an overhanging gable roof, while the stage building that serves as the gate and the other buildings are Ming and Qing, and steles record repairs in 1389 and 1824. It became a provincial monument in 2004 and a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Qinghua Temple, Tuandong
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in the middle of Tuandong village, founded in the Tang dynasty according to surviving fragments of stelae and repaired under the Yuan, Ming and Qing. It once had four courtyards; three main courtyards and two side courtyards remain, with Rulai (Tathagata) Hall, Sanfo Hall and Qifo Hall on the axis. Only Rulai Hall is Yuan, a three-bay building with a glazed ridge, and the other halls are Ming and Qing.

rows.name: Qinglian Temple
rows.summary: Qinglian Temple, founded in the Northern Qi dynasty, stands on the lower slope of Xiashi Mountain in two courts, the lower and upper temples, joined by a mountain path of about 500 m. The lower temple's Maitreya Hall holds six Tang-dynasty painted clay figures, among the few Tang temple sculptures to survive in China, with a 4.2 m Maitreya seated with both legs hanging; the upper temple keeps Song-dynasty timber halls and sculpture. The temple is run as an ancient-architecture museum.

rows.name: Qingmeng Daoist Temple, Gaoping
rows.summary: A Daoist temple in Tielu village, recorded on its stelae as founded in 1261, with two courtyards on a north-south axis. The Sanqing Hall at the centre is a Yuan building whose walls are painted with figures of Yin Xi and Zhang Daoling on the south wall and a sequence of scenes from the life of Laozi on the other three. The rear hall was rebuilt in the Ming dynasty and the remaining buildings are Qing.

rows.name: Quanshen Temple, Tianzhuang
rows.summary: A village temple to "all the gods" in Tianzhuang village, with a stage building, a main hall, side halls and a bell tower. The main hall is Yuan in style, three bays wide with an overhanging gable roof, and the east side hall keeps wall paintings of the Eight Immortals gathering. A tablet of 1611 records a Ming-dynasty restoration.

rows.name: Runcheng Dongyue Temple
rows.summary: Runcheng Dongyue Temple is a temple to the Dongyue god in Runcheng village, with Song-dynasty origins and a rebuilding of 1593 recorded on its steles. Of what was once a three-courtyard complex, an offering pavilion, the Tianqi Hall and a two-storey rear hall remain, all in Ming style; the pavilion stands on a platform ringed with stone railings carved with lions and monkeys. It lies a short walk from the walled settlement of Diji Fortress.

rows.name: Sanjiao Hall, Sirun
rows.summary: A small temple to the "three teachings" of Buddhism, Daoism and Confucianism in Sirun village, of which only the main hall survives. The hall is a Jin-dynasty building, square in plan and three bays on each side, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof and a veranda round the lower storey. Inside, diagonal beams set at 45 degrees at the corners carry the upper roof structure.

rows.name: Sansheng Ruixian Pagoda
rows.summary: A square, thirteen-tier brick pagoda of the Jin dynasty with closely stacked eaves, about 30 m high and 6 m along each side at the base, standing in the Zhaoqing Yuan temple compound in Jishan village. An inscription on its third floor records that a stone tortoise holding a relic, marked with a Sui-dynasty date of 601, was dug up on the site in 1166, and that the pagoda was then built over it and finished in 1169. The tower is hollow inside, and Jishan is on the national list of historic villages.

rows.name: Sanzong Temple, Sanwang
rows.summary: A temple to the mythical archer Hou Yi, worshipped in south-east Shanxi as Sanzong, on a slope south of Sanwang village. The main hall is a Jin-dynasty building with a front veranda and carved stone column bases; the gate building, offering hall and side halls are later, and a small patriarch hall stands in a side courtyard. Repairs are recorded under the Song dynasty in 1119–25.

rows.name: Shicun Dongyue Temple
rows.summary: A village temple to the Dongyue god, the Eastern Peak deity of Mount Tai, in Shicun, Xiacun township. It was listed as a national monument in 2013, with buildings that the register dates from the Yuan to the Qing dynasty. It is one of several Dongyue temples around Zezhou on the national list, among them those at Zhoucun and Yinxi.

rows.name: Shizhang Yuhuang Temple
rows.summary: A village temple to the Jade Emperor in Shizhang village, Lingchuan County, listed as a national heritage unit in 2006. The main hall is Jin-dynasty, three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof and a porch along the front; the gate, side halls and other buildings are Ming and Qing.

rows.name: Shousheng Temple and Glazed Pagoda, Yangcheng
rows.summary: Shousheng Temple is a Buddhist temple in Yangling village, Qinchi township, known for its glazed brick pagoda, recorded as built in 1608. It has been a provincial monument since 1986 and a national one since 2019. The village has been developing the site for visitors, with a visitor centre, a heritage display hall and a car park listed in a 2026 state-media report.

rows.name: Shuidong Cuifujun Temple
rows.summary: Shuidong Cuifujun Temple is a village temple to Cui Fujun, a Tang-dynasty magistrate whom villagers worshipped as a deity, listed as a national monument in 2013 with buildings dated from the Yuan to the Qing dynasty. The county tourism page counts it among the five national monuments of Jincun township, together with Qinglian Temple and Yuhuang Temple. A conservation project for the temple was tendered in 2022.

rows.name: Situ Town
rows.summary: A tourist town in the north-east of Jincheng, built in Ming and Qing street style, with restaurants, shops, craft workshops, amusement rides and stage shows. It is best known for the Situ iron-flower show, a folk fire display in which molten iron is struck against a wooden structure to throw sparks; a 2024 performance with 108 participants was recognised by Guinness World Records as the largest of its kind.

rows.name: South and North Jixiang Temples
rows.summary: Two Buddhist temples about 2 km apart in Liyi township, listed together as a single national monument. South Jixiang Temple, in Pingchuan village, dates from the Tang according to its steles and has a Song-dynasty middle hall of timber with bracket sets that include diagonal arms, and a Yuan rear hall. North Jixiang Temple, in Xijie village, was founded in 773 according to its steles, was given its name by imperial decree in 978, and keeps buildings from the Song to the Qing.

rows.name: Tangdi Temple, Dayang
rows.summary: A temple to Tang, the founder of the Shang dynasty, in the old town of Dayang, built in two courtyards on about 3,000 square metres. The main hall, Chengtang Hall, is a Yuan-dynasty building with an unusually wide central bay; the opera stage, gates and side halls are Ming and Qing.

rows.name: Tangdi Temple, Pingshang
rows.summary: A village temple to Tang, the founder of the Shang dynasty, in Pingshang village in Zhoucun town. The surviving buildings date from the Ming and Qing periods, and the temple joined the national list in 2013.

rows.name: Tangdi Temple, Xiajiao
rows.summary: A village temple to Tang, the founder of the Shang dynasty, in the north of Xiajiao village. Inscriptions record it as complete by 1116 and rebuilt in 1211; the worship hall is Jin-dynasty work, while the main hall and the opera building are Ming or Qing. More than twenty Ming and Qing stone tablets are kept in the halls.

rows.name: Tanlingtou Dai Temple
rows.summary: Tanlingtou Dai Temple stands on a mound north of Tanlingtou village in Beiyicheng township, listed as a national monument in 2013 with buildings dated to the Jin and Qing dynasties. Dai is an old name for Mount Tai, and temples of this type honour the Mount Tai god in the same way as the Dongyue temples nearby.

rows.name: Tianguan Wang Mansion
rows.summary: Tianguan Wang Mansion is a cluster of old houses in Shangzhuang village associated with Wang Guoguang, a Ming minister of personnel (the 'tianguan' of the name), and opened to visitors in 2012. Dwellings from the Yuan, Ming, Qing and Republican periods stand together, with an old Ming plum tree, a courtyard estate in mixed Chinese and Western style and an exhibition on Wang Guoguang. Costumed role-play shows and lantern tours at night are staged for visitors.

rows.name: Tiefo Temple, Gaoping
rows.summary: Tiefo (Iron Buddha) Temple is a one-courtyard temple in Mixi village, known for the Ming-dynasty painted clay figures in its main hall: a Buddha with two bodhisattvas, the Twenty-Four Devas ranged along the side walls and a hanging sculpture of scenes from Journey to the West behind. A doorstone inscription records the casting of an iron Buddha in 1167, and the temple holds more than thirty Ming figures in all. It drew crowds after 2024 as one of the real-world sites linked to the video game Black Myth: Wukong.

rows.name: Wangmangling
rows.summary: Wangmangling is a cliff-edged part of the southern Taihang range on the Shanxi–Henan border, and the scenic area covers four zones, Wangmangling, Xiyagou, Kunshan and Liuxiu City, falling from about 1,700 m to about 300 m. Paths and viewing points overlook precipices, gorges and caves, and the area is known for sunrise and sea-of-cloud views and, in winter, rime on the trees.

rows.name: Wanshou Palace, Dongfeng
rows.summary: A temple to the local holy woman Ma Xiangu, known as Shenggu, in Shang Dongfeng village, founded in 1284 according to an inscription. The Sanjiao Hall and the ancestral hall (Shenggu Hall) are Yuan timber buildings, with traces of Yuan Daoist wall paintings in the Sanjiao Hall, while the other buildings, including an opera stage and a stone pavilion, are Ming and Qing. More than twenty stelae of the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties stand in the compound.

rows.name: Xiangyu Old Fortress
rows.summary: A fortified village on a hillside above a stream, built for the Sun family, three brothers who held senior posts under the late Ming, and completed in 1634. The outer wall, about 760 m round and 5 to 25 m high, has tiers of vaulted soldiers' caves that earned it the name "honeycomb city", and inside are three gates, stone-paved lanes of Ming and Qing courtyard houses and a five-storey watchtower about 25 m high. It belongs to the group of castle villages in the Qin River valley for which Jincheng is known.

rows.name: Xianweng Temple, Bofang
rows.summary: A Daoist temple in Bofang village dedicated to Zhang Guolao, one of the Eight Immortals, built as a single courtyard with a gate, a tower, an offering hall and the main hall. The main hall is a five-bay Ming building, and its east, west and north walls carry Ming murals of a Daoist procession of deities and of the Tang emperor Xuanzong performing sacrifices on Mount Tai. The temple also keeps many stelae recording its repairs.

rows.name: Xiaohuiling Erxian Temple
rows.summary: A temple to the two Yue sisters on a ridge about 800 m south-east of Xiaohui village, built as a single courtyard about 50 m by 25 m. The main hall is a Song-dynasty building with heavy timbers and a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, standing behind a Qing offering hall and a gate building that doubles as a stage; the side halls are Ming or Qing. Six stone tablets are kept in the temple.

rows.name: Xicheng Mountain
rows.summary: Xicheng Mountain is a karst summit on the north-west side of the Wangwu range, where a ring of cliffs with four gaps like city gates encloses a bowl of subalpine meadow, a landscape that is rare in northern China; the main peak is about 1,888 m. The meadow, called Shengwangping, has sinkholes, a spring pool called Yaochi and sites linked to the Shang founder Tang's rain prayers and to ancient sky-watching, and it held its first flower festival in June and July 2026.

rows.name: Xilimen Erxian Temple
rows.summary: A temple to the two Yue sisters in Xilimen village, built round two courtyards covering 2,748 square metres. It was founded in the Tang dynasty and heavily repaired in 1157 and 1162; the middle hall dates from 1157 under the Jin dynasty and has a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, while the gate, rear hall and side halls are Ming or Qing. Two carved panels on the stone terrace in front of the middle hall, one of a scarf dancer and one of actors in a stage scene, are counted among the earliest surviving pictures of Chinese drama.

rows.name: Xixi Erxian Temple
rows.summary: A temple to the two Yue sisters, also called Zhenze Palace, in a wooded valley just outside Lingchuan, with its back to a stream instead of the usual hill behind and water in front. Sixteen buildings from the Jin to the Qing stand in two courtyards; the rear hall and the two-storey dressing towers on either side are Jin-dynasty work, and 29 stone tablets include one carved with a poem by the Jin-dynasty writer Yuan Haowen. Old cypresses beside the offering hall have knots that local people read as the twelve zodiac animals.

rows.name: Xuansheng Temple, Shimo
rows.summary: A Confucian temple in the middle of Shimo village, founded in 1304. The main hall is a Yuan building with a yellow-and-green glazed ridge, and the two-storey gate building at the front doubles as an opera stage. Two Yuan stelae, dated 1304 and 1326, still stand in the temple.

rows.name: Xuezhuang Yuhuang Temple
rows.summary: A village temple to the Jade Emperor on the north-west side of Xuezhuang village, with buildings that range from the Yuan to the Qing dynasty. It was listed as a national heritage unit in 2013 and is one of several Jade Emperor temples of the Jincheng area, which also include the larger temple at Fucheng.

rows.name: Yandi Mausoleum, Gaoping
rows.summary: The Yandi Mausoleum at Zhuangli village is one of four places in China that hold a tomb of Yandi, the legendary Emperor Yan or Shennong, remembered as the teacher of farming and herbal medicine. A large temple compound stands around the tomb mound, beside the older Wugu Temple, and the site has a stele dated 1611 that is the earliest known marker of the tomb. Memorial ceremonies are held here, including a yearly folk-culture exchange event that brings visitors from Taiwan.

rows.name: Yangcheng Confucian Temple
rows.summary: Yangcheng Confucian Temple is a two-courtyard temple in the south-east of the old county town, first built in the Song, rebuilt in the Ming and repaired in 1839 after its main hall was destroyed in 1689. Only the Confucius temple and some twenty other rooms survive, in Ming and Qing style. In 1946 it served as the headquarters of the Taiyue military region.

rows.name: Yangtou Mountain and Grottoes
rows.summary: Yangtou Mountain rises to about 1,300 m where Gaoping meets Changzhi, and local tradition places Yandi's first sowing of grain here; the scenic area marks the sites of his legendary town, spring, well and field plot, with a lake and a ceremonial square at the foot. Halfway up the southern flank are the Yangtoushan Grottoes, a national heritage site and the largest group of Buddhist carving in Jincheng, with dozens of small caves and niches cut into sandstone blocks from the Northern Wei to the Tang dynasty. Stone stupas and a Northern Wei carved stone with a sheep-shaped base stand on the ridge above.

rows.name: Yinxi Dongyue Temple
rows.summary: Yinxi Dongyue Temple is a village temple to the Dongyue god on the east side of Yinxi village, Beiyicheng township, listed as a national monument in 2013. The register dates its buildings from the Jin to the Qing dynasty, and its main hall is the Tianqi Hall, the usual name for the hall of the Dongyue god.

rows.name: Youxian Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple laid out in three courtyards up a hillside, with a gate, the Chunqiu Tower, and Pilu, Sanfo and Qifo halls on its axis. Pilu Hall is a Northern Song building of 990, with a carved Song-dynasty Buddha platform inside, and Sanfo Hall is a Jin-dynasty building overhauled under the Yuan; the other buildings are Ming and Qing. Its setting between hill and stream, with the "dawn bell" of Youxian, was counted among the old eight views of Gaoping.

rows.name: Yuhuang Temple, Nanzhuang
rows.summary: A temple to the Jade Emperor on a hill beside Nanzhuang village, built in an upper and a lower courtyard up the slope. The main hall is a Yuan-dynasty building with a single-eave overhanging gable roof, main beams made of unsawn logs and slanting bracket arms, while the other buildings are Qing in style. Inscriptions record repairs under the Tang and Jin dynasties and later.

rows.name: Yuquan Dongyue Temple
rows.summary: Yuquan Dongyue Temple is a single-courtyard temple of about 2,400 sq m on the east side of Yuquan village, laid out along one axis with a stage-gate building, a prayer hall and the main hall, flanked by side towers and rooms. The main hall is Jin-dynasty, the gate Ming and the other buildings Qing, and steles record repairs in 1579, 1660, 1770, 1832 and 2004.

rows.name: Zezhou Dai Temple
rows.summary: Zezhou Dai Temple is a hillside temple to the Mount Tai god in Yedi village, which holds national-level status as a historic and cultural village. The compound of about 3,700 sq m steps up the slope in two yards; its Tianqi Hall is Song-dynasty work, with stone pillar inscriptions dated 1080, and the other halls are Ming and Qing. Its grounds also hold an old opera stage, a large ginkgo, two cypresses joined in a V shape and stone carvings of dragons.

rows.name: Zhongping Erxian Palace
rows.summary: A temple to the two Yue sisters on the south slope of Cuiping hill, north-west of Zhongping village. It was first built in the Tang dynasty and repaired in 1172, and the main hall is a Jin-dynasty building three bays wide and three deep with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof. The gate building doubles as an opera stage facing the courtyard, and the side towers and other halls are from later periods.

rows.name: Zhoucun Dongyue Temple
rows.summary: Zhoucun Dongyue Temple stands on a high platform on the north side of Zhoucun, with five halls in a row at the back joined by long covered corridors, and a stage building flanked by bell and drum towers facing the main hall across the courtyard. The central Dongyue Hall is Song-dynasty work, rebuilt in the early 1080s, with four octagonal blue-stone columns across its front; the two halls beside it are Ming and the stage building Qing. Other temples that once stood beside it, including a Confucian temple, have gone, leaving it as the local landmark.

rows.name: Anchan Temple
rows.summary: A temple in the old town of Taigu, founded in 857 under the Tang, of which two buildings survive. The Sutra Hall is an original Northern Song building of 1001, nearly square, three bays by three, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the rear hall dates from the Ming.

rows.name: Baiyun Temple, Liangjiatan
rows.summary: A hillside temple on Baofeng Mountain west of Liangjiatan village, founded in the Tang dynasty and anciently called Xiyu Temple, built along the slope and cliff over about 7,800 sq m. The surviving buildings, dated by the national list from the Ming to the Republican period, include the gate, Heavenly Kings, Weituo, Dizang, Guanyin and Ancient Buddha halls and the main hall, with a pagoda grove of six tombs of senior monks east of the temple. Two old locust trees and nine ancient cypresses stand in front of the gate.

rows.name: Cao Family Mansion
rows.summary: The mansion of the Cao family, a Jin merchant family, in Beiguang village, also called Sanduotang. It was built in stages from the late Ming into the Qing and covers about 98 m by 108 m, with three large courtyards side by side divided into fifteen small ones, and a west garden with an underground kitchen. It suits visitors who have seen the Qiao or Wang compounds and want to compare merchant house design.

rows.name: Chang Family Manor
rows.summary: The fortified manor of the Chang family, Qing-dynasty merchants who traded tea to Russia, in Chewang village south-west of Yuci. A stone-paved street runs through it past restored courtyard houses, a family temple, the Shiyunxuan study with carved stone tablets, and a large landscaped garden known as Jingyuan. Carved stone and brick, such as the Fish Leaps the Dragon Gate relief at the west gate, reward a slow visit.

rows.name: Chongjiao Temple, Xiyang
rows.summary: A small temple in the north of Xiyang county town, founded in 1069 under the Northern Song and grouped with Shousheng Temple as the "North Temples" by 1381. Four halls joined around one courtyard survive: front and rear halls five bays wide with hip-and-gable roofs and bracketed eaves, and two three-bay side halls. The national listing dates the surviving halls to the Yuan dynasty.

rows.name: Chongsheng Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple on Chanyin Mountain in Shangchiyu village, founded in the Tang dynasty, renamed Chongsheng in the Northern Song and rebuilt under the Jin. It has an upper and a lower courtyard, with a gate, a through-hall and the main hall on the central axis; the main hall dates from the Jin and was repaired in 1349. Two Yuan stone pagodas and a Ming solid brick pagoda stand in the grounds, with a Bailong shrine to the east and an opera stage to the south.

rows.name: Cisheng Temple, Xiangyuan
rows.summary: A village temple in Xiangyuan with two courtyards, an opera stage and the main hall on its central axis, and meditation courtyards on either side. A stele records its rebuilding in 1332 under the Yuan, and it was repaired in 1790 and 1835 under the Qing. The main hall is a Ming-dynasty building three bays wide, and the opera stage is Qing.

rows.name: City God Temple, Jiexiu
rows.summary: A temple on East Street built in 1370 and extensively repaired in 1495, whose gate, opera stage, bell and drum towers, main hall, side halls and galleries are all decorated with coloured glazed tile. It was used for a long time by the local Jin opera troupe. It is one of four nationally listed monuments in central Jiexiu, with Houtu Temple, Xianshenlou and Wuyue Temple, that the city plans to link as a glazed-tile trail.

rows.name: City God Temple, Pingyao
rows.summary: A three-courtyard temple complex of about 7,300 sq m in which the City God temple stands on the main axis, with a Kitchen God temple and a God of Wealth temple to either side. The axis runs from a gate archway through a two-storey opera tower and an offering hall to the main hall and a sleeping hall, and the main hall's west wall carries a mural of the City God's procession. The buildings were rebuilt between 1864 and 1869 after a fire in 1859.

rows.name: Cixiang Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Jiguo village whose three courtyards run north from the gate through a Guandi shrine and bell and drum towers to the main hall and the Lutai Pagoda. The main hall is original Song-dynasty timberwork, three bays wide with an overhanging gable roof, and the octagonal nine-storey brick pagoda, 48.2 m high, was built under the Jin dynasty between 1123 and 1137. The temple goes back to the Tang dynasty and took its present name in the Northern Song, and most other buildings are Ming or Qing.

rows.name: Dazhai
rows.summary: A village in the Taihang foothills that was promoted nationwide in the 1960s and 1970s as a national model for agricultural production, under the slogan "In agriculture, learn from Dazhai". The scenic area takes in the former Dazhai People's Commune buildings (a national heritage unit dated 1966), the Dazhai Exhibition Hall and a cultural exhibition hall, and a walking route up Hutou Mountain. It suits visitors interested in the history of China's rural collectivisation.

rows.name: Dongyue Temple, Jiexiu
rows.summary: A temple to the Eastern Peak in Xiaojin village, rebuilt in 1270 under the Yuan dynasty after an earlier founding of unknown date. The compound covers about 3,100 square metres and keeps a screen wall, gate, opera stage, bell and drum towers, a front offering hall, the double-eaved main hall and a rear hall known as the Holy Mother Palace. It suits visitors interested in Shanxi's rural temple architecture.

rows.name: Eighth Route Army Headquarters Memorial, Matian
rows.name_zh: 麻田八路军总部纪念馆
rows.summary: From 1941 to 1945 the Eighth Route Army's front headquarters and the Communist Party's Northern Bureau were based at Matian, a village in the Taihang mountains near the Hebei border. The old compound has courtyard houses with their plain period furnishings kept as they were, including the former residences of Deng Xiaoping and Zuo Quan, and a memorial hall nearby holds more than 6,000 historical items. Zuoquan county was renamed in 1942 after General Zuo Quan, the army's deputy chief of staff, who was killed in action near Matian that year.

rows.name: Former Residence of Kong Xiangxi
rows.summary: A Qing-period gentry house in the old town of Taigu that the banker and Nationalist finance minister Kong Xiangxi (Kung Hsiang-hsi), a Taigu native, bought in 1930. It covers about 6,300 sq m in eight courtyards, including a stage courtyard and a garden, and has exhibitions on Kong's life and on Chiang Kai-shek's stay here in 1934. It suits visitors interested in Republic-era history or in Shanxi courtyard houses.

rows.name: Former Residence of Lei Lütai
rows.summary: The former home of Lei Lütai, co-founder and first general manager of the Rishengchang draft bank, built in the Daoguang period of the Qing (1821–1850) as a typical Pingyao courtyard house. Two main courtyards and two side courtyards face south, with a south hall, a middle hall and side wings of one storey and a two-storey rear hall called Jinyuan Lou. Rishengchang itself is a separate site elsewhere in the old city.

rows.name: Futian Temple
rows.summary: A compact Buddhist temple of about 800 sq m in Heishui village, Pingtou town, founded in the Tang dynasty and rebuilt in 1333 under the Yuan. The main hall is the Yuan building, three bays square with an overhanging gable roof, and the passage hall in front of it dates from the Ming. Side halls flank the courtyard.

rows.name: Fuxiang Temple, Yushe
rows.summary: A temple founded in 946 under the Later Jin on the north shore of Yunzhu Reservoir, with water on three sides. Only two buildings remain: the five-bay main hall, a Jin-dynasty survivor with a hip-and-gable roof and elaborate bracket sets, and the three-bay south hall from the early Ming.

rows.name: Guanghua Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Baicheng village, founded in the Tang dynasty as Longxing Temple and given its present name by imperial decree in 999. Three buildings survive: the main hall, rebuilt in 1326 under the Yuan, a rear hall and a west side hall. The main hall is five bays wide with a front veranda and a hip-and-gable roof, and the rear hall is a smaller three-bay building.

rows.name: Hongfu Temple, Liangcun
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Liangcun village founded in 713 under the Tang and repaired repeatedly in the Ming, Qing and Republican periods. The main hall is a Yuan-dynasty building, the south hall is Ming and the other buildings are Qing. It was listed as a national monument in 2019.

rows.name: Hongya Canyon
rows.summary: A forested canyon in the Taiyue range, named for the red rock of its steep cliffs, and one of the scenic areas of Taiyueshan National Forest Park. Forest covers over 97 per cent of the area, and the canyon has a ski area in winter. It suits walkers looking for a mountain day out within reach of Jiexiu and Lingshi.

rows.name: Hougou Ancient Village
rows.summary: A loess-plateau farming village in Dongzhao township, near the border with Shouyang county, where the houses are cave dwellings cut into the hillsides in stone, earth and brick. The village has 18 small temples and an ancestral hall, and an underground drainage system that runs through its courtyards. It suits visitors interested in traditional farming life in rural Shanxi.

rows.name: Houtu Temple, Jiexiu
rows.summary: A large Taoist temple complex of about 9,000 square metres in the north-west corner of Jiexiu's old town, extended in 1516 and given its present layout in 1730. It is best known for its glazed-tile work, with more colours than the usual yellow, green and blue and a main hall roofed entirely in yellow glaze, and for its many coloured clay figures, a large share of them Ming. The main buildings stand on two parallel axes, the western one running from the gate hall through the Sanqing Tower and an opera stage to the Houtu hall.

rows.name: Houtu Temple, Jingsheng
rows.summary: A one-courtyard temple dedicated to Nüwa, standing in farmland west of Jingsheng village, founded in 1266 and rebuilt in 1304. The offering hall and the three-bay main hall are Yuan buildings: the square offering hall has an elaborate caisson ceiling under a hip-and-gable roof, and the main hall has a front veranda. The gate, with its stage, and the flanking buildings were rebuilt in old style after modern concrete structures were removed.

rows.name: Huiji Bridge, Pingyao
rows.summary: A stone arch bridge on nine piers over the Huiji River, 80 m long and 7.4 m wide, built in 1671 under the Kangxi emperor. It stands outside the east wall of Pingyao Ancient City and is a quick stop on a walk around the walls.

rows.name: Huiluan Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Xingdi village at the foot of Mount Mian, founded in the Tang dynasty and rebuilt in 1133 under the Jin. The five-bay main hall, with a front veranda and an overhanging gable roof, is Yuan-dynasty work; the gate hall and side halls date from the Ming and Qing. It suits visitors interested in early timber architecture.

rows.name: Jinci Temple, Lingshi
rows.summary: A small temple of about 1,400 sq m in Mahe village, begun under the Yuan in the Zhizheng era and repaired many times in the Ming and Qing. The main hall, dated 1343, and the square offering hall in front of it are Yuan buildings, while the gate stage, bell and drum towers and side halls are later. It is a different temple from Jinci in Taiyuan.

rows.name: Jingsheng Confucian Temple
rows.summary: A village Confucian temple founded in the 1330s under the Yuan, with its present buildings from the Qing, set out in three parallel strings of courtyards just north of Jingsheng's central crossroads. A carved stone screen wall 3 m high, showing carp leaping the dragon gate, stands at the front, and the four-storey hexagonal Kuixing Tower marks the south-east corner. The main axis runs past a pool and bridge to the main hall, sleeping hall and scripture pavilion, with a school hall to the west and a granary to the east.

rows.name: Jingxin Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Yangyi village beside the S319 provincial road, founded in the Tang dynasty and now made up of Ming and Qing buildings on two courtyards. Its gate doubles as an opera stage facing into the front courtyard, with a peacock-blue glazed roof, and the courtyard is lined with two-storey bell and drum towers, side halls and the Sanfo Hall, all under coloured glazed-tile roofs. The main hall behind has Ming murals.

rows.name: Jinzhuang Confucian Temple
rows.summary: A three-courtyard Confucian temple of about 1,000 sq m in Jinzhuang village, first built in 1315 under the Yuan and rebuilt several times in the Ming and Qing. Its main hall, rebuilt in 1802, holds fifteen painted clay figures dated to the early Yuan, led by a seated Confucius 1.85 m tall with the Four Correlates and Ten Philosophers beside him. The axis also has a Lingxing gate, a lecture hall and a ceremonial pool.

rows.name: Jiulong International Cultural and Ecological Tourism Park
rows.name_zh: 九龙国际文化生态旅游区
rows.summary: A leisure and holiday resort of about 3,900 mu (some 2.6 sq km) in the hills of Yuci District, close to Taiyuan. It combines a mountain lodge, a ski resort, an RV campsite and an off-road vehicle club. The ski resort hosted the opening of Shanxi's first Ice and Snow Carnival in December 2024, so it suits skiers and families on a short trip from Taiyuan rather than visitors looking for heritage.

rows.name: Lixiang Temple, Xiyang
rows.summary: A village temple in Chuankou, Zhaobi township, whose buildings range in date from the Song to the Qing dynasty. It was listed by Jinzhong city in 2003 and by Shanxi province in 2016, and became a national heritage unit in 2019.

rows.name: Liyinghou Temple
rows.summary: A small Yuan-dynasty temple beside Zhenguo Temple in Haodong village, dedicated to Hu Tu, a Jin state official of the Spring and Autumn period. Only the main hall survives, three bays wide on a one-metre platform with an overhanging gable roof, and it holds nine painted clay figures of the Yuan period. It pairs naturally with Zhenguo Temple about 150 m to the east.

rows.name: Longfu Temple, Nanzheng
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Nanzheng village founded in 1298 under the Yuan, repaired in the Ming and again in 1800, on two courtyards of about 2,900 sq m. The central axis runs from a screen wall through a gate, flanked by arched cave rooms topped with bell and drum towers, to the Sansheng Hall and the five-bay Qifo (Seven Buddhas) Hall at the back, which has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof.

rows.name: Mengjiagou Longquan Temple
rows.summary: A hillside temple of about 2,400 sq m at Mengjiagou village, begun in the Tianqi period of the Ming dynasty. Its gate, passage hall, stele hall, dragon pool, pavilion and old stage are terraced up the slope with 37 cave rooms, and a thirteen-storey brick pagoda about 25 m high belongs to the complex. It suits visitors interested in cave-style temple building in Shanxi's hills.

rows.name: Miaojue Temple, Xincun
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Xincun village built in the Ming and Qing dynasties, with its Qianfo (Thousand Buddhas) Hall of the Qing and other buildings in Ming style. The hall's walls are covered in murals. The village committee once used the temple as offices, and press reports in 2015 described the hall's west roof as collapsed and much of the mural damaged.

rows.name: Mingxian School Site, Taigu
rows.summary: The old campus of Mingxian School, which Kong Xiangxi founded in Taigu in 1907 in memory of Oberlin missionaries killed in the Boxer uprising of 1900. Oberlin College sent graduates to teach here from 1918 until the early 1950s. The listed site, dated from the Qing dynasty to the Republic, lies within the campus of Shanxi Agricultural University, which grew out of the school's farming faculty after 1951.

rows.name: Mount Shigao
rows.summary: A forested mountain scenic area in the Taiyue range, rising to 2,532 m, of which about 20 of its 75 sq km are open to visitors. More than 70 sights are linked by about 25 km of visitor roads, including temples in the hills and a red-leaf zone. The area opened to visitors in 2011 and suits a day of walking in the hills.

rows.name: Nanshen Temple, Gankeng
rows.summary: A temple dedicated to the Bodhisattva of Light in Gankeng village, rebuilt in the Ming dynasty and known in turn as Yeshu Furen Temple, Nanshen Temple and today Yuanxiang Temple. Its halls include the Heavenly Kings Hall, the Bodhisattva of Light Hall, halls for Guanyin and Dizang and a rear stone Buddha hall, with a chanting hall and the Sansheng Hall alongside. Ming and Qing steles and a Ming stone sutra pillar stand in the grounds.

rows.name: Pingyao Confucian Temple
rows.summary: A Confucian temple in the south-east corner of Pingyao Ancient City whose Dacheng Hall dates from 1163 under the Jin dynasty, with later Ming and Qing buildings around it. The Shaoshan Academy is attached, where the late-Qing scholar Xu Jiyu served as head for ten years. It suits visitors who want to see Jin-dynasty timber architecture inside the old town.

rows.name: Pingyao Market Tower (Shilou)
rows.summary: A three-eaved timber tower, 18.5 m high, that stands over South Street in the middle of Pingyao Ancient City, with a roof of yellow and green glazed tiles. A passage runs north to south through its square base, and the well just south of it, with water the colour of gold, gives the tower its other name, the Golden Well Tower. It was repaired in 1688 and several times since.

rows.name: Puguang Temple
rows.summary: A small Buddhist temple of about 1,100 sq m in Baidao village, Xiluo town. The main hall is Song-dynasty, the side halls Ming and the remaining rooms and courtyard buildings Qing. The main hall is three bays square and about 120 sq m of Ming and Qing wall paintings survive inside it.

rows.name: Puming Temple, Changze
rows.summary: A village temple in Changze, repaired in the Ming dynasty. Its main hall is a typical Ming building and keeps fine Ming-dynasty murals.

rows.name: Puzhao Temple, Siping
rows.summary: The surviving main hall of a temple founded in the Later Jin dynasty and repaired in the Ming and Qing, in Siping village. It is a large seven-bay hall of 376 sq m built in Yuan style, with a roof decorated in yellow and green carved glazed tile, and nothing else of the temple remains. The hall stands in the grounds of the village care home for older people.

rows.name: Qingliang Temple, Pingyao
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Yongcheng village, founded in 1342 under the Yuan and repaired in the Ming and Qing. Its two courtyards hold a gate, a middle hall and, at the back, the five-bay Qifo (Seven Buddhas) Hall, where seven seated Ming painted figures nearly 3 m high stand on a U-shaped platform before gilded halos. A conservation project approved in 2016 was the first full repair of the temple since 1949.

rows.name: Qingxu Temple, Pingyao
rows.summary: A Taoist temple complex just inside the east gate of Pingyao's town wall, traditionally founded in 657 in the Tang dynasty and given its present name in 1064. The Dragon-and-Tiger Hall at the entrance is Yuan-dynasty, while the Hall of the Three Pure Ones and the other buildings are Ming and Qing. No Taoist priests live here now, and the buildings house Pingyao County Museum, whose collection includes Buddhist and Taoist carvings; the Hall of the Three Pure Ones keeps a Yuan-dynasty decree stele in Phags-pa script.

rows.name: Qu Family Compound
rows.summary: The home of the Qu family, Qing-dynasty merchants of Qi County, built from the Qianlong reign and reaching its present size by 1925. The castle-like compound covers 5,317 sq m with 8 large and 19 small courtyards and about 240 rooms, including a stage courtyard and a balustrade courtyard, and has housed the Shanxi Jin Merchant Culture Museum since 1996. The listing also covers the former Changyuchuan tea house on Duanjia Lane.

rows.name: Rishengchang
rows.summary: The former headquarters of Rishengchang, regarded as China's first draft bank (piaohao), which grew out of a dye business and began issuing drafts cashable at branches in other cities in the early nineteenth century. The courtyards on West Street are now a museum, where displays include the coded marks once used to stop drafts being forged. Draft banks like this one made central Shanxi a financial centre of Qing China by the late nineteenth century.

rows.name: Shima Temple Grottoes
rows.summary: A group of rock-cut Buddhist carvings at Shima village, with more than a thousand surviving stone images dating from the Northern and Southern Dynasties to the Tang. The temple here was known as Shousheng Temple in the Song dynasty, and the site has been protected at provincial level since 1986. It suits visitors interested in early Buddhist sculpture in rural Shanxi.

rows.name: Shitie Tombs
rows.summary: A group of six earth-mounded tombs of the Northern Qi grand marshal Han Gui and his family, listed as a national heritage unit. The mounds stand in open farmland near Shitie village. It is of interest mainly to those tracing Northern Dynasties burials in Shanxi.

rows.name: Shousheng Temple, Weize
rows.summary: A Yuan-dynasty temple in Weize village, Tongyu town, standing in front of the village primary school. Its gate and main hall survive, and both roofs are decorated with yellow and green glazed tile. It was listed as a national monument in 2013.

rows.name: Taihang Longquan Scenic Area
rows.summary: A large national forest park and scenic area in the Taihang Mountains south of Zuoquan, with a waterfall, lakes, temples and an alpine meadow. It suits a summer day in the hills.

rows.name: Taiheyan Glazed Archway
rows.summary: A glazed-tile archway of 1897 in Beixinwu village, built by a local merchant as the front gate of a Zhenwu temple that has since disappeared. It has four pillars, three bays and three roofs and is faced almost entirely in blue, yellow and green glazed tile, including the pillars, plaques, couplets and imitation timber brackets. Scenes of a carp turning into a dragon decorate the east side of the archway and a tiger under a pine the west.

rows.name: Wubian Temple
rows.summary: A walled temple in the old town of Taigu, best known for its White Pagoda, a hollow octagonal brick pagoda built in 1090 under the Northern Song. The pagoda imitates a timber tower, with seven storeys outside and nine inside, stands 43 m high and has a wooden staircase within. After a fire in the Tongzhi era left only the pagoda standing, the temple around it, with a gate and opera stage, a pavilion and the main hall, was rebuilt in 1904–06.

rows.name: Wujin Mountain National Forest Park
rows.summary: A forested mountain park on the boundary between Taiyuan and Yuci, run as a leisure resort that combines religious sites, walking paths and an amusement park. Peach blossom on the slopes in late March and early April is a seasonal draw. It suits a half-day outing from Taiyuan or Yuci.

rows.name: Wuyue Temple, Jiexiu
rows.summary: A temple in the south-east of Jiexiu's old town, founded in 1456, destroyed in 1750 and rebuilt in 1763, on a site of about 4,100 square metres. Its gate, opera stage and bell and drum towers are joined into one tall structure known as the Haishen Tower, with a five-bay stage raised on a high platform and richly decorated bracket sets under the eaves. The main hall, front hall, side halls and rear hall stand behind it.

rows.name: Xianshenlou
rows.summary: A pavilion-style tower over the street, combining a gateway, a stage tower and an overhead passage, first built in 1048 as part of a Zoroastrian temple and regarded as the only surviving Zoroastrian building in China. The temple was later turned into a temple of the three sworn brothers Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei, and the tower and hall behind it were rebuilt in the 1660s and restored in the 1980s. It stands near the old east gate of Jiexiu and suits a short stop with the town's other temples.

rows.name: Xiaohe Lotus Bay
rows.summary: A riverside leisure area on the Xiaohe River in south-east Yuci, laid out around 2020 as the first part of the planned Xiaohe Arts Town. It has a central plaza used for fountain and light-show performances, a footbridge shaped like a lotus stem, a snack street, about 3 km of woodland, sports pitches and large seasonal flower displays such as autumn chrysanthemums. It suits families and evening outings from Jinzhong.

rows.name: Xiaoxigou Tourist Town
rows.summary: A purpose-built tourist town that opened in July 2021 on the site of a former quarry in the hills east of Taiyuan, after the quarry had been cleaned up and replanted. It holds shops and stalls selling Shanxi snacks, crafts and intangible-heritage products, together with guesthouses, a children's play area and a traditional Chinese medicine wellness theme. It suits families and short day trips from Taiyuan or Jinzhong.

rows.name: Xingfan Temple
rows.summary: A Song-dynasty hall, all that remains of a temple founded in 1025 at Xiguan village and moved to its present site in 1687. The main hall is five bays wide and six rafters deep under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof and is original Song timberwork.

rows.name: Yiji Holy Mother Temple
rows.summary: A hillside temple complex of about 8,400 sq m on a ridge south-east of Heshan village, founded in the Song dynasty and repaired in 1321 and 1338 under the Yuan. It has an upper and a lower courtyard plus a separate shrine to Marquis Xianze; the Holy Mother Hall in the upper courtyard is Yuan-dynasty and the other halls are Ming and Qing. The lower courtyard has an entrance archway, gate and opera stage, and side halls in the upper courtyard are named for eyesight, smallpox and the Medicine King.

rows.name: Yongfu Temple, Beiyijian
rows.summary: A village temple in Beiyijian whose through-hall, between the Heavenly King hall and the main hall, was rebuilt in 1469 and is the listed building. It stands on a high platform, is five bays wide and uses large timbers, and is typical of Ming construction. An opera stage stands opposite the temple gate.

rows.name: Yuanshen Temple, Jiexiu
rows.summary: A temple beside the Hongshan spring at the foot of Huqi Mountain, protected by the province in 2004 and by the State Council in 2013.
