A Song-dynasty stele of 1008 records a rebuilding in 997, and the compound of about 700 sq m now runs from a wooden gateway with a yellow glazed-tile roof through a through-hall, an opera stage and side halls to the main hall and a rear hall, with 21 old steles in the grounds. It suits a short stop on a trip around Jiexiu's temples.

rows.name: Yuanzhi Temple, Fancun
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Fancun town. Its founding date is unrecorded, but inscriptions record work under the Jin, and it was repaired many times in the Ming and Qing, when most of its present buildings were made. Its through-hall, the Qianfo (Thousand Buddhas) Hall, was a beamless hall painted all round with rows of small Buddha figures; a fire in 2014 destroyed the hall and its murals.

rows.name: Yuci City God Temple
rows.summary: A temple of about 6,000 square metres on East Street, founded in 1362 in the Yuan dynasty and moved to its present site in 1431, with its final layout in place by 1523. Its centrepiece is the two-storey Xuanjian Tower, 17 m high and roofed in peacock-blue glazed tile, which stands in front of a covered stage and the main hall. It is one of the few historic buildings kept in the rebuilt Yuci Old Town, where it has also been used as a filming location.

rows.name: Yuci Old Town
rows.summary: A large quarter built from around 2000 on the site of the old Yuci county town and laid out as old-style streets. Most of the original houses were cleared for it, and a few listed buildings were kept, among them the City God Temple, the Qingxu Pavilion and the Confucian temple. It has served as a location for dozens of television dramas, and suits a short stop for anyone passing through Yuci.

rows.name: Zhangbi Castle
rows.summary: A walled fortress village with gullies on three sides and a convex-shaped wall about 374 m by 244 m, entered through a barbican at its north gate. Inside, a stone-paved main street runs past temples to Guandi, Zhenwu and Erlang, a Yuan-dynasty opera stage and dozens of Ming and Qing houses, with a network of Sui and Tang tunnels beneath. The village was laid out on astrological lines and stages seasonal events, including light shows on its south gate.

rows.name: Zhaoyu Ancient City
rows.summary: The old centre of Qi County, a town on the Great Tea Road whose Ming and Qing courtyard houses have been renovated for visitors. Sights include the Qu Family Compound (a national heritage unit, now a museum of Jin merchant culture), the old Sanjinyuan draft bank and a museum of the tea-trade route. The streets host seasonal events, such as the lantern festival at Chinese New Year.

rows.name: Zhenguo Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Haodong village, listed with Pingyao Ancient City and Shuanglin Temple as part of the 1997 World Heritage site. Its Ten Thousand Buddha Hall, dated by an inscription to 963 under the Northern Han, is one of the oldest surviving timber halls in China and is known for its large bracket sets, and it holds eleven painted clay figures of the same period. The walled complex has two courtyards, with the Tianwang Hall as its gate and a Qing-dynasty Sanfo Hall at the back.

rows.name: Zhenhe Tower
rows.summary: A Ming-dynasty tower in Jialing village, known locally as Silou Men. It stands three storeys and 15.5 m high with four tiers of eaves under a hip-and-gable roof, and measures 15.5 m east-west by 13.5 m north-south. Its name means roughly "river-subduing tower", and one plaque reads "Guard the Changyuan for ever", after the Changyuan River.

rows.name: Zhensheng Temple
rows.summary: A small Buddhist temple in Pifu village. Its main hall was built in 1157 under the Jin dynasty and repaired in the Ming and in 1842; it is three bays wide with a front veranda and a flush gable roof. The gate in front is a Qing-dynasty seven-bay stone structure.

rows.name: Zishou Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Suxi village, founded in the Tang, burned at the end of the Jin, rebuilt in 1467 after lying derelict in the early Ming and brought to its present scale in 1622. The front courtyard has the gate, an inner gate, and the Vajra and Heavenly Kings halls with bell and drum towers, while the rear courtyard is centred on the main hall and ringed by halls of Amitabha, the Medicine Buddha, Dizang, Erlang, Maitreya and the Three Great Bodhisattvas. The halls hold about 248 sq m of murals and some 100 painted clay figures.

rows.name: Zuoquan Confucian Temple
rows.summary: The former Confucian temple of Liaozhou, now in the county town of Zuoquan, where the Dacheng Hall was rebuilt in 1297 under the Yuan and is the only original building left. The hall is five bays wide and three deep on a footprint of about 459 sq m, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof and a covered aisle running all round it. The other buildings in the compound are modern rebuilds.

rows.name: Baishan Dongyue Temple, Pu County
rows.summary: A large temple to the Lord of Mount Tai (Dongyue) on wooded Baishan hill east of Pu county town, with roots in the Tang and rebuilt in 1316–18 after the 1303 Pingyang earthquake. It covers about 20,000 sq m in several groups, among them the Dongyue palace, a Hell hall and the Huaqing pool; only the palace's main hall is Yuan, five bays wide and deep under a double-eave hip-gable roof, and the rest is Ming and Qing. The temple appears on a national rural-tourism route for Linfen promoted in 2024, alongside Xiaoxitian and the Guangsheng area.

rows.name: Dabei Temple, Quwo
rows.summary: A small temple compound in Qucun town, founded in the Tang dynasty and covering about 4,000 square metres. Its three-bay offering hall is original Jin-dynasty work with a hip-gable roof, while the Heavenly Kings Hall, the passage hall and the side ranges are Qing.

rows.name: Dingcun
rows.summary: Dingcun is a village on the east bank of the Fen River whose Ming and Qing courtyard houses are run as a folk museum, with more than 30 courtyards; the earliest dates from 1593. The Dingcun Palaeolithic site, excavated from 1954 on the river terraces around the village, produced human fossils about 120,000 years old and over 2,000 stone artefacts, which a culture exhibition hall presents. Both appear on Shanxi government tourism routes through Linfen.

rows.name: Dongyang Houtu Temple
rows.summary: A temple in the middle of Dongyang village, founded in 1283 as an Eastern Peak temple, wrecked in the great earthquake of 1303 and rebuilt in 1345, and later renamed for the earth goddess Houtu. Its Yuan-period stage has a cross-gabled hip roof and a stacked bracket-set ceiling, the Houtu Hall dates from 1622 and holds Ming painted clay figures, and the double-eaved gate has honeycomb-like brackets. After 1949 the temple was used as a school, and several halls were pulled down in the 1970s.

rows.name: Fandian Guandi Temple
rows.summary: A temple to Guan Yu in Fandian village, founded in 1505 and repaired in 1831. The stage and main hall on the central axis are Ming, the gate and the front range of rooms are Qing, and the two side gates sit tight against the stage under the inscriptions 'both civil and martial' and 'both god and sage'.

rows.name: Fencheng Ancient Town
rows.summary: Fencheng was the seat of Taiping county and still has more than forty historic buildings from the Jin to the late Qing, including a City God Temple, a Confucian temple, a Guandi temple, a drum tower, the county yamen hall, a brick pagoda and a stretch of Ming town wall. The City God Temple, rebuilt in 1627, is flanked by two Ming timber archways, and a covered stone bridge first built in 1183 crosses a channel on the south side. The town is a national historic and cultural town (2007) and is promoted in Linfen's tourism routes.

rows.name: Fenhe Culture and Ecology Scenic Area, Linfen
rows.summary: A riverside park about 17 km long along the Fen River through Linfen, laid out around the idea of one river, five lakes, ten gardens and eighteen views. People's Daily describes it as combining themes of the Yao and Shun legends, river ecological restoration and everyday leisure, with museums and a library set among the planting. It is a city park rather than a historic site.

rows.name: Former Taiyue Administrative Office, Xiaoli Village
rows.summary: The former seat of the Taiyue Administrative Office, a regional wartime government for the Taiyue mountains of southern Shanxi, in Xiaoli village, Liangma town; the listed buildings date from 1942–44. The State Council listed it as a national monument in 2019 in the category of modern historic sites and representative buildings, and the scenic area around it covers about 1.8 sq km across the villages of Ducun, Xiaoli and Sangqu. Anze keeps 18 sites from the Taiyue base area, of which this is one.

rows.name: Gu County Peony Garden
rows.summary: A peony garden at Sanhe village in the hills of Gu county, built around an old peony plant that is acclaimed locally as the finest in China. Shanxi Daily gives the plant's age as more than 1,300 years and counted 621 blooms on that single plant in 2026. The grounds are laid out as a visitor park, so the spring flowering season is the time to go.

rows.name: Guajiashan Cliffside Sculptures
rows.summary: Figure carvings on the cliffs of Guajia Hill, on the southern edge of Ji County town, which the national list dates from the Northern Dynasties to the Ming dynasty. They became a provincial protected site in 1986 and a national one in 2019.

rows.name: Guandi Temple, Hongtong
rows.summary: A temple to Guan Yu in the centre of Hongtong county town, founded in 1306 under the Yuan and enlarged in the Ming and Qing. Its gate tower, the three-storey Chunqiu Building of 1531 (repaired in 1710), has a cross-shaped passage through its base and is the town's best-known landmark, with the stage, offering hall and main hall behind it and bell and drum towers at the sides.

rows.name: Guanyin Temple, Huozhou
rows.summary: A temple on the east side of Huozhou, begun under the Yuan and extensively repaired in the Jiajing reign of the Ming, covering 2,021 sq m. It has a gate, a Sansheng hall, a Guanyin hall, a main hall and a street-spanning pavilion with a colonnaded passage beneath it. The pavilion is Yuan and has a double-eave hip-gable roof; the other buildings are Ming and Qing.

rows.name: Hongtong Locust Tree Ancestor-Worship Park
rows.name_zh: 洪洞大槐树寻根祭祖园
rows.summary: The park commemorates the Hongtong locust tree, remembered by families across northern and eastern China as the point of departure of the Ming-era resettlements from Shanxi, of which Ming records list 18 between 1373 and 1417. It is a modern park built around that memory, with a yearly ancestor-worship ceremony (the 36th, in April 2026, drew descendants from 18 provinces and cities), stage shows such as the Daming Qianminshu and a genealogy advice centre. The ancestor-worship customs are on China's national intangible heritage list.

rows.name: Houma Jin Capital Site
rows.summary: The remains of Xintian, the capital of the state of Jin from 585 BCE, lie where the Fen and Kuai rivers meet at Houma and include walled-town sites, ancestral-temple foundations, bronze-foundry and sacrificial areas and cemeteries. Most of it is buried, so the place to start is the Jin Ancient Capital Museum in the city centre, which shows finds from the site; the Houma Covenant tablets, jade and stone slips inscribed with oaths, were found here in 1965. A site park marks the foundations of the ancestral-temple complex.

rows.name: Huozhou Drum Tower
rows.summary: A Ming and Qing drum tower in the middle of Huozhou city. It was listed as a provincial site in 2004 and as a national monument in 2019. It stands a short walk from the Prefectural Office and Zhusheng Temple.

rows.name: Huozhou Prefectural Office
rows.summary: The surviving prefectural office of Huozhou, on East Street in the old centre of Huozhou city, now a museum. Most of the compound was destroyed at the end of the Yuan dynasty and only the main hall survived; the ceremonial gate and an admonition-stone pavilion were rebuilt in the Ming and Qing, and the gate tower is a modern reconstruction. The hall is three bays wide and eight rafters deep under a single-eave overhanging gable roof.

rows.name: Jin Museum (Qucun–Tianma Site)
rows.summary: A site museum on the Qucun–Tianma site, where archaeologists found the early capital and royal cemetery of the Western Zhou state of Jin, in use between about 1000 and 800 BC. The excavations uncovered 19 tombs of Jin marquises and their consorts, with chariot-and-horse pits, sacrificial pits and many bronzes and jades. The museum opened in 2014 on the cemetery site, with galleries on Jin history, the excavation and the marquises' tombs.

rows.name: Jingshi Palace, Hongdong
rows.summary: A complex of historic buildings in Ganhe village, Dicun township, Hongtong, dated by the national list to between the Ming dynasty and the Republican period. It was listed as a provincial protected site in 2004 and as a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Jinyuan Garden, Quwo
rows.summary: A landscaped park in Quwo county town, laid out as a classical-style garden on the culture of Jin, the ancient state of this region. It has a lake with timber boardwalks and Chinese-style pavilions, a large public plaza, a theatre and a conference hall, and it stages short historical plays built around Chinese idiom stories. It suits an easy hour or two for anyone visiting the Jin-period sites around Quwo.

rows.name: Langzhai Brick Pagoda
rows.summary: A dense-eaved brick pagoda of the Tang dynasty in Langzhai village, Mabi township. It was listed as a provincial protected site in 2004 and as a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Laojun Cave, Fushan
rows.summary: A small Daoist hall in Liang village, Zhangzhuang township, the only building left of a temple founded in 619. The three-bay hall is built of brick and stone in imitation of timber, stands 4.4 m high and faces south. Inside are 39 stone panels of 1531 carved with the eighty-one transformations of Laozi, and a mural of 1561 covering about 78 square metres.

rows.name: Lingguang Temple Glazed Pagoda
rows.summary: A seven-storey octagonal brick pagoda more than 20 m high, built in imitation of timber construction, standing in the fields west of Beiliang village. It is all that remains of Lingguang Temple, founded in 652 and rebuilt under the Jin; the 1695 earthquake left only seven of its thirteen storeys, the temple was destroyed in 1948, and its site was later buried by Fen River silt and turned to farmland. The pagoda was restored in 2020.

rows.name: Longquan Temple, Nanlinjiao
rows.summary: A village temple in Nanlinjiao, Beidong township, whose buildings are dated by the national listing to between the Yuan and Qing dynasties. It was listed as a county protected site in 1987 and as a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Longshuyu Scenic Area
rows.summary: Longshuyu is a hill-country scenic area above Huangya village in Xiangling town, on the western edge of Xiangfen County. A county official describes its tourism as built around Zen Buddhist practice and mental well-being. A November 2024 Shanxi government release lists it, with the Dingcun museums, the Taosi site museum, Yaojing Winery and Lotus Town, among the attractions of a themed tourist route through Xiangfen.

rows.name: Lotus Town, Xiangfen
rows.summary: A hot-spring leisure town beside the Fen River in Dengzhuang town, north of Xiangfen county town. Shanxi's culture and tourism department listed it in 2023 among the province's night-time culture and tourism consumption zones and named its hot springs among Shanxi's ten hot-spring wellness destinations, and it appears on a 2024 rural-tourism route through Linfen themed on ancestral roots.

rows.name: Mayi Temple Brick Pagoda
rows.summary: A Jin-dynasty dense-eaved brick pagoda on the Nanshan ridge in the hills north of Anze, about 2 km west of Lingnan village. It was listed as a provincial protected site in 1996 and as a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Nanhan Dongyue Temple, Yicheng
rows.summary: A village temple to the Lord of Mount Tai (Dongyue) at Nanhan, covering 2,660 sq m, with a stage, an offering hall and a main hall flanked by side halls and corridor rooms. The offering hall and main hall are Yuan and the other buildings Qing. Both Yuan halls are three bays wide with overhanging gable roofs, and the main hall has the more elaborate bracketing.

rows.name: Niuwang Temple Stage, Linfen
rows.summary: A Yuan-dynasty opera stage built in 1283 and repaired in 1321, at the Niuwang (Ox King) Temple in Hecun village, Weicun town, north of Linfen. The stage is about 7.5 m square, with a single-eave hip-gable roof and open on three sides, while the hall, offering pavilion and side halls behind it are Ming and Qing. It was long thought to be China's oldest surviving wooden stage until a Jin-dynasty stage at Gaoping was identified in 2002.

rows.name: Peng Zhen Former Residence, Houma
rows.summary: The memorial hall at the birthplace of Peng Zhen (1902-1997), a Communist Party leader who held senior posts in the party and the state, in Dieshang village, now part of Houma. Government reports describe exhibition halls with more than 300 historical photographs and over a hundred objects on his life, and a bronze statue of him stands at the memorial. The house is a provincial-level monument (listed in 2004).

rows.name: Pujing Temple, Xiangfen
rows.summary: A temple compound of about 5,600 square metres in the fields near Shiwei village, with a gate, a Heavenly Kings Hall, an arhat hall, a Guandi hall, a Great Buddha Hall, a Medicine King hall, a pavilion and a bell tower. The five-bay Great Buddha Hall, over ten metres high, was rebuilt in 1303 after a major earthquake and is the oldest building; the rest dates from the Ming and Qing. It is also known as Nanshi Temple.

rows.name: Qiankun Bay, Yonghe
rows.summary: Qiankun Bay is a stretch where the Yellow River winds in tight S-shaped meanders between Shanxi and Shaanxi, and this scenic area looks over it from the Shanxi bank in Yonghe County; a separate scenic area faces it across the river in Yanchuan, Shaanxi. Provincial authorities list the Yonghe bends among Shanxi's twenty notable geological relics, and the Yellow River No 1 tourist road runs through Yonghe County.

rows.name: Qiaoze Temple Stage, Yicheng
rows.summary: The stage is all that remains of the Qiaoze Temple, a water-god temple at Wuchi village in Nanliang town, founded in 1324 under the Yuan. It is square, covers 140 sq m and stands on a platform 1.6 m high under a single-eave hip-gable roof, and it is regarded as the largest surviving Yuan-dynasty stage in China.

rows.name: Qilijiao Thousand Buddha Grottoes, Xixian
rows.summary: A group of rock-cut Buddhist grottoes, also called the Xixian Thousand Buddha Caves, on the east bank of the Chengchuan River at Qilijiao village north of Xi county town. The carvings date from the Northern and Southern dynasties to the Tang. The site was listed provincially in 1986 and nationally in 2013.

rows.name: Qiliyu Scenic Area, Huozhou
rows.summary: A mountain valley scenic area on the Huozhou side of Mount Huo, in Licao town east of Huozhou, with forested slopes and a ski area at its entrance. Provincial reports describe a forest-wellness town here and say it became a popular regional destination in summer 2026. Mount Huo is the central one of China's five traditional guardian mountains.

rows.name: Reliu Guandi Temple
rows.summary: A temple to Guan Yu in Reliu village, Guyang town, in Gu County; the national listing dates its buildings to the Ming and Qing. It was listed as a provincial monument in 2004 and as a national one in 2019.

rows.name: Renzu Mountain
rows.summary: Renzu Mountain is a forested mountain area in Ji County, named for Fuxi and Nüwa, the legendary ancestors of humankind. Provincial media describe more than a hundred old temples and shrines on its slopes, of which the Renzu Temple, the Xuantian Shangdi Temple, the Kongshan Temple and the Beidou Qixing Temple are best known. The scenic area is developed as a mountain leisure destination, with walking trails and seasonal events such as a locust-blossom festival and an autumn-leaf festival.

rows.name: Rongzi Winery
rows.summary: A winery estate in Xiangning County that makes red wines from vineyards on the Loess Plateau. Shanxi government media report a foreign media delegation being taken to the estate in 2025 to taste its wines, and the winery was listed in a 2025 notice of Shanxi time-honoured brands.

rows.name: Sanqing Temple Offering Hall, Dongxu
rows.summary: A Yuan-dynasty offering hall, the hall in front of the main shrine where offerings were made, belonging to the Sanqing Temple in Dongxu village, Gaoxian town. It was listed as a county protected site in 1987 and as a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Shangshan Temple (Sanhuang Temple), Hongtong
rows.summary: A single-courtyard temple in Sunbu village to the three legendary Sovereigns Fuxi, Shennong and Xuanyuan (the Yellow Emperor), also called the Sanhuang Temple. The main hall and the east side hall are Yuan work, the ear halls are Yuan and Qing and the rest is Qing, with repairs recorded in 1578, 1758 and 1838.

rows.name: Shijiagou Historic Village
rows.summary: A hillside village in Sengnian town of mostly brick and cave-dwelling courtyard houses, begun in 1769 and well developed by the Tongzhi reign (1862–1874). The houses climb a south-facing slope with a hill behind and a gully in front, and most are three- or four-sided courtyards. It is a China Historic and Cultural Village (2008), and its old buildings have been a national heritage unit since 2006.

rows.name: Shousheng Temple, Xiangning
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in the county town of Xiangning, founded in 1049 and repaired under the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties. What survives is a three-bay main hall and a two-storey bell tower built in 1312, which has a hip-gable roof. It has been a national heritage unit since 2006.

rows.name: Sisheng Palace, Yicheng
rows.summary: A temple in Cao Gong village, Xiyan town, named for the four sage-kings it enshrines: Yao, Shun, Yu and Tang. It was founded under the Yuan and covers about 2,300 square metres, with an opera stage, an offering hall and the main hall on its axis, flanked by side halls and galleries. The five-bay main hall and the stage are Yuan buildings, and the rest is Ming and Qing.

rows.name: Stone and Wooden Archways, Yicheng
rows.summary: Two four-faced memorial archways stand on the main street of Yicheng's old town, about a hundred metres apart, both promoted by the local censor Shi Xueqian. The stone archway, built in 1611, is carved with the Eight Immortals and other scenes and has a timber roof; the larger wooden one was finished in 1613 and carries inscribed plaques on all four sides. The old town around them is a residential district of historic courtyards.

rows.name: Taosi
rows.summary: Taosi is the site of a walled town of the Longshan period (about 2300 to 1900 BC), where excavations found a rammed-earth enclosure of about 280 hectares, palace foundations, a large elite cemetery and an observatory platform. The Taosi Site Museum opened in November 2024, and since 2025 the archaeological park around it has opened the reconstructed observatory, the palace area, a stretch of palace wall and an astronomy archaeology hall. Chinese archaeologists see it as showing the first features of an early state, and it is popularly identified with the capital of the legendary king Yao.

rows.name: Tiefo Temple (Dayun Temple), Linfen
rows.summary: A temple in the south-west of Linfen's old town, founded in 632 and now run as a museum, with a gate, an entrance hall, a sutra library and a brick pagoda that was begun in 1715 and finished in 1728. The pagoda's hollow ground floor holds an iron Buddha head 6.8 m high that is dated to the Tang, and the upper floors cannot be climbed. The present buildings are Qing, rebuilt after the earthquake of 1695.

rows.name: Wahuang Temple, Huozhou
rows.summary: A Qing-dynasty temple to Nüwa, the mother goddess of Chinese myth, in Jia village, Dazhang town. The south-facing compound covers about 1,300 square metres, with an opera stage, a main hall of three bays with flanking side halls, side rooms and bell and drum towers. It has been a national heritage unit since 2006.

rows.name: Wangqu Dongyue Temple, Linfen
rows.summary: A village temple to the Lord of Mount Tai (Dongyue) at Wangqu, north of Linfen, begun in the early Yuan and repaired in the Ming and Qing; its Yuan-dynasty stage and Qing main hall survive. The stage combines a Yuan rear section, 7.25 m wide, with a Qing porch in front, and has sixteen bracket sets under its eaves. Inside, a caisson ceiling rises in three tiers of brackets.

rows.name: Xiangling Confucian Temple
rows.summary: The Dacheng Hall of the Confucian temple at Xiangling is a large hall of the Yuan period, five bays wide and about 22 m across, with a hip-and-gable roof and twelve bracket sets under its long front architrave. The temple was first built in 1209 under the Jin and the hall was rebuilt in 1306. It stands inside the Xiangling grain station in Xiangling town.

rows.name: Xingtangsi Scenic Area, Mount Huo
rows.summary: A mountain scenic area on the Hongtong side of Mount Huo, named after Xingtangsi village. Mount Huo is the central one of China's five traditional guardian mountains, and the village was the site of the Zhongzhen Temple where the mountain god was honoured; it was demolished in 1970 with the neighbouring Xingtang Temple, and in 2012 only a side hall and a Ming stele survived. The area includes Yunshan Valley, named in 2023 as a national forest-wellness pilot site.

rows.name: Xixian Drum Tower
rows.summary: A Ming-dynasty drum tower in the centre of Xi county town, listed as a provincial site in 2004 and as a national monument in 2013. It stands about 1 km from Xiaoxitian, so the two can be seen on one walk.

rows.name: Xue Family Compound, Quwo
rows.summary: A Qing-dynasty courtyard house of three courtyards in sequence in the old town of Quwo, with a south range, passage halls and a north tower, decorated with stone and wood carving and painted ornament. After 1949 it was used by the housing office and other offices, and since 1995 it has been in the care of the cultural-relics authorities.

rows.name: Yao Mausoleum
rows.summary: The tomb of Yao, one of the legendary Five Emperors, stands in the hills east of Linfen on the north bank of the Lao River. The earth mound is the ancient core, with Ming and Qing buildings and a number of stone tablets, and repairs are recorded from the Tang dynasty onwards. Since 2007 the city has restored the site and added new ceremonial buildings, among them the Guozu (State Ancestor) Hall, huabiao pillars and a glazed screen wall.

rows.name: Yao Temple, Linfen
rows.summary: A temple complex to the legendary emperor Yao on the southern edge of Linfen, moved to its present site on the east bank of the Fen River in 658 and restored after the earthquakes of 1303 and 1695. Its main hall, Guangyun Hall, was rebuilt in 1999 after an arson fire the year before, and the complex also has the three-storey Wufeng Tower, about 19 m high, and four ancient cypresses in the courtyard of the main hall. The scenic area also takes in Huamen, a plaza and park to the west.

rows.name: Yaojing Winery
rows.summary: A wine estate in Shangxiliang village, Dadeng township, Xiangfen County, rated as a 4A scenic area. It combines vineyards, wine-making, a wine-culture display and countryside leisure, with a campsite. A November 2024 Shanxi government release lists it, with the Dingcun museums, the Taosi site museum, Lotus Town and Longshuyu, among the attractions of a themed tourist route through Xiangfen.

rows.name: Yingli Thousand Buddha Grottoes
rows.summary: A group of Buddhist rock-cut grottoes on a cliff above Yingli village, just east of Xiangning county town, carved between the Northern Qi and the Tang dynasty. They were listed as a provincial site in 1996 and as a national monument in 2019.

rows.name: Yonghe Confucian Temple
rows.summary: The Dacheng Hall of Yonghe's Confucian temple, a Ming-dynasty building in the old county town on Dongmen Lane off Zhenggou Street. It became a provincial monument in 2004 and a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Yuhuang Temple, Hongtong
rows.summary: A village temple founded in 1229 of which only the rear courtyard survives, with three halls of the Yuan period standing side by side: the Jade Emperor Hall, the Guan Gong Hall and the Erlang Hall. The Jade Emperor Hall keeps fragments of Yuan wall paintings.

rows.name: Yunqiu Mountain
rows.summary: A mountain scenic area in Xiangning County, rated 5A in 2020, with a total area of 210 sq km, a core visiting zone of 35 sq km and a highest point of 1,629 m. Visitors come for its ice caves, the old village of Tar'erpo and the cave-dwelling courtyards of Kangjiaping, and the area hosts an annual trail-running race and a yearly culture festival. It was named a national civilised-tourism demonstration unit in 2024.

rows.name: Zhaigeta Wellness Area, Fushan
rows.summary: A health-and-wellness resort area in Zhaigeta township, in the hills east of Fushan county town. Shanxi media reported in 2023 that, helped by the building of southern Shanxi's wellness cluster, it had become a leisure destination for visitors from neighbouring provinces, and that it held food and farm-produce events over the autumn holiday. It is a modern resort development rather than a historic site.

rows.name: Zhusheng Temple, Huozhou
rows.summary: A temple in the old centre of Huozhou, on Qianjin Street, with buildings from the Yuan to the Qing dynasties. It was listed as a provincial site in 2004 and as a national monument in 2019.

rows.name: Anguo Temple, Lishi
rows.summary: A hillside temple compound in a forested valley of Wuya Mountain, west of central Lüliang, founded in 637 under the Tang as Anji Temple and renamed in the Song dynasty. The buildings are Ming and Qing, with a main hall holding three Buddha figures about 4.8 m high, a two-storey copper-pagoda tower, a bell and drum tower, and a cliffside villa built in the Yongzheng period by the grandson of Yu Chenglong. Yu Chenglong, a Qing governor-general known for his integrity, studied here before taking office, and the temple is now run as a clean-governance education site.

rows.name: Baima Xiandong Cave
rows.summary: A cave on Jiufeng Hill at Donggou village in Wucheng town, south-east of Lishi, set among wooded hills. The Lüliang government says about 1,000 m of the cave is developed, with a drop of more than 260 m from the mouth to the lowest developed point, and its walls carry inscriptions dated 1121, 1337 and 1406 that mostly record rain prayers and exploration. Stalactites and other limestone formations line the passages, and the cave was a traditional place for rain-making rites.

rows.name: Central Rear Committee Site, Shuangta
rows.name_zh: 临县中央后委机关旧址
rows.summary: A group of former Party offices and residences in Shuangta village, Sanjiao town, where the Party's Central Rear Committee was based in 1947–48. The Lüliang government lists the former Central Foreign Affairs Group office, the Secretariat's special accounts office and the residences used by Mao Zedong, Ye Jianying, Yang Shangkun and Deng Yingchao. There is an exhibition room on site, and the county counts it among its three national classic red-tourism sites.

rows.name: Cisheng Temple, Xiaoyi
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Suzhuang village, now part of Xiaoyi's built-up area, founded in the Jin dynasty and expanded and repaired in the Ming and Qing periods. The city government says the compound keeps old buildings from the Ming dynasty onwards and Ming-dynasty statues. Central-government conservation funds paid for repairs there in 2018.

rows.name: Dadonggou Forest Scenic Area
rows.summary: A forest leisure area in the Guandi Mountains in Xinyi town, in the hills north-east of Lishi, where the road climbs past Qiannian village into birch woods along a stream below Guji Mountain. It began operating in May 2023 and is laid out mainly for camping, with several camps, capsule-cabin lodging, forest-wellness activities and a restaurant, and in 2023 it was named a national forest-wellness pilot site. It suits a day trip or a camping night from Lüliang.

rows.name: Dawu Drum Tower
rows.summary: A Ming-dynasty drum tower in Dawu town, in the south of Fangshan county, in the area now being built up as Lüliang's new district. The Fangshan government's tourism notes call it finely built, and it is one of the county's listed sights alongside Mount Beiwudang. It became a provincial protected site in 1986 and a national one in 2019.

rows.name: Donglongguan Tombs
rows.summary: A cemetery of Song and Jin dynasty tombs at Donglongguan village in Yangcheng town, about 300 m long, where 27 tombs were excavated in 2008 ahead of road building: 16 with brick chambers and 11 cut into the earth, in hexagonal, octagonal and square plans. The Fenyang government says the brick carving, painted decoration and murals in the chambers are well preserved, and the finds included pottery, porcelain, ironwork and coins. It was listed nationally in 2013.

rows.name: Dongyue Temple, Xingdongyuan
rows.summary: A village temple to the Dongyue (Eastern Peak) god at Xingdongyuan in Longjiao township, Shilou county, laid out on a north-west to south-east axis of about 35 by 65 m with a screen wall, gate, opera stage and main hall. The main hall is original Jin-dynasty timber, three bays wide, with a hip-gable roof of yellow, green and blue glazed tiles added in the Ming or Qing and about 36 m² of late-Ming murals inside; the other buildings are Ming and Qing, with repairs recorded in 1338 and 1641. It has been a national protected site since 2001.

rows.name: Fan'an Temple Pagoda, Shangxian
rows.summary: A seven-storey octagonal brick pagoda about 40 m high at Shangxian village, also called the Shangxian Pagoda, hollow inside with an arched doorway on each floor. It stands directly on the ground without a foundation platform or a finial, which local accounts call a pagoda without a base; inscriptions inside date it to the Song dynasty, and it was repaired under the Ming and again in 2017-2019. The village has built a small rural tourism area around it, with fruit-picking in season.

rows.name: Fenjiu Culture Scenic Area, Xinghuacun
rows.summary: A liquor-heritage visitor area built around the Fenjiu distillery in Xinghuacun town, the home of Fenjiu, a light-aroma Chinese grain spirit. The sights include the Fenjiu Museum, a workshop rebuilt in Ming–Qing style, the aged-liquor cellars and the distillery gardens. It also includes the Old Workshop, a courtyard complex with six surviving late-Qing buildings and an old well, which is a national monument and where liquor is still made by traditional methods.

rows.name: Former Jinsui Daily Office, Gaojiacun
rows.summary: The former office of the Jinsui Daily, the newspaper of the Jinsui Border Region, in Gaojiacun village, where the writers Ma Feng and Xi Rong wrote the novel Heroes of Lüliang. The national heritage list dates its use to 1940–49, and in 2025 the village was being developed as a rural-tourism village under a conservation plan for the border-region sites that the county approved.

rows.name: Former Residence of Yu Chenglong
rows.summary: The family home of Yu Chenglong (1617-1684), a Qing official who rose to governor-general of the Lower Yangtze provinces and whom the Kangxi emperor praised as the most incorruptible in the empire. Three courtyards of the early Qing survive at Laibao village, the homes of his father, his elder brother and himself, restored in 2014 and shown with period scenes and exhibits as part of the Yu Chenglong Clean Governance Culture Park. Laibao is a listed historic and cultural village, and the site is also used as an education base for officials.

rows.name: Guandi Temple, Fenyang
rows.summary: A temple to Guan Yu, the Three Kingdoms general worshipped as a god of loyalty and war, in the southern part of Fenyang's old centre, built in 1515 in the Ming dynasty and popularly known as the Iron Horse Guan Yu Temple. It has two courtyards, with an offering hall, a main hall and a rear hall decorated with Ming glazed ridge ornaments, and a pair of Ming glazed lions. The temple has housed Fenyang Museum since 1997, and the museum opened a new building at Xinghuacun in 2025.

rows.name: Guashan Tianning Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple complex on Gua Mountain, 3 km from Jiaocheng, which the county government dates to 627 and describes as a major Huayan temple of the Tang dynasty. The Stone Buddha Hall was founded in the early Tang, and the Ming and Qing periods added a Holy Mother temple, a shrine hall, a Wenchang palace and an academy. The hill is also known for its ancient cypresses, which grow out of the cliff faces.

rows.name: Heichashan April 8 Martyrs' Memorial
rows.name_zh: 黑茶山四八烈士纪念地
rows.summary: A memorial museum at the foot of Mount Heicha in Xing county, built for the people killed when a flight from Chongqing to Yan'an crashed into the mountain in fog on 8 April 1946. Those killed included the Communist Party figures Wang Ruofei, Qin Bangxian (Bo Gu) and Deng Fa and the New Fourth Army commander Ye Ting. The halls hold portraits, biographies and stone memorial tablets, a pavilion marks the crash site on the summit, and a separate martyrs' cemetery for the Jinsui area lies at the south-west foot of the mountain.

rows.name: Houtu Shengmu Temple, Fenyang
rows.summary: A temple to Houtu, the Earth Mother goddess, at Tian village north-west of Fenyang, rebuilt in 1549 in the Ming dynasty, of which the main hall and a side hall survive. The hall walls hold Ming murals of about 60 sq m, a banquet and music scene on the rear wall and processions on the side walls, painted in heavy colour with gilded relief lines. Fenyang's tourism bureau names it, with Taifu Daoist Temple, among the city's heritage sites noted for murals and relief sculpture.

rows.name: Houtu Shengmu Temple, Shilou
rows.summary: A temple to the earth goddess Houtu Shengmu on the hillside at Dianshan, about 2.5 km south-west of Zhangjiahe village, in the hills of Shilou county; the national list dates it to the Ming and Qing dynasties. The Ministry of Culture and Tourism's route page describes a compound of about 1,500 m² facing south, with a gate, an opera stage and a main hall built of brick and stone without beams, three bays wide with a timber porch, which holds five Ming clay figures. It became a provincial protected site in 2004 and a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Hujiagou Brick Pagoda
rows.summary: A 12 m octagonal brick pagoda of the Ming dynasty at Hujiagou village in Caijiaya township, standing on a three-tier stone base. The tower is solid; its eaves imitate timber brackets and rafters, and the window frames and balustrades carry brick relief of flowers, figures and insects. It became a provincial protected site in 2004 and a national one in 2019.

rows.name: Jiajiazhuang Village Tourist Area
rows.name_zh: 贾家庄文化生态旅游区
rows.summary: A tourist area built around Jiajiazhuang, a village north-east of Fenyang that was a national model for agriculture from the 1950s to the 1970s and has since turned to rural tourism. Its main street, Jia Street, opened in 2016: it is 533 m long with 240 shopfronts, including snack stalls, a bar street and an art corridor, built in old-street style on the old village site. The wider area adds folk-custom, farming-culture and Party-history themes.

rows.name: Jinlong Mountain Scenic Area
rows.summary: A hillside complex of Buddhist and Daoist shrines at Xiatujing village, west of Xiaoyi, built around the site of an old Dragon King temple on the hilltop. Its listed sights include the Chongxiao Temple, a large Guanyin statue, the Wenchang Pavilion, a stepped approach called the Eighteen Steps of the Blue Cloud and the Jinlong Spring, and the site mixes Buddhist, Daoist and local filial-piety culture.

rows.name: Jinsui Border Region Memorial Hall, Caijiaya
rows.summary: A memorial museum at Caijiaya village in Xing county, set in the compound that was the seat of the Jinsui Border Region government and military headquarters during the war against Japan and the civil war. Displays cover the border region's history, and the preserved buildings include the residences used by Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Ren Bishi and He Long, the hall of the 1948 Jinsui cadres' conference and the Six Willows Pavilion. Mao, Zhou and Ren stopped at Caijiaya in March 1948, and Mao addressed the conference there.

rows.name: Jinsui Branch Bureau Site, Beipo
rows.name_zh: 北坡中共中央晋绥分局旧址
rows.pinyin: Běipō Zhōnggòng Zhōngyāng Jìnsuí Fēnjú Jiùzhǐ
rows.summary: A former Party regional headquarters in Beipo village, about 1 km west-north-west of the Caijiaya memorial hall, where the Jinsui Branch Bureau of the Party's Central Committee worked in the 1940s. It is a hillside group of Qing-dynasty cave dwellings, 53 of which survive, restored from 2015 as part of the village's red-tourism project. Bureau secretary Lin Feng and deputy secretary Zhang Jiafu were among those who lived here.

rows.name: Joint Defence Army Headquarters Site, Shayuan
rows.name_zh: 临县陕甘宁晋绥联防军指挥部旧址
rows.pinyin: Línxiàn Shǎngānníng Jìnsuí Liánfángjūn Zhǐhuībù Jiùzhǐ
rows.summary: A former military headquarters in Shayuan village, Linjiaping town, dated to 1947 in the national heritage list and associated with the Shaan-Gan-Ning and Jin-Sui Joint Defence Army. The Linxian government counts it among the county's three national classic red-tourism sites, alongside the Central Rear Committee site and the Party Northwest Bureau site at Nangeda.

rows.name: Longtian Tudi Temple, Baicaopo
rows.summary: A small one-courtyard temple at Baicaopo village in Yudaohe town, with an opera stage, an offering hall and the main Dragon King hall on one axis and three side halls. Inscriptions date the main hall to the Jin dynasty with rebuilding under the Yuan, while the stage and offering hall are Qing, and the Fenyang government describes the site as intact. It has been a national protected site since 2013.

rows.name: Mount Beiwudang
rows.summary: A mountain scenic area in Fangshan county, in the Lüliang range, which is a national-level scenic area and one of northern China's Daoist holy mountains. The county government gives its area as 88 sq km, of which fewer than 20 sq km are open, with 72 peaks, 36 cliffs and 24 ravines; visitors climb a stepped path of about 1,455 steps past ancient pines and rock formations to the temples on the summit, and there are also 5.5 km of wooden walkways. A temple fair is held in the first days of the third lunar month.

rows.name: Nancun City Site (Zuoguocheng)
rows.summary: The ruins of a walled hill city on the ridge east of Nancun village in Yukou town, identified by the county government as Zuoguocheng, the base of the Xiongnu leader Liu Yuan, and dated by the national list from the Warring States period to the Jin dynasty. The defences form an inner city, an outer city and an east city on the ridge; the north-west part survives only as broken wall stumps, while the rammed-earth wall bases in the south-east are largely intact. Emergency stabilisation of the walls has been completed, and a small exhibition hall on Xiongnu culture is planned beside the site but not yet funded.

rows.name: Sanhuang Temple, Xiaoyi
rows.summary: A temple to the Three Sovereigns of Chinese legend, Fuxi, Shennong and the Yellow Emperor, who are honoured together in one hall in Jiajiazhuang village on the western edge of Xiaoyi. The Sanhuang Hall keeps its Yuan-dynasty structure and the other surviving buildings are Qing, including a side hall and an opera stage; the temple was repaired in 2005. It stands on the village's old merchants' road, which is about 1,200 m long and once had 13 large inns for carts and horses.

rows.name: Shanqing Temple
rows.summary: A small Buddhist temple at Fudi village in Dayu township, south of Linxian town, founded in 583 and rebuilt in 1269 under the Yuan dynasty. The Yuan main hall survives, five bays wide with an overhanging gable roof, together with the gate, side halls and galleries in a compound of about 1,200 sq m. The Lüliang government's overview of religion described it in 2017 as one of the city's better-preserved temples, with resident monks.

rows.name: Shanshenyu Thousand Buddha Grotto
rows.summary: A temple built around a grotto cut into the sandstone hillside at Shanshenyu village, which the county government dates to the Yuan dynasty. The main hall is the grotto itself, about 5.5 m deep, with a seated Shakyamuni figure and roughly a thousand small Buddha figures carved in niches around the walls. The two courtyards in front, with a gate, a passage hall and a nine-bay building, are Ming or Qing, and an 11 m Qing pagoda stands beside the temple.

rows.name: Shengxi Lake Forest Park
rows.summary: A large city park in Xiaoyi laid out around a lake, which Shanxi named a five-star urban park in 2013. Its design draws on Suzhou-style gardens, with lotus gardens, lakeside paths, pavilions and bridges, a gallery on filial-piety themes and a children's amusement area. It adjoins the Xiaohe wetland park to the west.

rows.name: Shushifo Cliff Carvings
rows.summary: A group of Buddhist rock carvings on a cliff near Shushifo village in the northern hills of Jiaocheng county, which the national list dates from the Northern Qi to the Tang dynasty. The village now belongs to Tianning town, having been part of Lingdi township until 2021. The carvings became a provincial protected site in 1996 and a national one in 2019.

rows.name: Taifu Daoist Temple
rows.summary: A Daoist temple at Shangmiao village in Xinghuacun town, where inscriptions record the founding of the altar in 1200 in the Jin dynasty. The main hall, dedicated to the Jade Emperor, keeps its Jin-dynasty structure and the other halls are Ming; inside are painted clay figures, relief ("hanging") sculpture and a full set of murals of the deities' homage procession. Local media describe it as the most complete Daoist complex of the Jin to Qing periods in western Shanxi, and Fenyang runs it as a visitor site with guided visits.

rows.name: Tianqi Temple, Xiaoyi
rows.summary: A village temple at Zhongwangtun in Wutong town, south-east of Xiaoyi, which the city's heritage register dates to the Yuan dynasty and the national list to the Yuan and Qing periods. It is one of four national monuments in Xiaoyi, and central-government conservation funds paid for repairs there in 2018.

rows.name: Tianzhen Daoist Temple
rows.summary: A Daoist temple built into the slope of Fengshan, a hill on the northern edge of Lishi, in upper and lower courtyards. It honours the Song-dynasty Daoist Chen Tuan and was rebuilt in the Ming dynasty; the surviving halls include the double-eaved Jade Emperor Tower and the Chen Tuan Hall, which holds a Ming mural of the palaces of Wudang Mountain. A temple fair held here around the 26th day of the first lunar month is on the provincial intangible heritage list.

rows.name: Wenfeng Pagoda, Fenyang
rows.summary: A 13-storey octagonal brick pagoda about 85 m high, on the south-eastern edge of Fenyang and part of the Wenhu Cultural Park, built at the end of the Ming dynasty on the initiative of a local scholar-official to improve the town's feng shui. Its interior holds a Guanyin figure on the ground floor and the twelve zodiac animals on the upper floors, and the Fenyang government's tourism page ranks it first among Chinese brick pagodas by height. It appears in Jia Zhangke's 2015 film Mountains May Depart.

rows.name: Wuyue Temple, Fenyang
rows.summary: A village temple to the Five Sacred Mountains at Beiyuyuan village, Sanquan town, west of Fenyang. A temple inscription records a rebuilding in 1299 and the addition of the Water Immortal Hall in 1300, and the Wuyue Hall and Water Immortal Hall are still Yuan-dynasty buildings with Yuan murals, while the other halls are Ming and Qing. The Water Immortal Hall also keeps a Yuan brick altar.

rows.name: Xiangyan Temple, Liulin
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in the north of Liulin county town, founded in the Tang dynasty, whose surviving buildings are of several dynasties, mainly Jin, Yuan and Ming. The main hall is of the Jin period, and the Heavenly Kings, Vairocana and Ten Kings halls and others are Yuan, which the Lüliang government's tourism page sums up as one Jin and seven Yuan halls. The temple was conserved in 2003–04 and has been open to visitors since.

rows.name: Xiaohe National Wetland Park
rows.summary: A wetland park around a reservoir on the Xiao River on the western side of Xiaoyi, with a planned area of 5.47 sq km of which about 3.28 sq km is water. It has reed beds, lotus and water-lily ponds that flower in summer, and long wooden boardwalks, and it is a stopping place for migratory birds in spring. It adjoins Shengxi Lake Forest Park to the east.

rows.name: Xuanzhong Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in the Shibi valley that Chinese and Japanese Buddhists regard as the ancestral temple of the Pure Land school, founded in 472 in the Northern Wei period according to the Lüliang government. The monks Tanluan, Daochuo and Shandao taught here, and Japanese Pure Land delegations have come to pay their respects since the 1950s. The main halls are Ming and later, including the Hall of the Heavenly Kings rebuilt in 1605, and a Song-dynasty brick pagoda, the Qiurong Pagoda, stands on a hilltop to the south-east.

rows.name: Yiju Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple at Zaogeda village in Sanjiao town, on a hillside beside a river, which was formerly called the Fotang Temple and served as a branch of the Tiangong Temple; the county government gives its area as 56,000 sq m. The axis runs from a Ming gate and front hall to a Yuan-dynasty main hall and a Qing sutra library, with a cave shrine, the Wanfo Cave, at the rear. The county counts it with Qikou as one of its two 4A scenic areas.

rows.name: Yukou Shengmu Temple
rows.summary: A village temple to the Holy Mother at Yukou in the Yudaohe valley, built around 1307 under the Yuan dynasty judging by an inscription on a gate stone, and repaired in 2006–08. The main hall and a side hall are Yuan, the Holy Mother hall and side halls Ming, and the rest Qing, in a two-courtyard layout with a three-cave gate and a small Lü Dongbin shrine above it. It is one of the sights listed for the Yudaohe scenic area.

rows.name: Yuxu Palace, Liulin
rows.summary: A Daoist temple on the hillside of Baoning Hill at Qinglong, just east of Liulin county town, dedicated to the god Zhenwu (Xuantian Shangdi) and first built in 1600 under the Ming dynasty, with a repair in 1654. The main hall holds a Zhenwu statue over 3 m high under a roof ridge of coloured glass, glazed dragon plaques are set into the screen walls at either end, and a shrine to the Holy Mother stands at the top of the hill. It has been a national protected site since 2013.

rows.name: Zetian Temple, Wenshui
rows.summary: A temple at Nanxu village, north of Wenshui, dedicated to Wu Zetian, whose family came from Wenshui; the county tourism page calls it the only temple to the empress in China. The main hall was rebuilt in 1145 under the Jin dynasty on a Tang foundation and has a sculpted dragon hanging above its shrine, and the compound now serves as the Wu Zetian Memorial Hall, with side halls of exhibits and a corridor of inscribed steles. It was listed nationally in 1996.

rows.name: Zhongyang Tower, Xiaoyi
rows.summary: A four-storey timber tower with a passage through its base, standing over the crossroads in the old town of Xiaoyi, with four tiers of eaves and a cross-gabled roof of coloured glazed tiles. The present building dates from 1909, after a lightning fire in 1868 and an earlier earthquake collapse, on a site where a tower has stood since the Han-Wei period according to the city's tourism page. The same page calls it the largest and best-preserved tower of its kind in the Jinzhong and Lüliang area, and the painted ceiling over the ground floor shows scenes from classic novels.

rows.name: Baoning Temple, Youyu
rows.summary: A Ming-dynasty temple in Youwei, an old garrison town in north-west Shanxi, founded in 1460 and added to the national list in 2019. Only two halls remain, the Tianwang (Heavenly Kings) hall and a seven-bay main hall, and the temple's 136 water-and-land ritual paintings, usually dated to the Ming, are now kept in the Shanxi Museum in Taiyuan. The paintings mix Buddhist and Daoist deities with scenes of everyday life.

rows.name: Chongfu Temple, Shuozhou
rows.summary: A large Buddhist monastery in the middle of Shuozhou, founded in the Tang dynasty and best known for its two Jin-dynasty halls, the Mituo Hall of 1143 and the Guanyin Hall. The Mituo Hall keeps its Jin glazed roof tiles and wall paintings, and the other halls line the central axis, from the entrance hall and the bell and drum towers through the Thousand Buddha Pavilion to the main hall. Visitor numbers rose after the 2024 video game Black Myth: Wukong brought attention to the monastery.

rows.name: Guangwu Great Wall
rows.summary: A stretch of Ming-dynasty Great Wall on the hills above New Guangwu village in Shanyin County, running east towards Yanmen Pass; this card stands for the Shanxi sections of the Great Wall in the national listing. The surveyed core of the wall is about 5 km long, and it is regarded as one of the better-preserved brick-faced Ming sections in China, with watchtowers along the ridge. The best-known spot is the Moon Gate, a brick archway left when a watchtower partly collapsed; footpaths and a visitor centre have been built, and farmhouse restaurants have opened in the nearby villages.

rows.name: Guangwu Han Tombs
rows.summary: A large Han-dynasty cemetery on open ground north of the villages of Old and New Guangwu, where several hundred earth burial mounds still stand above ground. The tombs opened so far include Western Han shaft graves with wooden chambers and Eastern Han brick-chambered tombs. It makes a short stop on a trip to the nearby Guangwu Great Wall and fortress.

rows.name: Jingtu Temple, Yingxian
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in the north-east corner of Ying County town, known locally as the North Temple and founded in 1124 under the Jin dynasty; only its main hall survives. The Jin-dynasty timber hall is known for its richly decorated ceiling, with nine coffered caisson vaults. It stands about 500 m east of the Yingxian Wooden Pagoda and is run as a visitor site alongside it.

rows.name: Jinshatan Ancient Battlefield
rows.summary: A themed park outside Huairen built around the folk story of the Yang family generals' legendary battle against the Liao at Jinshatan, the 'Golden Sand Beach'. It has reconstructions of a Song army camp gate and tents, a general's review platform with a group of stone figures of the Yang family, a hall for the family, a peony garden, and the Tianmen Array, a labyrinth with an underground section. Visitors can also try archery and period costume, and the park suits families and school groups interested in the story.

rows.name: Old Guangwu Fortress
rows.summary: A Ming frontier fortress town in Old Guangwu village, a few kilometres from Yanmen Pass, whose rectangular earth walls, faced with brick in the Ming rebuilding, still enclose the village. There are gate towers on the east, south and west sides, and a lived-in village of courtyard houses inside the walls. It lies about 2 km west-north-west of the Moon Gate on the Guangwu Great Wall, so the two are easily combined.

rows.name: Ashoka Pagoda, Jinyuan
rows.summary: A brick lama-style stupa about 25 m high, the only survivor of Huiming Temple, which once stood in the old city of Jinyang. A bell-shaped dome on a square stone base carries a cone of 13 rings and a glazed finial; the present pagoda was rebuilt in 1385 in the Ming on the site of a Sui-dynasty pagoda of 602. Local tradition ranked it among the eight views of the old Taiyuan county town, as 'the ancient pagoda against the sky'.

rows.name: Baoyuan Old Vinegar Workshop
rows.summary: A vinegar workshop and museum rebuilt in 2006 by a local vinegar company in Qingxu, the county titled China's vinegar capital. Its halls reproduce the Ming and Qing way of making vinegar with period tools and costume, alongside exhibits on farming and vinegar culture, and visitors can taste vinegars of different ages. It suits visitors interested in Shanxi's food traditions.

rows.name: Buer Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist hall dismantled and re-erected in 1987–89 in Yangqu county town from Xiaozhiyu village, where it first stood. Inscriptions on the ridge beam show that the three-bay Sansheng Hall was first built in 956 under the Northern Han and restored in 1195 under the Jin, and it keeps nine painted clay figures of the Ming, with Samantabhadra on the Buddha's left and Manjusri on his right, the reverse of the usual order. Ming murals of about 80 sq m cover the side walls, and a Ming sutra pillar and a Yuan brick pagoda stand in front.

rows.name: Changjing Tower
rows.summary: A two-storey Ming building in the old city, named for the announcement of the top five candidates in the Five Classics at the provincial examination. The tower, a connecting passage, a rear hall and the Chunqiu pavilion form an I-shaped group roofed in peacock-blue glazed tile. It is run as part of the Guandi Temple Museum, with a long-term exhibition on the imperial examination.

rows.name: China Coal Museum
rows.summary: A national first-grade museum on the history of coal, opened in 1989 on the western side of Taiyuan. Its Coal Sea Exploration area has seven themed halls on how coal forms and how it has been mined and used, a four-dimensional cinema and a full-scale simulated mine where visitors wear miners' helmets and try out mining equipment. It suits families and anyone curious about Shanxi's coal industry.

rows.name: Chongshan Temple
rows.summary: A royal temple built by Zhu Gang, Prince of Jin, in memory of his mother and completed in 1391, which was almost wholly burnt down in 1864 and now covers about a forty-sixth of its original area. The survivor is the Dabei Hall, about 20 m high with a double-eave roof, whose three Ming clay bodhisattvas, 8.3 m high, include a Thousand-armed Guanyin; an iron bell of 1506 hangs in the bell tower and a pair of Ming iron lions flank the gate. The temple is the seat of the Shanxi Buddhist Association and keeps a large collection of Song-to-Ming printed sutras.

rows.name: Chunyang Palace, Taiyuan
rows.summary: A Taoist temple dedicated to Lü Dongbin (Chunyang), called the largest and best preserved in Taiyuan by the city government, founded in the late Song or early Yuan and greatly enlarged in 1597 by the Princes of Jin. Five courtyards climb from a wooden pailou and the Daode Gate to the Ming Lüzu Hall and a Jiugong Bagua courtyard laid out on the eight-trigrams plan, with caves and pavilions in the upper courtyards. It now houses the Shanxi Ancient Architecture Museum, whose collection includes steles, statues, painted sculpture and murals.

rows.name: Dawang Temple, Yangqu
rows.summary: A small Ming temple hall of 1467 in Fanzhuang village, known as the Beamless Hall, which served as a shrine to Zhao Wu, the god of Mount Cang in Yu County. The 9.7 m square hall has no inner posts and no cross-bay beam frames: its hip-and-gable roof is carried by tiers of brackets and diagonal corner beams, a structure the county government calls rare in China. Murals of 88 sq m survive on three walls.

rows.name: Donghu Vinegar Garden
rows.summary: A visitor site at a Taiyuan vinegar maker, laid out as a working factory museum on how Shanxi aged vinegar is produced, with displays of both the traditional and the modern process. It has been named a national industrial-tourism demonstration base. It suits visitors interested in Shanxi's best-known condiment and in food heritage.

rows.name: Dou Dafu Temple
rows.summary: A temple to Dou Chou, a minister of the state of Jin in the Spring and Autumn period, at the foot of Mount Erlong beside the Fen River. It covers about 1.7 hectares, with buildings in Yuan style along an axis of Qing-dynasty theatre pavilion, gate, offering hall and main hall, where a seated statue of Dou Chou stands. The Lieshi cold spring below the temple, dry from the 1980s, was restored and reopened in 2021.

rows.name: Duofu Temple
rows.summary: A hill temple near the top of Mount Jueweishan, founded in 786 in the Tang dynasty and rebuilt in the early Ming. Its main hall holds Ming painted clay figures of three Buddhas and four bodhisattvas and 84 wall paintings of the Buddha's earlier lives. The scholar Fu Shan, who lived through the Ming–Qing transition, studied in a cave beside the temple, and the slopes around it are known for autumn colour.

rows.name: Fen River Scenic Area
rows.summary: A 43 km riverside park along the Fen River through Taiyuan, running from the low-water bridge at Shanlan in the north to about 2 km beyond Yingbin Bridge in the south and crossed by 24 bridges. North of Shengli Bridge about 17 km is natural wetland, while the 26 km to the south is a landscaped reservoir stretch; the park has two riverside cycle lanes, more than 40 cultural features and 165 recorded bird species. It suits a walk or a bike ride rather than a single visit point.

rows.name: Former Shanxi Daxuetang (Shanxi University Hall)
rows.summary: The surviving 1904 building of Shanxi Daxuetang, the forerunner of Shanxi University, founded in 1902 with Boxer Indemnity funds at the suggestion of the British missionary Timothy Richard and, by the Taiyuan government's account, the third university in China after those of Beijing and Tianjin. The two-storey Western Learning College building has a Gothic-style castle façade and a square clock tower, combined with a Chinese-style parapet. It is now a school building.

rows.name: Gao Junyu Former Residence and Memorial Hall
rows.summary: The family home of Gao Junyu, an early Communist Party leader who founded the party and youth organisations in Shanxi, in Fenglingdi village, Loufan County. The residence is the middle courtyard of the old Gao family compound, a Qing-dynasty brick cave-dwelling house restored and opened in 1996, where he lived and studied until he was 16. A memorial hall beside it covers his career and the history of Loufan as a revolutionary base area.

rows.name: Grand Guandi Temple, Taiyuan
rows.summary: A temple to Guan Yu that the museum running it calls the largest and best preserved in Taiyuan, with Ming buildings on Jin-Yuan foundations arranged in two courtyards: the Chongning Hall, where Guan Yu sits in imperial dress, and behind it the two-storey Chunqiu Tower, with bell and drum towers and side halls. It was included in China's World Heritage tentative list in 2019 as Taiyuan's only nomination point on the Great Tea Road. It is run by the Guandi Temple Museum, which holds changing exhibitions on Guan Yu, the Shanxi merchants and local history.

rows.name: Hutu Temple
rows.summary: A temple to Hu Tu, a minister of the state of Jin in the Spring and Autumn period, venerated locally as a rain god. Founded in 1123 and rebuilt in the Yuan and Ming, it has a wide Ming offering hall whose side walls carry Qing murals of the god's rain procession and his return, a rear hall with clay figures of Hu Tu and his wife, and steles of the Yuan to Qing periods in the courtyards. The temple lies at the foot of Ma'an Mountain, and its front opera stage burnt down in 1983.

rows.name: Immaculate Conception Cathedral, Taiyuan
rows.summary: The cathedral of the Catholic diocese of Taiyuan, founded by Jesuits in 1635 and rebuilt after the earlier church was destroyed in 1900; the present building was completed in 1905. It is a Romanesque Revival church in rust-red brick with two bell towers about 36 m tall, standing on Jiefang Road among former church buildings. It was listed as a national monument in 2013.

rows.name: Jin Merchants Museum (Former Shanxi Military Governor's Office)
rows.summary: The compound of the Qing governor's office, where the Shanxi military government was set up in 1911 and where Yan Xishan later governed as military governor; it served as the seat of the provincial government until 2017. The surviving buildings include a two-storey gate tower, the Zixing Hall, now the Meishan conference hall, and a small artificial hill topped by a Gothic-style clock tower rebuilt in 1952. Since 2020 the compound has housed the Jin Merchants Museum, with exhibition zones on the origins of the Shanxi merchants, their draft banks, long-distance trade and family traditions.

rows.name: Jingyin Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple below Mount Jueweishan whose founding date is uncertain; a plaque of 930 is recorded, and it was rebuilt in 1205 under the Jin and repaired several times in the Ming and Qing. Its Great Buddha Pavilion is set into the hillside and holds an earthen Buddha more than 9 m high with two attendant bodhisattvas, inside a niche about 10 m high. Old cypresses grow in the grounds, and the temple faces Dou Dafu Temple across the Fen River valley.

rows.name: Jinyang Ancient City Site
rows.summary: The site of Jinyang, a walled city founded in the late Spring and Autumn period that later became a northern capital under the Tang and the Five Dynasties, until Song forces burned and flooded it in 979. The city covered about 20 sq km and is now mostly farmland and villages, but excavated remains are shown in a national archaeological site park. Its museum, opened in January 2024, displays nearly 1,000 finds such as stone Buddhas, roof ornaments and fragments of a Diamond Sutra stele.

rows.name: Jinyuan Confucian Temple
rows.summary: The Confucian temple of the Ming county town of Taiyuan, founded in 1373 and the only national-level monument inside the restored walled town of Jinyuan. Its Ming core runs along one axis from a pailou gate and a rectangular pond with a stone bridge to the Dacheng Gate and the five-bay Dacheng Hall, with galleries and a shrine to local worthies at the sides. The town walls, 3,700 m round and 11 m high, were rebuilt and reopened in 2021, and the temple sits among restored shops, temples and houses.

rows.name: Kaihua Temple, Xinzhuang
rows.summary: A village temple in Xinzhuang in the hills of Gaocun township, laid out from a gate hall and a Heavenly Kings hall to the main hall, with a Thousand Buddha hall and Guanyin and Ksitigarbha halls on either side. The county government describes the three-bay main hall, with a glazed-edged overhanging gable roof and double-bracket sets, as a Song-Jin style building moved here in 1141–49. It holds eleven painted clay figures, including the three bodies of the Buddha, bodhisattvas, disciples and guardians, and the hall plaque is in the calligraphy of the Buddhist leader Zhao Puchu.

rows.name: Liuweizhai Yunmengwu
rows.summary: The visitor area of the Liuweizhai food-factory park in Qingxu County, run by a Taiyuan food company founded in 1738 that is known for cooked meats. It combines factory viewing, a company history museum, hands-on food making, tasting, gardens and outdoor barbecue and camping areas, and it has been named a national industrial-tourism demonstration base. It suits families and study groups.

rows.name: Longquan Temple, Taishan
rows.summary: A mountain temple on Mount Tai (Taishan) in the Fengyu valley, founded in 710 under the Tang and rebuilt in the Ming and Qing, of which only the lower of its three original courtyards survives. It is known for the octagonal Guanyin Hall with its suspended clay sculptures, and for a Tang pagoda crypt found in 2008 that held a nested set of five caskets. The site is run as the Taishan Museum, with a rebuilt reliquary pagoda, a lookout and new temple halls around the old buildings.

rows.name: Longshan Grottoes and Tongzi Temple Site
rows.summary: A small group of nine Taoist cave shrines on the summit of Mount Long, most of them cut from 1234 under the Quanzhen priest Song Defang, with Yuan-dynasty figures of the Three Pure Ones and the Seven Perfected. Many of the statues have lost their heads to theft. Close by are the remains of Tongzi Temple, founded in 556 under the Northern Qi, with a worn cliff-side Buddha relief and a six-sided stone lamp tower about 4 m high, in hills known for lilac in spring and red leaves in autumn.

rows.name: Loufan Ancient City Ruins
rows.summary: The earthen ruins of a walled city of the Loufan people, a northern herding state of the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods that was conquered by the state of Zhao under King Wuling. The Π-shaped walls enclose roughly 1,200 m by 600 m and are cut in two by the Nanchuan River; rammed-earth stretches survive 4 to 11 m high on the eastern side, climbing to a raised platform on Huangdimao hill, the highest point. Survey finds on the surface include cord-marked pottery and roof tiles.

rows.name: Mengshan Giant Buddha
rows.summary: A giant seated Buddha carved into a cliff on Mount Meng from 551 under the Northern Qi, which Taiyuan's heritage pages describe as the largest cliff Buddha of the Northern Dynasties period. The head was lost and the body was found buried in rubble in 1980; a new head 12 m high was added in the 2000s, and the whole figure now stands about 38 m high. The scenic area also has the ruins of Kaihua Temple, two small Song-dynasty brick pagodas known as the Lianli Pagodas and an iron Buddha of the late Sui or early Tang.

rows.name: Mingxiu Temple
rows.summary: A small village temple in Wangguo village, Jinyuan district, nicknamed the glazed-tile temple for its green glazed roofs. Its two courtyards hold a Qing-dynasty front hall and a main hall with Ming gilded clay figures of the three Buddhas, their attendants and about 80 sq m of Ming wall paintings of a thousand Buddhas and Buddhist stories. The gate and the bell and drum towers are modern rebuilds.

rows.name: Peng Zhen Memorial Hall and Former CCP Taiyuan Branch Site
rows.summary: The former Shanxi First Provincial Middle School, set in the old provincial examination compound beside Wenying Lake, where a socialist youth group was formed in 1921 and the Taiyuan branch of the Communist Party, the first party organisation in Shanxi, in 1924. It is now a memorial museum with exhibitions on Peng Zhen, Gao Junyu and He Chang, who studied there, and on the history of the party in Shanxi, including a reconstructed Republic-era classroom. Three rows of Qing-style classrooms and the principal's office from the school stand beside the newer memorial building.

rows.name: Qianfo Temple, Gujiao
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Gujiao named for the more than a thousand small stone Buddhas of Tang date set into the rear wall of its main hall, on 79 panels, each figure about 8 cm high. The Ming main hall was dismantled and re-erected on the present site in 1990 from the north bank of the Fen River, and the gate hall, bell and drum towers and side halls around it are new. It is a modest compound of a single courtyard in the built-up part of Gujiao.

rows.name: Qinglong Ancient Town
rows.summary: A group of Ming- and Qing-style buildings in Qinglong village, Yangqu County, presented as a tourist old town with temples, gardens, an ancestral hall and an underground passage, plus a food street and folk performances. It lies by the road that northern Shanxi towns use to reach Taiyuan. It suits a short stop on a day trip north of the city.

rows.name: Qingyuan Confucian Temple
rows.summary: The Confucian temple of Qingxu, which the Taiyuan government calls the oldest surviving Confucian temple in the city, first built in 1203 under the Jin dynasty. Its Dacheng Hall, a square three-bay building with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof edged in blue glazed tile, keeps the frame and style of the Jin original and is one of the few Jin-period halls in Shanxi. The compound runs back through three courtyards, from three pailou gates and a half-moon pond to the Dacheng Gate, the hall and the Minglun lecture hall.

rows.name: Taiyuan Ancient Mosque
rows.summary: A working mosque in the old city, laid out as two courtyards on an east-west axis in Chinese timber style. Inscriptions date its foundation to the Tang dynasty, but the surviving buildings are Ming and Qing: a gate, a two-storey Ming tower called Xingxin Tower, a lecture hall and a prayer hall with Arabic-style patterns painted on its walls. Two hexagonal pavilions in the front courtyard shelter steles, one carrying a Qing imperial edict protecting Muslims.

rows.name: Taiyuan Botanical Garden
rows.summary: A botanical garden of about 2,730 mu (roughly 1.8 square kilometres) in Jinyuan district, opened in 2020 on land that had held coal depots and polluting factories. It has 25 themed plant gardens, a bonsai hall and three glasshouses under timber domes, the largest spanning 88 m, and part of a former coal-storage pit was turned into a lake. It suits a relaxed half day outdoors.

rows.name: Taiyuan Confucian Temple
rows.summary: The Confucian temple of Taiyuan prefecture, rebuilt in 1882 by the governor Zhang Zhidong on part of the burnt-out Chongshan Temple site after a Fen River flood destroyed the earlier temple. The red-walled compound runs along a central axis through a screen wall, the Lingxing gate, a pond, the Dacheng Gate and Dacheng Hall to a rear shrine hall. It now houses the Shanxi Archaeology Museum, the museum of the provincial institute of archaeology.

rows.name: Taiyuan Forest Park
rows.summary: A city forest park of 224 hectares on the northern edge of central Taiyuan, planned from 1990, with more than 100,000 trees around an artificial lake of 378 mu, an arboretum and a bird garden. The arboretum holds mostly native Shanxi species, and the bird garden keeps brown eared pheasants, peafowl, golden pheasants and ostriches. It suits a walk or picnic close to the city.

rows.name: Taiyuan Zoo
rows.summary: The city zoo of Taiyuan, in the north-east of the city, with about 2,000 animals in zones for birds, tropical and subtropical animals, primates and grassland herbivores. A new zone for medium-sized carnivores and small mammals opened on 1 October 2026, with North China leopards, white lions and red pandas. It suits families with children.

rows.name: Tianlongshan Grottoes
rows.summary: A group of Buddhist cave temples cut into two peaks of Mount Tianlong, begun in the Eastern Wei dynasty in the 6th century and extended through the Northern Qi, Sui and Tang. There are 25 caves with about 500 surviving figures, among them the open-air Cave 9, where a seated Maitreya sits above an eleven-headed Guanyin. Many heads and whole figures were cut away in the early 20th century and are now in museums abroad; a site museum shows a 3D-printed replica of Cave 8 and the head of its main Buddha, which returned from abroad and went on show in 2021.

rows.name: Tiemu'er Pagodas
rows.summary: Three Yuan-dynasty tomb pagodas standing together about 200 m east of Shijiazhuang village. The central stone pagoda, 3 m high with five tiers on an octagonal plan, was built in 1305 for Shi Zhongxian and carries the names of ancestors and a Buddhist sutra text, while the two flanking brick pagodas, three-tier pavilions about 6.5 m high, date from 1350 and 1353 and commemorate his son Yexian Tiemuer and Yexian's brother. Yexian Tiemuer, whose Chinese name was Shi Yanchang, held a Yuan military post in Yunnan.

rows.name: Twin Pagoda Temple
rows.summary: Yongzuo Temple, popularly called the Twin Pagoda Temple, is a Ming-dynasty Buddhist complex in the south-east of Taiyuan whose two octagonal brick pagodas, each of 13 storeys and more than 50 m high, were built between the 1590s and 1612 and appear on the city's emblem. The grounds also hold a brick beamless main hall, a gallery of about 260 steles and peonies that include Ming-dynasty plants. One of the pagodas can be climbed for a view over the city.

rows.name: Xu Xianxiu Tomb and Northern Qi Fresco Museum
rows.summary: A museum built over the Northern Qi tomb of Xu Xianxiu, a senior Northern Qi minister and prince whose 326 sq m of wall paintings were uncovered in 2000–02 and named among China's ten major archaeological finds of 2002. The original murals of a grand procession stay in place on both sides of the tomb passage, and the museum, opened in December 2023, also shows Northern Qi murals from other Shanxi tombs. The Taiyuan government calls it the best-preserved mural tomb of the Northern Dynasties found so far.

rows.name: Xuanquan Temple
rows.summary: A temple built into a cliff on Guanshan beside the Fenhe Second Reservoir, once a family temple of the Ming princes of Jin. Its halls stretch about 150 m along the rock face, from the gate, bell and drum towers and the main hall, which has Ming wall paintings, to a Ksitigarbha hall, a Guanyin hall, a Seven Buddha Cave and a Dragon King hall with relief clay sculpture; several buildings were rebuilt after 1991. A walkway of about 1 km follows the cliff towards the reservoir.

rows.name: Xuanyuan Temple, Yangqu
rows.summary: A village temple to the Yellow Emperor (Xuanyuan) in Xidian village, built on a rise at a road junction and rebuilt in 1537, with Yuan-period inscriptions still visible on the roof frame. Two courtyards run from an opera stage that doubles as the gate, through a Qing offering hall, to the Ming main hall, whose side walls carry twelve seated portraits of famous physicians from the Shang dynasty to the Ming.

rows.name: Yao Temple, Qingxu
rows.summary: A temple to the legendary Emperor Yao inside the old walled town of Yaocheng, where about 200 m of Ming rammed-earth wall still stands. The Yao Hall, a Ming double-eave building, has no beams or inner posts: six tiers of brackets form a caisson ceiling over the statue. Beside it stand a two-storey brick 'beamless' hall with a Guanyin shrine below, an opera stage and a Mother Goddess hall.

rows.name: Zilin Vinegar Park
rows.summary: A vinegar-factory visitor site run by the Zilin vinegar company in Qingxu, the county titled China's vinegar capital, built around a vinegar museum. Taiyuan's authorities list it among the city's industrial-tourism sites and its old-brand museums. It suits visitors interested in Shanxi's vinegar industry.

rows.name: Ayuwang Pagoda
rows.summary: A bottle-shaped brick stupa of about 40 m in the Tibetan Buddhist style, built in 1275 on a round base carved with lotus petals and topped by thirteen rings and a copper gourd-shaped finial. It replaced earlier pagodas on the site, the first a Sui-dynasty timber tower of 601. The architects Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin visited in 1937 and praised its proportions as the best of the surviving bottle-shaped pagodas.

rows.name: Bethune Model Ward, Songyankou
rows.summary: A courtyard in Songyankou village that the Canadian surgeon Norman Bethune had converted from a temple into a model ward for the Eighth Route Army, finished on 15 September 1938. Japanese forces destroyed it soon afterwards and it was rebuilt in 1974 on the original plan, with an operating room in the former Dragon King hall, a sterilisation room and a statue of Bethune. A memorial exhibition hall beside it shows photographs, letters and medical instruments.

rows.name: Bianjing Drum Tower
