rows.summary: A three-storey timber drum tower on a high masonry base at the central crossroads of Daixian's old town, rebuilt in 1476 after a fire destroyed the first tower of 1374. The base is about 13 m high with an arched passage through it, and the tower rises to roughly 40 m with four tiers of eaves and a plaque reading 'First Tower of Yanmen'. It was built for military observation and signalling on the approach to Yanmen Pass, and a steep, narrow stair leads up inside.

rows.name: Daixian Confucian Temple
rows.summary: The Confucian temple of the former Daizhou prefecture, built mainly in the Ming dynasty and called by the Dai County government the largest surviving prefectural Confucian temple in North China. Four courtyards run along a north-south axis from a decorated memorial archway through the Lingxing Gate and a semicircular pool to the seven-bay Dacheng Hall on a white-marble base, with the buildings roofed in peacock-blue glazed tiles. After 1949 the compound was used as a grain store, which helped it survive.

rows.name: Daizhou Ancient City
rows.summary: The walled town of Daixian, the seat of Dai County, whose walls were rebuilt in 1373 and are about 12 m high and 4.3 km round. Four gates once pierced the wall; the west gate tower, a corner tower and 1.2 km of the west wall have been rebuilt, and monuments such as the Bianjing Tower and the Ashoka pagoda stand in the streets inside. State media list Daizhou among the old towns of the Sino-Russian tea road, and Dai County is a national historic and cultural city.

rows.name: Eighth Route Army Headquarters Site, Nanru
rows.summary: The village courtyard in Nanru where the Eighth Route Army headquarters was based from 23 September 1937, its first command post after the army reached the Shanxi front. From here the headquarters sent telegrams and directed operations, issued an instruction on mobilising civilians for guerrilla warfare, and restored the political commissar system that had been dropped when the Red Army was reorganised. The site is now an education site with a display that includes oil paintings and replicas of the communications equipment, and guides on hand.

rows.name: Fanshi Glazed Pagoda
rows.summary: A Ming-dynasty glazed pagoda at Shiziwo in Zhuangzi village, Yantou township, in the mountains south-east of Fanshi, built between 1599 and 1604 as part of the Dahuguo Wenshu Temple. The octagonal brick tower has thirteen tiers and stands about 32 m high, faced with yellow, green and blue glazed bricks. It was listed as a provincial monument in 2004 and as a national one in 2019, and is also known as the Shiziwo Glazed Pagoda.

rows.name: Former Residence of Xu Xiangqian
rows.summary: The Qing-dynasty courtyard house in Yongan village where Xu Xiangqian, who was made a marshal of the People's Liberation Army in 1955, was born and lived. It is a typical northern Shanxi courtyard of brick houses with a two-storey building at the back, restored in the early 1990s and opened to visitors in 1992. Its seven exhibition rooms cover his life, and a separate Marshal Xu Xiangqian Memorial Hall opened in 2011.

rows.name: Former Residence of Yan Xishan, Hebian
rows.summary: A large courtyard compound built from 1913 to 1937 in his home town of Hebian by Yan Xishan, who controlled Shanxi's government and army from 1911 until 1949. The museum's own website counts 27 courtyards and nearly 1,000 rooms, over 700 of them still standing, including the multi-storey Deyi Lou. It has been open as the Hebian Folk Museum since 1989, and the compound was listed as a provincial monument in 1986 and as a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Gongzhu Temple
rows.summary: A three-courtyard temple covering about 4,300 m², named for Princess Chengxin, a daughter of the Northern Wei emperor Wencheng, who is credited with founding it; the present buildings date from a rebuilding in 1503 and from the Qing. The Mahavira Hall and the hall behind the gate are Ming, and the Mahavira Hall has about 90 m² of frescoes and thirty Ming statues. Sakyamuni, Amitabha and the Medicine Buddha sit on the altar, with eighteen arhats along the side walls.

rows.name: Guangji Temple, Wutai
rows.summary: A Yuan-dynasty temple in Taicheng, the county town of Wutai, whose five-bay Mahavira Hall holds Yuan clay statues of a Buddha with two bodhisattvas, three great bodhisattvas and eighteen arhats. A Tang-dynasty sutra pillar stands in front of the hall, and the temple houses the Wutai County Museum and the county heritage office.

rows.name: Guanwang Temple, Dingxiang
rows.summary: A temple to Guan Yu founded in 1123 under the Northern Song, of which a single hall survives, three bays wide under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof. It stands in the grounds of Dingxiang No. 2 Middle School in the county town and was listed as a national heritage site in 2006.

rows.name: Guoyang Confucian Temple
rows.summary: The county Confucian temple of the former Guo County, whose seat was Guoyang town, founded in the Yuan dynasty and once covering nearly 20,000 m². War damage, unrest and decades as a grain depot left it in poor repair, but its main buildings survive, including the Lingxing Gate, the Halberd Gate and the Dacheng Hall. A restoration has since been completed.

rows.name: Hanshan Cultural Park, Fanshi
rows.summary: A hillside cultural tourism park of about 81 hectares in Shahe town, in the north of Fanshi County, on the northern approach to Mount Wutai. The Ministry of Culture and Tourism's rural-tourism route lists an art museum, a former county-government compound, a Hanshan temple and several plazas among its sights, and Shanxi's culture and tourism authorities list it among the province's clean-governance culture sites. It staged an evening 'night-tour carnival' over the 2025 Dragon Boat holiday.

rows.name: Hongfu Temple, Beishe
rows.summary: A walled temple in Beishe village that stands on a raised platform inside a fortress-like wall, with the gate hall doubling as the wall gate. Its Jin-dynasty main hall, the Vairocana Hall, has five bays and oblique brackets, and holds an altar of nine clay statues arranged as the Huayan Three Sages with hanging sculpture on the side walls. The Qing-dynasty east hall has clay figures of Ksitigarbha and the Ten Kings of Hell.

rows.name: Hongfu Temple, Liuhui
rows.summary: A temple of Ming and Qing date in Liuhui village, in Nanwang township of Dingxiang County. It was listed as a provincial monument in 2004 and as a national one in 2019, in the eighth batch. It is a different temple from the Jin-dynasty Hongfu Temple at Beishe, also in Dingxiang County.

rows.name: Hongmenkou Underground Great Wall
rows.summary: A network of narrow defensive tunnels dug in the 20th century around Shuiquan village in Pianguan County and known as the underground Great Wall. Visitors go in through a cave dwelling in an ordinary village courtyard and walk a restored section of more than a kilometre, much of it so low that visitors have to stoop. It lies on the Great Wall Number 1 tourist road, which links it with Great Wall sections and with Laoniuwan on the Yellow River.

rows.name: Huiji Temple, Yuanping
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Lianjiagang village, north-east of Yuanping, whose gate, Manjusri Hall, bell tower and Galan Hall stand around a five-bay Great Buddha Hall. The national list dates the temple Ming to Qing, but the Ministry of Culture and Tourism's 2024 route page describes the Great Buddha Hall as original Song timberwork under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, with a broad brick terrace in front. It became a provincial monument in 1986 and a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Huyuan Riverside Park, Fanshi
rows.summary: A riverside park on the Hutuo River at the southern edge of Fanshi county town, with paths along a broad stretch of water. The Hutuo rises in Fanshi County, which gives the park its name ('source of the Hutuo'), and local people use the banks for evening walks, when coloured lanterns light the water. It is a short urban stroll rather than a major sight.

rows.name: Jindong Temple
rows.summary: A small Buddhist temple founded in 1093 in Xihuyan village, west of Xinzhou, whose corner hall is original Northern Song timberwork with bracketed eaves. The Manjusri hall dates from 1528 and holds a small area of Daoist murals, and a Song-dynasty sutra pillar stands in the courtyard; the other buildings are Qing.

rows.name: Jingju Temple Grottoes
rows.summary: A group of Tang-dynasty rock-cut caves in a cliff beside Fengrun village, south of Jingle. A scholarly survey records nine Tang caves and one Northern Dynasties cave, the largest number of Tang caves at any site in Shanxi. Most are square chambers with a three-Buddha altar against three walls, and donor inscriptions in Caves 4 to 6 date their opening to the reign of Emperor Gaozong.

rows.name: Jingle Confucian Temple
rows.summary: The Confucian temple of the former Jingle County, moved to its present site in the Ming dynasty and rebuilt in 1587, with two courtyards: the temple itself and the Censhan Academy. In the temple courtyard only the Dacheng Hall and its flanking galleries remain, while the academy keeps its Minglun Hall and two side studies. The five-bay Dacheng Hall has a single-eave hipped-gable roof.

rows.name: Laoniuwan, Pianguan
rows.summary: Laoniuwan is the village where the Yellow River enters Shanxi and the Great Wall meets the river, on the border with Inner Mongolia. An old fort stands above the village, and from it the view takes in a long reservoir lake created by the Wanjiazhai dam, below loess hills and Great Wall beacon towers. The Pianguan side is Shanxi's 4A scenic area; a separate scenic area of the same name lies across the river in Inner Mongolia.

rows.name: Luohou Temple
rows.summary: A Tibetan Buddhist temple of the Gelug school in Taihuai, beside Xiantong and Tayuan temples and named for Rahula, the Buddha's son. Founded in the Tang dynasty, rebuilt in the Ming and converted to the Yellow Hat school in 1705, it is laid out in three courtyards, from a Hall of Heavenly Kings with a pair of Tang stone lions to a rear scripture pavilion. The pavilion holds a mechanical lotus that opens to reveal a Buddha.

rows.name: Mimi Temple
rows.summary: A temple on Weiping Mountain, named after Mimi Rock, and one of the temples around Mount Wutai that lie outside the central Taihuai area. It was founded in the Northern Qi dynasty and flourished under the Tang and Song, but most of its surviving buildings are Qing.

rows.name: Mount Luya
rows.summary: The highest peak of the Guancen range in Ningwu County, rising above 2,700 m and named for its stacked peaks that resemble reed shoots. The scenic area protects larch and spruce forest and is a main refuge of the brown eared pheasant, a nationally protected bird, and it counts among the four national forest parks that state media list for Xinzhou. Other sights in the area include a cliff-side walkway, lakes, waterfalls and the Malun grassland, with the ice cave and the Fen River source as separate stops.

rows.name: Nanchan Temple
rows.summary: A small temple whose main hall, dated by a beam inscription to 782, is the oldest surviving timber building in China. The three-bay hall has no interior columns or ceiling and holds a group of painted clay statues of the Tang period on a U-shaped altar. Architectural historians found the hall in 1953 and it was listed as a national monument in 1961.

rows.name: Nanshan Temple, Mount Wutai
rows.summary: A large temple complex climbing the hillside south of Taihuai, assembled from three older temples, Jile Temple, Shande Hall and Youguo Temple, in works that began in 1875 and continued into the Republican period, and arranged in seven tiers. A flight of 108 steps leads up from a marble gateway, and the upper Youguo Temple is known for nearly a thousand stone carvings of folk tales and legends.

rows.name: Puji Bridge, Yuanping
rows.summary: A Jin-dynasty stone arch bridge at the south gate of Guoyang, an old town north of Yuanping, built in 1203 and once known as the South Stone Bridge. It is an open-spandrel arch about 30 m long, 8 m wide and 7 m high, with two small arches that let floodwater pass and carved relief along the arch edges. It became a provincial monument in 1986 and a national one in 2019, and state media list Guoyang's old town among the stops on the Sino-Russian tea road.

rows.name: Sansheng Temple, Fanshi
rows.summary: A two-courtyard temple whose Mahavira Hall dates from the Jin dynasty, while the gate, bell and drum towers and side halls are Qing and the Ksitigarbha hall was rebuilt in 1495. The Jin hall has three bays, a single-eave hipped-gable roof and five-step bracket sets. Shrines to the Grain God and to the Grandmother goddess stand on the west side.

rows.name: Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei Military Region Headquarters Site, Jingangku
rows.name_zh: 金岗库村晋察冀军区司令部旧址
rows.pinyin: Jīngāngkù Cūn Jìnchájì Jūnqū Sīlìngbù Jiùzhǐ
rows.summary: From March 1938 this village was the base of the Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei Military Region headquarters, the first base the Eighth Route Army built behind Japanese lines. The headquarters occupied a two-courtyard house at the foot of the hill, and the commander and political commissar Nie Rongzhen lived upstairs in its west wing. A memorial hall opened in 2003 and has exhibitions on the war history, on Nie's life and on the resistance offices around Mount Wutai.

rows.name: Songjiagou Village
rows.summary: A resettlement village built to rehouse residents of 14 poor mountain villages around Kelan, now run as a rural-tourism destination. Stone-paved lanes run between grey-tiled courtyard houses, some of them turned into guesthouses, and a greenhouse farm north of the village offers fruit and vegetable picking and craft and game activities for children. The Song-dynasty Great Wall, Heyeping meadow and Luya Mountain are among the sights nearby.

rows.name: Source of the Fen River
rows.summary: The headwaters of the Fen River, the longest river in Shanxi and the second-longest tributary of the Yellow River, which rises in the Guancen Mountains of Ningwu County. The source area lies in a mountain valley at the foot of the Luya Mountain resort, and state media single out its clear, lively water. From here the river runs south through Taiyuan and on to the Yellow River.

rows.name: Tianya Mountain, Yuanping
rows.summary: A scenic area of granite peaks and a small lake east of Yuanping, built around the story of Jie Zitui, the Spring and Autumn official remembered for carrying his mother into the mountains. Sights include a drum-shaped boulder about 20 m across that sounds in the wind, a lotus-shaped peak above a lake with a 14.88 m white marble Guanyin, and a Ming-Qing shrine to Jie Zitui. A 13.88 m bronze statue of him stands in the filial-piety area, where the steps are carved with the twenty-four filial exemplars.

rows.name: Wannian Ice Cave
rows.summary: A large natural ice cave in a forested gorge in the Luya Mountain area of Ningwu County. Xinzhou's tourism promotion names it alongside the forests of Luya Mountain as one of the area's main draws.

rows.name: Xihetou Tunnel Warfare Site
rows.summary: A village whose houses are linked by about 5 km of tunnels, dug from 1942 and extended into a network by 1947, which local militia and armed work teams used in the Anti-Japanese War and the civil war. The tunnels run on three levels, from connecting passages to command rooms and an arsenal, and their entrances were hidden in places such as stove flues, double walls and animal troughs. A village museum tells the story, including the fight of 17 February 1948, when about 50 militia and work-team members held out underground against more than 2,000 Nationalist troops.

rows.name: Xinkou Battle Site
rows.summary: The site of the Battle of Xinkou, fought from 11 October to 2 November 1937, when Nationalist and Communist forces together defended the northern approach to Taiyuan. The main remains are 47 cave dwellings cut into the cliffs in 1935, 15 at Hongya Bay and 32 at Hougou, which served in the battle as command posts, field hospitals and cavalry stables, along with trenches on nearby Hill 204. A 2.6 km trail with a wooden walkway opened in 2024 for walking part of the battlefield, and a memorial wall honours those who fought.

rows.name: Xinzhou Ancient City
rows.summary: The restored old quarter of Xinzhou, once the walled town of Xiurong, where lanes and buildings were repaired and rebuilt in a programme that began in 2017. The same programme covered Xiurong Academy, a college founded in 1775 on a ridge at the south-west of the old town, with hillside pavilions dating from 1725 and 1819. State media describe the old town as a stop on the Sino-Russian tea road that keeps local intangible-heritage crafts alive.

rows.name: Yanqing Temple
rows.summary: A small temple in Shanwen village whose Jin-dynasty main hall, the Great Buddha Hall, is the only original building left; the other halls were rebuilt in recent years. The hall has three bays under a hipped-gable roof with very wide eaves, few columns inside, and oblique bracket arms that are unusual in a building of this size. The hall no longer holds its original statues, and the lower part of a Song-dynasty sutra pillar dated 1035 stands in the front courtyard.

rows.name: Yanshan Temple
rows.summary: A small temple on the northern side of Mount Wutai, founded in 1158 in the Jin dynasty and formerly called Lingyan Temple, best known for the Jin murals in its Manjusri Hall. The murals cover more than 90 m² and were painted by the court painter Wang Kui and others, showing the life of the Buddha and other Buddhist stories in settings of palaces, streets and shops. The hall also keeps Jin painted sculptures including a Water-Moon Guanyin, and a local saying sets the temple beside the Yongle Palace: Yongle Palace in the south, Yanshan Temple in the north.

rows.name: Yunzhong River Scenic Area
rows.summary: A landscaped riverside area along the Yunzhong River, a tributary of the Hutuo, in the northern part of Xinzhou city. Lakes and planted banks line the water, and the provincial tourism department promotes the Yunzhong River hot springs on a 2026 summer wellness route. State media cite the area's calm, ecological setting alongside the Fen River source and the Yellow River gorge at Laoniuwan.

rows.name: Yuwang Cave
rows.summary: A karst cave and national forest park in the hills south-east of Xinzhou, named for Yu the Great, the legendary tamer of floods. State media list it as one of the four national forest parks of Xinzhou and promote the cave as its main attraction, set among mountain forest.

rows.name: Zhengjue Temple, Fanshi
rows.summary: The Mahavira Hall of Zhengjue Temple, a Jin-dynasty hall standing in the town of Fanshi. It was listed as a city-level monument in 2007 and as a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Zhu Memorial Archway, Yangwu
rows.summary: A late-Qing memorial archway in Yangwu village, built by the official Wu Fangchou in honour of his mother, née Zhu. It was originally a set of three stone arches, of which two survive: a main arch with four pillars and three roofs, and a smaller one about 500 m away. The main arch is carved with the Twenty-four Filial Exemplars, dragons and phoenixes, has a pair of stone qilin guardians in front and carries a tablet reading 'Imperial Edict'.

rows.name: Zunsheng Temple
rows.summary: A hillside temple of seven courtyards on the old southern route to Mount Wutai, founded in the Tang dynasty and given its present layout in the Republican period. The courtyards rise from the Hall of Heavenly Kings to a pagoda at the top, and the east courtyard has two stone sutra pillars, one dated 1026 and one a Republican-era copy. Much of the temple was rebuilt from 1986 after damage in the Cultural Revolution.

rows.name: Cangshan Temple
rows.summary: A group of temple halls and pavilions set in a mountain gorge north of Yu County, built around the legend of the Zhao Orphan, in which a child of the Zhao family of the ancient Jin state is hidden in these hills; the legend is listed as national intangible cultural heritage. The scenic area includes the Cave of the Hidden Orphan, the Orphan-rearing Garden, the Lotus Temple and a Loyalty Pavilion that looks over the gorge, and the temple buildings are Ming and Qing in date. Spring peach blossom and autumn leaves are the main seasons for walking the paths.

rows.name: Cuifeng Mountain Scenic Area
rows.summary: A forested mountain scenic area south-west of Yangquan, with forest cover above 97 per cent and more than 300 plant species recorded, including over 100 rare tree species. A walking route of about 5 km called the Green Wild Fairy Valley passes named gateways, an old tree and a valley, and the hillsides turn red and yellow with smoke trees and maples in autumn. A camping base opened in 2025 and a winter snow-play park in December 2025, so the area suits day walkers and families in both seasons.

rows.name: Dachang Hot Spring Resort
rows.summary: A hot-spring resort in a deep mountain valley in the far north of Yu County, with open-air pools in several themed zones and a reception building that has a lounge, cinema and spa rooms. The spring water comes from about 100 m underground at around 60 degrees Celsius and contains radon and sodium sulfate. Dachang ancient village, known for its stone houses, is a separate stop on the same rural-tourism route.

rows.name: Dawang Temple, Yu County
rows.summary: A temple on the west side of Yu County town, beside the Beihe stream, which the county government's own guide calls the county's oldest and best-preserved old building. It was founded in the Jin dynasty and keeps its mountain gate, music stage, Ming-dynasty main hall and a rear hall with Jin-dynasty features, with stone tablets in the grounds and two old locust trees in front. The temple honours Zhao Wu, a minister of the ancient Jin state linked to the Cangshan legend.

rows.name: Fujun Temple
rows.summary: A temple to the deity Cui Fujun in Zhongshebei village in the north of Yu County, rebuilt in 1315 under the Yuan dynasty. The main hall is a Yuan building, the front hall is Ming and the remaining halls are Qing. It is a small compound that suits anyone interested in Yuan timber architecture.

rows.name: Guanshan Academy
rows.summary: A traditional academy on wooded Guanshan hill west of Pingding town, the best known of several academies whose remains lie on the hill. It began as the thatched study of a local clan, was enlarged in the Yuan dynasty by the official Lü Sicheng, and its present buildings date from the Qing. Carved verses and inscriptions on the stones around the hill record its long history as a place of study.

rows.name: Guanwang Temple, Yangquan
rows.summary: A temple to the deified general Guan Yu on the side of Yuquan Hill in Linli village, north of central Yangquan. The main hall keeps a Northern Song timber frame from the temple's rebuilding in 1122, and Chinese sources regard it as the oldest surviving Guan Yu temple building in the country. The compound was extended in the Yuan, Ming and Qing periods, and the site suits visitors interested in early timber architecture.

rows.name: Hongyanling Scenic Area
rows.summary: A mountain scenic area in the Taihang Mountains in north-east Pingding County, beside the Hebei border, with a planned area of 40 km² and a core of 8 km² of peaks, pine forest and karst. Its best-known sight is Yuhuang Cave, a karst cave of five linked chambers called Dragon Palace, Crystal Palace, Jade Pool, Lingxiao Hall and Arhat Court, and a path leads up to a viewing platform on the ridge. It suits visitors who want a cave visit and a forest walk in the hills.

rows.name: Kaihe Temple Grottoes
rows.summary: A group of Buddhist rock carvings and inscribed tablets cut into the cliff of Kuitou Hill beside Luanliu village in Pingding County. The carvings date from the Northern and Southern Dynasties to the Sui, and the site was added to the national list in 2013. It suits visitors interested in early Buddhist art in a small rural setting.

rows.name: Machiyan Temple
rows.summary: A small mountain temple in Mashan village in the far east of Pingding County, on the Taihang Number One tourist road. Its middle hall dates from the Jin dynasty and holds Qing murals, and the Tianwang (Heavenly Kings) hall also survives. The temple was added to the national list in 2019.

rows.name: Niangzi Pass
rows.summary: A Ming-dynasty fortified pass on the Shanxi–Hebei border, known as the ninth pass of the Great Wall, where the railway and road cross the Taihang Mountains; the present walls date from 1542. Visitors climb the walled pass and its gate towers, and the scenic area also takes in sections of Great Wall, a waterfall and an old village in the valley. In legend the Tang princess Pingyang garrisoned the pass with a force of women, which gave it the name 'Ladies' Pass'.

rows.name: North China Yifeng Ecological Park
rows.summary: A farm-based leisure park near Qianyuanji village in Niucun town, Yu County, developed from a coal company's transformation project. It has a large tree nursery, fruit-picking orchards, an agricultural science education camp, an animal exhibit of more than 40 species, fishing and a riding track, with a hotel and restaurants on site. It suits families and school groups looking for an easy rural day out.

rows.name: Potou Taishan Temple
rows.summary: A village temple to the Taishan deity in Potou village in the hills east of Yu County town, rebuilt in 1347 under the Yuan dynasty. The main and rear halls are Yuan timber buildings, while the stone archway, gate, bell and drum towers and side halls are Ming and Qing. It suits visitors tracing early timber architecture in the Yu County hills.

rows.name: Sansheng Temple Main Hall, Yu County
rows.summary: The surviving main hall of Sansheng Temple, founded in 1064 to honour the Three Sages of the Huayan school: Shakyamuni, Manjusri and Samantabhadra. The five-bay hall, listed as Ming, keeps Jin-style features and escaped demolition because it was used as a township hall; the rest of the temple was pulled down in the 20th century. It stands in the grounds behind the Yu County government offices.

rows.name: Taolingou Scenic Area
rows.summary: A peach-orchard park in the hills just north-west of central Yangquan, nicknamed the city's back garden, where old peach trees fill the valley. The peach blossom festival is held here each April, and the park also has a peach-blossom themed garden, a farm sightseeing and fruit-picking area, a 'water village' area and play areas for children. It suits families and day-trippers from the city.

rows.name: Tianning Temple Twin Pagodas
rows.summary: Two octagonal, three-storey brick pagodas standing in a small park in the middle of Pingding town, the survivors of Tianning Temple, which was founded in the Northern Song. The pagodas imitate timber construction, with carved brick beams and brackets under the eaves. The west pagoda's date was fixed by an inscribed stone found inside it during repairs in 2005, and the east pagoda, which is solid, was repaired in the Ming.

rows.name: Xiaohe Ancient Village
rows.summary: A hillside village on the eastern edge of Yangquan with Ming, Qing and Republican-era courtyard houses, about 178 courtyards in all, and the ancestral home of the modern writer Shi Pingmei. Among the buildings are the Shi family garden, a memorial exhibition to Shi Pingmei, a Guandi temple and a Guanyin nunnery, with carved stone, brick and wood decoration, and the village also keeps a small lake and old wells and millstones. It holds national status as a historic and cultural village and a traditional village, the first in Yangquan to do so.

rows.name: Yangquan Memory 1947 Cultural Park
rows.summary: A cultural park built on the site of the former Yangquan Water Pump Factory and opened in 2021. The old E-shaped foundry halls now hold an exhibition on the city's recent past, with rebuilt shopfronts and streets of the 1970s to 1990s, a wall of local dialect, a city library and a display of the writer Liu Cixin's science fiction. There are also cafes, shops and a night market, and the park suits an easy evening in the city.

rows.name: Yubei Taishan Temple
rows.summary: A village temple in Xi Yubei village north of Yu County town, with a Yuan-dynasty main hall that keeps wall paintings including a procession of the Jade Emperor. A stage and two side halls also survive, one of them Ming. The temple joined the national list in 2019.

rows.name: Baitai Temple, Xinjiang County
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple compound near Guangma village, named for the white lotus base of its Shakyamuni image and also called Shanhua Temple. The Shakyamuni Hall is a Jin-dynasty building of the Mingchang era (1190–1196) and the rear hall dates from 1355, while the two-storey Fazang Pavilion is built against an earth cliff and holds Yuan-dynasty statues. The grounds also keep stone tablets from the Tang to the Ming, a Tang relic pagoda and a Northern Song dharani pillar.

rows.name: Balong Temple Pagoda, Zhonglizhuang
rows.summary: A square, seven-storey Song-dynasty brick pagoda about 24 m tall, in Zhonglizhuang village, Ronghe town, and the only part left of the Balong (Eight Dragons) Temple. A Republican-era county gazetteer dates the temple to 1012, when Emperor Zhenzong passed through on his way to sacrifice at Fenyin, and the pagoda's eaves carry brick imitations of timber brackets. It was listed as a provincial site in 2004 and as a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Beixin Sarira Pagoda
rows.summary: A Ming-dynasty sarira (relic) pagoda in Beixin village, Ronghe town, Wanrong County. It was listed as a provincial site in 2004 and as a national one in 2019.

rows.name: Beiyangcheng Brick Pagoda
rows.summary: A Northern Song brick pagoda in Beiyangcheng village, Jishan County, built in 1039 by a villager for his mother. It is square in plan and was originally nine storeys, of which eight survive, about 10 m high, with eaves stepped out in corbelled brick and a stone Buddha in the arched niche on the ground floor. It was listed as a provincial site in 2004 and as a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Bian Que Temple, Yongji
rows.summary: This temple honours Bian Que, the Warring States physician traditionally regarded as the earliest known doctor in China, and stands in the countryside near Xima village. The national listing records its surviving buildings as Ming-dynasty. It is a small rural temple, mainly of interest to visitors following the history of Chinese medicine or Shanxi's timber architecture.

rows.name: Changchun Temple, Jiang County
rows.summary: A Taoist temple in Dongjingxia village, founded in 1320 and laid out as a single courtyard about 71 m long and 24.5 m wide. Its Hunyuan Hall is a Yuan-dynasty building, the east side hall is Ming and the remaining buildings are Qing, so the small compound shows three dynasties of timber building. It is of most interest to visitors following Yuan-era architecture in southern Shanxi.

rows.name: Changping Guandi Temple
rows.summary: The Guan family temple stands in Changping village, the village held to be Guan Yu's birthplace, on the site of his former home. Beyond a Ming stone arch of 1523 inscribed 'Home Village of King Guan' the path passes the eight-sided, seven-storey brick Ancestral House Pagoda, about 10 m high and repaired in 1177, and reaches the Qing-dynasty Chongning Hall, flanked by separate halls for Guan Yu's wife, his sons and his ancestors, a layout that is rare among temples to him. It is a separate site from the larger Guandi temple at Xiezhou, with its own entrance.

rows.name: Dayudu Yellow River Scenic Area
rows.summary: Dayudu is a ferry crossing on the Yellow River in the south of Ruicheng, facing Henan across the water and named for Yu the Great, the legendary flood-controller. The scenic area runs along the river bank and cliff, with a temple hall to Yu, an old cypress traditionally linked to him and Buddhist features. Beside it the Dayudu pumping scheme, built in the 1970s to lift river water for irrigation, still supplies irrigation water to most of Ruicheng's irrigated farmland.

rows.name: Dongcun Opera Stage
rows.summary: A Ming-dynasty opera stage in Dongcun village, Qingtou town. It was listed as a provincial monument in 2004 and as a national one in 2019.

rows.name: Dongfeng Opera Stage
rows.summary: The main surviving building of a Mount Tai temple in Dongfeng village, an opera stage rebuilt in 1612, in the Wanli reign, with a projecting porch for viewing from three sides added in 1799. The stage faces north, is three bays square with separate front and rear stage areas, and stands on a brick platform 0.9 m high under a hip-and-gable roof. It covers about 102 square metres, and a Qing-dynasty row of side rooms and the old temple gate tower also survive beside it.

rows.name: Dongyaowen Memorial Archways
rows.summary: Two memorial archways built to honour local widows, a Ming stone archway of 1628 and a Qing brick archway of 1775, both facing east. The stone archway is about 9 m tall with four pillars and five roofs. The brick archway is 12 m tall with three roofs, and its body carries 164 brick carvings including the Twenty-four Filial Exemplars and the Eight Immortals.

rows.name: Dongyue Temple and Feiyun Tower, Wanrong
rows.summary: Dongyue Temple stands in the middle of Wanrong's county town, and its landmark is the Feiyun Tower at the front: a 23 m timber tower of three visible storeys under yellow, green and blue glazed-tile roofs, held up by four tall pillars that run its full height. The temple was rebuilt in 1291–1297 under the Yuan and repaired repeatedly in the Ming and Qing; behind the tower the main axis runs through the Wu gate, an offering hall, and halls for the Dongyue emperor and the king of hell. The tower is also a real-world reference for a location in the video game Black Myth: Wukong.

rows.name: Duiyun Cave Taoist Temple, Xiaxian
rows.summary: A Taoist temple complex founded in the early Yuan dynasty, built in terraces of courtyards and cave rooms in a loess gully at Shangniu village in Shuitou town. In 1922 Jia Kangjie founded a secondary school at the temple, and in 1928 the Chinese Communist Party's Hedong Special Committee was formally set up here. It has been a provincial-level protected monument since 1985 and is used for patriotic education.

rows.name: Erlang Temple North Hall, Yuanqu
rows.summary: A single Yuan-dynasty hall in Beiyang village, the only building left of the Erlang Temple. It is three bays wide and covers about 74 square metres, under an overhanging gable roof with bracket sets below the eaves. It is worth a stop for anyone tracing early timber halls in southern Shanxi.

rows.name: Fawang Temple, Nanyang
rows.summary: A temple to Fang Yin, a Daoist adept known as the Dharma King, with buildings rebuilt in the Yuan and repaired in the Ming and Qing. The main hall and the flanking Seven Stars and Nine Luminaries halls stand in one row, with side halls to Houtu and the Ten Marshals, all arranged around a large music pavilion. The pavilion is three bays square under a double-eaved cross-gable roof edged in yellow and green glaze.

rows.name: Fenghuang Valley Forest Park
rows.summary: Fenghuang Valley is a forest park in the Zhongtiao hills just south of Yuncheng, in Yanhu District, made up of Fenghuang Mountain and five valleys, with walking trails and a viewing corridor on the ridge. Part of the park has been developed as a leisure resort, with amusement rides and, according to the city tourism bureau, a glass suspension bridge and a cableway.

rows.name: Five Dragons Temple
rows.summary: This was a rain-praying shrine to King Guangren, the spirit of the springs that once flowed out of the slope in front of it, which is why villagers call it the Five Dragons Temple. Its main hall, dated to the 830s under the Tang dynasty, is the second oldest dated timber building in China after the main hall of Nanchan Temple on Mount Wutai. The five-bay hall has a hip-gable roof and no columns inside, with a Qing-dynasty opera stage in front; it was dismantled and repaired in 2013–15 and reopened to visitors in January 2015.

rows.name: Fusheng Temple, Xinjiang County
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Guang village with a gate, Mituo Hall and a rear hall, known for its Yuan and Ming painted sculpture, of which more than 30 figures and reliefs survive. Mituo Hall, on a platform 5 m high, holds a seated Amitabha flanked by standing bodhisattvas, with a hanging-relief Guanyin crossing the sea on the back of the main image. The three vaulted cave shrines on the lower floor of the rear hall, closed since the 1950s, opened to visitors in stages from October 2025 and in full by mid-2026.

rows.name: Guanwang Temple, Yuncheng
rows.summary: Hedong salt merchants founded this temple to Guan Yu in the Yuan dynasty so that they could pay their respects before shipping salt from the nearby lake, and in the Ming it was the largest Guan temple in Yuncheng city. After an earthquake destroyed it in 1555 it was rebuilt from 1597 with the merchants' money; today only the gate, offering hall and main hall are old, and the rebuilt rear tower holds a Guan Yu culture display and a Hedong folk-culture exhibition. Notable pieces include a stele of 1108 written by Emperor Huizong of Song and a stone tablet of oracle slips dated 1613.

rows.name: Hanquan Pagoda, Wanrong
rows.summary: A square brick pagoda with eleven tiers of closely spaced eaves, about 31 m of it still standing, rises on the west foot of Gufeng Hill near Zhuoli village in south Wanrong. It dates from the Song or Jin period and began as the Kanquan Pagoda of a hill temple that has since gone; the lowest four storeys have brick-carved imitation timber brackets, and the upper eaves step out in plain corbelled brick. The tower now stands alone on the hillside.

rows.name: Houji Temple, Wenxi
rows.summary: A village temple dedicated to Houji, the legendary patron of farming, in Wulü village in the west of Wenxi County. Only two buildings remain on the central axis: the Houji Hall and the opera stage facing it. The hall, three bays wide under a single overhanging-gable roof, carries an inscription dating it to 1292, the stage was repaired in the Ming and Qing dynasties, and a temple fair with opera is still held here.

rows.name: Houtu Temple, Guduo
rows.summary: A village temple south of Guduo, in Hejin, where only two buildings remain: the main hall and the opera stage that faces it, both Yuan-dynasty. A surviving stele records that the temple was founded in 1296 and extended in 1318, and the stage was divided into front and rear stage areas under the Qing. Both buildings are three bays wide with overhanging-gable roofs and early-style bracket sets under the eaves, so the temple suits anyone interested in early timber architecture and village opera stages.

rows.name: Houtu Temple, Wanrong
rows.summary: This is the successor to the Han-dynasty shrine where emperors came to sacrifice to Houtu, goddess of the earth: Emperor Wu of Han made it the imperial site for the rite in the second century BC, and Tang and Song emperors also made offerings here. After Yellow River floods and shifts in its course the temple was moved more than once and settled on its present site in 1870; it covers about 25,000 square metres, with a Yuan-dynasty gate that doubles as a stage, an offering hall and main hall of the late Qing, and the Qiufeng Tower, a Ming-dynasty three-storey tower about 33 m high at the rear of the main axis. A ceremony honouring Houtu has been held here every year since 2003.

rows.name: Jiangbei Grand Canyon, Jiang County
rows.summary: A mountain gorge scenic area on Xiaobeishan in the Zhongtiao hills, in Moli township east of Jiang County, developed since 2012 around a river-rafting course of about 5 km through the canyon, which drops about 200 m. The park also has water-sports and adventure activities in summer and a snow-play area in winter.

rows.name: Jiangxian Confucian Temple
rows.summary: Founded in 932 under the Later Tang, the Confucian temple in the middle of Jiang County town is now the county museum. Of a once large complex only two halls survive: the Ming-dynasty Dacheng Hall, three bays square under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof with dense bracketing, and the Qing-dynasty Minglun Hall. The front courtyard has been turned into a square.

rows.name: Jiangzhou Confucian Temple
rows.summary: The surviving buildings of this Confucian temple in the north-east of Xinjiang town are a screen wall, a ceremonial pool, a stone gate of 1521 and the Dacheng Hall, a large hall rebuilt in 1448 with a surrounding veranda, a double-eaved hip-gable roof and glazed ridge ornaments. The rest of the compound was destroyed in the civil war and the Cultural Revolution, and the side halls and the Dacheng gate are new. Stelae from the Song dynasty onwards stand in the grounds, among them a Song stele whose text was assembled from characters by the calligrapher Wang Xizhi.

rows.name: Jiangzhou Prefectural Office and Main Hall
rows.summary: Xinjiang town was the seat of Jiangzhou prefecture, and its government offices stood on a high bluff in the west of the old town; only the main hall and a second hall survive. The main hall was rebuilt under the Yuan dynasty and is seven bays wide, more than the usual five for a prefectural office, with a hip-gable roof and fewer interior columns than normal. A Northern Song stele of 1101 set into its north wall lists seven rules for officials, and the town's bell, drum and music towers stand close by on the same rise as part of the Jiangzhou Shu scenic area.

rows.name: Jingyun Palace Jade Emperor Hall
rows.summary: The only building left of the Jingyun Palace, a Taoist complex founded in 634 that burned down in 1933 apart from this hall. The Jade Emperor Hall is five bays wide under an overhanging gable roof and is Yuan-dynasty in style. It was repaired in 1984 and again with national funds in 2009.

rows.name: Jishan Banzao Jujube Park
rows.summary: This park of old jujube orchards around Yao, Taoliang and Jijiazhuang villages, north-west of Jishan town, holds more than 17,000 ancient jujube trees, many around a thousand years old. Since 2022 the villages have also been developed as a farm-tourism area with a jujube museum, a staged show performed largely by local jujube farmers, a sightseeing train and a children's dinosaur park. Autumn is the picking season, and the park holds a harvest festival.

rows.name: Jishan Giant Buddha
rows.summary: A seated clay Buddha 16.68 m tall stands in the main hall of Dafo Temple, formerly Qingliang Monastery, in Jishan; it was modelled against a loess cliff, with a carved earth lower body and a clay-modelled upper body, and its colours have faded with age. The temple was founded under the Jin dynasty in 1142, and Yuan-dynasty clay figures survive in its Ten Kings and Luohan caves. Much of the older temple was lost in war, and the buildings around the hall are modern rebuilds in the Yuan style.

rows.name: Jiwang Temple, Beichi
rows.summary: This small temple to Houji, the legendary Lord of Millet, stands in the north-west of Beichi village in Yangwang town and covers 1,241 sq m. An inscription on the main hall's ridge beam records its foundation in 1503 under the Ming; the main hall and the stage are Ming, while the side halls, for the Heavenly Kings, the god of wealth, Guan Yu and the Holy Mother, are Qing.

rows.name: Jiwang Temple, Jishan
rows.summary: This temple in the middle of Jishan town honours Houji, the legendary Lord of Millet and patron of farming. Along the main axis stand a gate, an offering hall, the tall Houji Tower, a pool with an eight-sided pavilion and the Jiang Yuan hall, which is the one Yuan-dynasty building; the rest is Ming and Qing, with bell and drum towers under glazed-tile roofs. The Houji Tower rises about 30 m on a raised platform, with a surrounding gallery of stone columns and carved balustrades.

rows.name: Jiwang Temple, Wanrong
rows.summary: Only the main hall and an opera stage survive of this temple to Houji, the legendary Lord of Millet, in Taizhao village. An inscription found during repairs in 2011 dates the main hall to 1023 under the Northern Song; it is a five-bay hall with a hip roof and no long beam spanning the interior, a rare surviving Northern Song form. The stage was rebuilt under the Yuan, moved in the 1920s and joined to the gate.

rows.name: Jiwangshan Pagoda, Wanrong
rows.summary: An octagonal, seven-storey brick pagoda with closely spaced eaves stands on the summit of Jiwang Mountain in the east of Wanrong County, about 23 m of it still standing. An inscription inside records that it was built in 1087 under the Northern Song, and it once belonged to a temple of Houji, the legendary god of grain, which no longer exists. The first storey has brick-carved timber-style brackets and a corbelled ceiling inside, the upper storeys are plain, and the top finial has been lost to earthquakes and weather.

rows.name: Jiyi Temple, Xinjiang County
rows.summary: A temple to the legendary figures Hou Ji and Boyi in Yangwang town, popularly called Yangwang Temple. Only the main hall and the stage survive, both of the Ming dynasty. The hall's east, west and south walls carry 131 square metres of Ming murals completed in 1507, with more than 400 figures illustrating the legends of the Three Sovereigns, Yu the Great, Hou Ji and Boyi.

rows.name: Li Family Mansion, Yanjing
rows.summary: Begun in the Daoguang reign (1821–1850) by the Li family, who moved from farming and study into trade, this courtyard compound in Yanjing village is often grouped with the Qiao and Wang family compounds as one of Shanxi's three great merchant houses. Eleven of its original twenty courtyards survive, with carved brick, stone and wood, tall Huizhou-style fire walls and a few courtyards with Gothic-style details linked to a family member who studied in England. Look for the screen wall carved with 365 different forms of the character for 'good' and for the family ancestral hall.

rows.name: Linjin County Yamen
rows.summary: The former county government compound of Linjin, founded in the Dade era (1297–1307) under the Yuan and covering about 16,000 square metres. Three halls stand on the main axis: the great hall, five bays wide, is the Yuan original, while the second and third halls date from the Qing.

rows.name: Lishan Scenic Area, Yuanqu
rows.summary: Lishan is a mountain scenic area in the south-east of Yuanqu County, made up of sections with separate entrances: Shunwangping, the meadow on the 2,358 m main summit, named for the legendary sage-king Shun, whom Chinese tradition places farming on Mount Li; Huangguman, the second-highest peak at 2,134 m; and Mihouyuan, where a large colony of wild macaques gathers. Shunwangping's subalpine meadow is nicknamed the 'grassland in the clouds', and a fourth section lies on the Xiaolangdi reservoir on the Yellow River. This is the Yuanqu side of Mount Li; the Qinshui side, in Jincheng, has its own scenic area.

rows.name: Longxiang Guandi Temple
rows.summary: A village temple to Guan Yu on a site of about 2,300 square metres, founded in the Song dynasty and repaired in the Yuan, Ming and Qing. Its main hall is a Yuan-dynasty building with a reduced-column frame and holds seven Yuan-dynasty painted figures, among them Guan Yu, Zhou Cang and Guan Ping, while the stage in front dates from 1831 and the offering hall is later. The temple survived the Cultural Revolution.

rows.name: Longxing Temple, Xinjiang
rows.summary: A temple on a high mound at the north end of the main street of Xinjiang, where the Tang-era Biluo Stele was carved. Its main hall is a Yuan building holding painted Buddha figures in Song-Jin style, and behind it stands a 13-storey octagonal brick pagoda 42.4 m tall, rebuilt in 1784. The temple was founded in the early Tang as a Daoist temple and renamed Longxing Temple in 670.

rows.name: Macun Brick-carved Tombs
rows.summary: A family cemetery of the Duan clan dating from 1118 to 1181, under the Song and Jin, of which nine of the fourteen tombs have been excavated. Each underground chamber is built in brick as an imitation timber courtyard house, with carved doors, windows and brackets and, in some, a carved opera stage with actors and musicians. Visitors go down a stairway to a long passage with chambers leading off it, and guides explain the carvings.

rows.name: Main Hall of Taishan Temple, Guocun
rows.summary: All that survives of a Taishan temple (dedicated to the god of Mount Tai) in Guocun village, Yanhu District, is its main hall, which beam inscriptions show to be Yuan in origin and to have been repaired several times in the Ming and Qing; the founding date of the temple is not recorded. The hall is five bays wide and six rafters deep, with a flush gable roof, bracket sets under the front eaves and two octagonal stone columns carved with dragons that were fitted in the Ming. It is one of several Yuan-period village halls on the Yuncheng plain listed as national monuments.

rows.name: Mausoleum and Temple of Emperor Shun
rows.summary: This is the tomb and temple of Emperor Shun, a legendary ruler of ancient China, on the Mingtiao ridge near Xiquma village in Beixiang town. The precinct has an outer city, a tomb garden with a brick-built mound about 3 m high and a temple compound with a stage, offering hall and main hall; the sleeping hall was rebuilt on its original site, and the national listing dates the temple buildings to the Yuan to Qing periods. Shundi Park and the Yanhu District Museum lie next to it and make up the wider scenic area.

rows.name: Nanfan Stone Archway and Stele Pavilion
rows.summary: A Qing-dynasty memorial archway of blue limestone, built in 1804 to honour a local widow, the grandmother of a salt official. It is 12 m high and 8.5 m wide, with six pillars, and is carved from base to top with beasts, flowers and figures. Beside it, a small pavilion holds 15 inscribed stones in shapes such as fans, peaches, pomegranates and bells, written in several scripts.

rows.name: Niandui Jade Emperor Temple
rows.summary: A small village temple in Niandui, covering about 480 square metres, with a stage and a main hall that were both built in the Yuan dynasty. The stage is three bays square and the main hall three bays wide, each under an overhanging gable roof with bracket sets below the eaves. It suits a short stop for anyone interested in early opera stages and timber halls.

rows.name: Offering Hall of Guandi Temple, Zhaili
rows.summary: Zhaili's Guandi temple, dedicated to the war god Guan Yu, has lost all but one building: the Yuan-dynasty offering hall, where offerings were presented before the main shrine. It is five bays wide and four rafters deep under an overhanging gable roof, with bracket sets along the eaves; the columns flanking the central bay are shifted slightly inward, a technique rare in surviving timber buildings.

rows.name: Pagoda of Master Fanzhou
rows.summary: A single-storey round brick pagoda about 10 m high stands in Sibei village on the site of the vanished Baoguo Temple; it was built in 793 as the tomb pagoda of the monk Fanzhou, a member of the Tang imperial clan. The body is divided into eight bays by square pilasters, with a door on the south side, a finial of lotus petals and a flame jewel, and an epitaph dated 822 set into the north face. Most Chinese pagodas are polygonal, so a round plan is unusual; the pagoda was repaired in 2013–14.

rows.name: Pujin Ferry and Puzhou Ancient City
rows.summary: The site of the ancient Pujin crossing of the Yellow River, where the Tang rebuilt a pontoon bridge in 724 and anchored it with iron oxen on both banks. The iron oxen, iron figures, iron mountains and pillars excavated here are described as the largest iron group of their period found in China, and are displayed outdoors beside a site museum. The ruined city of Puzhou lies nearby, with Tang earthen walls and a Ming brick-faced inner wall, parts of which were restored in 2012–16.

rows.name: Pujiu Temple
rows.summary: Pujiu Temple is the setting of the love story in The Story of the Western Wing, in which the scholar Zhang Sheng and Cui Yingying meet, and its brick pagoda is nicknamed the Yingying Pagoda after the heroine. The temple is recorded from the Sui dynasty at the latest, was destroyed by fire in 1920 and left only the Ming-dynasty pagoda and three cave shrines, and its main buildings were restored from 1986. The Yongji culture and tourism bureau counts the pagoda among China's four famous ancient echo structures, with a toad-like croak heard from around its base.

rows.name: Qiangxia Guandi Temple
rows.summary: A village temple to Guan Yu in Qiangxia village, Peijie town, founded in 1347 under the Yuan and repaired or extended in the Ming, Qing and Republican periods. Its walled yard, about 53 m by 38 m, still holds a stage tower, a viewing pavilion, an offering pavilion, the main hall and side halls to the ox king and the earth god. It was raised to national-monument status in 2019.

rows.name: Qiaogoutou Jade Emperor Temple
rows.summary: A village temple to the Jade Emperor in Qiaogoutou, laid out around a main hall dated to the Yuan dynasty. In front of the hall stand two Ming-dynasty stages side by side, once part of a row of three, and their walls still carry inscriptions left by Qing-dynasty Puju opera troupes. A side hall, the Mawang Hall, keeps 17 square metres of Qing murals.

rows.name: Qiaosi Stele Tower
rows.summary: A memorial tower of 1837 built by the Zhou family and their circle in honour of the wealthy Zhou Wanzhong, in Qiaosi village. It rises about 15 m from a stone platform, with five stele chambers holding seven steles on its front, and its upper part is carved on all four sides with brick balustrades, window tracery and hanging flowers. Lotus ponds lie around it, and the inscriptions are written in regular, clerical and seal script.

rows.name: Qingliang Temple, Ruicheng
rows.summary: A hillside temple near Potou village, also called Potou Temple, of which only the Great Hall survives. An inscription dates its foundation to the Tang and the hall to 1303, in the Yuan dynasty. The hall is five bays wide and three deep, stands on a 2 m platform with a front terrace, and its interior uses a reduced-pillar plan, with two main pillars nearly 1 m across.

rows.name: Qinglong Temple, Jishan
rows.summary: A small temple in Ma village, founded in 662 under the Tang and kept in Yuan style through later repairs. Its two courtyards hold eight halls, and the main, middle and Qielan (guardian-deity) halls carry about 196 square metres of Yuan and Ming murals. It is one of several national monuments around Jishan, and the Macun brick tombs lie a short walk away.

rows.name: Qiu Family Stone Archway, Guojiazhuang
rows.name_zh: 郭家庄仇氏石牌坊及碑亭
rows.summary: A finely carved stone archway 15 m high, with six pillars and five gateways under a triple-eaved hip-and-gable roof, built in the Tongzhi and Guangxu reigns (1862–1908) to honour the mother of the Qing salt commissioner Qiu Jiamo. It stands on the road at the entrance to Guojiazhuang village, with five stele pavilions to members of the Qiu family on either side.

rows.name: Qiyan Temple Pagoda Forest
rows.summary: A pagoda forest of memorial and relic pagodas, in brick and stone, at the site of the Upper Qiyan Temple in the Zhongtiao Mountains. The national list dates them from the Tang dynasty to the Qing, so the group spans about a thousand years of pagoda building.

rows.name: Quanzhang Guandi Temple
rows.summary: Only the main hall survives of the Guandi temple in Quanzhang village, at the foot of the Linggong Terrace site in Xinjiang County. It is a Ming-dynasty hall five bays wide and five deep, with a double-eaved hip-gable roof and glazed tiles, repaired in 1495 and several times after. A veranda of carved stone columns runs around it, with dragons whose claws grip objects of many kinds, and some columns carry dates from the Chenghua and Hongzhi reigns.

rows.name: Ruan Twin Stele Towers
rows.summary: Two Qing-dynasty memorial towers standing side by side in Xiliang village, built to honour the virtue of a father and son: Ruan Tingshi, who held the Qing military title of Wude Zuoqiwei, and his son Ruan Lingyun. The western tower is the father's and the eastern the son's, and each carries four stone plaques, one on each side, inscribed with two-character words praising upright conduct and loyalty. It is a small village monument, worth a short stop for visitors exploring Hejin's rural heritage.

rows.name: Ruicheng City God Temple
rows.summary: The city god temple of Ruicheng, known locally as the South Temple, a large group of old buildings in the middle of the county town. Its main hall dates from the Song dynasty and the forecourt pavilion from the Yuan, with the other halls from the Ming and Qing, so the compound shows about 800 years of building styles. A gallery of steles holds many stones from the Northern Wei onwards, including a Tang stele of 798.

rows.name: Sanguan Temple, Xinjiang
rows.summary: A small Yuan-dynasty temple built in 1341, known locally as the Gourd Temple, in a lane in the town of Xinjiang. Its square offering hall with a cross-gable roof is joined directly to the two-bay main hall, which holds Yuan painted clay figures of deities, generals and attendants.

rows.name: Sheng'an Temple Pagoda, Zhangcun
rows.summary: A Song-dynasty brick pagoda in Zhangcun village, in the north of Linyi County, and the only part left of Sheng'an Temple, which was demolished in 1958. Brick carved to imitate timber brackets, doors and windows decorates the lower storeys, and the ground-floor chamber, about 2.5 m high, has a corbelled ceiling. It was listed as a provincial site in 2004 and as a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Shengmu Temple, Shangfeng
rows.summary: A village temple named for the Holy Mother (Shengmu) in Shangfeng village, Niangzhang township, added to the national list in 2013. The list dates its buildings from the Yuan dynasty through the Ming and Qing.

rows.name: Shengtian Lake
rows.summary: A lake on the Yellow River shore in Ruicheng County, run as a leisure scenic area with lakeside paths and boating. The main seasonal draw is winter, when wild white swans gather from about November, with numbers rising through December before they leave in late February or early March; the beach they use is fenced off from visitors. It suits a relaxed half-day outing, especially for bird-watching.

rows.name: Shentan Grand Canyon, Yongji
rows.summary: Shentan Grand Canyon is a gorge scenic area in the Zhongtiao Mountains just south of Yongji. In spring 2026 it reopened as 'Shentan · Bull Demon King Carefree Valley', an immersive attraction themed on the novel Journey to the West, with evening performances and a food street.

rows.name: Shousheng Temple Brick Pagoda, Ruicheng
rows.summary: A 13-storey octagonal brick pagoda, 46 m tall, which survived the destruction of its temple in 1941 and is a landmark in the north-east of Ruicheng town. Built in the Northern Song, it has imitation-timber brackets on its lower three storeys and a hollow interior with about 20 square metres of Song Buddhist murals. The temple buildings around it are recent, and the pagoda was restored in 2012.

rows.name: Shousheng Temple Pagoda, Nanyang
rows.summary: A Song-dynasty brick pagoda from the former Shousheng Temple in Nanyang village, Liwang township, Wanrong County. It is octagonal, with its eaves stepped out in corbelled brick, brick-carved timber-style brackets under the first storey and a square chamber inside; the finial is lost. Two other national monuments share the temple name, in Ruicheng and in Xinjiang County, so check the village before setting out.

rows.name: Shousheng Temple, Beisu Village
rows.summary: Only the main hall survives of a temple founded in 961, in the middle of Beisu village in Xinjiang County. The five-bay hall has an overhanging gable roof with glazed ridge ornaments and a column-reduced interior plan, and its form marks it as Yuan. The temple's painted clay figures are lost.

rows.name: Sima Guang Tomb and Shrine, Xiaxian
rows.pinyin: Sīmǎ Wēngōng Cí · Sīmǎ Guāng Mù
rows.summary: This is the family burial ground of Sima Guang (1019–1086), the Northern Song chief minister and historian who compiled the Zizhi Tongjian, on the Mingtiao ridge north-west of Xiaxian, with a shrine complex built around it. It has a stele hall holding his broken spirit-way stele, an ancestral shrine whose present form dates from 1762, the Yuqing Chan Temple (founded in 1065 as the tombs' incense temple, with painted clay figures in its hall) and the Sushui Academy. A bronze statue of Sima Guang stands in the square outside.

rows.name: Stork Tower
rows.summary: The Stork Tower is a modern reconstruction of a tower on the Yellow River bank made famous by a short poem of the Tang poet Wang Zhihuan, and it is counted as one of China's Four Great Towers. The original was a Northern Zhou military watchtower that was destroyed in the wars of the early 13th century; the present 73.9 m tower, built in Tang style on a steel and concrete frame, was finished in 2002. Its six interior floors carry exhibits on the history and culture of Puzhou, and the surrounding scenic area covers about 2 sq km.

rows.name: Taipingxingguo Temple Pagoda (Anyi Pagoda)
rows.summary: This octagonal brick pagoda in the Anyi district is built in Song style and is taken by scholars to be the tomb pagoda of a monk of Taiping Xingguo Temple, which no longer stands. It was originally thirteen storeys and now has eleven, after earthquakes shook off its top, and estimates of its height before repair range from about 60 m to 71 m. Cracks were repaired and a new top built in a state-funded restoration from 2012 to 2015.

rows.name: Taishan Temple, Dayang
rows.summary: The Taishan temple (dedicated to the god of Mount Tai) in Dayang village keeps one building, a main hall whose beam inscriptions record repairs in 1304 and 1571 and whose frame still has Yuan-dynasty character. It is five bays wide under an overhanging gable roof, with a porch along the front where only two columns stand under the eaves, so from outside it reads as three bays.

rows.name: Taishan Temple, Nanliu
rows.summary: A temple to the Mount Tai god standing alone in the fields about 1 km south-west of Nanliu village, on a site of about 7,300 square metres. Its main hall and the Houtu and Shengmu halls on either side keep Yuan-dynasty structures, and the main hall has a glazed-tile ridge. It is of most interest to visitors who follow early timber architecture in southern Shanxi.

rows.name: Taitou Temple, Hejin
rows.summary: A temple complex in the town centre of Hejin, dedicated to the Eastern Peak god of Mount Tai, with ten halls still standing along a long north-south axis. From the south the axis runs through the main gate, a middle gate, the offering hall and the Dongyue Hall, with a Houtu shrine, a Western Peak hall and side halls on either flank. The buildings range from the Yuan to the Qing dynasty, and inscriptions record repairs in the Ming and Qing periods.

rows.name: Taiyin Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple beside Zhangshang village, founded in the Northern Wei period and rebuilt several times since, including in 1180 under the monk Ciyun. Its south hall, five bays wide, is a Jin-dynasty building and houses a reclining Buddha carved from a single piece of wood; a Yuan inscription records that it was carved during the 1180 restoration. A fire in 1916 destroyed the north hall, which was replaced by a family shrine moved here from nearby, and the Jin murals and the heads of three Buddha figures were sold off in 1923.

rows.name: Tongshan Charitable Granary, Xiezhou
rows.summary: A charitable granary compound of 1880 in Xiezhou, built under Yan Naijue, son of Yan Jingming, as one of the Tongshan granaries he set up in the Yuncheng area. The compound runs about 164 m from north to south and about 60 m across, and what survives is the entrance gatehouse, seven bays wide, a front courtyard and a rear yard. It is a quiet stop for visitors interested in late Qing local charity and architecture, and can be combined with a visit to the Guandi Temple.

rows.name: Twin Pagodas of Miaodao Temple
rows.summary: Two square brick pagodas face each other about 80 m apart in Linyi County town, all that survives of the former Miaodao Temple, once also called Yanta or Shuangta Temple; the east pagoda stood just outside the temple. The west pagoda, about 22 m tall, originally had nine storeys and keeps six; an inscription from its underground chamber dates it to 1069 under the Northern Song. The east pagoda, about 23 m tall and intact at seven storeys, is of similar form and probably of a similar date.

rows.name: Wangu Temple, Yongji
rows.summary: Wangu Temple is a Buddhist temple of Northern Wei origin at the foot of the Zhongtiao Mountains in Puzhou town, and the national listing dates its surviving buildings to the Ming dynasty. Only three structures remain of the old complex: the Yaoshi Cave, the thirteen-storey Duobao Buddhist pagoda standing on the hillside among old cypresses, and the two-storey, five-bay Wuliang Hall, a 'beamless hall' of blue brick with no timber frame inside.

rows.name: Wangxian Grand Canyon, Yuanqu
rows.summary: Wangxian Grand Canyon is a gorge scenic area in Wangxian village, in the hills of south-eastern Yuanqu County, where a stream cuts through a narrow rock canyon. Its main sights are the chain of waterfalls and pools known as the Three Pools of Wangxian and, at the head of the gorge, the Houhe reservoir. It lies in the same township as the Lishan scenic area, so the two can be combined.

rows.name: Wanquan Confucian Temple
rows.summary: The Confucian temple of Wanquan, a former county town, where the Dacheng Hall enshrining Confucius was rebuilt in 1439 under the Ming. The five-bay hall has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and painted beams, and the courtyard holds seven old cypresses. Only the hall and a glazed-tile screen wall with a dragon relief are original; the gate, pond and other halls are recent rebuilds.

rows.name: Wulao Peak, Yongji
rows.summary: Wulao Peak is a mountain scenic area in the southern Zhongtiao Mountains, once known as Donghua Mountain and counted among the famous Taoist mountains of northern China. The forestry ministry approved a national forest park here in 1992 covering about 104 sq km. Visitors can climb through the woods or take the cable car, and the area has a glass-floored walkway on a cliff and a forest slide.

rows.name: Xiaxian Confucian Temple
rows.summary: The Dacheng Hall of Xiaxian's Confucian temple is the only building that survived the 1556 Jiajing earthquake, which destroyed the rest of the temple. It is seven bays wide and five deep under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, with some interior columns left out to open up the floor, and it has ridge ornaments and gable decoration in glazed tile.

rows.name: Xihoudu
rows.summary: A Palaeolithic site on a terrace above a bend of the Yellow River, found in 1959 and excavated in 1961, 1962 and 2005, which produced stone tools, fossils of 22 vertebrate species and burnt animal bones that are taken as China's earliest evidence of human use of fire. A 2020 study put the deposits at about 2.43 million years old, replacing earlier estimates of about 1.8 million. The site is set up for visitors, with an exhibition hall of stone tools and fossils, a protection stele beside an original excavation point and a torch platform above the river.

rows.name: Xuandi Temple, Fancun
rows.summary: A Taoist temple to Xuandi (Zhenwu, the Perfected Warrior) in the north-east corner of Fancun village, begun in 1569 and finished at the start of the 17th century with the backing of officials that included a minister of war and a grand secretary. Four Ming buildings stand on the central axis across three courtyards, the gate, an incense pavilion with three tiers of eaves, the main hall and a rear hall, and fragments of the blue and green glazed roof tiles survive; it is nicknamed the Glazed Tile Temple (Liuli Miao). After 1949 it served as a grain store, which helped it survive the Cultural Revolution, and the heritage department repaired it in 2014.

rows.name: Xue Xuan Family Temple and Cemetery
rows.summary: The family temple and cemetery of Xue Xuan (1389–1464), a Ming official and Neo-Confucian scholar from Hejin whose tablet was placed in the Confucian temple in 1572. The single-courtyard family temple in the middle of Pingyuan village, Wanrong County, was founded in 1619 by a sixth-generation descendant and its present buildings are Qing; his tomb, a mound about 1.5 m high, lies on the east side of the cemetery.

rows.name: Yellow River Great Ladder Cliff
rows.summary: A zigzag stone stairway cut by hand into a sheer cliff on the Yellow River bank in Banpo village, Xiahua township, is the centrepiece of this scenic area; the provincial tourism department dates it to more than 1,500 years ago. The steps are between about 2 and 4 m wide, and the chisel marks are still clear on the cliff face. A path along the top leads on to a stream valley with small waterfalls, and the summit looks down on the Yellow River as it comes out through the Shimen ('Stone Gate') gorge.

rows.name: Yellow River Longmen Scenic Area, Hejin
rows.summary: At Yumenkou the Yellow River leaves the long Shanxi–Shaanxi gorge and widens onto the plain, the spot behind the saying about carp leaping the Dragon Gate to become dragons. The village-run scenic area has a street built in Ming and Qing style, a boat route up the river gorge, a viewing platform on Longmen hill and a monument to the Yumenkou campaign of the Anti-Japanese War. Seven bridges of different types span the river here, from an iron-chain bridge first built in 1949 to modern cable-stayed spans.

rows.name: Yellow River Plank Road Remains, Pinglu
rows.summary: A cliffside plank road and towpath ran along the north bank of the Yellow River in Pinglu County between Sanmen township and Laoyashi and was in use from the Han to the Qing dynasties; remains survive in more than 20 places, adding up to over 3 km. The timber is gone; what remains is the rock-cut ledge with rows of beam sockets, grooves worn by haulage ropes and inscriptions including some dated to the Tang and Song. The best-known stretch, near Dujiazhuang hamlet, keeps more than 680 m of the road above the river, with netting fitted above it to stop falling rock.

rows.name: Yongxing Temple Pagoda, Lüyuantou
rows.summary: A square brick pagoda of the Northern Song, dated by its form, stands in fields about 200 m north-east of Lüyuantou village, just south of Linyi. It was listed as a provincial site in 2004 and as a national one in 2013.

rows.name: Yongxing Temple, Songcun
rows.summary: A village temple, also called Chongxing Temple, at the south-east corner of Songcun in Huafeng township, in the hills of south-east Yuanqu County. Its north hall, five bays wide, is the main building and keeps Jin-dynasty features, and a hexagonal Qing-dynasty brick pagoda with dense eaves stands in the compound; the county gazetteer dates the temple's founding to the Western Wei, in 548. The gate and offering hall are modern reconstructions.

rows.name: Yuban Ancient Salt Road
rows.summary: An old salt-carrying road about 8 km long through the Zhongtiao hills, linking Zhangdian town in Pinglu County with the Yuncheng Salt Lake basin. Rock walls on both sides give it a trough-like cross-section, hence its other name, the Green Stone Trough, and its surface, 2 to 4 m wide, still shows cart ruts and hoof marks. A modern road replaced it in 1956 and it was rediscovered in the 1980s.

rows.name: Yubi City Ruins
rows.summary: The remains of Yubi, a Northern Dynasties fortress built on a loess plateau with cliffs on three sides, now lying among farmland and houses in Jishan County. The Western Wei built it in 538, and in 546 the Eastern Wei chancellor Gao Huan besieged it for more than 60 days in the Battle of Yubi. About 300 m of the rammed-earth south wall survives, standing 2–8 m high, and the walled area covered some 2.6 sq km.

rows.name: Yuwangcheng Ruins
rows.summary: The remains of Anyi, an early capital of the Wei state in the Warring States period and later a Han-dynasty county seat. Stretches of its rammed-earth walls survive, best on the north and west sides of the 13 square kilometre outer city, along with a mound about 9 m high that marks the Yu King Temple site in the south-east corner of the inner city. Most of the ground is farmland, so it is a place for walking the walls rather than for seeing buildings.

rows.name: Taihang Honggu National Forest Park
rows.summary: A national forest park in south-east Shanxi, where the Taihang, Taiyue and Zhongtiao mountain systems meet, made up of three sections: Taihang Honggu, Longgang and Shanbianyan. Honggu is named after the Five Dynasties landscape painter Jing Hao, who took the name Hongguzi, and an observing platform in the park is listed as a dark-sky site. It is one of the first national forest-wellness bases named in 2020.

rows.name: Ancient Juyan Marsh
rows.summary: Ancient Juyan Marsh is a scatter of small lakes among dunes and red-grass flats in Ejin Banner, in the old Juyan area. The Ejin Banner authorities promote it for its sunset views over the lakes, which they call 'Sunset on Nine Lakes', and for the Tang poet Wang Wei's lines about Juyan.

rows.name: Badain Jaran Temple
rows.summary: Badain Jaran Temple is a small Gelug-school Tibetan Buddhist temple built in 1755 beside the lake of Sumin Jaran in the heart of the Badain Jaran Desert, originally a branch of Yanfu Temple in Bayanhot. Its two-storey sutra hall, with a hipped roof and corner towers, and a single stupa make it the only old temple in Alxa Right Banner whose buildings survive largely intact. It has been a national protected unit since 2013.

rows.name: Ceke Port International Cultural Tourism Area
rows.name_zh: 策克口岸国际文化旅游区
rows.summary: Ceke is a road and rail land port of entry (kou'an) in the Gobi of Ejin Banner, used mainly for coal imports. Its international cultural tourism area is promoted by the Ejin Banner authorities as a place to see the port's national gate and to learn about the banner's culture and history. It suits visitors curious about how a working land port looks.

rows.name: Dingyuanying Old Town
rows.summary: Dingyuanying, also called Wohu Cheng, is a walled Qing-dynasty garrison town in the old centre of Bayanhot, founded in 1730 and handed to the Alxa Mongol prince as his seat the following year. Its surviving buildings include the prince's mansion, Yanfu Temple (the princes' family temple, begun in 1731), traditional houses and remains of the wall and gates, and the site was renovated in 2017. It suits visitors interested in Qing frontier history and Mongol princely rule.

rows.name: Dongfeng Space City
rows.summary: Dongfeng Space City is the tourism name for the area around the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in Ejin Banner, the launch site for China's crewed Shenzhou spacecraft. Ejin Banner and national ethnic-affairs materials describe it as a national study-tour demonstration base and one of the first ten science-tourism bases in China, and recall how the Ejin people moved their banner seat three times from 1958 to give up their best pastureland for the site. Access to the launch centre itself is controlled; the banner's publicity department has advertised launch-viewing trips from a designated viewing point at Bayan Bogd in Dongfeng town.

rows.name: Fuyin Temple (Beisi)
rows.summary: Fuyin Temple, known as Beisi (North Temple), is a Gelug-school Tibetan Buddhist monastery in a mountain valley of the Helan range, founded in 1804 and named by the Jiaqing Emperor in 1806. About fifteen temples and more than a hundred buildings make up the complex, with a white stupa some 10 metres tall beside the main hall. After Nansi it is the largest Tibetan Buddhist monastery in Alxa.

rows.name: Guangzong Temple (Nansi)
rows.summary: Guangzong Temple, known as Nansi (South Temple), is a Gelug-school Tibetan Buddhist monastery in a pine-wooded valley on the western side of the Helan Mountains, built in the 1750s–1760s and named by the Qianlong Emperor in 1760. At its height it had nearly 2,900 rooms and more than 1,500 monks, earning the nickname 'little Ta'er Temple'. Visitors see the archway gate, the halls and stupas, and painted Buddha figures carved into the cliff face at the valley mouth.

rows.name: Juyan Lake
rows.summary: Juyan Lake is the end of the Heihe, or Ejin, River, which runs more than 800 km through Qinghai, Gansu and Inner Mongolia before filling two hollows in the Gobi to form an east and a west lake, together called Juyan Hai. The scenic area on the shore has reed beds, waterbirds and Gobi scenery, with horses, cattle and camels grazing nearby. It suits birdwatchers and photographers.

rows.name: Khara-Khoto (Heicheng)
rows.summary: Khara-Khoto, or Heicheng ('Black City'), is a ruined walled city in the Gobi beside the Ejin River, founded under the Western Xia and expanded under the Yuan, when it was the seat of Yijinai Circuit; it was abandoned after the Ming army took it in 1372. Its rammed-earth walls, about 450 by 380 metres and up to 9 metres high, still stand around the foundations of Buddhist, Taoist and Islamic buildings, though drifting sand has buried parts of the interior. Russian and British expeditions in the early 20th century carried off large numbers of Tangut-language manuscripts and Buddhist paintings.

rows.name: Mandela Mountain Rock Art
rows.summary: Mandela Mountain has more than 6,000 known rock engravings on dark rock faces, of which 4,234 in a core area of about 18 square kilometres have been catalogued. They show ibex, argali sheep, deer, horses and camels, hunting and herding scenes and dancers, pecked, ground and incised mostly in the Bronze Age and early Iron Age, with later Tibetan, Mongolian and Tangut inscriptions. Some panels have been fenced and are watched by staff since vandalism in 2001.

rows.name: Tengger Dalai Moon Lake
rows.summary: Tengger Dalai Moon Lake is a lake of about three square kilometres in the heart of the Tengger Desert, with a dark-sand beach about a kilometre long on one shore. A lakeside resort runs activities including dune-bashing in six-wheeled vehicles, go-karts, sandboarding, paragliding, camel and horse riding and boating. It suits a desert-and-lake day trip or overnight stay from Bayanhot.

rows.name: Tengger Desert Swan Lake
rows.summary: Swan Lake is a narrow lake on the eastern edge of the Tengger Desert, ringed by dunes with oleaster trees along its shore. Migratory swans and other waterbirds stop here in spring and autumn, and the ger camp beside the lake offers meals, overnight stays and activities such as sandboarding, camel and horse riding and boating. It suits a short desert-and-lake trip from Bayanhot.

rows.name: Tonghu Grassland
rows.summary: Tonghu is a sandy lake basin in the south of the Tengger Desert, with reeds, grass and scrub around its lakes and dunes on all sides. Visitors stay in ger groups and camp tents, ride camels or horses, and can take a camel trek north into the dunes to an artificial oasis.
