rows.summary: The riverside grounds of the Shanghai Port International Cruise Terminal, now officially the North Bund International Passenger Center, built on the site of 19th-century wharves and brought into service between 2006 and 2009. Its lawns and riverside promenade are open to the public, look across the Huangpu to the Lujiazui skyline and are used for outdoor events and brand launches.

rows.name: Oriental Land
rows.summary: A large outdoor activity camp and park in Qingpu run for Shanghai's school students since 2002, which also admits the public. Among its lakes and woods are a full-size replica of a US Nimitz-class aircraft carrier with exhibition halls, an avenue lined with statues of scientists and thinkers, an island of rare plants and a course of 18 swing and wave bridges. It suits families with children.

rows.name: Park Hotel
rows.summary: An Art Deco tower on Nanjing Road West, designed by Ladislav Hudec and completed in 1934 for the Joint Savings Society, which remained Shanghai's tallest building until the 1980s and is the origin point of the city's survey coordinate grid. It is still a working hotel, so visitors see the dark-brick and black-granite exterior and the restored Art Deco lobby.

rows.name: Pujiang Country Park
rows.summary: One of Shanghai's first five pilot country parks, opened in 2017 on woods, farmland and waterways along the east bank of the Huangpu River in Pujiang, Minhang. It is split by roads into separate sections, among them the Miracle Garden with its large spring flower displays, forest areas, a farmland section named for its willows and egrets and a riverside promenade, and it suits families and anyone after a green day out near the city.

rows.name: Qianwei Eco-Village
rows.summary: A farming village in Shuxin town on Chongming that began hosting farm-stay (nongjiale) tourism in 1999 and now forms the Haishang Huadao ('Flower Island') scenic area, with rose fields, lawns, a rose-themed garden and hotel, and children's play areas. Its Xiyuan Garden displays Ming and Qing carvings and old wooden beds on the theme of traditional Chinese weddings, and many of the village's former farmhouse inns have become boutique guesthouses.

rows.name: Qibao Old Town
rows.summary: An old market town on the Puhuitang River in western Minhang, which had taken shape by the Northern Song and is usually said to be named after its Qibao Temple. Its old streets on both sides of the river are now a busy shopping and snack street, with small attractions such as the memorial hall of the painter Zhang Chongren, Hergé's friend and the model for Chang in The Adventures of Tintin, and a house devoted to Qibao's fighting crickets.

rows.name: Qinglong Town Site and Qinglong Pagoda
rows.summary: The remains of Qinglong Town, a port founded in 746 that was Shanghai's main harbour for overseas trade in the Tang and Song dynasties until its river silted up. Most of the site lies under fields and villages, and the thing to see is the Qinglong Pagoda beside Qinglong Temple: a seven-storey brick pagoda rebuilt in the Northern Song that survives as a hollow shell about 30 metres high, without its eaves or spire.

rows.name: Second CPC National Congress Memorial
rows.summary: The shikumen house where the Chinese Communist Party held part of its Second National Congress in July 1922, then the home of the early party member Li Da; the congress adopted the party's first constitution and manifesto. The memorial hall, opened in 2002 and enlarged in 2009, also covers the site of the Pingmin Girls' School behind it, and forms part of the scenic area of the First, Second and Fourth Congress memorials.

rows.name: Shanghai Auto Expo Park and Auto Museum
rows.summary: A 76-hectare lakeside park in Anting's International Automobile City, completed in 2006 around the Shanghai Auto Museum, which opened in 2007 and is described by the city as China's first specialised car museum. Since a 2022 refit the museum's first three floors trace the history of the motor car with more than 100 vehicles from around 50 makers, and the top floor is a car-themed play area for children.

rows.name: Shanghai Baoshan International Folk Art Museum
rows.name_zh: 上海宝山国际民间艺术博览馆
rows.pinyin: Shànghǎi Bǎoshān Guójì Mínjiān Yìshù Bólǎnguǎn
rows.summary: A museum of folk art and folk customs from China and other countries, opened in October 2010 in a building whose design is based on a Chinese knot. It stands at the edge of Gucun Park and pairs easily with a walk there.

rows.name: Shanghai Blooming Garden
rows.summary: A flower park of about 87 hectares spread over small islands west of Zhujing town, with four zones: a sea of flowers, a plum garden, a fragrance garden and an autumn garden. Plum blossom covers the islands in early spring, lilies, sunflowers, hydrangeas and lotus follow in summer and maples colour in autumn, and children can ride horses, take boats and use the play slides.

rows.name: Shanghai Botanical Garden
rows.summary: A large botanical garden in southern Xuhui, opened to the public in 1978 on the site of the former Longhua nursery, with themed sections for penjing (Chinese bonsai), peonies, magnolias, roses, osmanthus, conifers, maples and bamboo, plus an orchid house and a tropical glasshouse. The penjing garden is particularly well known, and the garden holds flower shows every spring and autumn.

rows.name: Shanghai Chenshan Botanical Garden
rows.summary: Shanghai's second botanical garden and its largest, opened in 2010–2011 around Chenshan hill and covering 207 hectares. Its central display area has more than 20 themed gardens, among them one set in a former quarry pit, and large exhibition glasshouses, while the wooded hill is kept for conserving native plants. In 2026 the State Council approved its upgrade to Shanghai Chenshan National Botanical Garden.

rows.name: Shanghai Fashion Center
rows.summary: A fashion and shopping complex in the former Yufeng cotton mill on the Yangpu riverside, whose saw-tooth-roofed brick sheds were built by a Japanese textile company between 1922 and 1935 and ran as a state cotton mill until 2007. Converted between 2010 and 2012, it now holds catwalk venues, designer studios, fashion shops, restaurants and the Zotter Chocolate Theatre, with a riverside walk along the old dock.

rows.name: Shanghai Film Park
rows.summary: A film and television studio lot built by the Shanghai Film Studio in Chedun, with streets and buildings recreating old Shanghai, opened to visitors in 2000. Period dramas are regularly shot here, and since July 2024 visitors can also walk the replica of Huanghe Road built for the TV series Blossoms Shanghai.

rows.name: Shanghai Flower Port
rows.summary: A large flower park near the East China Sea coast in Pudong's Lingang area, best known for its spring tulip show of about 3.2 million bulbs in more than 500 varieties. The tulips usually bloom from late March to early May, with flowers on show through the rest of the year, and the park reopened in March 2024 after an upgrade that added new garden areas.

rows.name: Shanghai General Post Office
rows.summary: Shanghai's head post office, completed in 1924 on the north bank of Suzhou Creek to a classical design by Stewardson & Spence, with giant Corinthian columns and a corner clock tower crowned by statues of Hermes, Eros and Aphrodite. Part of the building houses the Shanghai Postal Museum, which reopened in December 2024 after new displays were installed, while a working post office still occupies part of the old main hall.

rows.name: Shanghai Grand View Garden
rows.summary: A large garden of traditional-style halls and courtyards on the west shore of Dianshan Lake, built from 1979 and opened in 1988 to recreate the Grand View Garden described in the Qing novel Dream of the Red Chamber. Its courtyards are named after the characters' residences in the novel, such as Baoyu's Yihong Court and Daiyu's Xiaoxiang Lodge, and the grounds add a large plum grove and a modern seven-storey pagoda. It is a modern re-creation rather than a historic garden and suits readers of the novel.

rows.name: Shanghai Haichang Ocean Park
rows.summary: A marine theme park beside Dishui Lake in Lingang, opened in 2018 by Haichang Ocean Park Holdings, with one half themed as a polar tundra under an artificial snowy mountain and the other as a tropical island with a volcano. It combines aquarium and animal exhibits, rides such as a launch roller coaster and a river-rapids ride, and staged shows with killer whales and other marine animals. It suits families with children and fills a full day.

rows.name: Shanghai Haiwan National Forest Park
rows.name_zh: 上海海湾国家森林公园
rows.summary: A planted forest park of more than 1,000 hectares in Haiwan town, Fengxian, begun in 1999, whose lakes, woods and meadows hold more than 300 species of trees. It has an amusement area, a water-sports area and a dozen cultural exhibition areas, and its 135-hectare plum garden of nearly 42,000 trees is the main draw in the blossom season.

rows.name: Shanghai International Circuit
rows.summary: The motor-racing circuit in Anting that has hosted the Formula One Chinese Grand Prix since 2004 (with a break from 2020 to 2023), its 5.45 km track laid out in the shape of the character 上, the first in Shanghai's name. The main grandstand has wing-like viewing platforms over the track and the team buildings stand like pavilions in a lake, a design modelled on Yu Garden; besides F1 the calendar includes Formula E, touring-car and GT races.

rows.name: Shanghai Jewish Refugees Museum
rows.summary: A museum built around the former Ohel Moshe Synagogue, put up by Russian Jews in 1927, that tells the story of the roughly 20,000 Jewish refugees from Nazi Europe who found shelter in Shanghai, most of them confined to a restricted sector in Hongkou from 1943. The restored synagogue and the halls added in a 2020 expansion show documents, photographs, personal belongings and reconstructed scenes, and a name wall lists more than 18,000 refugees.

rows.name: Shanghai Lavender Park
rows.summary: A flower park in the Shanghai International Resort area near Shanghai Disneyland, planted mainly with lavender, which holds a lavender festival when it flowers in late May and early June. It suits a short stroll and flower photographs and is easily combined with the resort.

rows.name: Shanghai Museum of Glass
rows.summary: A museum about glass opened in 2011 on the site of a former glass-instrument factory in Baoshan, covering how glass is made, the history of the glass industry and its uses, alongside galleries of glass art and exhibitions of contemporary art. Glass-blowing demonstrations and hands-on workshops make it a good choice for families.

rows.name: Shanghai Ocean Aquarium
rows.summary: An indoor aquarium beside the Oriental Pearl Tower, opened in 2002, with about 450 species laid out as a journey from the Yangtze through South America, Australia, Africa, South-East Asia and Antarctic waters. Highlights are the China Zone of Yangtze species such as the Chinese sturgeon and giant salamander, and a long underwater tunnel where sharks and rays swim overhead. It suits families and rainy days.

rows.name: Shanghai Science Hall (former French School)
rows.summary: A French Renaissance-style building with Art Nouveau details on Nanchang Road, completed in 1917 as the French Club and given to the French Concession's French School in 1926. Since 1958 it has been the Shanghai Science Hall, home of the Shanghai Association for Science and Technology, so it is a working office and conference venue and visitors see its north front and entrance porch from Nanchang Road.

rows.name: Shanghai Science and Technology Museum
rows.summary: A large science museum on Century Avenue in Pudong, opened in 2001 around the theme of nature, people and technology. After a renovation that closed it from March 2023, it reopened in stages from February 2026, and its ten permanent exhibition areas, including a large rainforest zone opened in April 2026, sit alongside giant-screen and dome cinemas. It suits families and anyone who likes hands-on science displays.

rows.name: Shanghai Smurfs Park
rows.summary: A largely indoor Smurfs theme park inside Shimao's Dream City complex beside the InterContinental hotel built into a former quarry, described by China Daily as the first Smurfs park in China. Visitors walk among mushroom houses in the Smurf village, watch a character parade, ride a small berry-car roller coaster and a forest tram and play games against Gargamel, and it is aimed at families with young children.

rows.name: Shanghai Urban Planning Exhibition Center
rows.summary: A six-storey exhibition hall on People's Square, opened in 2000 and described by the city as China's first venue dedicated to urban planning, that explains how Shanghai has grown and how it plans to develop. Its displays, renewed during a closure from late 2019 to 2022, use planning maps, scale models, films and interactive exhibits in themed galleries on the city's culture, innovation and ecology.

rows.name: Shanghai Urban Vegetable Garden
rows.summary: A vegetable-themed farm park in Haiwan town, built by the Bright Food group and described by the city as China's first vegetable theme park. Its venues show more than 200 kinds of fruit and vegetables and the history and techniques of farming, visitors can plant and pick their own, and a small tourist train, karting and a children's playground make it a family outing.

rows.name: Shanghai Wild Animal Park
rows.summary: China's first national-level wild animal park, opened in 1995 on the southern outskirts of Pudong, with more than 200 species and over 10,000 animals. Shuttle buses carry visitors through drive-through enclosures where zebras, rhinos, big cats and bears roam, and a walking area has giant pandas, elephants, giraffes and primates; keepers stage animal-behaviour demonstrations at set times. It suits families and fills most of a day.

rows.name: Shanghai Zoo
rows.summary: One of Shanghai's two main zoos, laid out on a former golf course near Hongqiao Airport and opened as Xijiao Park in 1954 before taking its present name in 1980. Mature trees, wide lawns and the Swan Lake surround enclosures for Chinese species such as golden snub-nosed monkeys and South China tigers as well as animals from other continents, and it suits a relaxed family day.

rows.name: Sheshan Hills
rows.summary: Two low wooded hills, East and West Sheshan, rise from the Songjiang plain and form the core of a national forest park. West Sheshan is crowned by the Basilica of Our Lady of Sheshan, a Catholic pilgrimage church reached by a path lined with the Stations of the Cross and made a minor basilica in 1942. Beside it stands the Sheshan Observatory, built by French Jesuits in 1899–1901 and since 2004 the Shanghai Astronomical Museum, which reopened in 2023 after two years of restoration with its original 40 cm twin refractor on show.

rows.name: Sihang Warehouse
rows.summary: A six-storey concrete warehouse on the north bank of Suzhou Creek, built in 1931, where more than 420 soldiers of the Chinese 88th Division under Xie Jinyuan held out against Japanese forces in October 1937 in full view of crowds in the International Settlement across the creek. The restored west wall still shows shell and bullet holes, and the Sihang Warehouse Battle Memorial, opened inside the building in 2015, tells the story with dioramas, battle scenes and films.

rows.name: Site of the First National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party
rows.summary: The pair of two-storey shikumen lane houses on Xingye Road where the Chinese Communist Party held its first national congress in July 1921, with the downstairs room where the delegates met arranged as it was at the time. A new memorial hall next door, opened in June 2021, holds the main exhibition on the party's founding, and the delegates' lodgings at the former Bowen Girls' School, about 200 m away and part of the same listed site, opened to visitors in March 2026 after restoration. The 5A scenic area also includes the memorial halls of the Second and Fourth Congresses in Jing'an and Hongkou districts.

rows.name: Songjiang Tang Sutra Pillar
rows.summary: This octagonal stone pillar, inscribed with a Buddhist dharani sutra and set up in 859 under the Tang dynasty, is regarded by Shanghai's cultural heritage authorities as the oldest structure standing above ground in the city. About 9.3 m tall in 21 stacked tiers, it is carved with crouching lions, coiled dragons, bodhisattvas and the Four Heavenly Kings, and was taken apart, repaired and reassembled in 1963–64 after long standing half-buried in an earth mound. It stands in the grounds of Zhongshan Primary School, which is not open to visitors.

rows.name: Songze Site
rows.summary: The Neolithic site that gave its name to the Songze culture, with layers going back about 6,000 years, excavated repeatedly from 1960 and now covered by a small site museum opened in 2014 as a branch of the Shanghai History Museum. Displays include a replica of one of China's earliest known wells, a reconstruction of the face of the earliest human skull found in Shanghai, and pottery and jade from the excavations.

rows.name: Soong Ching-ling Mausoleum
rows.summary: The cemetery on Hongqiao Road, formerly Shanghai's International Cemetery, where Soong Ching-ling, Sun Yat-sen's widow and later Honorary President of the People's Republic, was buried in June 1981 in her family's plot beside her parents. The memorial area has a white marble statue of her and an exhibition hall on her life, and the grounds also hold a section of foreigners' graves; the writer Lu Xun was buried here from 1936 until 1956.

rows.name: Soong Ching-ling Memorial Residence
rows.summary: The 1920s garden villa at 1843 Middle Huaihai Road, built for a foreign shipowner, that was the Shanghai home from 1948 of Soong Ching-ling, Sun Yat-sen's widow and later Honorary President of the People's Republic. It became a memorial after her death in 1981 and keeps the rooms and furniture as they were in her lifetime, set in front and back gardens.

rows.name: St. Ignatius Cathedral
rows.summary: The twin-towered Gothic Revival cathedral of Xujiahui, designed by William Doyle and built by French Jesuits between 1906 and 1910 at the heart of the old Zikawei mission, and the seat of the Bishop of Shanghai since 1960. Badly damaged during the Cultural Revolution, it returned to religious use in 1979 and reopened in December 2017 after a restoration of its stonework, windows and floors that took two and a half years.

rows.name: St. John's University Historic Campus
rows.summary: The campus of St. John's University, founded by American missionaries in 1879 on a bend of Suzhou Creek and closed in 1952, now the Changning campus of East China University of Political Science and Law. Its 27 protected buildings combine Western verandah architecture with Chinese roofs, from Huaishi Hall (now Taofen Hall) with its clock tower to Gezhi Hall of 1899, which houses an exhibition on the campus's history. Since 2021 the campus and its creek-side promenade have been fully open to the public.

rows.name: Tilanqiao Prison
rows.summary: Built from 1901 as the gaol of the Shanghai International Settlement (the Ward Road Gaol) and once billed as the largest prison in the Far East, Tilanqiao keeps cell blocks and other buildings dating from 1917 to 1935 behind walls more than 5 metres high. Its inmates were moved to a new prison in Qingpu in 2024, and that year the city and Hongkou District were studying how to reuse the old compound.

rows.name: Tomb of Lu Xun
rows.summary: The grave of Lu Xun (1881–1936), a leading figure of modern Chinese literature, who was reburied here in 1956 in a park he had visited near his last home. The granite tomb in the north-west of Lu Xun Park has a bronze statue of the seated writer and a headstone inscribed in Mao Zedong's hand, and the Shanghai Lu Xun Memorial Hall stands in the same park.

rows.name: Tomb of Xu Guangqi
rows.summary: The grave of Xu Guangqi (1562–1633), the late-Ming official and scholar who translated Euclid's Elements into Chinese with the Jesuit Matteo Ricci and was a leading figure among the Chinese Catholics of his time, buried here with members of his family in 1641. The low oval mound, rebuilt in 2003 to its 1903 form, stands in Guangqi Park near the creek junction where his descendants settled, which gave Xujiahui, the 'Xu family junction', its name.

rows.name: Top of Shanghai Observatory, Shanghai Tower
rows.summary: The visitor observatory of the 632-metre Shanghai Tower, China's tallest building, reached by high-speed lifts that climb to the 118th floor at 546 metres. It gives a 360-degree view down onto the Jin Mao Tower, the Oriental Pearl Tower and the Bund, and a separate show on the 125th and 126th floors presents the building's giant tuned mass damper.

rows.name: Wendao Garden
rows.summary: A landscaped garden in Luodian, northern Baoshan, opened in 2006, with woodland, ponds and Huizhou-style buildings. Its main interest is a large collection of ornamental stones, shown with old stone carvings in two museums, alongside calligraphy and painting studios and a tea area.

rows.name: Wusong Paotaiwan Wetland Forest Park
rows.name_zh: 吴淞炮台湾湿地森林公园
rows.summary: A riverside park at Wusongkou, where the Huangpu River joins the Yangtze estuary, laid out from 2005 on mudflats that had been filled with steel-mill slag since the 1960s and named after the Qing navy's Wusong forts. Paths and boardwalks run through woods, ponds and tidal wetland, with a long riverside promenade facing the shipping lanes, a memorial square for the Wusong forts and the Yangtze Estuary Science Museum.

rows.name: Xisha Mingzhu Lake
rows.summary: A scenic area at the western end of Chongming Island made up of Mingzhu Lake, described as the island's largest freshwater lake and ringed by water-conservation forest, and the Xisha National Wetland Park on the Yangtze shore. Boardwalks lead through flooded woodland, reed beds and tidal creeks where herons, gulls and cormorants feed, and a small fish-specimen hall shows species from the lake and the Yangtze estuary.

rows.name: Xujiahui Origin heritage area
rows.summary: An open-street scenic area, rated 4A in 2012, that links the historic buildings and museums of Xujiahui, the district named after the descendants of the Ming scholar Xu Guangqi who settled here. Besides St Ignatius Cathedral and Xu's tomb in Guangqi Park, its sites include the Bibliotheca Zi-Ka-Wei library of the old Jesuit mission, the former Xujiahui Observatory, now the Shanghai Meteorological Museum, the T'ou-Sè-Wè Museum and the Pathé building where the national anthem, The March of the Volunteers, was first recorded. It also takes in the Shanghai Film Museum and the historic Jiao Tong University campus.

rows.name: Yangshupu Waterworks
rows.summary: One of China's earliest modern waterworks, built for a British company in 1881–1883 and still supplying part of the city, with brick buildings and walls designed to look like an English castle, complete with battlements and mock turrets. It is a working plant, so visitors see the castle-like buildings from outside, best from the Yangpu Riverside promenade along the Huangpu; part of the site houses the Shanghai Waterworks Science and Technology Museum, reopened after renovation at the end of 2024.

rows.name: Yuan Dynasty Water Gate Museum
rows.name_zh: 上海元代水闸遗址博物馆
rows.summary: A museum built over a Yuan-dynasty stone sluice gate found during building work at Zhidan Road in the early 2000s, one of six gates built around 1325 under the hydraulic engineer and painter Ren Renfa to control the silting Wusong River. The gate floor, about 42 m long, with its posts and walls laid on a dense bed of numbered timber piles, lies more than 7 m below street level and is seen from a glass walkway inside the hall; the find was named one of China's top ten archaeological discoveries of 2006.

rows.name: Yunbao Future City Art Town
rows.summary: An arts and leisure complex in Dongjing town, presented in 2025 as the arts quarter of the Sheshan National Tourist Resort. It combines an art museum, a music centre, a bookshop, a Songjiang experience centre of the Shanghai Astronomy Museum and a waterside market, with seasonal exhibitions and monthly events, and suits a relaxed afternoon or evening.

rows.name: Zhangma Village
rows.summary: A rural tourism village at the southern tip of Zhujiajiao, on the upper reaches of the Huangpu River, where waterways and farmland are laid out with field paths and small visitor facilities. Its best-known sight is the Maota Pagoda, a five-storey brick-and-wood pagoda first built in the Tang dynasty that also served as a lighthouse for boats on the Mao River. It suits a quiet half-day in the countryside, combined with Zhujiajiao.

rows.name: Zhaojialou Ancient Town
rows.summary: A small water town in Pujiang in south-east Minhang, named after a tower built in the Southern Song to summon farmers to work newly reclaimed land, to which a bell was added in the Ming. Restored and reopened in 2010, its old street, stone bridges and courtyard halls such as Ligeng Hall held small museums, including memorial halls to the local figures Qin Yubo and Ye Zongxing and an exhibition on the educator Huang Yanpei. Since 2023 the whole area has been under redevelopment as a new residential and commercial district, in which the Liyuan garden is to be kept and the old-town core revived.

rows.name: Zhenru Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple in Putuo whose main hall, built in 1320, is regarded as the oldest timber building in Shanghai and its only mid-Yuan structure. Restored to its original single-eaved form in 1963–1964, when workers found part names brushed onto its timbers by the Yuan carpenters, the hall stands in a rebuilt temple that has been an active monastery again since 1991.

rows.name: Zhujiajiao Ancient Town
rows.summary: A canal town beside Dianshan Lake in Qingpu District that grew from Song- and Yuan-dynasty country fairs into a busy rice-trading town in the Ming and Qing. Its old streets and waterways keep Fangsheng Bridge (first built in 1571 and rebuilt in 1812), Kezhi Garden, the City God Temple, Yuanjin Buddhist Temple and a Qing-dynasty post office, and boats still carry visitors along the canals.

rows.name: Zuibaichi Garden
rows.summary: One of Shanghai's five classical gardens, rebuilt in the mid-17th century by Gu Dashen, who named it 'Drunken Bai Pond' in homage to the Tang poet Bai Juyi. The pond, halls and corridors keep their Qing layout, and two of its stone carvings survived the Cultural Revolution because staff disguised them as propaganda boards; a larger public park was added around it in 1959.

rows.name: Shanghai Museum of Traditional Chinese Medicine
rows.summary: A museum of Chinese medicine on the Zhangjiang campus of Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine in Pudong, with displays on the history of Chinese medicine, herbs, instruments and the city's own medical traditions. It was listed in 2018 as a national TCM health-tourism base.

rows.name: Changzhou Museum
rows.summary: Changzhou's main city museum, founded in 1958 and housed since 2007 in a large modern building beside the civic square in Xinbei District. Its history galleries run from Liangzhu-culture jades and early green-glazed stoneware to Song and Yuan lacquer and porcelain and Ming and Qing painting, and it also has a natural history museum for children. It is rated a national first-grade museum.

rows.name: China Dinosaurs Park
rows.summary: A dinosaur-themed amusement park in Xinbei District, opened in 2000, with rides, shows and parades built around its theme. At its heart is a large museum of Chinese dinosaur fossils, and the wider Dinosaur City resort around it adds a hot-spring complex and a shopping street. It suits families with children.

rows.name: China Filial Piety Park
rows.summary: A themed park of about 860 mu (some 57 hectares) on the shore of Lake Tai at Xueyan, backed by the Lu'e hills and devoted to the Confucian virtue of filial piety. It combines Lu'e Chan Temple, on the site of an older temple, with a Guanyin hall, a grotto hall, a pagoda, an ancestral hall and a museum of filial piety, and it has held ancestor-worship ceremonies at Qingming.

rows.name: Chunqiu Yancheng (Yancheng Ruins)
rows.time_needed: Half a day (ruins and museum) to a full day
rows.summary: The earthworks of Yancheng, a walled town of the late Spring and Autumn period, form the core of this tourist area in Wujin: three rings of ramparts and three moats set one inside another, an arrangement rare among early Chinese city sites. A museum at the entrance presents the site and its finds. Around the ruins are a Spring and Autumn-themed amusement park and a wildlife park, which make up the rest of the 5A area.

rows.name: Former Jiangnan Command of the New Fourth Army, Shuixi
rows.name_zh: 新四军江南指挥部旧址
rows.summary: The Li family ancestral hall in Shuixi village, where the New Fourth Army set up its Jiangnan Command on 7 November 1939 under Chen Yi, with Su Yu as deputy, to direct its anti-Japanese operations around Maoshan and southern Jiangsu. The hall and a memorial museum beside it present the history of the command.

rows.name: Former Residence of Qu Qiubai
rows.summary: The Qu family ancestral hall on Yanling West Road, where Qu Qiubai, an early leader of the Chinese Communist Party and a writer and translator, lived with his family from 1912 to 1916. Its rooms are furnished as in his youth, and the adjoining memorial hall, built in 1999, covers his life with photographs, documents and manuscripts, including his translation of 'The Internationale'.

rows.name: Former Residence of Zhang Tailei
rows.summary: The house in Zihe Li, a lane off Qingliang Road, where Zhang Tailei, an early leader of the Chinese Communist Party, lived with his family from 1918 to 1925. His rooms at the back of No. 3 are furnished as a memorial hall, with an exhibition on his life in the neighbouring courtyard of No. 4 and a newer two-storey gallery beside them.

rows.name: Hongmei Park
rows.summary: A large city park east of Changzhou's old centre, opened in 1960 and named after the Hongmei (Red Plum) Pavilion, one of its two old buildings together with the Wenbi Pagoda. Its lake, gardens and plum trees make it a popular place in early spring, and it lies next to Tianning Temple.

rows.name: Huagu Qiyuan Flower Valley
rows.summary: A commercial flower park in the Maoshan resort area, laid out as ten themed gardens with a hillside of planted flower fields. Spring is the main flowering season, and it suits families and garden lovers.

rows.name: Jin Garden
rows.summary: A small private garden laid out in 1668–1672 by the retired official Yang Qingyan, with the painter Wang Hui involved in its design, and counted among Changzhou's four classic gardens. Its roughly 4,600 square metres keep the early-Qing plan: a pond around a yellow-stone rockery island, ringed by pavilions, studies and climbing corridors, with the Xiye Thatched Hall as the main building.

rows.name: Maoshan Forest World
rows.summary: An outdoor activity park covering about 3,500 mu (some 230 hectares) of forest and bamboo on the Jintan side of Maoshan, with forest-themed attractions such as a 'magic black forest' and a rafting run through the woods. Tea-field tents and forest villas allow overnight stays, and it is aimed mainly at families.

rows.name: Old Grand Canal and Nandajie District
rows.summary: The historic centre of Changzhou along the old course of the Grand Canal, combining Nandajie, the city's main pedestrian shopping street, with canal-side Xiyingli, where Xiying Gate and about 220 metres of wall are all that survive of the city walls. The canal's Changzhou urban section is part of the Grand Canal World Heritage Site, and old lanes such as Qingguo Lane lie close by.

rows.name: Oriental Salt Lake City (Dao Tianxia)
rows.summary: A modern leisure resort at the foot of Maoshan, the Taoist holy mountain, themed on Taoist culture and on the area's hills, water, tea, salt, herbs and hot springs. Its Dao Tianxia section has costumed characters who interact with visitors and folk performances, and the resort has hot-spring hotels.

rows.name: Qingfeng Park
rows.summary: A large public park in western Changzhou, opened in 2008 after four years of building and laid out with lakes, low man-made hills, woodland and a big central lawn. It is a favourite with local families for walks and spring kite-flying, and has hosted the city's chrysanthemum festival in autumn.

rows.name: Tang Family Residences, Qingguo Lane
rows.summary: Two Ming-dynasty courtyard houses of the Tang family on Qingguo Lane, a restored historic street along an old arm of the Grand Canal in central Changzhou. Zhenhe Hall, home of the Ming official, writer and anti-pirate commander Tang Shunzhi (Tang Jingchuan), is now a memorial museum to him, and Lihe Hall is the birthplace of the linguist Zhou Youguang. The rest of the lane is lined with former homes of noted Changzhou families.

rows.name: Tianmu Lake and Nanshan Bamboo Sea
rows.summary: Tianmu Lake is a reservoir in the hills south of Liyang, built in 1958–61 as the Shahe Reservoir and renamed in 1992 when it was opened for tourism. The 5A scenic area has two parts: the Shanshui Garden on the lake, with lakeside parks and islands, and the Nanshan Bamboo Sea, a bamboo-covered valley on the Anhui border with walking trails and a cable car into the hills. The lake is known locally for its fish-head soup.

rows.name: World Joyland
rows.summary: A theme park on the shore of Lake Tai at Xueyan in Wujin, opened in 2011 and built around video-game and animation themes, with roller coasters and other rides. Its original look drew on online games such as World of Warcraft. It is aimed at teenagers and families.

rows.name: Ancient Huai River Culture and Ecology Scenic Area
rows.summary: A riverside park of about 1.6 km² along the Gu Huai He, the old channel of the Yellow River, which flowed through Huai'an until 1855, on the north side of Qingjiangpu; Ninglian Road divides it into two parts. The eastern part has foot and cycle paths through landscaped banks and a cluster of museums, among them the China Huaiyang Cuisine Culture Museum, a Journey to the West exhibition hall and the Guhuai Tower with a display of local wedding customs. The western part holds a museum of Chinese urbanisation, a library and a culture square.

rows.name: Baima Lake Eco-Tourism Area
rows.summary: Baima Lake is a shallow lake on the border of Huai'an and Yangzhou that also serves as a through-lake for the eastern route of the South–North Water Diversion. The eco-tourism area in the north-west of the lake's tourist resort has a plum garden, an eco-amusement park, a campervan campsite and the "Three Islands Adventure", a set of small themed islands in the lake. It mainly draws families for a day by the water.

rows.name: China Water Transport (Caoyun) Museum
rows.summary: China's first museum devoted to caoyun, the imperial system that shipped tax grain along the Grand Canal to the capital, opened in May 2011 on Caoyun Square in Huai'an's old town. It stands at the north end of the excavated site of the Office of the Governor-General of Grain Transport, which ran the system from here under the Ming and Qing; the foundations and column bases of its great hall are laid out as a park in front. Five galleries hold about 6,000 m² of displays on the canal, the grain fleets and the city's role in them.

rows.name: Diyishan (First Mountain) and its Inscriptions
rows.summary: A wooded hill above the Huai River in the north of Xuyi town, named after the Song calligrapher Mi Fu, who climbed it in 1097 on his way to a post in Lianshui and wrote a poem calling it the "First Mountain"; a later copy of his three characters stands by the entrance. Its cliffs and steles carry well over a hundred inscriptions from the Song to the Republic, among them verses left by Southern Song envoys on their way to the Jin court and a Su Shi poem carved in the Northern Song and rediscovered in 1983. Below the hill, the restored lanes of the Diyishan historic quarter, such as Huangpai Street, are lined with restaurants and shops.

rows.name: Dragon Palace Ocean World (Journey to the West Culture Park)
rows.summary: A theme-park complex in Huai'an's economic development zone built around Journey to the West, the Ming novel credited to Huai'an's Wu Cheng'en. Its main part is Xiyou Amusement Park, a Journey to the West theme park opened in July 2021 with themed areas, rides, parades and evening shows. Next to it, Dragon Palace Ocean World, named after the Dragon King's undersea palace in the novel and rated 4A as Dragon Palace Beluga World by 2018, is now centred on a summer water park.

rows.name: Former Residence of Wu Cheng'en
rows.summary: Wu Cheng'en, the Ming writer credited with the novel Journey to the West, lived in this courtyard house in the Hexia quarter of Huai'an; it was restored in 1982 and is a city-level protected site. The compound of about 1 ha has his main hall with a bust reconstructed from his skull, a bedroom and a small garden, flanked by memorial halls to Wu and to the Monkey King, including an art gallery on the Monkey King family of actors. It lies at the edge of Hexia old town, whose lanes are worth a stroll.

rows.name: Former Site of the CPC Central China Sub-bureau
rows.name_zh: 中共中央华中分局旧址
rows.summary: From October 1945 to September 1946 the Central China Sub-bureau of the Communist Party's Central Committee and the Central China Military Region had their headquarters here, in the former Jiangsu Provincial Huai'an Middle School, directing party, government and military work in 73 counties and cities under Deng Zihui and Tan Zhenlin, with Zhang Dingcheng and Su Yu in military command. The east and middle buildings, a small north building and the assembly hall survive in their original form. A memorial hall opened in 2010, with displays on the period including the 1946 land-reform pilot and the Central Jiangsu Campaign.

rows.name: Former Site of the Jiangsu–Anhui Border Region Government
rows.summary: The Jiangsu–Anhui Border Region Government, set up by the Communist Party on 1 November 1945 to join its four liberated areas in central and northern Jiangsu and Anhui, had its seat in this compound in Qingjiang, now Huai'an, until it withdrew in September 1946. The compound of about 10,000 m² keeps its original layout, including the two-storey courtyard where talks between Communist, Nationalist and US representatives were held. A memorial hall opened here in 1986, and a new permanent exhibition on the border region's history opened in 2021.

rows.name: Hongze Lake Levee (Gaojiayan) and Ancient Dike Scenic Area
rows.summary: The great dike along the east shore of Hongze Lake was begun as a 30-li embankment in AD 200 and extended under the Ming and Qing to hold back the lake, protect the plains to the east and feed water to the Grand Canal; between 1580 and 1751 its lake face was clad with a wall of dressed stone about 60 km long and 7–8 m high. Now some 67 km long and part of the Grand Canal World Heritage listing, it can be toured from the Ancient Dike scenic area in Hongze District, whose sightseeing cars run along the top. Stops include the Zhouqiao breach, where floodwater broke the dike in 1824 and the stone wall was rebuilt with iron cramps, and some of the more than 300 Ming and Qing inscriptions carved along the dike.

rows.name: Huai'an Museum
rows.summary: Huai'an's museum of local history, rated a national first-grade museum in 2024, holds about 31,000 objects. Its main exhibition traces the area from prehistory through the Warring States, the canal grain trade, the salt monopoly and river works to its famous natives; highlights include Warring States bronzes from the Gaozhuang tomb found in 1978 and a carved wooden drum carriage from a tomb at Yunhe village excavated in 2004. Further galleries are devoted to the film director Xie Tieli and to collections of calligraphy and painting.

rows.name: Huai'an Prefectural Yamen
rows.summary: The seat of Huai'an Prefecture from 1370 until prefectures were abolished in 1913, on the old town's central axis north of the Governor-General of Grain Transport's office and the Zhenhuai Tower. Its great hall, seven bays and 26 by 18.5 m, was rebuilt after an 1861 fire with timber from a Hexia salt merchant's mansion, and it survived with the second hall through later use as a factory. Restored and opened in 2007 over some 12,000 m², it is described by the provincial tourism department as the only surviving Ming–Qing prefectural yamen along the Grand Canal.

rows.name: Huanghuatang New Fourth Army Headquarters Site
rows.name_zh: 黄花塘新四军军部旧址
rows.summary: Huanghuatang village in southern Xuyi County was the seat of the New Fourth Army's headquarters from early 1943 to early 1945, during the later years of the war against Japan. The memorial site comprises the former headquarters buildings and leaders' quarters, an exhibition hall of photographs and objects on the war in central China, and landscaped grounds. It was listed as a national heritage unit in 2019.

rows.name: Inner Canal (Liyunhe) Cultural Corridor
rows.summary: The Liyunhe, the section of the Grand Canal between the Yangtze and the Huai, runs 32 km through Huai'an, and this scenic corridor centres on a 15.6 km stretch through Qingjiangpu. Along it are parts of the Grand Canal World Heritage site – the Qingjiang Great Lock, the Qingkou hydraulic hub and the Huai'an section of the Huai–Yang Canal – together with the rebuilt Qingjiangpu Tower, a city memory museum, a hall of famous Huai'an people, an opera museum and the "south by boat, north by horse" stele marking where travellers once changed from boat to road.

rows.name: Jinhu Lotus Marsh (Hehuadang)
rows.summary: A wetland of about 22 km², most of it water, on the shore of Gaoyou Lake in south-eastern Jinhu County, planted with lotus fields that bloom in summer. More than 300 lotus varieties are grown, and the scenic area also has a lotus garden, a lotus culture hall, an exhibition on water plants and farming, a stele corridor of lotus poems and the Qingshan Temple. It is at its best in the summer flowering season.

rows.name: Jinhu Water Forest
rows.summary: A plantation of metasequoia (dawn redwood) standing in water in Tugou town, Jinhu County, planted in the 1980s as northern Jiangsu's largest man-made forest farm and opened as a privately run scenic area in 2017. Rows of trees rise from the water, with egrets in the canopy and the trees' breathing roots poking above the surface, seen from bamboo rafts, a forest train, a glass walkway and paths. Added attractions such as a maze, go-karts and flower fields make it a family day out.

rows.name: Jinshiyuan (King's Luck) Distillery, Gaogou
rows.summary: The baijiu maker Jiangsu King's Luck (Jinshiyuan), successor to the old Gaogou distillery, runs a factory tour at its base in Gaogou town that is listed as a national industrial-tourism demonstration site. One part shows the modern works – a culture square, an automated brewing hall seen from a viewing gallery, a store of large pottery jars and the bottling line – and the other, the Gaogou liquor heritage zone, has a liquor culture hall, displays of starter-making and distilling and a field of old fermentation pits still in use. It suits visitors curious about how Chinese grain spirit is made.

rows.name: Ming Ancestors Mausoleum
rows.summary: The first imperial tomb of the Ming dynasty, built from 1386 to about 1413 by the Hongwu Emperor and his son the Yongle Emperor beside Hongze Lake for the founder's grandfather, great-grandfather and great-great-grandfather; only the grandfather is actually buried here. Swamped by the lake around 1680 together with the city of Sizhou, it re-emerged in the 1960s and is now ringed by a protective embankment. The main sight is the spirit way lined with Ming stone statues of qilin, lions and other figures and carved pillars, while the burial chamber lies under a pond at its end and the halls survive only as foundations.

rows.name: Qing Yan Garden
rows.summary: A garden in central Qingjiangpu that grew from a lodge set up in 1678 by the river-works chief Jin Fu on the site of a Ming revenue office, and from 1729 belonged to the office of the Director-General of the Southern Rivers, who ran the river and canal works of the region. Its one original building is the Hefang Academy of 1750, built for the Qianlong Emperor's southern tour and flanked by stele pavilions and a stele corridor on the history of river works; the other halls, pavilions, Guandi temple and rockeries are later rebuildings in traditional style. Rated 4A in 2023, it is a compact garden of ponds, lotus and old trees.

rows.name: Qingliangang Neolithic Site
rows.summary: The site that gave its name to the Qingliangang culture, a Neolithic culture of the Huai River region, lies in Qinglian village north-east of Huai'an District and was first investigated in the early 1950s; new excavations in 2016–19 opened nearly a hectare. Little is visible: most of the core area is now a pond up to 5 m deep, the small on-site display room shows mainly photographs and text, and a planned site park had made little progress by 2024. Jade and stone artefacts of the culture are kept in the Huai'an Museum.

rows.name: Tieshan Temple National Forest Park
rows.summary: A forested area of low hills, up to about 200 m, in the far south of Xuyi County on the Anhui border, around the 9 km² Tianquan Lake reservoir. Its secondary broadleaf woodland mixes northern and southern plants, as it lies where the warm-temperate and subtropical zones meet. Within the park are the rebuilt Tieshan Chan Temple, an observing station of the Purple Mountain Observatory with a public astronomy park, and walking routes with a suspension bridge and a long stone stairway.

rows.name: Wentong Pagoda
rows.summary: An octagonal seven-storey brick pagoda, 23 m tall with yellow walls and dark eaves, in Shaohu Park in the north-west corner of Huai'an's old city beside the canal. It was founded in 708 as the 13-storey Zunsheng Pagoda, renamed after the neighbouring Wentong Temple when rebuilt in 1629, and cut down to two storeys by the Tancheng earthquake of 1668, after which it was rebuilt with only seven; the national heritage list dates the present structure to the Song. The lakeside park makes a pleasant stop between the old town and Hexia.

rows.name: Wudao Lake Scenic Area, Lianshui
rows.summary: A lake park in the middle of Lianshui town, laid out in 1930 around a lake with five small islands, grouped with the neighbouring Nengren Temple and the Lianshui County Museum into one scenic area. The temple's Song-dynasty Miaotong Pagoda was destroyed in 1948; after excavation of its crypt in 1998 yielded gold and silver reliquaries and other finds, a 68.88 m concrete pagoda with a lift was built on the spot in 1999–2002, and the temple was rebuilt in 2004–07. One island has a pavilion and an ink-washing pond recalling the Song calligrapher Mi Fu, who once held office in Lianshui.

rows.name: Yue Pagoda (Yueta), Tangji
rows.summary: A Song-dynasty brick pagoda in Yueta village, Tangji town, in eastern Lianshui County. Octagonal and built wholly of brick in imitation of a wooden pavilion-style pagoda, it has a stair that turns upward inside the walls, the only one of its kind in Jiangsu; repairs in 1974 and 1995 made good its damaged base and top, leaving it 20.04 m high. Local legends tie it to the early Tang general Xue Rengui, but heritage authorities date it to the Song.

rows.name: Zhou Enlai's Hometown: Former Residence and Memorial Hall
rows.summary: Zhou Enlai, the first premier of the People's Republic of China, was born in 1898 in this pair of Qing courtyard houses on Fuma Lane and lived here until 1910; restored in 1978 and opened in 1979, its 32 rooms show his birth room, family rooms, an old well and displays on his childhood. The 5A scenic area also takes in the Zhou Enlai Memorial Hall about 1 km to the north-east, opened in 1992 among artificial lakes, where an 800 m axis links the main hall, an exhibition on his life, a bronze statue and a copy of his Xihuating residence in Beijing's Zhongnanhai. The hearse from his 1976 funeral has been on display there since 2016.

rows.name: Chaohe Bay, Guanyun
rows.summary: A rural leisure area on a reed-fringed stretch of water east of Guanyun county town, with an eco-restaurant, a fishing centre and a campervan and camping base. It is aimed at local families and day-trippers, with holiday events such as hot-air balloon gatherings, markets and boat trips.

rows.name: Dayi Mountain, Guanyun
rows.summary: A cluster of twelve low peaks, the highest 226.7 m, on the northern edge of Guanyun county town, with the centuries-old Stone Buddha Temple (Shifo Si), a large bronze seated Buddha completed in 2009 and old rock carvings such as a Yuan-dynasty sika deer. On the eastern foot lies the Dayishan stone-coffin cemetery, a Neolithic burial ground about 6,500 years old whose graves were lined with natural stone slabs, described as the earliest stone-coffin cemetery found in China.

rows.name: Donghai Crystal City and Crystal Museum
rows.name_zh: 东海水晶城·水晶博物馆
rows.summary: The crystal quarter of Donghai, a county that brands itself the 'World Crystal Capital' because of its large deposits of rock crystal and quartz. It is made up of the China Donghai Crystal City, a large market where crystal jewellery and carvings are sold, and the China Donghai Crystal Museum, which is devoted to crystal. It suits visitors interested in minerals or shopping rather than sightseeing.

rows.name: Erlang Shen Cultural Park, Guannan
rows.summary: A temple park on the northern outskirts of Guannan county town devoted to Erlang Shen, the river-taming god of Chinese myth whom Journey to the West places at the mouth of the Guan River, a name the town links with its own Guan River. Its Tang-style halls and pavilions, among them the Zhenjun Hall and the Cixiao Pavilion, tell Erlang's story with an emphasis on filial piety, and visitors can strike the temple bell.

rows.name: Haiqing Temple Pagoda
rows.summary: A nine-storey octagonal brick pagoda built between 1023 and 1031 under the Northern Song, the only survivor of Haiqing Temple, which has since disappeared. It is also called the Ashoka Pagoda because it was built to enshrine Buddhist relics, and it stands by a lake at the western foot of Mount Huaguo, close to the scenic area's visitor centre.

rows.name: Haishang Yuntai Mountain
rows.summary: A forested mountain area in the coastal Yuntai hills above Sucheng, in Lianyun district, whose summit viewpoints look over Lianyungang port and Lian Island. Paths climb through wooded valleys past the Tao Yuanming culture garden and the Faqi Temple towards the summit area.

rows.name: Kongwang Mountain
rows.summary: A small hill on the southern edge of Haizhou, Lianyungang's old town, named after the story that Confucius climbed it to look out to sea. Its cliff carvings, made in the late Eastern Han, mix Taoist figures such as Laozi and the Yellow Emperor with some of the earliest Buddhist imagery in China, including a Nirvana scene and the tale of a prince who gave his body to a starving tigress.

rows.name: Lian Island
rows.summary: Jiangsu's largest island, joined to the mainland at Lianyungang port by a long sea wall, with wooded hills, the sandy Dashawan beach and the quieter Sumawan bay linked by a seaside boardwalk. Near Sumawan a Han-dynasty inscription cut into the rock marks the old boundary between the Donghai and Langya commanderies and is a national heritage site. The island was rated a national 5A scenic area in 2024.

rows.name: Lianyungang Museum
rows.summary: The city's main museum, a national first-grade museum that presents the history and culture of the Lianyungang area. It stands on Chaoyang East Road next to the Lianyungang Revolutionary Memorial Hall, so the two are easily seen together.

rows.name: Lianyungang Revolutionary Memorial Hall
rows.summary: A museum of the Lianyungang area's modern revolutionary history, including the War of Resistance against Japan, told through photographs and objects. It stands beside the Lianyungang Museum on Chaoyang East Road, and the two can be visited together.

rows.name: Mount Huaguo
rows.summary: The mountain that the novel Journey to the West made the home of the Monkey King, now a scenic area of 136 peaks crowned by Yunü Peak, at 624.4 m the highest point in Jiangsu. Paths, shuttle buses and a cable car lead to the Water Curtain Cave, the Sanyuan Temple, first built in the Tang, and woods where macaques roam. More than 200 cliff inscriptions from the Tang onwards are scattered over the slopes, among them the Yulin Guan group near the visitor centre, a national heritage site.

rows.name: Qinshan Island
rows.summary: A narrow islet of about 0.19 km² in the sea off Ganyu, roughly a kilometre long with three low peaks along its ridge. At the lowest spring tides a shingle causeway about 4 km long, the 'Divine Road', emerges from the water, and the island has Xu Fu's Well, old stone inscriptions and the sea-sculpted General Rock, all tied to legends of the First Emperor's eastern tour and Xu Fu's voyage in search of immortality.

rows.name: Tanggou Distillery, Guannan
rows.name_zh: 汤沟酒生态文化旅游区
rows.summary: A visitor area at the working distillery of Tanggou baijiu, a strong-aroma liquor made in Tanggou town, where the old workshops were merged into one state distillery in 1952. The visit is built around the distillery's fermentation pits and brewing halls, and its old cellar is a provincial heritage site.

rows.name: Taohuajian and the General Cliff Petroglyphs
rows.summary: A wooded valley on the southern slopes of Jinping Mountain, south-west of Haizhou, with a stream, pools and paths up to a summit viewpoint; its western part holds the General Cliff petroglyphs. Carved into a sloping rock face, they show human faces linked to plant-like lines, star symbols and animals, and archaeologists read them as a prehistoric farming ritual site of the Dongyi people. Micro-erosion dating suggests the carvings were made over a long span, between about 10,000 and 3,000 years ago.

rows.name: Xishuang Lake, Donghai
rows.summary: A reservoir on the south-western edge of Donghai county town, built in 1960 on the Yuejin River, whose shores are now laid out as the Xishuang Lake National Wetland Park. It is an open town park for a lakeside walk, easily combined with a visit to Donghai's crystal market.

rows.name: Yiyuan Park, Guanyun
rows.summary: A leisure park east of Guanyun county town built around large flower fields and a fairy-tale-style small town, with children's play areas and themed restaurants. It is run together with Guanyun's Chaohe Bay and plum-garden scenic areas and fills public holidays with markets, shows and fireworks, so it suits local families more than sightseers.

rows.name: Yuwan Scenic Area
rows.summary: A steep valley in the Yuntai Mountains east of Mount Huaguo, where a stream drops through a chain of waterfalls and pools, known as the Three Pools, between cliffs and woods that turn red and gold in late autumn. A via ferrata along the stream and a children's play area themed on Journey to the West have been added for families.

rows.name: Chaotian Palace
rows.summary: Rebuilt from 1384 as Nanjing's leading Taoist temple, where the Ming court's Taoist registry sat and officials rehearsed court ceremonies, the complex on Yeshan hill was wrecked in the Taiping war and rebuilt in 1865–69 as the Confucian temple and school of Jiangning prefecture. Its Qing gates, Dacheng Hall and the halls on the hill behind are described as the largest and best-preserved group of official-style historic buildings in the Jiangnan region, and in 1936 a vault was built in the grounds for Palace Museum treasures evacuated from Beijing. It now houses the Nanjing Municipal Museum, whose permanent exhibitions cover the city's history, highlights of its collection and Song and Ming dress excavated in Nanjing.

rows.name: Drum Tower of Nanjing
rows.summary: Built in 1382 on a rise at the centre of the Ming capital, where drums sounded the hours and ceremonies were held, the tower keeps its original brick base, shaped like a city gate with three arched passages on each side. The two-storey timber hall on top was rebuilt in 1684 around a stele recording the Kangxi Emperor's instructions to local officials on his southern tour, so it is also known as the Stele Tower. The surrounding Drum Tower Park, opened in 1923, reopened after renovation on 1 October 2025.

rows.name: Former Academia Sinica Buildings
rows.summary: Three buildings of the Academia Sinica, the Republic of China's national research academy, all designed by Yang Tingbao in a Chinese palace style: the Institute of Geology of 1931, where Li Siguang led research from 1932 to 1937, the Institute of History and Philology of 1936, and the headquarters of 1947, where the academy elected its first academicians in 1948. They stand just south of Jiming Temple in the compound of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Nanjing branch.

rows.name: Former Beijige Meteorological Observatory
rows.summary: On the 62 m summit of Beiji Ge (Jilong Hill), used for watching the sky since the 5th century and the site of the Ming imperial observatory, Zhu Kezhen founded the Academia Sinica's Institute of Meteorology in 1927, and in 1930 the Qing Beiji pavilion was replaced by an observatory, regarded as the start of modern meteorological research in China. Its 1930s buildings, a two-storey traditional-style building by Yang Tingbao and a 14 m hexagonal observation tower, have housed the China Beijige Meteorological Museum since 2010, with exhibits on Chinese meteorology from ancient times to the present and a bronze statue of Zhu Kezhen.

rows.name: Former British Embassy, Nanjing
rows.summary: Known locally as the Little White Building, this was the seat of the British legation in Nanjing, raised to an embassy in 1935; the embassy moved to Chongqing in 1938, returned in 1946 and closed in 1949. Two buildings survive from the compound: an office building in English classical style with a colonnaded front on a raised terrace, and a country-villa-style residence with a red-tiled roof. Both now belong to the Shuangmenlou Hotel, where the former embassy building is used as a restaurant.

rows.name: Former Macklin Hospital
rows.summary: The first building of the mission hospital that grew into today's Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital, a two-storey brick block of 1892 in American colonial style, named after its first director, the Canadian missionary doctor Macklin, with round-arched windows, dormers and a doorway bearing the date. Since 2007 it has housed the hospital's history memorial hall.

rows.name: Former Nanjing Office of the Eighth Route Army
rows.name_zh: 八路军驻京办事处旧址
rows.summary: A two-storey 1930s Western-style house that belonged to Zhang Boling, president of Nankai University, and was rented in August 1937 as the Nanjing office of the Communist-led Eighth Route Army, after the Communists and Nationalists agreed to cooperate against Japan. Headed by Li Kenong, with Ye Jianying and Bo Gu among those working here, the office secured the release of hundreds of Communist political prisoners and helped prepare the formation of the New Fourth Army before leaving for Wuhan in November 1937. It has been a memorial hall since 1987 and is now a branch of the Meiyuan New Village Memorial Hall.

rows.name: Former National Central University
rows.summary: Southeast University's Sipailou campus keeps the core of the former National Central University, the national university of Republican-era Nanjing, with buildings mostly of the 1920s and 1930s in a Western classical revival style. A copper-domed auditorium of 1930–31 seating about 2,700 faces Yang Tingbao's 1933 south gate along the campus axis, flanked by the 1923 Mengfang Library and the 1929 biology building. The 1923 gymnasium hosted lectures by Bertrand Russell, John Dewey and Rabindranath Tagore, and an old juniper known as the Six Dynasties Pine stands by the Mei'an building.

rows.name: Former Residence of Gan Xi
rows.summary: Begun in the Jiaqing reign (1796–1820) by Gan Fu, father of the scholar Gan Xi, this large family compound of linked courtyards in the old south of the city is popularly called the Gan Family Mansion. It now houses the Nanjing Folk Museum, with displays on local customs and crafts, and stands at the heart of the protected Nanbuting historic quarter.

rows.name: Gaochun Cittaslow (Yaxi)
rows.summary: A rural area of low hills, tea gardens and villages around Yaxi in eastern Gaochun, which became China's first member of the international Cittaslow ('slow city') network and hosts the network's China office. A scenic road winds between the villages and is popular for cycling and driving, with farm stays and seasonal family activities such as tea picking.

rows.name: Gaochun Old Street
rows.summary: The old main street of Chunxi, Gaochun's district town, which grew up as a market street from the Song dynasty and is lined with Ming- and Qing-period shop-houses now selling local snacks, crafts and souvenirs. Along the way are the Guanwang Temple and an old well associated with the Qianlong Emperor.

rows.name: Ginling College Campus
rows.summary: The campus of Ginling College, a Christian women's college founded in 1913, built in 1922–23 to a plan by the American architect Henry Murphy, with Chinese palace-style buildings in reinforced concrete set symmetrically around a great lawn and linked by covered walkways. During the Nanjing Massacre of 1937–38 the acting head, Minnie Vautrin, turned the campus into a refuge for thousands of women and children. Since 1952 it has been the Suiyuan campus of Nanjing Normal University.

rows.name: Great Bao'en Temple Heritage Park
rows.summary: The site of the Great Bao'en Temple, rebuilt by the Yongle Emperor from 1412 on the site of the older Changgan Temple, whose nine-storey, 78 m pagoda faced with white porcelain and glazed tiles was famous in Europe as the Porcelain Tower of Nanjing until it was blown up in 1856 during the Taiping war. A heritage park opened here in December 2015 with a light modern tower of steel and art glass over the excavated pagoda base, deliberately not a copy of the original, and glass walkways above the Song and Ming foundations. Displays cover the crypt of the Northern Song Changgan Temple, where an iron casket holding the Seven-Treasure Ashoka stupa was found in 2008, and a Ming imperial stele of 1428 survives on the site.

rows.name: Happy Valley Nanjing
rows.summary: A large theme park in Qixia District, opened in November 2020 as the eighth park of China's Happy Valley chain. It has more than 40 rides, among them several roller coasters such as a Bolliger & Mabillard wing coaster and an Intamin launched coaster, and stages seasonal themed festivals. It suits a full day out for families and ride enthusiasts.

rows.name: Hongshan Forest Zoo
rows.summary: A zoo of about 68 hectares spread over three wooded hills in northern Nanjing, Xiao Hongshan, Da Hongshan and Fangniu Shan, which opened in 1998 when the old Xuanwu Lake Zoo moved here. It keeps more than 3,000 animals of over 260 species in hillside enclosures, among them giant pandas, golden snub-nosed monkeys, South China tigers, Asian elephants, giraffes and red-crowned cranes, and runs a rescue centre for injured native wildlife. It ended animal performances in 2011 and stopped visitors feeding the animals in 2014.

rows.name: Jinling Arsenal (Chenguang 1865 Creative Park)
rows.summary: Founded by Li Hongzhang in 1865 as the Jinling Machinery Bureau, at the time China's largest arsenal, it made guns and ammunition for his Huai Army, was renamed the Jinling Arsenal in 1929 and moved its production to Chongqing in 1937. Its brick workshops from the late Qing and Republican years survive, among them the original machine hall of 1865, and since 2007 they have been reused as the Chenguang 1865 science and technology creative park.

rows.name: Jinling Scriptural Press
rows.summary: A Buddhist publishing house founded in 1866 by the lay scholar Yang Wenhui (Yang Renshan), often called the father of China's modern Buddhist revival, who taught figures such as the monk Taixu and the scholar Zhang Taiyan here. It still makes Buddhist books entirely by hand, carving the text on woodblocks, printing it and thread-binding the volumes, a craft listed as national intangible heritage in 2006 and included in China's block-printing entry on the UNESCO intangible heritage list in 2009. Staff can be seen at work in its craft display area.

rows.name: Jinniu Lake
rows.summary: Nanjing's largest artificial lake, a reservoir built in 1958 on the Babai River in the far north of Liuhe District, near the borders of Tianchang and Yizheng and overlooked by Jinniu Hill. It hosted water-sports events of the 2014 Nanjing Youth Olympic Games and has since staged dragon-boat and sailing races; visitors can take sightseeing boats or speedboats, paddle a kayak or try wakesurfing and a floating obstacle course. The surrounding countryside is one of the places that claim to be the home of the folk song Mo Li Hua (Jasmine Flower).

rows.name: Jinniu Lake Wildlife Kingdom
rows.summary: A safari park on the west shore of Jinniu Lake, laid out over hillsides and former quarry pits and holding more than 300 species of animals. In the drive-through section visitors follow a 3.2 km route in their own cars, with woodland and water used as barriers instead of fences; the walking section has a science hall, jellyfish and amphibian houses and animal-feeding areas. The walking section also puts on staged shows, including a circus, sea-lion performances and an animal parade, and has fairground rides, so it suits families with children.

rows.name: John Rabe House
rows.summary: The house where John Rabe, the Siemens representative in Nanjing and chairman of the International Committee for the Nanking Safety Zone, lived from 1932 to 1938 and wrote his diaries of the Nanjing Massacre; during the massacre he sheltered hundreds of Chinese refugees in the house and its garden. Restored with German support, it opened in 2006 as the John Rabe and International Safety Zone Memorial Hall, whose photographs, documents and objects tell the story of Rabe and the other foreigners who ran the Safety Zone.

rows.name: Liji Lane Comfort Station Exhibition Hall
rows.name_zh: 利济巷慰安所旧址陈列馆
rows.summary: A group of two-storey houses built in 1935 as a residential estate, which from the end of 1937 served the Japanese army as 'comfort stations' where women, many from the Korean peninsula, were held for sexual slavery. Identified in 2003 by Pak Yong-sim, a survivor from North Korea who had been held here, the derelict buildings were restored and opened in December 2015 as a branch of the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall. Seven buildings of about 2,000 m² hold exhibitions on the Japanese military's comfort-women system, with a statue based on a photograph of Pak taken at her rescue.

rows.name: Longjiang Treasure Shipyard Site
rows.summary: The dockyard by the Yangtze in north-western Nanjing where the great 'treasure ships' of Zheng He's early-15th-century voyages are believed to have been built, listed as the site of the Ming Longjiang shipyard. Three long water-filled docks survive of the original basins; excavations in 2003–04 found wooden building frames in them, and a huge rudder post was dug up here in 1957. The site is now a park with the docks, a replica treasure ship and a small display of finds.

rows.name: Meishan Steel Industrial Culture Tourism Area
rows.summary: An industrial tourism area inside the Meishan steelworks on Nanjing's south-western edge, a plant begun in the late 1960s as the '9424' project to supply iron to Shanghai and now one of Baosteel's main production bases. Old workshops have been turned into a steel experience hall, where a model blast furnace and projections show molten iron being poured, a factory history exhibition and a former locomotive repair shed with a steam engine on show, and giant cooling towers are painted with sky and clouds. Rated 4A in 2023, it is aimed mainly at school study trips and families.

rows.name: Meiyuan Xincun Memorial Hall
rows.summary: The group of houses in the Meiyuan Xincun residential quarter where the Communist Party delegation led by Zhou Enlai lived and worked from May 1946 to March 1947, during its negotiations with the Nationalist government in Nanjing. The memorial, opened in 1977, takes in the delegation's former offices and residences, an exhibition hall on the Nanjing negotiations opened in 1990, a bronze statue of Zhou Enlai and a Zhou Enlai library opened in 1998.

rows.name: Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders
rows.name_zh: 侵华日军南京大屠杀遇难同胞纪念馆
rows.pinyin: Qīnhuá Rìjūn Nánjīng Dàtúshā Yùnàn Tóngbāo Jìniànguǎn
rows.summary: The memorial museum to the victims of the mass killings carried out by Japanese troops after they captured Nanjing, then China's capital, on 13 December 1937. It stands at Jiangdongmen, where prisoners of war and civilians were killed and buried, and opened in 1985; enlarged in 1995 and 2005, it holds the main historical exhibition, an excavated burial pit with human remains, memorial squares and sculpture, and a peace park. The national listing also covers the other killing and burial sites around the city, most marked by memorial steles erected from 1985 onwards.

rows.name: Ming Palace Ruins
rows.summary: The ruins of the early Ming imperial palace, the model for Beijing's Forbidden City, which decayed after the court moved to Beijing in the 1420s and was later cut in two by an airfield and by Zhongshan East Road in the 1920s. South of the road, Wumen Park keeps the stone base of the Meridian Gate with its five archways, the inner Five Dragon Bridges and the site of the Fengtian Gate; north of it, the Ming Palace Ruins Park shows the bases and stone column plinths of the three great halls. The Donghua Gate and Xi'an Gate survive as separate gate ruins nearby.

rows.name: Mochou Lake Park
rows.summary: A lake park in western Nanjing, west of the Qinhuai River and Hanzhongmen, laid out around Mochou Lake, which takes its name from Mochou, a virtuous young woman of local legend. Halls, pavilions and covered walkways stand among rockeries and trees on the shore, among them the two-storey Shengqi Pavilion, the Yujin Hall and a white marble statue of Mochou beside a lotus pool. By tradition the Ming founder Zhu Yuanzhang gave the lakeside garden to his general Xu Da, and in summer boats can be taken out among the lotus.

rows.name: Nanjing Eye Footbridge & Hexi Riverside
rows.summary: A riverside park area of about 61 hectares on both banks of the Jiajiang, the arm of the Yangtze between Nanjing's Hexi new town and Jiangxinzhou island, taking its name from the Nanjing Eye, a cable-stayed footbridge across the channel. The bridge was completed in 2014 for the Nanjing Youth Olympic Games, described at the time as the first bridge over the Yangtze for pedestrians only, and links the riverside of the Youth Olympic quarter with the Youth Olympic Forest Park on the island. The area is themed on the river landscape and the 2014 Games, and is a place to stroll the riverfront and cross the Yangtze channel on foot.

rows.name: Nanjing Great Hall of the People
rows.summary: Built in 1935–36 as the National Assembly Hall, where the Republic of China's National Assembly met in 1946 and 1948, this four-storey hall on Changjiang Road pairs a modern symmetrical façade with simplified Chinese ornament and seats more than 3,400; it now hosts Nanjing's annual congress sessions and stage performances. Sharing its wall to the east is the former National Art Gallery, finished in 1936 to the same competition-winning design by Xi Fuquan as China's first national art museum. The gallery is now the old building of the Jiangsu Art Museum and reopened for exhibitions in 2017 after renovation.

rows.name: Nanjing Man Site (Tangshan Ape-Man Cave)
rows.summary: Hulu (Gourd) Cave on the northern slope of Tangshan, a limestone cave where workers found two fossil human skulls and many mammal fossils in 1993; the skulls belong to Homo erectus and are known as Nanjing Man. The cave is now the centre of a fossil-site park of about 75 hectares, where a time tunnel leads from the cave to a site museum, opened in 2014, that traces the area's geology and human evolution and displays the two skulls. The female skull has been dated to roughly 600,000 years ago and the male one to about 300,000 years ago.

rows.name: Nanjing Museum
rows.summary: Jiangsu's provincial museum, founded in 1933 as the preparatory office of the National Central Museum, with a collection of more than 400,000 objects that is especially strong in Ming and Qing imperial porcelain. Its main hall, begun in 1936 and finished in 1948 in the style of a Liao-dynasty temple with Liang Sicheng and Liu Dunzhen as advisers, houses the history of Jiangsu from prehistory to the Qing. Other halls, enlarged in an expansion finished in 2013, cover Chinese art, the Republic of China period, intangible heritage such as Nanjing brocade, and changing special exhibitions.

rows.name: Nanjing Science and Technology Museum
rows.summary: Nanjing's main science museum, set beside Huashen Lake in Yuhuatai District, with hands-on halls on scientific principles, space and the Earth. After nearly a year of renovation it reopened in July 2025 with new space exhibits, including a full-size replica of a space-station core module with virtual-reality launch rides. It suits families with children.

rows.name: Niushoushan
rows.summary: A twin-peaked hill south of Nanjing, a Buddhist centre since the Southern Dynasties and the birthplace of the Niutou school of Chan, redeveloped as a Buddhist cultural park that opened in 2015 to enshrine a relic venerated as part of the Buddha's skull, found in 2008 in the crypt beneath the old Bao'en Temple. The relic is kept in the Usnisa Palace, a vast domed building set into a pit left by iron mining on the west peak, with a hall holding a jade reclining Buddha and a thousand-Buddha hall inside, beside a new nine-storey Tang-style pagoda and the old Hongjue Temple pagoda. Paths also lead to stone ramparts linked to Yue Fei's victory over the Jin here in 1130 and to the tomb of the Ming admiral Zheng He on the southern slopes.

rows.name: Pearl Spring Scenic Area
rows.summary: A hill-and-lake scenic area at the eastern foot of Laoshan in Pukou, facing the Yangtze, named after a spring whose bubbles rise in strings like pearls and praised in Ming and Qing times as the finest outing north of the river. It now mixes nature with built attractions: bamboo rafts and boats on Jingshan Lake, a wildlife park with tigers, lions, bears and monkeys, a mountain toboggan run, a cable car and a 3 km imitation of the Great Wall built along the ridge in 1995. Next to the scenic area stands Dingshan Temple, founded in 503 and rebuilt in Tang style, which tradition links with Bodhidharma.

rows.name: Pingshan Forest Park
rows.summary: A wooded hill park of about 22 km² in Liuhe District, north of the Yangtze, which the district describes as its largest green conservation area, with forest cover of more than 85% and a highest point of 161 m. Woodland paths and lakeside boardwalks run through the park, which also has a cherry-blossom valley, Shuangdie Lake and tea gardens. The gardens grow the local Huaping Yuhua green tea, and a small exhibition hall in the park is devoted to its tea culture.

rows.name: Presidential Palace, Nanjing
rows.summary: A 9-hectare compound on Changjiang Road that was in turn a Ming prince's mansion, the office of the Qing viceroy of Liangjiang, the palace of the Taiping Heavenly King Hong Xiuquan, the seat of Sun Yat-sen's provisional presidency in 1912 and the headquarters of the Nationalist government and presidency until 1949. Since 2003 it has been the China Modern History Museum: an axis of Chinese-style halls behind the 1929 gateway leads to the 1936 Zichao Building with the offices of Chiang Kai-shek and Li Zongren, while the west side holds Sun Yat-sen's presidential office and the Xu Garden with its stone boat. Other buildings hold a reconstruction of the Taiping throne room and exhibitions on the site's history.

rows.name: Pukou Railway Station
rows.summary: The British-designed southern terminus of the Tianjin–Pukou Railway on the north bank of the Yangtze, opened in 1914, where passengers from the north crossed by ferry to Nanjing until the Yangtze River Bridge opened in 1968. The protected group includes the station building, its covered walkways and the old booking hall, and the surrounding streets were restored as a historic quarter, completed in 2024, while the tracks still serve freight. The quarter draws on Zhu Ziqing's essay 'Back', set at this station, and has a statue of the writer.

rows.name: Putang Bridge
rows.summary: A nine-arched stone bridge across the Putang River in Putang village, Honglan, rebuilt in 1508–1512 with money from the local Zhao brothers on the line of the old post road from Lishui to Xuancheng. At 91.3 m long it is the largest old bridge surviving in Lishui District, built of local volcanic tuff, with pointed cutwaters on its eight piers and 72 balustrade posts each topped by a small carved lion. It carried road traffic until a new bridge was built alongside, and was restored as a footbridge in 2009–2010, when its stone deck was relaid.

rows.name: Qiqiaoweng Bridge
rows.summary: A seven-arched Ming stone bridge over the Qinhuai River south-east of the old city, completed in 1440 and first called Shangfang Bridge after the nearby gate of the Ming outer wall. About 90 m long and 13 m wide, it is the largest old bridge surviving in Nanjing; carved dragon heads line the arches and scaly guardian beasts with human faces rear up from the cutwaters to mark flood levels. Restored in 2008–09, when missing carvings were replaced, it still carries traffic and stands at the western end of Qiqiaoweng Wetland Park along the river.

rows.name: Qixia Mountain & Qixia Temple
rows.summary: A low wooded hill above the Yangtze north-east of Nanjing, known for its red autumn maples, with Qixia Temple at its western foot, founded in 489 in the house of the recluse Ming Sengshao and regarded as the ancestral seat of the Sanlun (Madhyamaka) school of Chinese Buddhism; its present halls date from a rebuilding begun in 1919. Beside the temple stand an octagonal five-storey stone stupa, rebuilt under the Southern Tang in the 10th century, and the Thousand Buddha Cliff, niches and statues cut into the hillside from 489 onwards. In a pavilion before the gate is the stele of 676 honouring Ming Sengshao, its text composed by Emperor Gaozong of Tang, and in the winter of 1937–38 the temple sheltered refugees from the Nanjing Massacre.

rows.name: Southern Dynasty Tomb Sculptures, Nanjing
