Themed zones of tanks show marine life from many seas, with jellyfish displays and mermaid performances, and it is aimed squarely at families with children.

rows.name: Laoyuhe Wetland Park
rows.summary: An urban wetland park on the eastern shore of Dian Lake in Chenggong district, laid out where the Laoyu River enters the lake. Paths run through planted wetland and lakeside woodland, and it is mainly a local spot for walking and cycling rather than a destination in itself.

rows.name: Lu Han's Mansion
rows.summary: The 1930s residence of Lu Han, chairman of Yunnan province, opposite the east gate of Green Lake Park: a two-storey house with red tiles, carved stone door and window surrounds and steep, Gothic-influenced roofs. On 9 December 1949 Lu Han detained several senior Nationalist figures here and declared the Kunming uprising, by which Yunnan changed sides peacefully in the civil war. After restoration it opened as a public museum in 2020, with displays on the uprising.

rows.name: Qinglong Gorge, Anning
rows.summary: A forested gorge of about 19 square kilometres in Qinglong subdistrict, north-west of central Anning, with streams, waterfalls and old climbing vines along its trails. It is run as a family day out, and the walks are combined with add-on activities such as rafting.

rows.name: Qiongzhu Temple
rows.summary: A Buddhist temple on Yu'an Mountain north-west of Kunming, known as the first Chan (Zen) temple in Yunnan: tradition dates it to the Tang, and it rose to prominence when the monk Xiongbian taught here in the early Yuan dynasty. Most of the present buildings date from late Qing rebuilding. It is famous for its 500 painted clay arhats, each about a metre tall, made between 1883 and 1890 by the Sichuan sculptor Li Guangxiu and his students, which line the main hall and two side pavilions.

rows.name: Shilongba Hydropower Station
rows.summary: Mainland China's first hydropower station, built in 1910–1912 on the Tanglang River, the only outlet of Dian Lake, with German Siemens generators and Austrian Voith turbines; it is still generating today. The old powerhouse keeps a 240-kilowatt Voith unit that still works, and the China Hydropower Museum, set up on the site in 2008, tells its history. A pond in the grounds fills a crater left by a Japanese air raid in 1940.

rows.name: Shizhaishan Archaeological Site Park
rows.summary: Shizhaishan, a low hill near the south-eastern shore of Dian Lake, was the burial ground of the rulers of the ancient Dian kingdom; excavations from the 1950s onwards yielded the 'Seal of the King of Dian' and bronze cowrie containers topped with scenes of sacrifice and oath-taking. The nearby Hebosuo site, thought to have been the kingdom's main settlement and later the seat of the Han commandery of Yizhou, has yielded more than 2,000 Han-dynasty official seal impressions and tens of thousands of bamboo and wooden slips. An archaeological park covering both began trial opening in May 2026, centred on an exhibition hall of finds at the Shizhaishan excavation station.

rows.name: Tomb of Sayyid Ajjal Shams al-Din
rows.summary: The tomb of Sayyid Ajjal Shams al-Din Omar (1211–1279), a Muslim official from Bukhara whom Kublai Khan sent to Yunnan in 1274 as the Yuan dynasty's first provincial governor; he founded a new city on the site of modern Kunming, where he had a Confucian temple, a Buddhist temple and mosques built, and the admiral Zheng He was descended from him. The rectangular stone tomb, restored and walled in 1985, lies on Ma'er Hill in the northern outskirts, while a stone cenotaph inscribed in Chinese and Mongolian stands in the city's Wujing area.

rows.name: Wang Renqiu Stele
rows.summary: A red-sandstone memorial stele raised in 698, under Empress Wu Zetian's Zhou dynasty, by the son of Wang Renqiu, a local official who helped the Tang put down a revolt; it is the only Tang stele surviving in the Kunming area. About 4 metres high on a tortoise base, it is topped with two dragons and a Buddhist niche, and its inscription of more than 1,600 characters includes over 150 of the new characters introduced under Empress Wu. Since 1991 it has stood in a pavilion within a small stele garden in the hills south-west of Anning.

rows.name: Wenquan Cliff Inscriptions, Anning
rows.summary: A 200-metre stretch of cliff above the Tanglang River at Anning's hot-spring town of Wenquan, carved with more than 160 inscriptions, mostly poems and descriptions of the springs by Ming and Qing visitors. The earliest, 'Listening to the Spring', was written by He Mengchun, who became the Ming governor of Yunnan in 1521. The carvings run in three groups from the 'Nine-Bend Dragon's Nest' to the spring called the 'Finest Hot Spring under Heaven'.

rows.name: World Horti-Expo Garden
rows.summary: The grounds of the 1999 Kunming International Horticultural Exposition cover about 220 hectares of wooded slopes in the north-eastern suburbs, next to the Golden Temple. The site keeps its exhibition halls, including a large greenhouse, along with themed gardens for tea, bamboo, bonsai, medicinal herbs, trees and vegetables, and dozens of gardens laid out by Chinese provinces and by other countries.

rows.name: Xinglin Grand View Garden
rows.summary: A park themed on traditional Chinese medicine in the Taiwan farmers' enterprise park of Shilin county, combining medicinal-plant gardens and displays on Chinese medicine with wellness activities and a hot-spring spa. It is a commercial wellness and agri-tourism development rather than a heritage site, and is sometimes added to a Stone Forest trip.

rows.name: Yulong Bay
rows.summary: A leisure park near Taiping in Anning, set among lakes and forested hills about 24 km from central Kunming and listed as a 4A site in 2022. It has an 'old Kunming' street area, lakeside and forest walks and family activities, alongside a golf course, a riding club and lakeside hotels.

rows.name: Yunnan Ethnic Village
rows.summary: An ethnographic theme park of about 89 hectares on the shore of Dian Lake, where replica villages show the houses, crafts and customs of Yunnan's ethnic groups, including the Bai, Dai, Yi, Wa, Naxi and Tibetans. Staff in ethnic dress explain local customs, and staged versions of festivals such as the Dai Water-Splashing and Yi Torch festivals are held for visitors.

rows.name: Yunnan Military Academy
rows.summary: The former campus of a military academy founded in Kunming in 1909, in the last years of the Qing dynasty, which trained more than 9,000 officers before it closed in 1935; its graduates included Zhu De and Ye Jianying as well as cadets from Korea and Vietnam. The surviving main building is a two-storey block built round a large courtyard, each side about 120 metres long. It houses the Yunnan Military Academy History Museum, opened in 2009, with exhibitions on the academy and on the Chinese Expeditionary Force of the Second World War.

rows.name: Yunnan Wildlife Park
rows.summary: A large zoo opened in 2004 on the forested slopes of Jindian (Golden Temple) National Forest Park in north-east Kunming. More than 200 species are kept in hillside enclosures, including big cats in a lion-and-tiger area, and sightseeing buses link the stops on the long circuit.

rows.name: Zheng He Park and Ma Haji Tomb Stele
rows.summary: The tomb stele of Ma Haji, father of the Ming admiral Zheng He, stands on the western slope of Yueshan hill in Zheng He Park in Kunyang. Its inscription, composed in Nanjing by the Minister of Rites Li Zhigang before Zheng He's first voyage, records the family's history, and a note on the back records that Zheng He returned to sweep the tomb in 1411. Two steles about Zheng He, put up in 1935, flank it, and the park also has a Zheng He memorial hall.

rows.name: Zhenqing Taoist Temple
rows.summary: Regarded as the largest group of historic buildings in central Kunming, it covers about 2 hectares at the junction of Tuodong Road and Baita Road and dates from the Ming and Qing dynasties. It is made up of three parts, the Zhenqing Temple itself, the Duleifu hall and the Yanlong Shrine, and is still a working Taoist temple and the seat of the Kunming Taoist Association.

rows.name: Baisha Murals and Dabaoji Palace
rows.summary: Baisha village, north of Lijiang and part of the Old Town of Lijiang World Heritage Site, was an early political centre of the Naxi, and its Ming-dynasty halls hold the best-known group of the Baisha murals. The Dabaoji Palace and the neighbouring Liuli Hall, protected together as a national monument, have wall paintings that mix Chinese Buddhist, Daoist and Tibetan Buddhist imagery, reflecting the Naxi rulers' support for several religions.

rows.name: Baoshan Stone Town
rows.summary: Baoshan Stone Town is a Naxi village built on top of a huge rock outcrop above the right bank of the Jinsha River, in the north-east of Yulong county. Founded in the early Yuan dynasty (1264–1294), it served as the seat of Baoshan prefecture, and it is still inhabited, listed among China's traditional villages.

rows.name: Black Dragon Pool
rows.summary: Black Dragon Pool lies in Jade Spring Park at the foot of Elephant Hill, just north of Lijiang Old Town, and its springs feed the streams that run through the old town. The park was laid out in 1737 and is known for the view of Jade Dragon Snow Mountain across the pool and its white marble bridge. Its Ming and Qing pavilions and halls, including the Moon-Embracing Pavilion (rebuilt in 1963 after a fire), are protected as a national monument.

rows.name: Guanyin Gorge
rows.summary: Guanyin Gorge, at Qihe south of Lijiang, is a scenic area described as the southern gateway to the Lijiang basin, where the old Tea Horse Road passed through the Yulong Pass. It combines the wooded gorge with Tea Horse Road and Naxi folk-culture attractions.

rows.name: Guanyin Pavilion, Yongsheng
rows.summary: Guanyin Pavilion, also called Lingyuan Guanyin Temple, sits beneath a cliff above the Lingyuan stream on the eastern edge of Yongsheng county town. Its hall, rebuilt in 1876 with marble balustrades and carved wooden screens, encloses a 1.78-metre image of Guanyin carved into the rock face. The carving is inscribed as after the Tang painter Wu Daozi, a design said to have reached Yongsheng in the Dali Kingdom period with Buddhist scriptures brought back from the Chinese interior.

rows.name: Jinlong Bridge
rows.summary: Jinlong Bridge is an iron-chain suspension bridge across the Jinsha River between Qihe in Lijiang and Zili in Yongsheng, built in 1876–1880 and long an important crossing on the Tea Horse Road between Lijiang, Yongsheng and Sichuan. Sixteen iron chains of about 500 links each carry its 138-metre plank deck, with two more as handrails, between stone abutments topped by gate pavilions. Because the site lies in a hydropower reservoir's flood zone, the bridge was rebuilt in place about 6 metres higher, a project completed in 2016.

rows.name: Lashi Lake
rows.summary: Lashi Lake lies at about 2,440 metres in a basin on the south-eastern slopes of Jade Dragon Snow Mountain, 8 km west of Lijiang, and is the core of a provincial wetland nature reserve set up in 1998. Some 20,000 to 30,000 migratory waterbirds winter here, among them black-necked cranes and bar-headed geese, and 57 bird species have been recorded in the wetland. A dam built since the 1980s keeps the once-seasonal lake at a steady level.

rows.name: Liming Danxia, Laojun Mountain
rows.summary: Liming, a Lisu township in western Yulong county, has about 240 square kilometres of red Danxia sandstone landforms within the Laojun Mountain area, part of the Three Parallel Rivers World Heritage Site. Its best-known sight is Qiangui ('Thousand Turtles') Mountain, a red sandstone dome whose cracked, weathered surface looks like rows of crawling turtles.

rows.name: Maojiawan, Yongsheng
rows.summary: Maojiawan, a village in Chenghai town at the foot of Fenghuang Mountain south-west of Chenghai Lake, is promoted locally as the ancestral home of Mao Zedong's forebears. The Shaoshan Mao clan genealogy traces the family to Mao Taihua, a Jiangxi man who served at the Lancang garrison in what is now Yongsheng before moving on to Hunan in the early Ming, and local tradition holds that some of his descendants stayed here, though sources differ on the dates. The village has a Mao clan ancestral hall.

rows.name: Puji Temple, Lijiang
rows.summary: Puji Temple stands at the foot of Puji Hill, about 6 km west of Lijiang Old Town, and is counted among the five main monasteries of the Karma Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism in the Lijiang area. Founded in 1771, it keeps Qing and Republican-era buildings that are protected as a national monument.

rows.name: Qina Old Buildings
rows.summary: In the Ming dynasty a post station, Qingshui, was set up on the official road through what is now Qina town, and garrison officers and wealthy families built houses, ancestral halls, temples and schools along it. The listed group comprises nine buildings, including Ruiguang Temple, the Dongyue Temple and several family halls and courtyards, with dated Ming timber structures preserved by the dry valley climate. Apart from the two temples, which are collectively owned, the buildings are privately owned.

rows.name: Shuhe Old Town
rows.summary: Shuhe, about 4 km north-west of Dayan, is one of the earliest Naxi settlements around Lijiang and grew into a market town on the Tea Horse Road, known from the Ming dynasty for its leatherworkers. Part of the Old Town of Lijiang World Heritage Site, it has a market square, the Qinglong Bridge, the spring-fed Jiuding Dragon Pool and the Qing-dynasty Sansheng Palace, while the Ming murals of its Dajue Palace are protected as a national monument. Like Baisha, it is usually quieter than Dayan.

rows.name: Yingpan Village Tombs
rows.summary: On a hillside above Yingpan village in Liude township, the Taliu, a Yi subgroup living around Taliu Mountain, built some 7,000 stone-faced tombs between the late Ming and the Republican era, most of them in the late 17th and 18th centuries. About 2,500 survive largely intact, many with archway-style headstones up to 2 metres high, carved in relief with auspicious animals and flowers.

rows.name: Yushuizhai
rows.summary: Yushuizhai, at the southern foot of Jade Dragon Snow Mountain on the northern edge of Baisha, is a Naxi Dongba cultural site built around a sacred spring that drops down the hillside in a three-tier cascade. It has a temple to Dongba Shiluo, regarded as the founder of the Dongba religion, and a gallery of murals in the Dongba painting style.

rows.name: Banhong Hulu Wang Di (Banhong Incident Site)
rows.summary: A scenic area around Banhong, a Wa village on the Myanmar border in Cangyuan county, where local Wa people clashed with British forces in 1934 as a silver-mining company moved in from Burma. The Banhong Incident led to renewed Sino-British boundary talks, and the village now has a memorial stele at the incident site and a memorial hall, with tea gardens on the surrounding hills.

rows.name: Cangyuan Rock Paintings & Sigangli Valley
rows.summary: Red rock paintings at 17 sites on limestone cliffs at 1,200–2,000 metres in Cangyuan county, made with haematite pigment, apparently by finger, and dated by uranium-series tests to about 3,800–2,700 years ago. The Sigangli Rock Painting Valley scenic area combines the main painting site with a sinkhole, caves including Sigangli, the cave of the Wa creation legend, and Bange village, where a new visitor centre opened in 2026.

rows.name: Guangyun Temple
rows.summary: A Theravada Buddhist temple in Mengdong, the county town of Cangyuan, also known as Xuetang ('school') Temple. Its Qing-dynasty main hall combines an entrance pavilion, whose extra false eaves make it appear five-tiered, with a long hall under a triple-eaved roof and carved, painted beams. Ten murals inside show Jataka tales of the Buddha's previous lives and processions of the local chieftain.

rows.name: Hulu (Gourd) Town, Cangyuan
rows.summary: A Wa-themed leisure quarter built on the edge of Cangyuan county town around Gourd Lake, with red-walled Wa-style buildings, totem carvings and large gourd sculptures recalling the Wa creation myth. Evening song-and-dance and craft workshops such as weaving and wood carving are put on for visitors. It is a modern development with no old buildings; for a traditional Wa village, go to Wengding.

rows.name: Liulang River Water Mills
rows.summary: A group of Qing-dynasty water mills along the middle reach of the Liulang River at Gumo village in Shili township, northern Fengqing county. Of the 27 mills, 21 are still in working order.

rows.name: Mengwang and Northwest Pagodas
rows.summary: Two Ming-dynasty pagodas north-west of central Lincang, listed together as a national heritage unit. The Northwest Pagoda stands on the north-western edge of the city, and Mengwang Pagoda about 6 km further north-west in Zhangtuo township.

rows.name: Mengxiang Wetland Park
rows.summary: A wetland park on the edge of Gengma county town, laid out around a lake with reed beds, groves of trees and boardwalks. Its square hosts local festivals such as the Dai Water-Splashing Festival, and it makes a pleasant evening stroll if you are staying in Gengma.

rows.name: Rongkangda Oolong Tea Estate
rows.summary: A company-run oolong tea estate and eco-cultural park in Shahe township just outside Shuangjiang county town, with tea gardens spread over the surrounding hills. Paths lead through the plantation to viewpoints over the valley, and the estate hotel offers tea-related activities.

rows.name: Wanyao Pottery Village, Boshang
rows.summary: A pottery village in Boshang town south of Lincang city, founded according to the county gazetteer in 1738 by three potters from Hunan who built dragon kilns to use the local clay. Its earthenware making is on Yunnan's provincial intangible heritage list, and around 60 households still work as potters, alongside pottery cafés, guesthouses and study programmes added in recent years.

rows.name: Wengding Wa Village
rows.summary: A Wa village in Cangyuan county long described as the most completely preserved traditional Wa settlement, with thatched stilt houses (people lived above, livestock below) and ritual posts once used in sacrifices. Fire destroyed almost all of its 105 houses in February 2021; the old village was rebuilt on the same site and reopened at the end of 2022, while most villagers now live in a new village nearby.

rows.name: Dulong River Valley
rows.summary: The remote valley of the Dulong River, a headwater of the Irrawaddy, in the far north-western corner of Yunnan, west of the Gaoligong range and bordering Tibet and Myanmar. It is the only area where the Derung (Dulong) people live together as a community, and almost all of the township's roughly 4,650 residents are Derung.

rows.name: Laomudeng and Zhiziluo
rows.summary: Two neighbouring places high on the eastern slopes of the Nu River canyon in Pihe Nu Township. Laomudeng is a Nu village with a plain Christian church, while Zhiziluo, about 2 km away along a footpath, was the seat of Nujiang Prefecture from 1954 to 1974 and of Bijiang County until 1986, and its largely empty buildings from that era now draw visitors as a 'city of memory'.

rows.name: China Pu'er Tea Expo Garden
rows.summary: A tea-themed park on Yingpan Mountain south-east of Pu'er city, set in the middle of some 1,500 hectares of tea gardens. Its core area holds a Pu'er tea museum covering the tea's origins, cultivation, processing and trade, along with tea-making workshops, a hall to the tea ancestor and tasting houses. Visitors can try picking and processing tea and look out over the tea hills from the higher viewpoints.

rows.name: Dai Buddhist Temples of Jinggu
rows.summary: A national heritage listing that groups three Dai Theravada Buddhist sites of Ming and Qing date in Jinggu county: the twin stupas of Mengwo Temple and the Qiannuo and Mangdao temples. The most accessible are the Mengwo twin stupas in the county town. Qiannuo Temple stands in a village some way to the south-west.

rows.name: Jingdong Confucian Temple
rows.summary: The Confucian temple of Jingdong, founded in 1442 under the Ming and moved and rebuilt several times since. The east-facing complex keeps its screen wall, semicircular pond, bell and drum towers, Lingxing Gate, side halls and a five-bay Dacheng Hall with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, with the former school laid out beside the temple. It was listed as a national heritage site in 2013.

rows.name: Laodabao Lahu Village
rows.summary: A Lahu village in Jiujing township, Lancang county, known as the home of the song 'Happy Lahu' and for villagers who sing Lahu folk songs to the guitar. In 2013 the villagers set up a performance company in which they hold shares, and it stages song-and-dance shows for visitors. The village is a base for two nationally listed intangible heritage traditions, the Lahu creation epic Mupa Mipa and the lusheng dance.

rows.name: Menglian Chieftain's Palace
rows.summary: The seat of the Dao family, hereditary Dai chieftains of Menglian, whose post the Qing raised to a pacification commission (xuanfusi) in 1709; in Dai it is called the 'golden palace'. The present compound, rebuilt from the late 19th century into the early 20th, combines Chinese-style gate towers and courtyards with raised Dai halls and houses the county's ethnic history museum, with the chieftains' robes, seals and documents on show. It stands at the top of Nayun, the old town of Menglian, whose upper, middle and lower quarters are still lived in.

rows.name: Mengsuo Dragon Lake
rows.summary: A natural freshwater lake at about 1,150 m beside Ximeng, a Wa autonomous county in western Pu'er, ringed by forest and regarded by the Wa as a sacred lake. In the woods behind it lies Longmoye, a Wa sacred site where buffalo skulls from sacrifices are kept among the trees and rites are held during the Wa wooden-drum festival each April.

rows.name: Mohei Ancient Town
rows.summary: An old salt-producing town in north-eastern Ning'er county, whose name comes from Dai words meaning 'salt well'. Local accounts trace salt working here to the Han dynasty, and production expanded under the Qing, making Mohei one of Yunnan's main salt districts and a busy stop on the Tea Horse Road. Caravan inns, shops, old houses, bridges and stretches of the old road survive in the town.

rows.name: Mojiang Confucian Temple
rows.summary: The former Confucian temple of Talang sub-prefecture, begun in 1821 in Lianzhu, now the county town of Mojiang. Surviving buildings include the Lingxing Gate, the Lingxiao and Kuixing pavilions, side halls, the Chongsheng Hall and a five-bay Dacheng Hall with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, while the pond and one gate have been rebuilt. It was listed as a national heritage site in 2019.

rows.name: Mojiang Tropic of Cancer Park
rows.summary: A hillside park on the western edge of Mojiang county town, built where the Tropic of Cancer passes through, with marker towers, a sundial square and sculptures on the theme of the sun along a path up the hill. It combines astronomy displays and a planetarium with features on Mojiang's 'twins' theme, and is the main venue of the town's International Twins Festival in early May.

rows.name: Monument to the National Unity Oath
rows.summary: A stone stele erected at the start of 1951 after a traditional Wa oath-taking ceremony held to promote unity among the area's ethnic groups under the new government. Abandoned for a time and later recovered, it has stood since 2000 in the National Unity Garden on the north side of Ning'er county town, where a small exhibition hall explains its history. It is presented in China as the first monument to ethnic unity of the People's Republic.

rows.name: Nakeli Tea Horse Road Post Station
rows.summary: A small village in Ning'er county that grew up as a staging post on the Tea Horse Road, where mule caravans rested and traded. Its sights are the Rongfa caravan inn, a covered wind-and-rain bridge more than a century old, and a stretch of the old road paved with dressed stone and cobbles, part of which has been cleared for walking. It makes a pleasant stop for a stroll and a caravan-style meal.

rows.name: Nuofu Church
rows.summary: A church built in 1921 by American Baptist missionaries in Nuofu, a Lahu area in southern Lancang county near the Myanmar border. It takes the form of a Lahu raised timber building wrapped in a veranda, while the interior was fitted out in the manner of a Western church. Services stopped in 1949 but have since resumed, and local Lahu Christians again worship here in their own language.

rows.name: Pu'er Tea Horse Road Heritage Park
rows.summary: A heritage park on the edge of Pu'er city built around a section of the Tea Horse Road, the caravan route along which tea from southern Yunnan was carried north; Pu'er was a gathering point for tribute tea bound for the imperial capital. A walking route of about 5 km follows the old road through the hills on the Banjiupo section, which is protected as part of the national Tea Horse Road listing, and a museum covers the history of the mule caravans. The park lies behind the Chama Ancient Town leisure quarter and stages a caravan-themed water show.

rows.name: Taiyanghe Forest Park
rows.summary: A forest park of about 216 km² in the hills south-east of Pu'er city, protecting a large, little-disturbed tract of southern subtropical monsoon evergreen broadleaf forest. Raised wooden walkways wind among the trees, and electric carts serve the core area, which is closed to private vehicles. More than 2,100 species of higher plants have been recorded here, and the park runs a rescue and breeding centre for rare animals such as white-cheeked gibbons and binturongs.

rows.name: Coloured Sand Forest, Luliang
rows.summary: At the foot of Wufeng Mountain south of Luliang town, the Coloured Sand Forest is about 6 square kilometres of weathered sandstone eroded into ridges, pinnacles and gullies in shades of red, yellow, white and grey. Sand sculptures have been carved among the natural formations, though rain erosion has worn many of them down and some of the named features have collapsed.

rows.name: Cuan Baozi Stele
rows.summary: Carved in AD 405, the Cuan Baozi Stele is the 1.83 m tombstone of Cuan Baozi, a local governor of the powerful Cuan clan, and its 403 characters are a celebrated example of calligraphy caught between clerical and regular script. Unearthed in 1778, it has stood in a stele pavilion here since 1937. Beside it is the Duan alliance stele, erected in 971 after the Duan rulers of the Dali kingdom swore an alliance with 37 tribes of eastern Yunnan.

rows.name: Cuan Longyan Stele
rows.summary: Erected in 458, the Cuan Longyan Stele is the 3.38 m memorial stone of Cuan Longyan, a regional governor from the Cuan clan that dominated eastern Yunnan for centuries. Its 904-character inscription traces the family's origins and offices in regular script with clerical touches, and the rounded head is carved with a dragon, a tiger, the Vermilion Bird and sun and moon symbols. Together with the smaller Cuan Baozi Stele in Qujing it is one of the 'Two Cuan' steles prized by Chinese calligraphers.

rows.name: Dahai Grassland Mountain
rows.summary: Dahai Caoshan ('Dahai grass mountain') is an expanse of high, open grassland in the Wumeng Mountains, in Dahai township south of Huize, ranging from about 2,570 m to 4,017 m. Since 2022 it has also had a ski area at an average altitude of about 3,500 m, open from mid-November to April.

rows.name: Dajue Temple, Luliang
rows.summary: Dajue Temple in the old centre of Luliang is a Buddhist temple whose listed buildings date from the Yuan and Ming dynasties. Its halls include a Hall of Heavenly Kings, and in its grounds stands a brick pagoda known as the Thousand Buddha Pagoda.

rows.name: Duoyi River
rows.summary: The Duoyi River flows through Lubuge township in south-eastern Luoping near the Guizhou border, dropping over dozens of small waterfalls between banks lined with old trees and bamboo. Bouyei villages sit beside it, and its banks are a gathering place for the Bouyei Sanyuesan festival on the third day of the third lunar month.

rows.name: Huize Guild Halls
rows.summary: Huize's old town keeps a group of Qing-dynasty guild halls, the 'eight great halls' built by merchant and migrant communities, mostly from other provinces, among them those of Jiangxi, Huguang, Guizhou, Fujian, Shaanxi and Sichuan. The Jiangxi Guild Hall, also called Wanshou Palace, and the Huguang Guild Hall, or Shoufo Temple, stand among the old streets, and walking between the halls is a good way to explore the town.

rows.name: Kedu Pass Post Road
rows.summary: At Kedu Pass, where the Kedu River marks the border between Yunnan and Guizhou, an old post road about 5 km long and 2 m wide survives beside Kedu village. It is described as the longest and most complete old post road left in Yunnan and is still used by villagers, and its heritage listing dates the route from the Qin to the Qing dynasty.

rows.name: Nizhu River Grand Canyon
rows.summary: The Nizhu River, the lower course of the Kedu River and a tributary of the Beipan, has cut a deep gorge along the Yunnan–Guizhou border in Puli township, Xuanwei. The G56 expressway crosses it on the Duge (Beipanjiang) Bridge, whose deck sits about 565 m above the floor of the gorge and which was the world's highest bridge from its opening in 2016 until 2025.

rows.name: Source of the Pearl River
rows.summary: The Pearl River is held to rise on Maxiong Mountain in Zhanyi, whose eastern slopes became a national forest park of about 12.5 square kilometres in 1993. More than 95 per cent of the park is forested, and it holds around 2,000 plant species, including rarities such as the ghost plant Monotropa uniflora and the giant tree rhododendron.

rows.name: Yulu Earth Crack
rows.summary: The Yulu 'Earth Crack' is a narrow karst slot gorge in Yulu township, south-east of Huize. Visitors explore it on a walking trail that follows the gorge.

rows.name: Bamei Village
rows.summary: Bamei is a Zhuang village in the north of Guangnan county, hidden in a small basin ringed by karst hills with no road in. Visitors arrive by boat through dark limestone river caves about 1 km long, and the village's secluded fields and traditional way of life have earned it the name of a real-life 'Peach Blossom Land'.

rows.name: Dawangyan Rock Paintings
rows.summary: On a cliff in Dawangyan Park above Malipo town, ancient rock paintings are known as the 'Great King' site after the two large human figures at the centre of the main panel. The national heritage list dates them to between the Neolithic and the Zhou dynasty, and they are often said to be over 4,000 years old.

rows.name: Laoshan Battlefield Memorial Site
rows.summary: Laoshan is a small range of peaks on the China–Vietnam border south of Malipo, where Chinese and Vietnamese forces fought a major battle in 1984 during the border conflict that followed their 1979 war. The scenic area covers the former battlefield, with the main peak, gun positions, memorials and an exhibition hall on local support for the front. The Laoshan Battle Memorial Museum and a martyrs' cemetery are near Malipo town.

rows.name: Xiyang River Grand Canyon
rows.summary: This scenic area, also promoted as Nongren Valley, follows a deep, steep-sided stretch of the Xiyang River gorge at Mulu village in Dongbao township, Guangnan county. A riverside boardwalk of about 2 km runs through the gorge, with a glass walkway and glass slide added more recently, and the township holds Zhuang folk festivals and performances here.

rows.name: Dai Ethnic Park
rows.summary: A ticketed area at Ganlanba (Menghan), south-east of Jinghong, that takes in five lived-in Dai villages. Among them is Manchunman, whose Theravada Buddhist temple dates from the Qing dynasty and is protected as a national heritage site. Water-splashing performances are staged every day, so this is where to see the custom outside the April festival.

rows.name: Dayi Tea Estate
rows.summary: A tea estate of about 100 hectares at Menghai, formerly the Tea Horse Road scenic area, renamed in 2016 when the Dayi tea company, a provincial tourism group and the Yunnan Academy of Agricultural Sciences' Tea Research Institute joined forces to run it. Visitors walk through the tea gardens and a reconstructed Tea Horse Road street with a caravan inn displaying artefacts from the old route, and can try pressing pu'er tea cakes by hand.

rows.name: Jingzhen Octagonal Pavilion
rows.summary: The ordination hall of Jingzhen Temple in Mengzhe, built in 1701 and the only original structure left after the temple was destroyed in 1853; the rest of the temple has since been rebuilt. Standing 15.42 m high on a brick base with an indented cross-shaped plan, it is crowned by a cone of eight-sided roofs in eleven tiers and a finial clad in silver floral ornament. It was among the national heritage sites listed in 1988.

rows.name: Manduan Temple
rows.summary: A Theravada Buddhist temple in Man'en village, Mengzhe, whose main hall, built in the late Ming or early Qing, is the oldest surviving timber building in Xishuangbanna. The hall stands on a 1.3 m base under a stepped roof made up of 22 curved planes, with dragon-shaped brackets under the eaves, painted outer walls and gilded stencil decoration inside. The gate, ordination hall, monks' quarters and drum house are modern rebuilds.

rows.name: Manfeilong Pagoda
rows.summary: A cluster of nine white brick stupas at Manfeilong village in Menglong, with a central stupa ringed by eight smaller ones on a plan shaped like an eight-petalled lotus. Dai records date the first building to 1204, but the present group probably dates from a rebuilding in the Qianlong reign of the Qing. Each small stupa has a niche holding a Buddha image; the plinth and niches carry relief carving, and the niche walls gilded stencil painting.

rows.name: Mengbala Resort
rows.summary: A resort development beside the Mengbala golf club on the G214 just outside Menghai town, combining hotels, a hot-spring resort, holiday housing and leisure facilities set in tropical gardens. It is a place to stay and relax rather than a sight in itself.

rows.name: Mengjinglai Dai Village
rows.summary: A Dai village of stilt houses in Daluo town, Menghai county, run as a scenic area by the villagers together with a tourism company; it was listed as a Chinese Traditional Village in 2013. The Daluo River loops past the village and forms the border with Myanmar, with boundary marker 229 on its bank. Visitors see a grove of carved stupas and demonstrations of more than ten traditional crafts, among them brocade weaving, papermaking, slow-wheel pottery, sugar-making and brewing, alongside peacock and elephant-foot-drum dances.

rows.name: Mengle Great Buddhist Temple
rows.summary: A large Theravada Buddhist temple complex on the southern edge of Jinghong, built from 2005 on the site of Jingpiao Temple, a royal temple of the old Dai kingdom destroyed in war in the 19th century; when it was consecrated in 2007 it was billed as the largest Theravada temple in China. Its halls climb a hillside, and since 2020 they have been in the care of the local Buddhist association. It is a modern reconstruction rather than a historic monument.

rows.name: Mengyuan Fairyland
rows.summary: A limestone area of seasonal tropical rainforest at Mengyuan village in Mengla county, with karst peaks, stalactite caves and an underground river. The main show cave, Baojiaoniu Cave, stays at about 21°C, and a cave route of about 1.6 km is divided into themed sections. The area also takes in Dai and Yao villages and forest trails.

rows.name: Single-Tree Forest, Daluo
rows.summary: A huge old banyan in Daluo town whose aerial roots have grown down from the branches and taken root as separate trunks, so that one tree looks like a small grove. Yunnan's forestry authority counts 36 such roots and estimates the tree at more than 1,000 years old, and locally it is called 'Meilongka', Dai for 'one tree makes a forest'. It stands in a small scenic area less than 1 km from the Daluo border crossing and is easily combined with Mengjinglai, about 5 km to the east.

rows.name: Wangtianshu Rainforest Scenic Area
rows.summary: A rainforest area near Bubeng, north of Mengla and within the Xishuangbanna nature reserve, named after the wangtianshu (Parashorea chinensis), a dipterocarp that grows 40 m tall or more and is under first-class national protection in China. Its best-known feature is a canopy walkway of cable and rope slung between the trunks about 36 m above the ground, and boat trips run on the Nanla River.

rows.name: Wild Elephant Valley
rows.summary: A visitor area in the Mengyang section of the Xishuangbanna National Nature Reserve, about 36 km north of Jinghong, where wild Asian elephants sometimes come out of the rainforest to feed and drink. A 2.3 km elevated walkway and a cableway cross the forest canopy to observation points, but sightings are a matter of luck. Captive elephants appear at an elephant 'science park', where since 2023 tricks and rides have given way to displays of natural behaviour such as bathing and feeding; the site also has an elephant museum, a feeding area and a butterfly garden.

rows.name: Xishuangbanna Primeval Forest Park
rows.name_zh: 西双版纳原始森林公园
rows.summary: A forest park created on about 25,000 mu (some 1,700 hectares) of tropical valley rainforest in the Caiyanghe area east of Jinghong, described as the closest primeval forest to the city. Paths lead through the forest, but the park is developed for tour groups, with a staged show in which hundreds of peacocks are released to fly over a lake, an Aini (Hani) village and song-and-dance performances.

rows.name: Xishuangbanna Southern Medicine Garden
rows.summary: A 20-hectare garden of medicinal plants on Xuanwei Avenue in central Jinghong, set up in 1959 by what is now the Yunnan branch of the Institute of Medicinal Plant Development. It grows more than 1,500 species used in Chinese, Dai and other traditional medicine under tall tropical trees, and labelled paths make it a shady hour or two in town that pairs easily with the nearby Tropical Flower Garden.

rows.name: Xishuangbanna Sunac Theme Park
rows.summary: An amusement park in the Sunac resort district on the western side of Jinghong, part of a large complex of hotels and holiday housing. It has rides and family attractions and suits travellers with children.

rows.name: Xishuangbanna Tropical Flower Garden
rows.summary: A tropical garden run by the Yunnan Institute of Tropical Crops on Xuanwei Avenue in central Jinghong, with palms, fruit trees, crop plants and more than a thousand kinds of plants along shady paths. It is an easy few hours in town; the much larger Xishuangbanna Tropical Botanical Garden at Menglun suits serious plant lovers better.

rows.name: Former Wenxingxiang Trading House
rows.summary: The former premises of the Wenxingxiang trading firm, built in 1934 in the old centre of Yuxi. It is listed as a national heritage site in the category of important modern historic sites and buildings.

rows.name: Lijiashan Bronze Museum
rows.summary: The museum for the Lijiashan tombs, a Warring States to Han cemetery of the ancient Yunnan bronze culture at the north-western corner of Xingyun Lake, named one of China's ten major archaeological discoveries of 1992. Excavations in 1972 and 1991 opened 85 tombs and recovered more than 3,000 objects, including weapons, tools, cowrie containers, gold, jade and the celebrated ox-and-tiger bronze table now in the Yunnan Provincial Museum. The museum, founded in 1993, stands in the district town about 13 km south of the cemetery.

rows.name: Longquan Forest Park, Yimen
rows.summary: A forest park on the western edge of Yimen county town, built around Dalongkou, a karst spring where an underground river emerges from the hillside. Lakes, waterside paths and old trees surround the springs, and Longquan Temple and the smaller Longyin Temple stand in the woods.

rows.name: Longxi Clan Manor, Gasa
rows.summary: A fortified manor built in 1938 on a hillside above Gasa for Li Runzhi, a local leader whose private armed force controlled much of the surrounding Ailao Mountains area under the Republic. High rammed-earth walls enclose dozens of rooms whose fittings mix Chinese and Western elements. It is promoted locally as the Ailao Mountain Tusi Mansion.

rows.name: Xiushan Hill Temples, Tonghai
rows.summary: A hill on the southern edge of Tonghai, laid out as Xiushan Park, where temples have stood since the Dali Kingdom and were enlarged and rebuilt under the Yuan, Ming and Qing. Paths climb past a string of buildings listed together as a national heritage site, among them Yongjin Temple, the Qingliang Terrace, the Jade Emperor Pavilion, Puguang Temple, Wanshou Palace and Tonghai's Confucian temple.

rows.name: Yingyuetan Hot Springs
rows.summary: A hot-spring leisure complex at Dayingjie on the western side of Yuxi's Hongta district, with many pools of different temperatures and themes set in gardens around a large pond. The Yuquan Temple stands within the same grounds.

rows.name: Yuxi Kiln Site
rows.summary: The remains of kilns in Yuxi's Hongta district that made porcelain from the Yuan to the Ming dynasty, including blue-and-white and celadon wares. The site is entered through a memorial archway and gate, and has excavated kiln remains, maps of the area's old kiln sites and displays of ceramics from Yuxi and other kilns in the region.

rows.name: Daguli Amusement Park
rows.summary: An amusement park and leisure complex on the edge of Zhenxiong county town in north-eastern Yunnan. It has a roller coaster, a large Ferris wheel with views over the town, a water park and a hot-spring hotel, and mainly serves local families.

rows.name: Dashanbao Black-necked Crane National Nature Reserve
rows.summary: A national nature reserve protecting about 19,200 hectares of high plateau marshland and grassland at 2,200–3,300 metres, west of Zhaotong city. It is one of the largest and densest known wintering grounds of the black-necked crane, a bird of the high plateaus, and has been a Ramsar wetland since 2004. The scenic area follows a loop road past the reserve's lakes and the Tiaodunhe reservoir.

rows.name: Huanglianhe Waterfalls
rows.summary: A river valley in the Wumeng Mountains just outside Daguan county town, which the county promotes as a 'home of waterfalls'. Waterfalls of different sizes line the Huanglian River, set among forest that includes rare dove trees.

rows.name: Jinsha Water Park, Suijiang
rows.summary: A water park on the Jinsha River reservoir at Suijiang county town, laid out on floating platforms on the river, with swimming areas and inflatable play courses. Jet skis and flyboarding are on offer, and the park hosts events such as dragon-boat and music festivals.

rows.name: Long Family Ancestral Hall
rows.summary: The ancestral hall built from the early 1930s by Long Yun, the ethnic Yi chairman of Yunnan's provincial government in the Republican era, about 7 km south of Zhaotong city. Enclosed by a wall and a lotus-planted moat, it pairs a shrine of three courtyards with a residential compound guarded by watchtowers, mixing Chinese temple layout, garden design, European details and features of Yi fortified manors. Its fine wood and stone carving includes a five-dragon stone relief in front of the entrance hall.

rows.name: Shaonuping Lakeside Resort
rows.summary: A lakeside resort town on the Xiangjiaba reservoir of the Jinsha River, redeveloped for tourism from 2023 on the site where 318 households displaced by the reservoir were resettled. It has a sand beach, a hot-spring centre with dozens of pools and an infinity pool, sightseeing boats and water sports, barbecue and camping spots and a lakeside walkway. Many of its guesthouses are run by or for the resettled families.

rows.name: Washi Hanging Coffins
rows.summary: Wooden coffins placed in a cliff face at Washi village in Weixin county, one of several hanging-coffin sites in north-eastern Yunnan. The national heritage list dates the burials to the Tang dynasty, and how the coffins were raised onto the cliff is not recorded.

rows.name: Western Grand Canyon Hot Springs
rows.summary: A hot-spring and water-park resort on Wenquan Avenue on the western side of Shuifu, above the Jinsha River just upstream of the Xiangjiaba dam at Yunnan's northern border with Sichuan. It has themed outdoor hot-spring pools, water slides and an on-site hotel. The original resort on the canyon floor was lost to the dam's reservoir, and this hillside site, which draws the hot water up from the valley, replaced it.

rows.name: Xiaocaoba
rows.summary: A forested upland around Xiaocaoba town, north-east of Yiliang county town, in the Chaotianma section of the Wumengshan National Nature Reserve, which protects large tracts of subtropical evergreen broadleaf forest. Xiaocaoba is promoted as the original home of tianma (Gastrodia elata), the wild orchid tuber used in Chinese medicine and cooking, and the forest also shelters dove trees (Davidia) and other rare plants.

rows.name: Yuan Zi Inscription at Doushaguan
rows.summary: A small cliff inscription of 794 at Doushaguan pass in Yanjin county, recording how the Tang envoy Yuan Zi passed this way on his mission to invest Yimouxun as king of Nanzhao. Its eight lines of 122 characters, now sheltered by a pavilion, sit beside the pass on the ancient Five-Foot Road from Sichuan into Yunnan, where a stretch of stone paving with worn hoof prints survives. Wooden hanging coffins wedged into the cliffs of the Guan River gorge can be seen from the road nearby.

rows.name: Zhaotong Old Town
rows.summary: The historic core of Zhaotong, a Qing town founded in 1732 whose wealth from silver mining in the Zhuti area drew merchants from other provinces; their guild halls, among them the Shaanxi and Guangdong halls, still stand. The protected old town covers about 2.3 square kilometres, and in recent years its lanes, guild halls and other heritage buildings have been extensively restored. The Fengchi Academy on Wenyuan Street, where the Han-dynasty Meng Xiaoju Stele (found near Zhaotong in 1901) has long been kept, reopened to visitors in August 2026.

rows.name: Zhaxi Meeting Memorial Site
rows.summary: Memorial sites in Zhaxi, the county town of Weixin, where the Chinese Communist Party Politburo held a series of meetings in early February 1935 during the Long March, completing the leadership changes begun at the Zunyi Conference. The Jiangxi Guild Hall on Zhaxi's old street, one of the meeting venues, survives, and a memorial hall displays several thousand artefacts and photographs from the Red Army's passage, including weapons, a radio set and an X-ray machine.

rows.name: Longyun Yangsheng Valley
rows.summary: A leisure and resort scenic area in Shiping County, developed by a local tourism company in the hills of Honghe prefecture. It was named in 2020 as one of the first national forest-wellness bases.

rows.name: Panmao Yequ Manor
rows.summary: A rural estate near Anning run by Yunnan Demao Biotechnology, in the hills west of Kunming, with gardens and woodland for day visits. It was named in 2020 as one of the first national forest-wellness bases.

rows.name: Dalü Palace, Gonjo
rows.summary: The old residence of the Dalü family, once rulers of Gonjo, known locally as the Dalü Gyalpo Lhakhang ('palace of King Dalü'), stands in Zongka hamlet about 1 km from the centre of Gonjo county town, and the family's descendants still live there. Its three-storey stone-and-timber building has a chapel that tradition says was built for the Sakya lama Phagpa when he stayed in 1255, with murals in Yuan-period style and a ceiling painted with dragons, tigers, leopards and elephants.

rows.name: Former Office of the Chamdo People's Liberation Committee
rows.name_zh: 昌都地区人民解放委员会办公旧址
rows.pinyin: Chāngdū Dìqū Rénmín Jiěfàng Wěiyuánhuì Bàngōng Jiùzhǐ
rows.summary: The Chamdo People's Liberation Committee, a provisional local administration, was formed at a congress held in Chamdo from 27 December 1950 to 1 January 1951, after the Battle of Chamdo that October. Its Soviet-style office building of 1955–59 was moved about 30 metres for city planning and now stands within the Chamdo Revolutionary History Museum, opened in 2016, whose exhibition traces the area's history through the 1950s with photographs and objects.

rows.name: Galden Jampaling Monastery
rows.summary: Galden Jampaling, regarded as Kham's largest Gelug monastery, stands on a terrace above the river confluence in the heart of Chamdo and was founded in the 1430s or 1440s by Jangsem Sherab Zangpo, a disciple of Tsongkhapa, as the first Gelug monastery in Kham. It is the seat of the Phagpa Lha incarnations. Its festivals include a butter-sculpture display on the 15th day of the first Tibetan month and masked dances at the end of the Tibetan year.

rows.name: Gangtuo Village
rows.summary: Gangtuo, on the west bank of the Jinsha River where National Road 317 crosses from Sichuan into Tibet, is where units of the People's Liberation Army's 18th Army crossed the river in October 1950 and raised the first PRC national flag in Tibet, which gave the village the title 'First Village of Tibet's Liberation'. The village keeps the river-crossing site, the ruins of a blockhouse, an old army supply-station granary and the former 18th Army barracks, now a small museum, alongside Tibetan-style houses, some of which take guests.

rows.name: Karuo Neolithic Site
rows.summary: Karuo, on a ridge where the Karuo river meets the Lancang (Mekong), is the type site of the Karuo culture, a farming village of some 4,000–5,000 years ago first excavated in 1978–79. Digs uncovered house foundations, stone and bone tools, incised pottery and foxtail millet, among the earliest evidence of farming on the Tibetan Plateau. In the site park, boardwalks lead past excavated house foundations and reconstructed scenes, and in 2026 it was named one of Tibet's first regional-level archaeological site parks.

rows.name: Nangba Langze Stone Sculptures
rows.summary: Inside a small temple hall at Randui village, Bangda township, sit nine stone figures carved in the late 8th or early 9th century: Vairocana in the centre with the Eight Great Bodhisattvas, four on each side. Some faces and crowns were later restored in painted clay, but the bodies and bases are original. An Old Tibetan inscription at the site was added to the national list of famous ancient inscriptions in 2023.

rows.name: Renda Cliff Carvings
rows.summary: A Buddhist relief cut into the cliff at Renda in 804 by monks of the Tibetan Empire to honour the king. The central Vairocana is flanked by bodhisattvas, disciples and two flying apsaras, with inscriptions in Old Tibetan and Chinese below. It belongs to a group of imperial-era carvings across the eastern Tibetan Plateau linked to the monk Yeshe Yang, whose team included Tibetan and Han craftsmen.

rows.name: Riwoche Monastery
rows.summary: A Taklung Kagyu monastery founded in the 1270s by Sangye Ön, which became the seat of the school's 'lower' branch in Kham and one of the largest monasteries of eastern Tibet. Its great assembly hall, the Tragyelma, finished in the early 14th century, gives the monastery its Tibetan name and is the listed national monument. It is also known for the philosophy and logic studied by its monks.

rows.name: Sanse Lakes (Three-Coloured Lakes)
rows.summary: Three small lakes lie close together in Puyu village, Banbar town, each a different colour, and are known as the black, white and yellow lakes. Listed among Tibet's first regional-level scenic areas in 2011, they have a viewing platform, and Puyu also leads to the Xianggela glacier and an ice cave, where villagers run off-road motorbike trips.

rows.name: Yanjing Ancient Salt Terraces
rows.summary: On the steep banks of the Lancang (Mekong) at Yanjing, families still make salt the traditional way: brine is carried up from wells by the river, poured onto flat terraces built on timber posts and left to dry in the sun and wind. Salt has been made here since the Tibetan imperial period; the terraces on the east bank give a pale salt and those on the west bank at Jiada a reddish one. The terraces lie in the Naxi and Quzika townships of southern Markam County.

rows.name: Zizhu Monastery
rows.summary: Zizhu Monastery, regarded as one of the oldest and most important monasteries of the Bön religion, is spread across the six limestone peaks of Zizhu mountain, one of Bön's four sacred mountains, at about 4,800 metres. Revived in the 14th century and rebuilt from 1982, it runs colleges of philosophy, debate and meditation, and pilgrims visit the meditation caves of past masters on the mountain. Every twelve years, in the Tibetan Year of the Rooster, it stages a multi-day masked dance known as 'Heaven and Hell'.

rows.name: Drak Lhalupuk Cave Temple
rows.summary: Regarded as Lhasa's only cave temple, it is set into the eastern foot of Chakpori hill opposite the Potala Palace and is traditionally counted among the shrines founded by King Songtsen Gampo in the 7th century. Two small buildings, one yellow and one white, front the caves; inside the white one a passage runs round a central rock pillar, and the rock walls carry dozens of relief images of buddhas and bodhisattvas carved between the Tibetan empire and the Qing period. It is a working Gelug shrine visited by pilgrims.

rows.name: Drepung Monastery
rows.summary: One of the three great Gelug monasteries of Lhasa, founded in 1416 by Jamyang Chöje Tashi Palden, a disciple of Tsongkhapa, on the slopes of Mount Gephel west of the city. A visitor in 1936–37 reported some 7,700 monks here, which made it the largest monastery in Tibet at the time, and its Ganden Phodrang palace, built in 1518, was the residence of the Dalai Lamas before the Potala Palace was built. Visitors walk up through the hillside complex to its assembly halls and chapels.

rows.name: Ganden Monastery
rows.summary: The first of the three great Gelug monasteries, founded in 1409 by Tsongkhapa himself on the top of Wangbur Mountain above the Lhasa River valley in Dagzê District. It was largely destroyed after 1959 and has been extensively rebuilt since the 1980s; the main sights are the Serdung with the rebuilt tomb of Tsongkhapa, the Tsokchen assembly hall and the chapel where he taught. A kora path around the hilltop gives wide views over the valleys.

rows.name: Lhasa Nanshan Park
rows.summary: A hillside park on the mountains south of the Lhasa River, directly across the river from the Potala Palace, created by planting trees on bare slopes since 2012. It covers about 2.3 km² and climbs to about 4,000 m, with walking trails and viewpoints looking back over the river to the Potala and the city. It has become one of Lhasa's most popular green spaces, though the climb is hard work at this altitude.

rows.name: Norbulingka
rows.summary: The summer palace and park of the Dalai Lamas, begun in 1755 by the 7th Dalai Lama on the western edge of Lhasa and used as their summer residence from the 1780s until 1959. Within the walled gardens are several palaces, among them the Takten Migyur Phodrang completed in 1956, and the site was added to the Potala Palace World Heritage Site in 2001. In summer the park is a favourite place for picnics, and it is a traditional venue for Tibetan opera during the Shoton festival.

rows.name: Nyethang Drolma Temple
rows.summary: A small temple dedicated to Tara at Nyêtang, south-west of Lhasa, associated with the Indian teacher Atiśa, who taught in the area and died there in 1054; it is now a Gelug temple. Its main hall holds statues of the 21 Taras, and the side chapels contain a large stupa and relics linked to Atiśa and his disciple Dromtön. The present buildings reflect a 1930s restoration, and the temple came through the Cultural Revolution relatively undamaged.

rows.name: Princess Wencheng Tibetan Culture Park
rows.name_zh: 文成公主藏文化风情园
rows.summary: A culture park in the Cijueling cultural and creative zone on the south bank of the Lhasa River, built around the open-air theatre of 'Princess Wencheng', a large stage show about the 7th-century marriage of the Tang princess to the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo. Staged against a hillside facing the Potala Palace across the river by a company of several hundred, the show has run in seasons since 2013 and passed 2,000 performances. The park also stages a second production, 'Princess Jincheng'.

rows.name: Qinghai-Tibet-Sichuan-Tibet Highway Monument
rows.summary: A monument on the bank of the Lhasa River, unveiled on 25 December 1984 to mark 30 years since the Sichuan–Tibet and Qinghai–Tibet highways opened to traffic. The three-sided column carries inscriptions in Tibetan and Chinese honouring the soldiers and the people of Tibet, Sichuan and Qinghai who built the two roads and those who died building them, and its title was written by Hu Yaobang. It was listed as a national heritage site in 2019.

rows.name: Ramoche Temple
rows.summary: A 7th-century temple in Lhasa's old town, traditionally said to have been founded by Princess Wencheng and regarded as the city's most important temple after the Jokhang. It houses the Jowo Mikyo Dorje, a statue of the Buddha associated with the Nepalese queen Bhrikuti. Fire destroyed the original building; the present three-storey temple goes back to a rebuilding of 1474 and was restored from 1986 after being gutted in 1959.

rows.name: Sera Monastery
rows.summary: One of the three great Gelug monasteries of Lhasa, founded in 1419 by Jamchen Chöje Shakya Yeshe, a disciple of Tsongkhapa, at the foot of the hills on the northern edge of the city. Besides its great assembly hall and colleges, it is known for the monks' debates, held on a set schedule in the debating courtyard and punctuated by loud claps and vigorous gestures, which many visitors come to watch. The monastery also looks after some 19 hermitages in the hills behind it.

rows.name: Tibet Museum
rows.summary: The regional museum of Tibet beside the Norbulingka, first opened in 1999 and reopened in July 2022 after being rebuilt and enlarged on the same site; it holds some 520,000 objects, more than 40,000 of them graded as precious. The history and culture galleries run from Neolithic finds of the Karuo culture and replica rock art from Ngari to early Tibetan medical texts, thangkas, statues and imperial documents such as a golden book granted to the 11th Dalai Lama in 1841. A second permanent exhibition covers folk culture, with costumes, tea sets, a yak-hair tent and a yak-skin boat.

rows.name: Tibet Museum of Natural Science
rows.summary: A large science museum in eastern Lhasa, opened on a trial basis in 2015 and formally in 2016, that combines a natural-history museum, a science centre and an exhibition hall in one 33,000 m² building. The natural-history halls cover the uplift of the plateau, Tibet's landscapes and wildlife and scientific expeditions, the science halls are hands-on, and a third section introduces Tibetan writing, religion, arts and customs. There is also a 4D cinema and a dome theatre.

rows.name: Tibet Planet Astronomy Experience Hall
rows.summary: An indoor astronomy science centre in the Lhasa Economic and Technological Development Zone, opened in December 2019 as the first astronomy-themed science museum in Tibet. Its galleries start with traditional Tibetan astronomy and the Tibetan calendar, including their links with Tibetan medicine, and move on to the Earth, the solar system and the wider universe through more than 50 interactive exhibits using projections, motion capture and VR, plus a 3D theatre. It suits families, or a gentle indoor visit while acclimatising in Lhasa.

rows.name: Tibet Wildlife Protection Park (Qushui Zoo)
rows.summary: A zoo and wildlife rescue centre beside the G318 at Chabalang village in Qüxü town, south-west of Lhasa, laid out in the late 2010s on woodland planted by local villagers and known locally as Qushui Zoo. In 2024 it kept about 377 animals of 46 species, among them elephants, lions, tigers, lynx, camels, alpacas and sika deer, in areas for plateau plants, rare species, big cats and wild animals, with a children's play area and picnic (linka) grounds. It also takes in injured wild animals such as brown bears and blue sheep, and releases those that recover.

rows.name: Tibet Yak Museum
rows.summary: A museum devoted to the yak and its place in Tibetan life, opened in May 2014 in Lhasa's Liuwu New District as a Beijing-funded aid project. Its galleries look at the yak in nature, history and art, drawing on a collection of some 7,900 objects, and one wall is hung with rows of yak skulls. It also holds temporary exhibitions and summer activities for children.

rows.name: Tromzikhang (Qing Ambans' Office Museum)
rows.summary: A Barkhor courtyard building just north of the Jokhang that from 1728 served as the first office and residence of the ambans, the Qing court's resident commissioners in Tibet. Two ambans were killed here in the unrest of 1750 led by Gyurme Namgyal, and a memorial shrine was then built on the site. After restoration in 2012–13 it opened in July 2013 as an exhibition hall in seven sections, with recreated offices, multimedia displays and wax figures.

rows.name: Xiangxiong Meiduo Cultural Tourism Town
rows.summary: A modern cultural tourism park in the Tolung (Duilong) river valley in Doilungdêqên District, west of Lhasa, named after Zhangzhung (Xiangxiong), the ancient culture of western Tibet, and open since 2020. Its grounds take in an equestrian arena used for horse shows and races, large flower fields, linka (picnic) parkland and an amusement area, and it has hosted evening light shows in summer and on holidays. It suits a relaxed outing from the city rather than a heritage visit.

rows.name: Xiuse Caina Flower Park
rows.summary: A flower and farm park beside the airport expressway at Caina in Qüxü County, part of the township's plateau agriculture projects. Its flower valley, opened in 2024, has nearly 1,000 mu (about 65 ha) of flower fields planted with tulips, roses, sunflowers and many other varieties, with walking paths, a petting area with alpacas and ponies, a children's playground, food stalls and linka (picnic) tents. It makes a short stop on the road between Lhasa and Gonggar airport when the flowers are out.

rows.name: Bangna Monastery
rows.summary: A Ming-period monastery west of Baxiu village in Xichang township. Its surviving main hall, with an assembly hall, chapel, porch and a later prayer-wheel room, is a traditional fortress-style Tibetan building with Han Chinese decorative touches, similar to buildings in Aba in Sichuan, and it has never been heavily rebuilt.

rows.name: Sapu Glaciers (Sepu Kangri)
rows.summary: Sapu lies below the peak of Sepu Kangri, on the boundary between Biru and Banbar counties, in an area of snow mountains, large maritime glaciers and glacial lakes; in Tibetan 'sa' means snow leopard and 'pu' the head of a valley. A paved road now reaches a glacial lake, and nearby villages offer guesthouses and tents for visitors.

rows.name: Tangra Yumco
rows.summary: Tangra Yumco, a holy lake for followers of the Bön religion, is a large salt lake in a basin on the north side of the Gangdise (Transhimalaya) range in Nyima County. Wenbu village at its northern end is the base for visiting the lake and the nearby Targo snow mountain, and the Bön monastery of Yuben stands on the eastern shore. Much of the shore can be driven, which makes it a goal for long overland trips.

rows.name: Khorzhak Monastery
rows.summary: A Sakya monastery in Khorzhak village on the Karnali (Peacock) River south-east of Burang town, founded in 996 and traditionally linked with the translator Rinchen Zangpo. Its main buildings are the Jokhang (Shakyamuni Hall) and the Hundred-Pillar Hall, and a red wall facing the river bears a large inscription of the mantra Om Mani Padme Hum. Masked dances are held at its anniversary festival in the first Tibetan month, and old thangkas are displayed once a year in the sixth.

rows.name: Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar
rows.summary: Mount Kailash (Kang Rinpoche, 6,638 m) and Lake Manasarovar (Mapham Yumtso in Tibetan) form a sacred landscape for Buddhists, Hindus, Jains and followers of Bön, and pilgrims come to walk around the mountain and bathe in the lake. The 53 km kora around Kailash starts and ends at Darchen (4,670 m) and crosses the Drölma La at about 5,650 m, usually over three days. The freshwater lake, about 320 km² at some 4,600 m, lies a short drive south of the mountain.

rows.name: Pangong Lake Scenic Area (Rutog)
rows.summary: A lakeside scenic area on the Rutog shore of Pangong Lake (Bangong Co), a long, narrow lake at about 4,240 m on the plateau of far western Tibet. Viewpoints and a lakeside resort look over the clear water and the bare mountains around it, and the lake is frozen for about six months of the year. The area was rated 4A in 2025.

rows.name: Piyang and Dungkar Cave Temples
rows.summary: The largest Buddhist cave site found so far in Tibet, spread across the cliffs above the villages of Piyang and Dungkar north of Zanda, with nearly a thousand caves once used for worship, meditation, living and storage. Some shrine caves keep murals of buddhas, bodhisattvas, flying apsaras and mandalas painted in mineral pigments, and the site also includes ruined temples and stupas from the Guge period. Archaeologists recorded it only in 1992, and it lies in the same eroded earth-forest country as Tsaparang.

rows.name: Tholing Monastery
rows.summary: The oldest monastery in Ngari, founded at the end of the 10th century by the Guge king Yeshe-Ö in what is now Zanda town, and a starting point of the later spread of Buddhism in Tibet. The translator Rinchen Zangpo worked here after studying in Kashmir and India, and the surviving halls, including the Gyatsa (Yeshe-Ö) temple, the White Temple and the assembly hall, keep important murals. Many of its stupas and chapels were damaged in the 20th century, and it is now a Gelug monastery.

rows.name: Tsaparang (Guge Kingdom Ruins)
rows.summary: The ruined capital of the Guge kingdom, which ruled this part of western Tibet from the 10th century until it fell in the 1630s, built up an earth hill above the Langqên Zangbo (Sutlej) valley. More than 300 rooms, over 300 caves, stupas, tunnels and the remains of palaces climb about 175 m from base to summit, and the White Temple, Red Temple and three other halls keep murals and sculpture that the Dunhuang Academy restored in 2012–13. The eroded earth-forest landscape around it is as striking as the ruins.

rows.name: Basum Tso
rows.summary: Basum Tso (Draksum Tso in Tibetan) is a long glacier-dammed lake in a deep valley of the upper Ba River in Gongbo'gyamda County, ringed by snow peaks and forest, and was Tibet's first natural-landscape 5A scenic area. On Tashi island near the south-western shore stands Tsozong Monastery, a Nyingma temple whose present buildings date largely from a 14th-century rebuilding. Boat trips run on the lake, and the lakeside village of Jieba is a traditional Kongpo farming village.

rows.name: Cuomujiri Lake
rows.summary: Cuomujiri, whose Tibetan name is usually translated as 'fairy's tears', is an old moraine-dammed lake in a forested valley just north of Bayi, with snow peaks behind it. The valley is best known for its autumn colours, when the forest along the winding road up to the lake turns red and gold.

rows.name: Cypress King Garden
rows.summary: This park protects a grove of giant Tibetan cypresses (Cupressus gigantea) at Baji village beside the G318, just south-east of Bayi. Close to a thousand trees grow here, and the largest, the 'King of Cypresses', is estimated to be more than 3,200 years old.

rows.name: Galang Lake
rows.summary: Galang Lake, about 2 km² in area, lies in the Galang National Wetland Park beside Galang village, at the mouth of the Bodui peach-blossom valley in Bomê County. Snow peaks and forest surround the lake, and across the road are hillside ruins associated with the old Galang kingdom; in spring the village orchards turn pink with peach blossom.

rows.name: Guoguotang Great Bend
rows.summary: At Guoguotang, about 12 km from Medog town, the Yarlung Tsangpo swings through a tight horseshoe bend around a forested spur, seen from viewing platforms above the river. Tea gardens cover the slopes nearby, and the low altitude and humid climate make the scene unusually green for Tibet.

rows.name: Kading Valley
rows.summary: Kading Valley is a steep, forested side gorge off the Nyang River valley north-west of Bayi, known for the Tianfo ('Heavenly Buddha') waterfall that drops down its cliffs. It makes a short stop on the G318 between Lhasa and Nyingchi.

rows.name: Linze Scenic Area
rows.summary: Linze village in Gongbo'gyamda County is home to several thousand wild Tibetan macaques that live in the surrounding forest and come down to meet visitors, who may feed them under staff guidance. The scenic area also includes the grey-stone manor of the aristocratic Ngapoi family, whose best-known member was the politician Ngapoi Ngawang Jigme, and a hill sacred to a local wealth deity, with murals.

rows.name: Lulang
rows.summary: Lulang is a high valley of meadows, streams and spruce forest at about 3,300 m on the G318 east of the Sejila pass, often wrapped in cloud. The scenic area takes in the forest viewpoints along the road, the Lulang International Tourism Town of hotels and guesthouses, built with aid from Guangdong province, and villages such as Tashigang where families run homestays.

rows.name: Midui Glacier
rows.summary: Midui Glacier flows down from the mountains above Midui village in Bomê County, where two great icefalls merge with a strip of forest between them, at the meeting of the Nyenchen Tanglha and Boshula ranges. The glacier tongue reaches down almost to the village fields, and villagers offer horse rides to the viewing area.

rows.name: Red Building of the Zamu Central County Committee
rows.summary: Known locally as the Bomê Red Building, this two-storey Soviet-style building of stone and timber in the Bomê county government compound was built in 1953 as an office of the Kham–Tibet Highway administration and from 1955 housed the Zamu Central County Committee of the Communist Party. In January 1959 armed Tibetan forces besieged it for about ten days, and the 60 or so officials and soldiers inside held it until reinforcements arrived. It now holds an exhibition of photographs and stories of the soldiers and officials who worked in the area in the 1950s.

rows.name: Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon
rows.summary: The 5A scenic area at Pai, in Mainling, covers the upper entrance of the Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon, where the river turns into the deep gorge that wraps around the peak of Namcha Barwa. From the visitor centre, roads and walkways lead to viewpoints and villages such as Suosong, with views of the mountain when the clouds clear and peach blossom in spring. Visitors must keep to the marked trails and viewing platforms; the undeveloped parts of the canyon, which lies in a national nature reserve, are closed to hiking and camping.

rows.name: Dajielin Monastery (Chödegong)
rows.summary: A Gelug monastery in Chödegong village in the Yartö valley, which began as the 11th-century residence of the translator Ra Lotsawa and reached its present size under the 13th Dalai Lama. Its four-storey main building holds an assembly hall, chapels with statues of Tsongkhapa and his disciples, and walls covered in murals with Tibetan captions. A giant thangka is shown each year on the 25th day of the fifth Tibetan month.

rows.name: Dratang Monastery
rows.summary: A monastery founded in 1081 by the scholar and physician Drapa Ngönshé and finished in 1093, built as a mandala with three rings of walls; it passed to the Sakya school in the 13th century. Only the ground floor of the main hall and parts of the outer wall survive, but its central chapel keeps early murals that have been conserved since the 1990s.

rows.name: Gongkar Chö Monastery
rows.summary: A Sakya monastery founded in 1464 by Dorje Denpa Kunga Namgyal as the seat of the Dzongpa (Gongkar) branch of the Sakya school. Its assembly hall has murals from the 16th century in the Khyenri style associated with the painter Jamyang Khyentse Wangchuk. It makes an easy stop on the way to or from Lhasa's airport.

rows.name: Jiedunzhu Dzong Ruins
rows.summary: The ruins of a Yuan–Ming period dzong, or fortress, stand on a cliff at about 3,300 metres south-west of Jiemai village in Painba township. Painba, known as the 'land of a thousand towers', has many more old stone towers on its cliffs, in its valleys and among its barley fields.

rows.name: Keru Lhakhang
rows.summary: A small temple in Keru village, Gyêrba township, founded under King Tride Tsugtsen; its main Shakyamuni chapel dates from the first half of the 8th century. The chapel keeps painted clay statues of the Buddha with his eight bodhisattva disciples and early carved brackets of dragons, tigers and lions. Old scriptures found here, many dating from around 800, were sorted and bound in 2002.

rows.name: Lhagyari Palace Ruins
rows.summary: The palace of the Lhagyari kings, a line descended from the Tibetan imperial family who kept their title through the Sakya and Phagmodrupa periods, stands on the south side of Qusum town. It has three phases: walls and gates of the 13th-century Tashi Chödzong, the 15th-century Ganden Lhatse palace with remains of murals, and an 18th-century summer palace that survives largely complete. Its buildings blend in Han Chinese features, which is rare among Tibetan palaces.

rows.name: Lhalung Monastery, Lhozhag
rows.summary: A monastery on a terrace above the north bank of the Lhozhag Nub Chu, founded as a Karma Kagyu seat in 1155 by Düsum Khyenpa and laid out as a mandala in the 16th century by Pawo Tsuglag Trengwa; the 5th Dalai Lama later made it Gelug. Tradition links it with Lhalung Palgyi Dorje, the monk said to have killed King Langdarma in the 9th century, and its black-hat dance recalls the story. The main hall has painted and carved brackets and murals, including a panorama of the monastery close in style to Chinese blue-and-green landscape painting.

rows.name: Mindrolling Monastery
rows.summary: One of the principal monasteries of the Nyingma school, founded in its present form in 1676 by Terdak Lingpa on the site of an earlier temple, and rebuilt after damage by Dzungar troops in 1718. The three-storey main hall has an assembly hall with murals of fierce protector deities and a chapel painted with the great Nyingma lamas. Mindrolling was long known for Tibetan calendar studies, calligraphy, medicine and incense making.

rows.name: Namseling Manor
rows.summary: The seven-storey earth-and-stone tower house of the Namseling family, aristocrats who held land in Dranang, built in the Ming period on the south bank of the Yarlung Tsangpo opposite Samye. With Pala Manor near Gyantse it is among the oldest tall manor houses in Tibet. The main tower survives inside a broken inner wall, with steep stairs, old chapels and traces of wall paintings on the upper floors.

rows.name: Quxi Watchtowers, Lhozhag
rows.summary: A group of stone watchtowers and walls on the hillside at Quxi village in Se township, built between the Northern Song and Ming periods. Old towers like these stand in villages, valleys and hilltops across Lhozhag; at Quxi their walls have rows of small rectangular openings, and some tops and walls have crumbled.

rows.name: Samye Monastery
rows.summary: Tibet's first Buddhist monastery, built in the 8th century under King Trisong Detsen with the Indian masters Shantarakshita and Padmasambhava, and the place where the first Tibetan monks were ordained. It is laid out as a three-dimensional mandala of the Buddhist universe: the central Utse hall, mixing Tibetan, Han Chinese and Indian styles, is ringed by four coloured stupas and a circular wall. About 500 metres to the south-west stands Khamsum Sangkhar Ling, a temple founded in the late 8th century whose four-storey main hall is second in size only to the Utse.

rows.name: Sekhar Guthok Monastery
rows.summary: Tradition says the nine-storey stone tower at the heart of this monastery was built in the 11th century by the yogi Milarepa as a trial set by his teacher Marpa; the top two floors were rebuilt in 1985. Beside it, the assembly hall added in the 16th century by the Kagyu scholar Pawo Tsuglag Trengwa has murals said to be by his own hand. Long a Kagyu house, the monastery has followed the Gelug school since 1944.

rows.name: Songkar Stone Stupas
rows.summary: Five stone stupas of different sizes, each carved from a single block, stand at the foot of a rocky hill beside the Yarlung Tsangpo west of Samye. They date from the same period as Samye, and tradition credits their design to Padmasambhava. Rock carvings nearby, mostly of Amitayus, belong to several later periods.

rows.name: Tradruk Temple
rows.summary: One of the earliest Buddhist temples in Tibet, founded in the 7th century under King Songtsen Gampo in the Yarlung valley and enlarged in the 14th century; its main assembly hall is laid out like that of the Jokhang in Lhasa. Legend says the king had a falcon defeat a dragon to drain the lake here, which gave the temple its name, and Princess Wencheng is said to have stayed. Its treasures include a thangka of Avalokiteshvara worked in pearls, made in the Phagmodrupa period.

rows.name: Valley of the Kings, Chonggye
rows.summary: The burial ground of the kings of the Tibetan Empire from the 7th to 9th centuries, a group of large flat-topped mounds of rammed earth and stone on and below Mura Hill at Chonggye. The mound identified as Songtsen Gampo's tomb has a rebuilt temple on top with statues of the king, his queens Wencheng and Bhrikuti and his ministers. The tomb of King Tride Songtsen keeps a tall inscribed stone stele on a carved tortoise base.

rows.name: Yumai, Lhünzê
rows.summary: Yumai is a small township in a deep valley of Lhünzê County, among fir forest and snow peaks, where rain and snow fall for much of the year. For decades it was known as the 'three-person township', when the herder Sangjie Quba and his daughters Zhuoga and Yangzong were its only residents; a paved road opened in 2019, and it now has two villages, Yumai and Niulintang, with about 250 people. Visitors see the family's old house, walk a forest trail with rhododendrons and waterfalls, and stay in village guesthouses.

rows.name: Yumbulagang
rows.summary: Yumbulagang, a tower-like palace on a ridge above the Yarlung valley, is held by tradition to be the first building in Tibet, the palace of the legendary first king Nyatri Tsenpo. The 5th Dalai Lama turned it into a temple and added the golden roof; the present building, restored from 1982, has statues of Songtsen Gampo and Princess Wencheng and murals telling of the first king, the first building and the first field.

rows.name: Zhongga Qude Monastery
rows.summary: A Gelug monastery in Ritang town that began as a Bön temple in the imperial period, became a Kadam house in the 11th–13th centuries and turned Gelug after the 15th century.
