Smaller sites nearby include a veterans' household museum and a memorial garden, and the town has guesthouses and a canteen themed on the early settlers.

rows.name: Tuerdi Aji Manor
rows.summary: A manor house dating to 1915, known as the manor of Tuerdi Aji, on what is now the Pishan Farm of the Bingtuan's 14th Division. It is a national heritage site, listed in 2013 in the category of modern historic sites and representative buildings.

rows.name: Shihezi Military Reclamation Sites
rows.summary: Three early buildings of Shihezi, the city founded in the early 1950s by the army's 22nd Corps: the Soviet-style corps headquarters of 1952, known as the 'first building of the reclamation army' and now the Xinjiang Bingtuan Military Reclamation Museum; the 1952 assembly hall, later the People's Cinema; and the 1951 single-storey office and residence of the commanders Tao Zhiyue and Zhang Zhonghan. They stand on one axis in the city centre, and the museum tells the story of the Bingtuan's farming and city-building through photographs and objects.

rows.name: Dorben Oirat Ancient City Ruins
rows.name_zh: 道尔本厄鲁特森木古城遗址
rows.summary: The earthen ruins of a walled town built in the 1640s by the Dzungar Oirats, whose Mongolian name means 'temple of the Four Oirats', and which served for a time as a political, economic and religious centre of the Dzungars. Its near-square rammed-earth walls, still several metres high, have gates on all four sides and enclose the foundations of two lama temples, a ruined Tibetan-style stupa and houses, on a rise among springs and wetland meadows. The town declined after the Qing conquest of the Dzungars, and the Torghut Mongols halted here in 1771 on their return migration.

rows.name: Emin Wild Fruit Forest
rows.summary: A mountain scenic area in the Wuerkaxiaer Mountains about 30 km south-east of Emin, where rock outcrops, woodland and waterfalls fill the valleys and the slopes flower in spring and summer. The lower ground is used for Kazakh folk events under Emin's 'home of Kazakh folk customs' banner, with farm-stay restaurants, sports grounds and water play, while the upper valleys are kept for scenery and walking. Its snow draws visitors in winter as well.

rows.name: Hanaka and Seyitqamal Mosque Minarets
rows.name_zh: 哈纳喀及赛提喀玛勒清真寺宣礼塔
rows.summary: Two red-brick minarets in Shuangta (Twin Towers) Park in central Tacheng, the surviving parts of the Seyitqamal mosque, founded in 1885 by the Uzbek mullah Seyitqamal, and the Hanaka mosque, built from 1910 by Uzbek Muslims, whose minaret was begun in 1928. The octagonal Hanaka tower has two railed balconies and carved floral and geometric panels, while the Seyitqamal tower rises from a square base with relief columns to a blue-glazed top. Both combine Uyghur and Russian architectural features.

rows.name: Lujiaowan (Antler Bay)
rows.summary: A mountain scenic area of more than 19,000 ha on the north slope of the Tianshan south-west of Shawan, made up of Big and Little Lujiaowan between the Bayingou River on the west and the Danangou valley on the east. Its name, 'antler bay', comes from the antlers that the Tianshan red deer shed each year and leave in the gullies and beside the streams.

rows.name: Songhai Bay
rows.summary: A forested valley on the south slope of the Saier Mountains, also called the Haergatu White Pine Forest Park and known locally as Songshugou ('pine valley'), through which highway G219 climbs at around 1,800 m. Siberian larch and tall poplars cover the slopes, and at the top lie the Yukuqiaolong summit pastures and the small 'Love Lake', reached by a 1,314-step trail and circled by a 900 m boardwalk. The area also takes in Niushitou grassland and ancient remains including stone-mound tombs and so-called 'beard tombs'.

rows.name: Tacheng Red Building
rows.summary: A Russian-style brick trading house in central Tacheng, built from 1910 and completed in 1914 as the business centre of the Jixiangyong firm of a Tatar merchant from Russia, and named for the iron-red paint of its street walls. It later served as a hospital, government offices and a newspaper office, and after restoration it houses the Red Building Museum, whose collection of some 7,900 objects covers the history of the Tacheng region. The L-shaped building keeps its green iron roof, white window frames and the date 1914 on its walls.

rows.name: Wusu Foshan National Forest Park
rows.summary: A national forest park of 39,000 ha in the Tianshan south of Wusu, made up of the Daifuseng, Bayingou and Wulansadeke areas of mountain forest, grassy slopes and river valleys. Its emblem is the 3,946 m Snow Buddha peak, likened to a giant natural Buddha, and it also has a sub-alpine botanical garden. Formerly Wusu's Nanshan park, it became a national forest park in 2008 and is a favourite summer outing for people from Wusu and nearby cities.

rows.name: Tang Wangcheng (Toqquz Saray) Ruins
rows.summary: Ruins of a walled town on a rocky hill north of Tumxuk, known in Uyghur as Toqquz Saray ('nine stations'), which was the seat of the small kingdom of Weitou under the Han and the Tang garrison town of Jushide on the road between Kucha and Kashgar. Three rings of earth-and-stone walls climb the hillside to a beacon tower at the top, with remains of Buddhist temples below. Excavations resumed in 2022, and some of the finds, including Buddhist figures, coins and pottery, are shown in Tumxuk's archaeology exhibition hall.

rows.name: Yong'an Lake
rows.summary: A lake-and-desert recreation area on Yong'an Lake, part of the wetlands of the lower Yarkand River south of Tumxuk, where open water, reed beds, desert poplars, sand dunes and a bare mountain ridge lie side by side. The wetland reserve around the lake is a stopover for migrating birds, and visitors come for boat trips, autumn colours and desert sunsets. A desert activity area offers sand-motorbike rides and in winter becomes a snow park with a 300 m ski run.

rows.name: Astana Cemetery
rows.summary: Astana was the main burial ground of the people of Gaochang from about the 4th to the 8th century, laid out in family plots on the gravel plain a few kilometres from the old city. The dry climate preserved silks, paper documents, food and natural mummies in the tombs, and much of what was found is now held by the Xinjiang Museum in Ürümqi and the Turpan Museum.

rows.name: Bezeklik Thousand Buddha Caves
rows.summary: Cut into a cliff above the Mutou Valley in the Flaming Mountains, Bezeklik was a Buddhist cave monastery used from about the 5th to the 14th century and served as a royal temple of the Uyghur Qocho kingdom; 83 caves survive, more than 40 with murals. Many paintings were cut away by foreign expeditions in the early 20th century and are now in museums abroad, but murals of Buddhas, bodhisattvas and Uyghur donors remain in the open caves, and since May 2026 the route climbs from the monks' living area to the caves, taking in a stupa ruin and Cave 9. Four caves of the nearby Shengjinkou Grottoes, part of the same protected site, opened to visitors in April 2025 with a daily limit and real-name booking.

rows.name: Boxiha Caves
rows.summary: A small Buddhist cave temple of the Uyghur Qocho kingdom in the Mutou Valley area near Bezeklik, with ten caves and stupa remains on the ground above. Its murals show strong Central Plains influence and include a rare scene from the Vimalakirti Sutra.

rows.name: Emin Minaret
rows.summary: The Emin Minaret is a tapering tower of sun-dried brick built around 1777 in honour of Emin Khoja, a Turpan ruler who sided with the Qing; it is also called the Sugong Tower in Chinese. Its walls are laid in more than ten geometric brick patterns, and it stands beside a large mud-brick mosque with domed halls and the Emin family cemetery. The complex sits among vineyards on the south-eastern edge of Turpan.

rows.name: Flaming Mountains
rows.summary: The Flaming Mountains are a long ridge of bare red sandstone across the Turpan basin, so deeply gullied that at certain times of day they look as if they are on fire; in the novel Journey to the West the Monkey King has to borrow a magic palm-leaf fan to put out their flames. The scenic area at their foot has underground galleries on the geology and the legend, a giant thermometer, and statues of Xuanzang and his companions. Since August 2025 the original and the newer neighbouring site have been run as one area, linked by shuttle carts, with donkey-cart and camel rides.

rows.name: Gaochang Ruins
rows.summary: Gaochang, also known as Qocho, was the leading city of the Turpan basin for some 1,400 years: capital of the Gaochang kingdom, a Tang county seat and then capital of the Uyghur Qocho kingdom, until war destroyed it in the 14th century. Within its eroded mud walls you can still trace the outer city, inner city and palace citadel, and the best-preserved buildings are the Great Buddhist Temple and the south-western temple. Boardwalks and shuttle carts link the ruins to a visitor centre opened in 2016, and the site is part of the Silk Road World Heritage listing.

rows.name: Grape Valley
rows.summary: Grape Valley is a green gorge cut into the Flaming Mountains on the north-eastern edge of Turpan, watered by the snow-fed Buyluk River and lined with vineyards, orchards and Uyghur villages. Walk among trellised vines and the airy drying houses used to make raisins, and explore old lanes such as Frog Lane, where karez water still runs past the houses. Grapes ripen from late summer, the season of Turpan's annual grape festival.

rows.name: Huoshanhong Winery
rows.summary: A modern winery and leisure resort in Turpan's Gaochang District, where visitors ride sightseeing carts round the estate. Its 3 km underground cellar has been turned into a gallery on the history of wine with tasting areas, the production hall is open as a factory tour, and the estate has a hotel built in the shape of oak wine barrels.

rows.name: Karez Folk Custom Park
rows.summary: A company-run park opened in 2000 on the West Gate karez, an old underground irrigation channel on the western edge of Turpan's old town. Visitors walk down to a stretch of the karez and its outlet, see a small karez museum, and can eat, shop and stay in the park's Uyghur-style hotel and guest rooms among the vines. The park also stages an outdoor song-and-dance show about the karez.

rows.name: Kumtag Desert Scenic Area, Shanshan
rows.summary: The dunes of the Kumtag Desert, whose Uyghur name means 'sand mountains', run right up to the southern edge of Shanshan town. Visitors play on the dunes by day, and the scenic area regularly runs evening bonfire parties, folk performances and star-gazing camps. It was designated a national key scenic area in 2002.

rows.name: Liuzhong Ancient City Ruins
rows.summary: Liuzhong, today's Lukqun, was a garrison town from the Eastern Han dynasty, when Ban Yong based his Western Regions headquarters here in AD 123, and later a Tang county seat. Little survives among the houses of the town: the main remnant is a tall stretch of the inner city's west wall, with further wall fragments in courtyards and the earth platform of an 18th-century prince's palace.

rows.name: Loulan Winery
rows.summary: A working winery of the Turpan Loulan Winery company at Shuangshuimo in Shanshan County, rated as a 4A scenic area in 2023. Visitors can tour the estate and its wine museum, which presents the grape-growing and winemaking of the Turpan basin.

rows.name: Taizang Pagoda Ruins
rows.summary: Taizang Pagoda is the ruin of a large Buddhist temple-stupa from the Tang and Uyghur Qocho periods, a square mud-brick and rammed-earth mass that still rises in stepped tiers lined with niches, some with traces of paint. It stands on the plain below the Flaming Mountains a short distance from the Gaochang ruins and the Astana cemetery. The ruin was consolidated in 2009–2010 and fenced, with a gate and a small management building.

rows.name: Turpan Karez Paradise
rows.summary: Turpan's karez are hand-dug underground channels that carry snowmelt from the Tian Shan across the gravel plain to the oases, and this park, opened in 1992 by the Xinjiang Karez Research Association, is a place to see one from the inside. A walkway more than 10 m below ground follows part of an old working karez past its tunnel and vertical shafts, and a museum explains with models and photographs how the system was dug and maintained. There is also a display of surface construction work, a vineyard watered by the karez and a raisin drying house.

rows.name: Turpan Museum
rows.summary: Turpan Museum is one of China's national first-grade museums and holds finds from the oasis's ancient cities and cemeteries. Its galleries, closed since 2025 for an extension, covered Turpan's history along the Silk Road, documents excavated at Astana and other sites, ancient coins and naturally preserved mummies with their grave goods, and a separate hall showed fossils of the giant hornless rhinoceros Paraceratherium.

rows.name: Tuyoq Valley
rows.summary: Tuyoq is an oasis village of mud-brick Uyghur houses in a gorge through the Flaming Mountains, with Buddhist cave temples cut into the valley walls above it. The caves, begun in the 5th century, are among the earliest in the Turpan basin: 157 caves, three temples and nine stupas survive, and after long conservation work several caves with murals opened to visitors in May 2025. The 4A scenic area takes in the restored village, with craft workshops and food stalls, the grottoes and walks or viewpoints over the canyon.

rows.name: Amalong Fantasy Park
rows.summary: An amusement park in the Ürümqi Economic and Technological Development Zone, on the western side of the city. It is a modern theme park for families with children rather than a sightseeing destination.

rows.name: Baishuijian Ancient Town
rows.summary: A tourist town built in old style beside the Baiyang River gorge at Dabancheng, reopened in 2014 after older buildings on the site were refitted, with a mock-Tang city gate where a staged welcome dance is performed, a folk-custom street, craft workshops, inns and a wetland park. It has an art museum for the composer Wang Luobin, whose 1938 song 'The Girl from Dabancheng' is named after the town, and next to it stands the small Xiakou fort on a rocky knoll, presented as the ruins of a Tang post although excavation in 2016 dated it to the Qing dynasty. It makes an easy stop on the road between Ürümqi and Turpan.

rows.name: Eighth Route Army Xinjiang Office
rows.name_zh: 八路军驻新疆办事处旧址
rows.summary: The former Eighth Route Army office in Xinjiang, which worked from 1937 to 1942, when the Communist Party kept representatives such as Chen Yun, Deng Fa and Chen Tanqiu in Dihua (Ürümqi) under the provincial ruler Sheng Shicai; Zhou Enlai and Wang Jiaxiang were among those who stayed there. The surviving two-storey building, put up as a private house in 1928–33, was used by the representatives from 1938. A memorial hall opened on the site in 1963, and an exhibition building completed in 2021 presents the office's history.

rows.name: Hongguangshan Scenic Area
rows.summary: A hill on the northern edge of central Ürümqi, between the Xinjiang International Convention and Exhibition Centre and the Olympic Sports Centre, crowned by the Hongguangshan Grand Buddha Temple, a Chinese Buddhist temple complex that opened to the public in 2021. A stairway lined with statues of the Buddha's ten disciples climbs to a large Buddha figure on a lotus platform.

rows.name: Hongshan Park
rows.summary: A hill park in central Ürümqi around Hong Shan, the 'Red Mountain' of Permian red sandstone that serves as the city's emblem, laid out in 1985 after decades of tree-planting. The Hongshan Pagoda on the summit is a regional heritage site, and the park also has old-style buildings including a viewing tower and a Buddhist temple, a statue of Lin Zexu and a lake with fairground rides; a temple fair is held around the Lunar New Year.

rows.name: Mao Zemin's Former Residence
rows.summary: The small office and home of Mao Zemin, Mao Zedong's younger brother, who lived here while serving as acting head of the Xinjiang provincial finance department in 1940–41. The two-and-a-half-room earth-and-timber house, which he designed himself and which was rebuilt in its original style in 1996, is furnished as reconstructed from later recollections and forms the core of the Mao Zemin Former Residence Memorial Hall.

rows.name: Shaanxi Grand Mosque
rows.summary: Ürümqi's largest Hui mosque, founded in 1883 by Muslims from the Wei River valley of Shaanxi, rebuilt between 1902 and 1906 and long counted first among the city's historic Hui congregations. Its prayer hall is built in Chinese timber-frame style with green-glazed tiles, a hip-and-gable front hall and a double-eaved octagonal moon-viewing tower over 17 m high at the back, a form rare among Xinjiang mosques.

rows.name: Shuimogou Park
rows.summary: The core park, about 4 km², of the Shuimogou scenic area in north-eastern Ürümqi, where the Shuimo River runs between hills replanted with trees since the late 1970s. It takes its name from the water mills that ground flour here from the Qing period until the 1950s, and has a replica water mill, pavilions, a riverside landscaped in 2005 and the Qingquan Temple, built from 1988.

rows.name: Silk Road Mountain Resort
rows.summary: A ski and mountain resort on the northern slopes of the Tian Shan in Shuixigou town, Ürümqi County, also known as the Silk Road International Ski Resort. The ski season usually starts in mid-November and runs into March, and Pingxiliang village below the slopes has a cluster of guesthouses serving skiers.

rows.name: Tianshan Grand Canyon
rows.summary: A mountain scenic area and national forest park covering about 1,038 km² of the Tian Shan's northern slopes in Ürümqi County, at an average altitude above 2,000 m. It holds the most complete old-growth Schrenk's spruce forest on the north side of the range, meadows where Kazakh herding families live, and the Zhaobishan reservoir and wetland.

rows.name: Wulabo Ancient City
rows.summary: The oldest and best-preserved walled town in the Ürümqi area, a rammed-earth enclosure of about 25 hectares whose walls, 2–7 m high, keep bastions, barbicans at the gates and three inner compounds; scholars variously identify it with the Tang town of Luntai or earlier Han-era settlements. It opened to visitors in September 2024, together with a history hall showing finds from the site such as lotus-pattern bricks, Kaiyuan Tongbao coins, grey pottery and bronze mirrors.

rows.name: Xinjiang International Grand Bazaar
rows.summary: A large market and tourist complex in the Erdaoqiao area of Ürümqi, opened in 2003 and extended with a pedestrian street from 2018, built in a mix of Islamic, Uyghur and Chinese styles. Besides the market halls it has a Silk Road tower over 70 m high, a theatre with resident song-and-dance shows and a food street.

rows.name: Xinjiang People's Theatre
rows.summary: A landmark theatre at Nanmen in central Ürümqi, completed in 1956 and opened in January 1957 as the new autonomous region's main venue for political meetings and performances. The symmetrical domed building combines Eurasian architectural forms with Uyghur-style plaster decoration in green and blue, and after a restoration begun in 2019 it still hosts shows, films and events.

rows.name: Xinjiang Tianshan Wildlife Park
rows.summary: A large wildlife park in Dabancheng District, south-east of Ürümqi, where a range of animals are kept in large enclosures. It is a common family day out from the city.

rows.name: Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region Museum
rows.name_zh: 新疆维吾尔自治区博物馆
rows.summary: Xinjiang's regional museum and a national first-grade museum, founded in 1959, in a building opened in 2005 and enlarged in 2022, with a catalogued collection of more than 24,000 objects. Its permanent galleries cover Xinjiang's history from the pre-Qin period to the Qing, ancient mummies preserved by the desert, ancient costumes and textiles, and excavated documents, and its best-known pieces include the Han-to-Jin brocade armguard inscribed 'Five stars rising in the east benefit China'.

rows.name: Ürümqi Confucius Temple
rows.summary: The Ürümqi Confucius Temple, on Qianjin Road in central Ürümqi, is described as Xinjiang's only surviving Confucian temple and its only intact temple complex in late-Qing style. The present buildings were put up in 1922 as a temple mainly to Shangdi, with Confucius honoured alongside, and the main hall was rebuilt as a Dacheng Hall for Confucius in 1945; the Ürümqi Museum now looks after it.

rows.name: Aberdeen Harbour
rows.summary: Aberdeen Harbour is a working fishing harbour and typhoon shelter between Hong Kong Island and Ap Lei Chau, where traditional fishing boats are still moored. Visitors can take a sampan or tour boat around the harbour, walk the Aberdeen Promenade or see the Aberdeen Wholesale Fish Market, which was built in 1950. Floating restaurants and harbourfront eateries are part of the draw.

rows.name: Aberdeen Promenade
rows.summary: Aberdeen Promenade is a tree-lined waterfront on the north shore of Aberdeen Harbour, running east from the Aberdeen Wholesale Fish Market along Praya Road. Traditional wooden junks and flat-bottomed sampans bob on the water, and locals can be seen buying fresh fish, practising tai chi or using the outdoor fitness corner. Sampans, ferries to nearby islands and floating seafood restaurants can all be reached from here.

rows.name: Aqua Luna
rows.summary: Aqua Luna is a red-sailed Chinese junk, launched in 2006, that carries passengers on Victoria Harbour cruises of about 45 minutes with views of the skyline. Some sailings include dim sum or afternoon tea, and an evening sailing is timed for the Symphony of Lights show. Its Chinese name, Cheung Po Tsai, comes from a 19th-century pirate.

rows.name: Argyle Street Footbridge
rows.summary: The Argyle Street Footbridge is an elevated pedestrian walkway at the junction of Argyle Street, Cherry Street and Tong Mei Road in Mong Kok. The Hong Kong Tourism Board describes it as a link between Mong Kok and Tai Kok Tsui, with views of the traffic below and a skyline where old and new buildings stand side by side. A scene of the mainland Chinese drama Our Generation (2025) was filmed on the bridge.

rows.name: Arsenal Street
rows.summary: Arsenal Street in Wan Chai takes its name from the army hospital, air-defence buildings and armouries that once stood here. Today it links Wan Chai, Admiralty and the Convention and Exhibition Centre, lined with government offices, office towers and hotels. The Hong Kong Police Headquarters on the street was a key location in the police film Cold War (2012).

rows.name: Art Park
rows.summary: Art Park is a waterfront park in the West Kowloon Cultural District, with open lawns, waterfront paths and wide views of Victoria Harbour and the Hong Kong Island skyline. Weekends and holidays bring live music, market stalls and street performers, and it is a popular spot for watching fireworks on special occasions. Cafés and restaurants line the promenade.

rows.name: Avenue of Stars
rows.summary: The Avenue of Stars is a waterfront walkway of about 400 metres on the Tsim Sha Tsui promenade, honouring the Hong Kong film industry and modelled on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. Along it are plaques, handprints and statues of film figures including Bruce Lee, Jackie Chan and Anita Mui, with interactive exhibits and panels on the industry's milestones. It looks across Victoria Harbour to the Hong Kong Island skyline.

rows.name: Bank of China Tower
rows.summary: Designed by I. M. Pei, the Bank of China Tower is one of the most recognisable buildings on the Hong Kong skyline. Its triangular frames and reflective glass facade are based on the form of bamboo, and catch the changing light against the sky. It houses the headquarters of Bank of China (Hong Kong).

rows.name: Bonham Road Government Primary School
rows.summary: The school building on Bonham Road was put up in 1940 and 1941 for Northcote Training College, the first full-time teacher training college in Hong Kong, and it has housed the primary school since 2000. Its three-storey, E-shaped main block is a prominent example of Streamline Moderne, with curved corners, horizontal lines and little ornament. Air-raid shelters from the war years survive inside, and the building was declared a monument in 2021.

rows.name: Bridges Street
rows.summary: Bridges Street is a street of about 300 metres in Sheung Wan, lined with historic buildings alongside newer creative spaces. The red-brick Chinese YMCA of 1918 stands on it, and the street also has galleries, antique shops, cafés and restaurants. The Hong Kong Tourism Board describes it as an arts and culture district.

rows.name: Broadway Cinematheque
rows.summary: Broadway Cinematheque is an art-house cinema in Yau Ma Tei, opened in November 1996 and run by the Broadway Circuit. It screens independent and international films and hosts festivals and retrospectives. Beside it are Kubrick, a bookshop that specialises in film and culture, and a café.

rows.name: Canton Road
rows.summary: Canton Road is a long street running through Tsim Sha Tsui, Jordan, Yau Ma Tei, Mong Kok and Prince Edward, from Salisbury Road in the south to Lai Chi Kok Road in the north. Its southern stretch in Tsim Sha Tsui is lined with luxury boutiques and shopping centres and links landmarks such as Harbour City and the former Marine Police Headquarters. Further north the street gives way to residential blocks and small neighbourhood shops.

rows.name: Cape D'Aguilar Lighthouse
rows.summary: Put into service in April 1875, this is the oldest surviving lighthouse in Hong Kong, a 9.7-metre round granite tower with a rusticated base and an arched doorway closed by an iron door. It was taken out of service in 1896 after Waglan Island Lighthouse opened, and its lantern was re-lit and automated in 1975. It stands on the south-east shore of Hong Kong Island, at the end of the Cape D'Aguilar peninsula.

rows.name: Central Government Offices
rows.summary: Opened in 2011 at Tamar on the Admiralty waterfront, the Central Government Offices house several government bureaus and departments. Architect Rocco Yim designed it around a door-always-open idea, with a central hollow arch and an open layout that lets air flow through to the harbour. Next door, Tamar Park has lawns where people picnic and walk, and a path to the waterfront promenade with views across Victoria Harbour.

rows.name: Central Market
rows.summary: Central Market is a Bauhaus-style market building from 1939, one of Hong Kong's first wet markets, restored between 2017 and 2021 as a Grade III historic building with shops, restaurants and community spaces. More than 500 red lampshades, a classic symbol of local wet markets, hang from the ceiling at the ground-floor entrance. Original red-brick walls and a hanging clock survive at the grand staircase.

rows.name: Central Plaza
rows.summary: Central Plaza is a 374-metre office skyscraper on Harbour Road in Wan Chai, completed in 1992. It has a triangular floor plan and a four-bar neon clock at the top that shows the time in colours at 15-minute intervals. It is a landmark of the Wan Chai skyline, seen mainly from the street and the harbourfront.

rows.name: Central–Mid-Levels Escalators
rows.summary: Opened in 1993, this 800-metre system of 16 escalators and three travelators carries commuters up the slope from Queen's Road Central to Conduit Road, and is one of the longest outdoor covered escalator systems in the world. The direction reverses during the day, running downhill in the morning rush and uphill for the rest of the day. It features in Wong Kar-wai's film Chungking Express (1994), and it does not go as far as The Peak.

rows.name: Cha Kwo Ling Promenade
rows.summary: Cha Kwo Ling Promenade is a harbourside park whose play platform sits on the roof of the Kwun Tong sewage pumping station, with views over Victoria Harbour and the sunset. It has five play zones themed on air, earth, sky, sunlight and water, with more than 60 play facilities including an 8-metre rope-net climbing structure, slides, a water play area, treehouses and mazes. The park is fully accessible and welcomes pets, so it suits families with young children.

rows.name: Che Kung Temple
rows.summary: A temple at Tai Wai dedicated to Che Kung, a Song-dynasty general worshipped as a protector against epidemics. The present temple was built in 1994 in front of the older one and renovated in 2012, and houses a large golden statue of Che Kung and a fan-bladed wheel of fortune that worshippers spin for luck. The busiest day is the Che Kung Festival on the second day of the first lunar month, which draws large crowds.

rows.name: Cheung Ancestral Hall, Shan Ha Tsuen
rows.summary: Built in 1815 by the Cheung clan of Shan Ha Tsuen, this grey-brick ancestral hall has two halls around an open courtyard and an altar carved with the Eight Immortals. The clan used it for gatherings and ancestral worship, and from the 1930s to the 1950s it also housed Wah Fung School. A major restoration was carried out in 1999.

rows.name: Cheung Chau Sai Tai Road
rows.summary: Sai Tai Road is a waterfront path on the western side of Cheung Chau, running along the coast from near the Fireboat station towards Sai Wan. Walkers and cyclists use the wide, easy path past fishing boats at their moorings. It leads on towards the Cheung Chau Family Trail, Cheung Po Tsai Cave, a cave linked in legend to a pirate's hidden treasure, and a Tin Hau temple.

rows.name: Cheung Kong Center
rows.summary: Cheung Kong Center is an office tower at 2 Queen's Road Central, designed by Cesar Pelli and completed in 1999. It stands between the HSBC Main Building and the Bank of China Tower, where its restrained design contrasts with its neighbours, and coloured lights play across its sides at night. Visitors see it from the street, as it is an office building.

rows.name: Cheung Shan Monastery, Ping Che
rows.summary: A two-hall Buddhist temple at Miu Keng in Ping Che, probably built in 1789 as Cheung Sang Nunnery. It stood halfway along the old route to Shenzhen via Sha Tau Kok and served as a rest stop where travellers were offered tea. The rear hall is about a metre higher than the front hall, plaster mouldings decorate the inside and outside, and the Buddha, Kwun Yum and Tei Chong Wong are worshipped within.

rows.name: Chi Lin Nunnery and Nan Lian Garden
rows.summary: Chi Lin Nunnery is a large Buddhist temple complex founded in 1934 as a retreat for nuns and rebuilt in the 1990s in the style of the Tang dynasty, with timber halls held together by interlocking joints rather than nails. Its halls hold statues of the Buddha and bodhisattvas, and visitors are asked to keep quiet and not to take photographs inside. A footbridge links it to Nan Lian Garden, a Tang-style landscaped garden opened in 2006 with a lake, hills, rocks, wooden pavilions and a red bridge.

rows.name: Chik Kwai Study Hall
rows.summary: Chik Kwai Study Hall was built before 1899 by Lai Kam-tai of the Lai clan in Pat Heung, as a place for both ancestor worship and the education of young clansmen. It is a typical two-hall, one-courtyard Qing building with a carved wooden altar for the clan's ancestral tablets, and the Antiquities and Monuments Office calls it one of the finest traditional study halls remaining in the Yuen Long area, for its woodcarvings, plaster mouldings and murals. After the Second World War it housed classrooms and then a kindergarten, which closed in the early 1970s.

rows.name: Chinese YMCA Bridges Street Centre
rows.name_zh: 香港中华基督教青年会必列者士街会所
rows.pinyin: Xiānggǎng Zhōnghuá Jīdūjiào Qīngniánhuì Bìlièzhěshì Jiē Huìsuǒ
rows.summary: Built in 1918 as the first headquarters of the Chinese YMCA of Hong Kong, this six-storey building of red brick and concrete has a symmetrical front facade. When it opened it had the city's first indoor swimming pool with warm water and the first elevated timber running track, and the pool, track, gymnasium and auditorium are all still there. It was declared a monument in 2023 and is still a working YMCA centre.

rows.name: City Art Square
rows.summary: City Art Square is the open-air plaza in front of Sha Tin Town Hall, laid out as part of the plaza's beautification and donated by the Sun Hung Kai Properties Charitable Fund. It displays sculptures and public art installations by 19 artists and designers from overseas, mainland China and Hong Kong, including Zaha Hadid, Dennis Oppenheim, Xu Bing and Sarah Tse, and the Leisure and Cultural Services Department lists works such as The Red Box, Miracle Horse, Vortex and Bauhinia Arc. The Hong Kong Tourism Board describes it as one of the city's largest collections of public art.

rows.name: Clock Tower, Tsim Sha Tsui
rows.summary: The Clock Tower, built in 1915, is the only part of the Kowloon-Canton Railway's Tsim Sha Tsui terminus left standing: the terminus opened in 1916, the trains moved to Hung Hom in 1975, and the old station was demolished in 1978. The 44-metre tower is built of red brick and granite in Edwardian Classical Revival style, with an octagonal domed belfry topped by a lightning rod. It stands on the harbourfront next to the Star Ferry pier, a good spot for the skyline view.

rows.name: Competition Pavilion
rows.name_zh: 香港新晋建筑及设计师比赛展亭
rows.pinyin: Xiānggǎng Xīnjìn Jiànzhú Jí Shèjìshī Bǐsài Zhǎntíng
rows.summary: The Competition Pavilion, nicknamed 'Growing Up', is a pavilion of slender timber columns on the West Kowloon waterfront, next to the Hong Kong Palace Museum, with views across Victoria Harbour. It was designed by New Office Works as the winning entry in the first Hong Kong Young Architects and Designers Competition and was built to host small concerts and performances. The nickname refers to Hong Kong's cultural growth.

rows.name: Cyberport
rows.summary: Cyberport is a technology business park on the Telegraph Bay waterfront in Southern District, with office buildings, a hotel and a shopping and entertainment complex. For visitors the draw is a waterfront promenade with views over the bay, open lawns for picnics and walks, and nearby shopping malls with dining and cinemas. It is a modern development rather than a historic site.

rows.name: Dialogue in the Dark
rows.summary: Dialogue in the Dark is an exhibition in which blind or visually impaired hosts guide visitors through darkened rooms set up as scenes from city streets to quiet natural landscapes, so that visitors rely on touch, sound and smell. It runs under the name Dialogue Experience, which also offers a Silence experience in which visitors communicate without sound. The organisers present it as a way to promote social inclusion, and the visit includes discussion with the hosts.

rows.name: Duddell Street Steps and Gas Lamps
rows.name_zh: 都爹利街石阶及煤气路灯
rows.pinyin: Dūdiēlì Jiē Shíjiē Jí Méiqì Lùdēng
rows.summary: A flight of granite steps at the southern end of Duddell Street, completed in 1883, with heavily moulded Tuscan-order newels and balusters and four gas lamps mounted on the balustrades. The lamps date from the early twentieth century and, since street lighting was electrified in 1967, have been the only working gas lamps of their type in the city. Super Typhoon Mangkhut damaged the steps and lamps in 2018, and the restoration was completed in December 2019.

rows.name: Dukling
rows.summary: Dukling is a red-sailed wooden Chinese junk with nearly 70 years of history, built as a fishing boat and later used for harbour sightseeing, with cruises that have included a Symphony of Lights night sailing and commentary on Hong Kong's fishing heritage. The operator has suspended its cruises for repair and maintenance until further notice.

rows.name: East Coast Boardwalk
rows.summary: The East Coast Boardwalk is a 2.2-kilometre harbourfront path beneath the Island Eastern Corridor on Hong Kong Island, running between Fortress Hill and Quarry Bay and opened in two sections in January and December 2025. It has paths for walking, jogging and cycling, cascade seating for sunset views, a children's play area, fitness equipment and a glass-floored observation deck over the water. Marine-life murals on the piers line up into a giant whale shark when seen from the right angle.

rows.name: East Coast Park Precinct
rows.summary: East Coast Park Precinct is a 1.1-hectare harbourfront park with about 425 metres of promenade at the end of Watson Road in North Point, opened in stages in 2021 and 2022. Its main feature is a barrier-free breakwater about 100 metres long, which the Harbourfront Commission describes as the first of its kind opened to the public in Victoria Harbour, with nearly 360-degree views of the harbour from its end. The park also has a lawn, a children's play area with slides, and a word-art installation that uses the names of Hong Kong's districts.

rows.name: Eliot Hall and May Hall, University of Hong Kong
rows.name_zh: 香港大学仪礼堂及梅堂
rows.summary: Two three-storey red-brick halls opened in 1914 and 1915 as student residences, designed by Denison, Ram and Gibbs and named after Sir Charles Eliot and Sir Francis Henry May. Their facades combine curved pediments, rusticated columns, Chinese-style ceramic grilles and balconies under double-tiled Chinese roofs. During the Battle of Hong Kong in December 1941, Eliot Hall served as a relief hospital and May Hall as the main residence for staff and students.

rows.name: Entrance Tower and Enclosing Walls of Lo Wai, Lung Yeuk Tau
rows.name_zh: 龙跃头老围门楼及围墙
rows.summary: Lo Wai is the earliest of the five walled villages that the Tang clan founded at Lung Yeuk Tau, after their ancestors branched out from Kam Tin in the 14th century. Brick walls enclose the village on all four sides and most of them are intact, and the entrance tower was moved from the north side to its present position facing east for feng shui reasons. The tower and walls were declared monuments in 1997 and fully restored in 1998.

rows.name: Entrance Tower of Ma Wat Wai
rows.summary: Ma Wat Wai was built by the Tang clan in the Qianlong reign as one of the Five Wais and Six Tsuens of Lung Yeuk Tau. Past development removed most of its walls and all four corner towers, leaving the entrance tower, whose red sandstone lintel carries two characters meaning a place of verdancy, and part of the enclosing walls. The tower was fully restored in 1995 and is on the Lung Yeuk Tau Heritage Trail.

rows.name: Exchange Square
rows.summary: Exchange Square is a complex of three office towers in Central that is home to the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, with banks, investment firms and several consulates among its tenants. Its plaza has landscaped terraces, fountains and outdoor sculptures, including works by Henry Moore.

rows.name: Fa Yuen Street Footbridge
rows.summary: The Fa Yuen Street Footbridge crosses the junction of Mong Kok Road and Fa Yuen Street in the middle of Mong Kok. From it you can watch buses, minibuses and taxis pass below, with neon signs, shops, older tenement buildings and street stalls around you. It features in a chase sequence in the film One Nite in Mongkok (2004).

rows.name: Facade of the Old Mental Hospital
rows.summary: The granite facade of a building completed in 1892 as medical staff quarters for the Government Civil Hospital and used from 1939 to 1961 as wards for mentally ill female patients. Its early-Baroque design, with a wide arched verandah, rusticated granite on the lower level and pediments and pinnacles above, is rare in Hong Kong. Only the facade survives, preserved on the site of the Sai Ying Pun Community Complex and nicknamed the 'High Street Haunted House'.

rows.name: Fan Lau Fort
rows.summary: Fan Lau Fort is a small coastal fort of 1729 on the Fan Lau peninsula at the south-western tip of Lantau, looking out over the sea passage into the Pearl River estuary. The rectangular enclosure measures 46 m by 21 m, with walls of semi-dressed stone and green brick; it was probably abandoned around 1898, after the New Territories were leased to Britain, and was restored in the 1980s and 1990s. The peninsula is also known for the line where muddy river water meets clearer sea water.

rows.name: Fan Sin Temple and Wun Yiu Kilns
rows.pinyin: Shàng Wǎnyáo Fánxiān Gōng Jí Wǎnyáo
rows.summary: Fan Sin Temple is the main temple of Sheung Wun Yiu and Ha Wun Yiu, villages that made blue-and-white porcelain from the Ming dynasty until the kilns closed in 1932. It honours Fan Tai Sin Sze, patron saint of potters, a dedication the Antiquities and Monuments Office says is unique in Hong Kong; a plaque in the main hall dates from 1790, and the temple was fully restored in 2000 after a fire in the 1970s. The remains of the Wun Yiu pottery kilns in Sheung Wun Yiu are a separate declared monument, where excavations in 1995 and 1999 found clay pits, water-mills, an animal-driven grinder, soaking tanks and dragon kilns.

rows.name: Fat Tat Tong, Ha Wo Hang
rows.summary: A two-storey Hakka family house built in 1933 by a trust of the four sons of Li To-wan, who had gone to Vietnam to earn a living before returning to Ha Wo Hang. Its long pitched tiled roof, colonnaded verandahs on both floors and ornamental parapet with a rolling-cloud pediment show the eclectic style favoured by returned overseas Chinese in the early twentieth century. It is still lived in by Li To-wan's descendants.

rows.name: Flagstaff House Museum of Tea Ware
rows.summary: Completed in 1846, Flagstaff House is the oldest surviving Western-style building in Hong Kong. It was the office and residence of the commander of the British forces until 1978 and has housed the Museum of Tea Ware, which shows Chinese tea ware, since 1984. The two-storey Greek Revival building has deep verandahs suited to the local climate and stands inside Hong Kong Park.

rows.name: Former French Mission Building
rows.name_zh: 前法国外方传道会大楼
rows.summary: Built in 1917 by the French Society of Foreign Missions as its base in Hong Kong, this three-storey granite and red-brick building is Neo-classical, with a chapel in one corner whose cupola rises above the roof. It stands on Government Hill and served as the temporary headquarters of the provisional Hong Kong government immediately after the Second World War. The Court of Final Appeal sat here from 1997 to 2015, and the building is now used by law-related organisations.

rows.name: Former Kowloon British School
rows.summary: Opened in 1902 for the children of foreign residents, the Former Kowloon British School is the oldest surviving school building built for Hong Kong's expatriate community. It is a Victorian building adapted to the climate with wide verandas, high ceilings and pitched roofs, and it was founded after a donation from Ho Tung (later Sir Robert Ho Tung) in 1900. After restoration it now houses the Antiquities and Monuments Office, and it was declared a monument in 1991.

rows.name: Former Marine Police Headquarters (1881 Heritage)
rows.summary: Completed in 1884, the former Marine Police Headquarters is one of the oldest surviving government buildings in Hong Kong. The compound has a main building, a stable block and a signal tower known as the Round House, which gave time signals to ships until the time ball moved to Signal Hill in 1907. The Marine Police left in 1996, and since 2009 the compound has been a heritage and tourism-themed commercial site with shops and restaurants in the historic buildings.

rows.name: Fortified Structure at Ha Pak Nai
rows.summary: A two-storey grey-brick fortified house with gun embrasures in its outer walls, built around 1910 by Tang Yam-nam after the failed New Army Uprising in Guangzhou. It served as a base and refuge for followers of Sun Yat-sen, working with the Castle Peak Farm in Tuen Mun, and looks across Deep Bay from the coast at Ha Pak Nai. The Antiquities and Monuments Office records its link with the late Qing revolutionary movement.

rows.name: Fung Ping Shan Building, University of Hong Kong
rows.summary: Built in 1931 as the library for the university's Chinese book collection, this three-storey red-brick building has a fan-shaped plan, giant pilasters and an atrium lit by a skylight. It has housed the University Museum and Art Gallery since the 1960s, the oldest museum of its kind in continuous operation in Hong Kong. Only the exterior is declared a monument.

rows.name: Gage Street
rows.summary: Gage Street is a market street in Central that begins near the Central–Mid-Levels Escalators and runs downhill to Aberdeen Street, with fresh-food stalls, cha chaan teng and dai pai dong. It has appeared in films including Rush Hour 2 and The Dark Knight. Together with Pak Tsz Lane it forms part of the Dr Sun Yat-sen Historical Trail.

rows.name: Gate Lodge of the Former Mountain Lodge
rows.name_zh: 旧总督山顶别墅守卫室
rows.summary: Gate Lodge is a small Neo-classical house on Mount Austin Road, built between 1900 and 1902 as one of two gatekeeper's lodges for Mountain Lodge, the governor's summer residence on the Peak. The main house was demolished in 1946, leaving only this lodge, with its rounded corners and three small triangular pediments. It stands in Victoria Peak Garden and is now used as a site office.

rows.name: Golden Bauhinia Square
rows.summary: Golden Bauhinia Square is a waterfront plaza in Wan Chai, next to the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre. Its centrepiece is the six-metre gilded Forever Blooming Bauhinia sculpture on a red granite base, a gift from the Central Government to mark the 1997 handover, beside the 20-metre Reunification Monument. A flag-raising ceremony is held here daily, and the square has wide views across the harbour.

rows.name: HSBC Main Building
rows.summary: Designed by Norman Foster and completed in 1985, the HSBC Main Building has its structural steel on the outside, which leaves an open, light-filled interior without columns. Visitors can walk through the atrium and look up at the building's workings. Two bronze lions, Stephen and Stitt, stand either side of the main entrance.

rows.name: Happy Valley Racecourse
rows.summary: Happy Valley Racecourse is one of Hong Kong's two horse-racing tracks, dating back to 1845. Many race meetings are held on Wednesday nights and add live music, food and drink, and a beer garden, and visitors can watch from the public stands. The grounds also include the Hong Kong Racing Museum.

rows.name: Harbour Cruise Bauhinia
rows.summary: Harbour Cruise Bauhinia runs dinner buffet cruises on Victoria Harbour from North Point, with Eastern and Western dishes served on board and an open deck for views of both shores. The whole trip takes about two hours, and one sailing is timed to take in A Symphony of Lights from the water. It suits visitors who want a sit-down meal combined with the harbour skyline.

rows.name: Hau Ku Shek Ancestral Hall
rows.summary: Hau Ku Shek Ancestral Hall stands in Ho Sheung Heung. It was built in the late Ming dynasty to commemorate the clan's 17th-generation ancestor Hau Ku-shek and renovated around 1762, and follows the traditional three-hall, two-courtyard layout, with red sandstone drum platforms and a door frame on the facade, richly decorated roof ridges and carved beams. The two-storey rear hall was once a village school, and the Hau clan still holds ceremonies in the hall.

rows.name: Hau Mei Fung Ancestral Hall
rows.summary: Hau Mei Fung Ancestral Hall in Kam Tsin was built in the late 18th century by Hau Cheuk-wan, who gained a juren degree in 1788, to commemorate his great-grandfather Hau Mei-fung (1634–1688), a student of the Imperial Academy. It is a two-hall, three-bay Qing vernacular building whose rear hall has a porch with a humpbacked roof, a feature rarely seen among traditional buildings in Hong Kong. Plaster mouldings decorate the ridges and wall friezes, and the timberwork and ancestral shrine carry carvings of animals, flowers and folk stories.

rows.name: Hau Wong Temple, Kowloon City
rows.summary: Hau Wong Temple in Kowloon City, dedicated to Hau Wong (Yeung Hau Tai Wong), is dated by the Antiquities and Monuments Office to 1730 or earlier, from a temple bell cast in 1730. It was patronised by Qing officials and soldiers from the Kowloon Walled City and keeps relics from that garrison, including an incense burner donated in 1847 and a stone inscription of the character for crane dated 1888. The stepped gables of the rear hall follow a style called 'five peaks pay tribute to heaven', which is very rare in Hong Kong.

rows.name: Hip Tin Temple, Shan Tsui
rows.summary: A temple to Kwan Tai, rebuilt in 1894–95 to replace an earlier one, and one of the few surviving main temples tied to Tung Wo Market, run by the Shap Yeuk village alliance that dominated the Sha Tau Kok economy from the 1830s to the 1930s. Five stone plaques in the front hall record the rebuilding, and the carved altar, fascia boards and plaster dragonfish corbels survive intact. Part of the building has also served as a village school since 1959, and villagers still mark the Kwan Tai festival on the 13th day of the fifth lunar month.

rows.name: Historic Structures of Aberdeen Reservoir
rows.name_zh: 香港仔水塘历史构筑物
rows.summary: Four structures from Aberdeen Reservoir, built in 1931 and 1932: the dam, valve house and bridge of the Upper Reservoir and the dam of the Lower Reservoir. The reservoirs were built to ease water shortages in the west of Hong Kong Island and were the fourth and last reservoirs built on the island. They lie within Aberdeen Country Park.

rows.name: Historic Structures of Kowloon Reservoir
rows.summary: Five waterworks structures built between 1901 and 1910 for Kowloon Reservoir: the main dam and its valve house, the spillway dam and two recorder houses. It was the fourth reservoir in Hong Kong and the first on the Kowloon Peninsula, and its stored rainwater replaced well water and the supply pumped from Yau Ma Tei. The structures lie in Kam Shan Country Park, also known as Monkey Hill for its macaques.

rows.name: Historic Structures of Pok Fu Lam Reservoir
rows.name_zh: 薄扶林水塘历史构筑物
rows.summary: Completed in 1863, Pok Fu Lam Reservoir was the first reservoir built in Hong Kong. Six of its structures were declared monuments in 2009, namely the former watchman's cottage, the gauge basin and four masonry bridges, and a further masonry bridge of granite at the east end of the reservoir, carrying Pok Fu Lam Reservoir Road on a semicircular arch, was declared in 2020. The reservoir lies in Pok Fu Lam Country Park, which the Hong Kong Trail crosses.

rows.name: Historic Structures of Tai Tam Group of Reservoirs
rows.name_zh: 大潭水塘群历史构筑物
rows.summary: Twenty-two waterworks structures dating from 1883 to 1936 around the Tai Tam reservoirs on the eastern side of Hong Kong Island: dams, valve houses, masonry bridges, a pumping station with its chimney and staff quarters, and the 21-arch section of the Bowen Aqueduct. The extra water they supplied allowed the city to spread east from Central and Western. The Tai Tam Waterworks Heritage Trail passes many of the dams and bridges in Tai Tam Country Park.

rows.name: Historic Structures of Wong Nai Chung Reservoir
rows.name_zh: 黄泥涌水塘历史构筑物
rows.summary: Wong Nai Chung Reservoir, completed in 1899, is the third oldest surviving waterworks construction in Hong Kong, and its masonry dam, valve house and weir were declared monuments in 2009. The reservoir later stopped serving as a water store and is now Wong Nai Chung Reservoir Park, a lakeside park.

rows.name: Hong Kong China Dragon Boat Association Shek Mun Training Centre
rows.name_zh: 中国香港龙舟总会石门训练中心
rows.pinyin: Zhōngguó Xiānggǎng Lóngzhōu Zǒnghuì Shímén Xùnliàn Zhōngxīn
rows.summary: The Hong Kong China Dragon Boat Association runs its training centre beside the Shing Mun River at Shek Mun in Sha Tin, where it holds certificate courses for paddlers at several levels and hosts local and international dragon boat races. The association also hires out boats and facilities. The Hong Kong Tourism Board lists the centre as a filming location of the 2018 film Men on the Dragon, whose paddlers' training scenes were shot here; it is a working sports venue rather than a sightseeing stop, so it suits dragon boat enthusiasts and film fans.

rows.name: Hong Kong City Hall
rows.summary: Opened in 1962 on Edinburgh Place, this Modernist complex was the first multi-purpose cultural centre for all citizens in Hong Kong, and it has a concert hall, a theatre, a public library and a marriage registry. A Memorial Garden between its two blocks has a 12-sided shrine to the soldiers and civilians who died defending Hong Kong in the Second World War. It was declared a monument in 2022.

rows.name: Hong Kong Coliseum
rows.summary: Opened in 1983, the Hong Kong Coliseum is an indoor arena shaped like an inverted pyramid, built from the roof downwards to leave the 1,600-square-metre arena floor without columns. It seats more than 12,500 and hosts concerts, sports events and conferences, so most visitors come for a show rather than the building itself. It is managed by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department.

rows.name: Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre
rows.summary: The Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai opened in 1988 and is one of the city's main venues for trade fairs, concerts and events, including the Art Basel Hong Kong art fair held each March. Designed by Skidmore, Owings and Merrill, it is known for its large glass curtain wall and an aluminium roof shaped to recall a seabird in flight. Most visitors see it from the harbourfront beside Golden Bauhinia Square.

rows.name: Hong Kong Disneyland
rows.summary: Hong Kong Disneyland is a theme park on reclaimed land at Penny's Bay on Lantau, opened in 2005. It has eight themed lands, including Fantasyland, Toy Story Land and World of Frozen, with rides, parades, live shows and character meetings, and the resort has three Disney hotels. It suits families with children and Disney fans.

rows.name: Hong Kong Museum of Art
rows.summary: The Hong Kong Museum of Art, the city's first public art museum, stands on the Tsim Sha Tsui waterfront and holds a collection of about 20,000 items. The collection centres on Chinese antiquities, Chinese painting and calligraphy, China trade art and modern Hong Kong art, and displays rotate alongside special exhibitions. The building, renovated between 2015 and 2019, has floor-to-ceiling windows with views over Victoria Harbour.

rows.name: Hong Kong Museum of History
rows.summary: The Hong Kong Museum of History presents the history of Hong Kong from ancient civilisation to its emergence as an international metropolis. Its 'Hong Kong Story' permanent exhibition, which reopened on 1 April 2026, has more than 2,800 exhibits in four chapters, and the National Security Exhibition Gallery on the second floor is dedicated to national security education. The museum moved to its present building on Chatham Road South in 1998, next to the Hong Kong Science Museum.

rows.name: Hong Kong Museum of the War of Resistance and Coastal Defence
rows.name_zh: 香港抗战及海防博物馆
rows.summary: A museum in the 1887 Lei Yue Mun Fort above the Lei Yue Mun channel, converted from the former Hong Kong Museum of Coastal Defence in September 2024. A permanent exhibition covers Hong Kong's coastal defence and military changes from the Tang dynasty to 1997, alongside material on the War of Resistance. Outdoors, a historical trail with 24 checkpoints marks significant events at the fort.

rows.name: Hong Kong Observation Wheel
rows.summary: The Hong Kong Observation Wheel is a 60-metre Ferris wheel on the Central harbourfront, with 42 air-conditioned gondolas. A ride lasts about 15 to 20 minutes and looks across the harbour, the Central skyline and Kowloon. The AIA Vitality Park around the wheel has a hand-painted carousel, street art and seasonal events.

rows.name: Hong Kong Observatory
rows.summary: The Hong Kong Observatory was established in 1883 and became the Royal Observatory in 1912, and its 1883 Building stands on a small hill off Nathan Road. It is a two-storey Victorian-Colonial block of plastered brick with arched windows and long verandas, declared a monument in 1984, and it now houses the directorate's offices while forecasting work has moved to newer buildings nearby. The Observatory describes its grounds as home to plants and wildlife that are uncommon in Hong Kong.

rows.name: Hong Kong Palace Museum
rows.summary: The Hong Kong Palace Museum opened in 2022 in the West Kowloon Cultural District and shows works from the Palace Museum in Beijing and other institutions, with highlights including ceramics, jade carvings and goldwork, across nine galleries. It also stages special exhibitions on Chinese art and culture and on other civilisations. The building was designed by Rocco Design Architects Associates, with stacked atriums that bring in natural light.

rows.name: Hong Kong Railway Museum
rows.summary: The old Tai Po Market Railway Station, completed in 1913 with a Chinese-style pitched roof when other stations on the Kowloon-Canton Railway were Western in design, is now an open-air railway museum. The station building holds an exhibition gallery, the old booking office and a signal cabin, and the grounds display a narrow-gauge steam locomotive, diesel-electric engines, historic coaches, trolleys and semaphores. The station closed when a new one opened nearby in 1983, and the museum opened in 1985.

rows.name: Hong Kong Science Museum
rows.summary: The Hong Kong Science Museum, opened in 1991, has at least 500 exhibits, most of them hands-on, in themed halls covering energy, light and sound, mechanics, mathematics, magnetism and electricity, and biodiversity. Highlights include the 22-metre-tall Energy Machine and Betsy, Cathay Pacific's first DC-3 airliner. It suits families and anyone curious about how things work.

rows.name: Hong Kong Science Park
rows.summary: Hong Kong Science Park is a 22-hectare technology campus at Pak Shek Kok on the Tolo Harbour waterfront, run by the Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation. Visitors can walk the Grand Plaza and the Pak Shek Kok Promenade beside it and see the auditorium known as the Golden Egg, which serves as the park's landmark, while the HKSTP Experience Centre shows the city's technology projects to booked visitors. The waterfront is a rest stop on the cycle route between Sha Tin and Tai Po.

rows.name: Hong Kong Space Museum
rows.summary: The Hong Kong Space Museum, open in Tsim Sha Tsui since 1980, is easy to spot by its egg-shaped dome, which houses the Space Theatre. Two permanent halls, the Hall of the Cosmos and the Hall of Space Exploration, hold more than 100 exhibits, over half of them interactive. The theatre screens astronomy shows and science documentaries.

rows.name: Hong Kong Water Taxi
rows.summary: Hong Kong Water Taxi runs air-conditioned boats with open decks around Victoria Harbour, combining sightseeing sailings with regular routes between piers such as Tsim Sha Tsui East, West Kowloon, Wan Chai and Central. On the water you pass landmarks including the Hong Kong Observation Wheel, the IFC towers and the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre. Routes have changed recently, so the operator's current notices are worth checking.

rows.name: Hopewell Centre
rows.summary: Hopewell Centre is a cylindrical tower on Queen's Road East, completed in 1980, which was the tallest building in Hong Kong when it opened. Its round plan and glass facade make it easy to pick out on the skyline. It stands on a steep hillside, so it has entrances on both Queen's Road East and Kennedy Road.

rows.name: Hung Hing Ying Building, University of Hong Kong
rows.summary: A two-storey Classic Revival red-brick building opened in 1919 as the university's student union, with a rotunda at the centre and a wing on each side. It later served as a senior common room and, from 1996 to 2012, as the music department, and it was named after Hung Hing-ying in 1986. It stands opposite the Main Building.

rows.name: Hung Shing Temple, Ap Lei Chau
rows.summary: Hung Shing Temple is the main temple on Ap Lei Chau, built in 1773 for Hung Shing, a deity worshipped as a protector of fishermen and merchants at sea. It is a Qing-style building of two halls with a covered courtyard, with Shiwan ceramic figurines on the roof ridges and two dragon-painted timber poles outside. It is one of the few traditional temples in Hong Kong to keep its original sea-facing setting, and the Hung Shing Festival on the 13th day of the second lunar month is still one of the island's main events.

rows.name: Hung Shing Temple, Kau Sai Chau
rows.summary: Hung Shing Temple stands near Kau Sai Fishermen Village at the southern end of Kau Sai Chau and was built before 1889 with donations from local people whose living came from fishing. It is a two-hall, three-bay building with altars to Hung Shing, the deity who protects people at sea, and two other deities. A restoration funded by the Hong Kong Jockey Club was completed in 2000 and won a UNESCO Asia-Pacific heritage conservation award.

rows.name: Hung Shing Temple, Wan Chai
rows.summary: One of Wan Chai's oldest surviving temples, estimated to date from 1847–1852 and dedicated to Hung Shing, the 'God of the South Sea'. It is an example of Lingnan vernacular architecture set against natural rock beside Queen's Road East, with stone carvings, plaster mouldings, granite figures and Shiwan ceramic ridge decorations made in 1909. The temple has long hosted religious ceremonies and was declared a monument in 2026.

rows.name: I Shing Temple
rows.summary: I Shing Temple, meaning 'temple of two gods', is dedicated to Hung Shing and Che Kung and serves the residents of six villages in Wang Chau. An inscription on its bell suggests it was built in 1718, and it is both a place of worship and a meeting place where villagers discuss important matters. It is a grey-brick, two-hall building with an open courtyard and a chamber on each side, restored in 1996, and it is one of the ritual sites for Wang Chau's Jiao Festival, held once every eight years.

rows.name: Ice House Street
rows.summary: Ice House Street runs from Lower Albert Road to Connaught Road in Central and takes its name from the ice store that once stood here, where American merchants kept imported ice for hospitals and the public. Its historic buildings include the Club Lusitano and the old Dairy Farm depot. Today the street is home to boutiques, restaurants and hotels.

rows.name: International Commerce Centre and sky100
rows.summary: The International Commerce Centre, completed in 2010 at the tip of West Kowloon, is Hong Kong's tallest building, mostly offices with a Ritz-Carlton hotel on the upper floors. Its sky100 observation deck on the 100th floor, 393 metres above sea level, is an indoor viewing deck with 360-degree views over Victoria Harbour, Hong Kong Island and Kowloon.

rows.name: Island House, Tai Po
rows.summary: Completed in 1906 on a small islet at the head of Tolo Harbour, Island House is a two-storey colonial building with open verandahs, built as quarters for the District Officer and used until 1985 as the official residence of the Secretary for District Administration. The islet is joined to the shore by a causeway. The house is now WWF-Hong Kong's Island House Conservation Studies Centre.

rows.name: JOYPOLIS SPORTS HONG KONG
rows.summary: JOYPOLIS SPORTS HONG KONG is an indoor sports-themed amusement centre spread over five levels of the Health and Wellness Centre in Kai Tak Sports Park, and the first overseas flagship of Japan's JOYPOLIS SPORTS brand. Its themed zones include a ninja obstacle course on the ground floor, a Sonic-themed sports arena licensed by SEGA and a floor of mixed-reality, virtual-reality and augmented-reality games such as VR horse racing and AR wall climbing. It suits families and groups looking for an all-weather activity.

rows.name: Jackson Road
rows.summary: Jackson Road is a short street in the heart of Central, home to the Hong Kong Club Building and the Court of Final Appeal Building. The neoclassical court building, which also housed the Supreme Court and the Legislative Council, has Ionic and Doric columns and a statue of Themis, goddess of justice, on top. The film A Better Tomorrow (1986) opens with a scene shot on the street.

rows.name: Jamia Mosque
rows.summary: Jamia Mosque on Shelley Street is the oldest mosque in Hong Kong. The present building dates from 1915 to 1916, paid for by the Bombay merchant Haji Mohamed Essack Elias to replace an 1849 mosque on the same site. It has a minaret topped by a dome, pointed multifoil archways, coloured glass windows and an octagonal dome over the prayer hall, and it remains an important place of worship for the city's Muslims.

rows.name: Jardine House
rows.summary: Jardine House is an office tower at 1 Connaught Place in Central, completed in 1973 and easily recognised by its hundreds of circular windows. It was originally called Connaught Centre and was the tallest building in Asia when it opened. Visitors can look at the facade from outside or go in to the shops and food hall on the lower levels.

rows.name: Kai Tak Cruise Terminal
rows.summary: Kai Tak Cruise Terminal stands on the former Kai Tak Airport runway and was designed by Foster + Partners, with a form that pays homage to the site's aviation past; the first ship berthed in 2013. Its roof is a public park of about 23,000 square metres with greenery, walking paths and wide views of Victoria Harbour and the skyline. Locals and visitors use the park even when no cruise ship is in port.

rows.name: Kai Tak Sports Park
rows.summary: Kai Tak Sports Park is a sports and entertainment complex on the former Kai Tak Airport site, opened in March 2025 and described by the Hong Kong Tourism Board as Hong Kong's largest. Its main venues are the 50,000-capacity Kai Tak Stadium with a retractable roof, the 10,000-seat Kai Tak Arena and a 5,000-seat youth sports ground, alongside open public spaces and a shopping mall. The stadium's facade of triangular aluminium panels changes colour with the light.

rows.name: Kang Yung Study Hall
rows.summary: One of the few study halls in Hong Kong built purely for teaching, this hall in the Hakka village of Sheung Wo Hang was built by the Li clan in the early Qing dynasty and enlarged in the Qianlong reign. It is a simple two-hall building of grey brick, mud-brick and rammed earth, with cocklofts that provided classrooms and living quarters. An inscription records a renovation in 1872, and a full restoration was completed in 1993.

rows.name: Kau U Fong
rows.summary: Kau U Fong is a short street in Sheung Wan lined with modern restaurants, independent shops and boutique hotels, among a few surviving tenement buildings with weathered facades and worn stone steps. The stairway scene in Wong Kar-wai's film In the Mood for Love (2000), where two neighbours brush past carrying wonton noodles, was shot here.

rows.name: King George V Memorial Park, Kowloon
rows.name_zh: 九龙佐治五世纪念公园
rows.summary: King George V Memorial Park is a historic park in Jordan, beside Canton Road, built in 1940 and officially opened in 1941. It keeps traditional Chinese touches, including a red-and-green tiled gateway, a palace-style compound wall, a pavilion and banyan trees growing along a stone wall. It makes a quiet, shaded stop after Temple Street or the nearby Kwun Chung streets.

rows.name: King Law Ka Shuk, Tai Po Tau Tsuen
rows.summary: King Law Ka Shuk is the ancestral hall of the Tang clan in Tai Po Tau Tsuen, named after their ancestor Tang King-law and once used as a study hall; the Antiquities and Monuments Office says it still serves for clan meetings and traditional functions. It is a traditional three-hall, two-courtyard building with geometric motifs on its roof ridges, and the murals above the main entrance and the carved timber altar in the middle hall date from renovations in 1932. Its restoration, completed in 2001, won an Award of Merit in the UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Awards.

rows.name: King Yin Lei
rows.summary: King Yin Lei is a mansion on Stubbs Road in Mid-Levels, built around 1937 for the wife of a Guangdong merchant, and it has appeared in films and television series. The Antiquities and Monuments Office describes its design as combining Chinese and Western architecture, a rarity in Hong Kong. It was declared a monument in 2008 and restored by 2010, and its façade is a popular spot for photographs.

rows.name: King's College
rows.summary: King's College is a government secondary school whose red-brick campus on Bonham Road, built between 1923 and 1926, is one of six surviving pre-war government school buildings in Hong Kong. It is designed in the Neo-classical style, with arched colonnades, verandahs and rusticated quoins. The Japanese army used it as a military stable during the occupation, and it reopened as a school in 1950 after repairs.

rows.name: Kom Tong Hall (Dr Sun Yat-sen Museum)
rows.summary: Built in 1914 for the businessman Ho Kom-tong, this Edwardian-era mansion has red-brick walls, granite dressings and ornate iron balconies, and was one of the first buildings in Hong Kong with a steel frame and concealed electrical wiring. Inside are a grand staircase, plaster ceilings picked out in gold leaf and Art Nouveau stained glass. It has been the Dr Sun Yat-sen Museum since December 2006; Sun received his secondary and university education in Hong Kong.

rows.name: Kowloon Peak
rows.summary: Kowloon Peak, also called Fei Ngo Shan, is the highest mountain in Kowloon, rising to about 600 metres at the north-eastern corner of New Kowloon, inside Ma On Shan Country Park. The summit has views over Victoria Harbour, Hong Kong Island, Kowloon and Sai Kung, and a viewing platform on Fei Ngo Shan Road can be reached by road. Hikers climb it by challenging trails, some steep and dangerous, including Stage 4 of the Wilson Trail, and it is popular for sunrise, sunset and autumn silvergrass.

rows.name: Kowloon Union Church
rows.summary: Opened in 1931, Kowloon Union Church was one of the earliest inter-denominational churches in Hong Kong, built by the London Missionary Society with support from Sir Paul Chater. It is in Perpendicular Gothic style, with red brick walls, grey granite window surrounds, a battlemented three-storey tower as the entrance and a rare double hammer-beam timber roof over the main hall. The Japanese army used it as a stable during the occupation, and it reopened for worship in 1947 and is still an active church.

rows.name: Kowloon Walled City Park
rows.summary: Kowloon Walled City Park stands on the site of the Kowloon Walled City, a garrison town built by the Qing government in 1847 that later became a densely built-up enclave before it was cleared and turned into a park. The 31,000-square-metre park is laid out as a classical Chinese garden of pavilions, ponds and themed gardens, and it keeps two declared monuments: the restored Yamen, once the office of the Qing assistant magistrate, and the excavated remains of the South Gate, where two original stone plaques were found. An outdoor display area has a bronze model, and the Yamen currently houses the movie set exhibition Kowloon Walled City: A Cinematic Journey, scheduled to run until May 2028.

rows.name: Kun Lung Wai (San Wai), Lung Yeuk Tau
rows.summary: Kun Lung Wai, also called San Wai, is one of the five walled villages founded by the Tang clan of Lung Yeuk Tau. Its grey-brick walls, built in 1744, have a watch tower at each corner and gun embrasures, and the gate tower in the south-west wall is an unusual pair of separate halls with a granite-and-brick front. The gate tower was restored in 1988 and the walls and corner towers in 1994.

rows.name: Kwong Fook Tsz
rows.summary: Also known as Pak Shing Temple, this temple on Tai Ping Shan Street was built in 1895 with funds raised by Chinese community leaders. It enshrines Ksitigarbha, Chai Kung, Shui Ching Pak and Tai Sui, and holds the soul tablets of Chinese workers who died in Hong Kong in the early years. Its three-hall, two-courtyard layout is rare among Hong Kong temples, and Shiwan ceramics decorate the ridge of the entrance hall.

rows.name: Kwun Tong Promenade
rows.summary: Kwun Tong Promenade is a harbourside park about one kilometre long, built on the former Kwun Tong Public Cargo Working Area and opened in two stages in 2010 and 2015. It has a boardwalk, a plaza with mist and music-synchronised lighting, lawns, pavilions, a children's play area and a sensory garden, with views across Victoria Harbour towards Kai Tak and Lei Yue Mun. Pets are welcome, and there is a pet-friendly park for dogs.

rows.name: LEGOLAND Discovery Centre Hong Kong
rows.summary: LEGOLAND Discovery Centre Hong Kong is an indoor LEGO-themed attraction in the K11 MUSEA mall, aimed at children aged 3 to 10 and their families. It has about ten themed play areas, including rides and a 4D film, and a Miniland of Hong Kong landmarks built from more than a million bricks. It suits families with young children.

rows.name: Lan Kwai Fong
rows.summary: Lan Kwai Fong is a nightlife district of more than 100 restaurants, bars, clubs and shops spread across small streets in Central. Evenings start with happy hours and dinner, and later at night and at weekends the streets fill with visitors, from dive bars that spill onto the pavement to wine bars high up in the towers. It also hosts public events such as the LKF Beer & Music Fest and holiday celebrations.

rows.name: Law Uk Folk Museum
rows.summary: Law Uk is a Hakka village house more than 200 years old, built for a family surnamed Law and the only one left intact in Chai Wan. It follows the typical 'three-bay, two-chamber' Hakka plan, with a central main hall, a light well and a forecourt once used for drying grain and laundry. Restored in 1989, it now operates as a branch of the Hong Kong Museum of History.

rows.name: Legislative Council Complex
rows.summary: The Legislative Council Complex faces Victoria Harbour in Central and is the seat of Hong Kong's legislature, opened in September 2011 as its first purpose-built home. Visitors can join a guided public tour that includes the Hall of History. Tours run in Cantonese, English and Putonghua and have to be booked in advance.

rows.name: Lei Cheng Uk Han Tomb
rows.summary: The Lei Cheng Uk Han Tomb is a brick burial chamber, dated by its structure, brick inscriptions and burial objects to the Eastern Han dynasty (AD 25–220), found in 1955 when a hillside was levelled for the Lei Cheng Uk housing estate. The tomb itself is closed for conservation, but visitors can look in through a glass panel at the entrance passage. An exhibition hall beside it, a branch of the Hong Kong Museum of History, displays the pottery and bronze finds and explains how the tomb was discovered and built.

rows.name: Lei Yue Mun Viewing Platform
rows.summary: The Lei Yue Mun Viewing Platform is a modern lookout built as part of the Lei Yue Mun Waterfront Enhancement Project, extending from Lei Yue Mun Rest Garden beside the channel at the eastern entrance to Victoria Harbour. It gives views along Hong Kong's eastern coast and access to Oyster Shell Beach. The fishing villages nearby are known for their seafood restaurants.

rows.name: Leung Ancestral Hall, Yuen Kong Tsuen
rows.summary: The Leung clan built this ancestral hall in Yuen Kong Tsuen, Pat Heung, about 200 years ago, after their ancestors moved to the New Territories from Dongguan in the 17th and 18th centuries. It is a typical two-hall, one-courtyard Qing vernacular building with a granite-block base and grey-brick walls, and the rear hall holds a wooden altar for the ancestral tablets. Fully restored in 2006, it is still used by the clan for traditional ceremonies and as a meeting place.

rows.name: Lin Fa Temple, Tai Hang
rows.summary: Lin Fa Temple, the Temple of Lotus, was probably built in 1863 for Kwun Yam, the goddess of mercy. It stands on a hill slope in Tai Hang, with a half-octagonal front hall on a granite arched terrace and a main hall built against an exposed boulder. The Tai Hang Fire Dragon Dance, which is on China's national list of intangible cultural heritage, is blessed here before its procession through the neighbourhood.

rows.name: Lion's Pavilion View Point
rows.summary: The Lion's Pavilion is a multi-level, Chinese-style pavilion on Findlay Road at the Peak, which the tourism board says is named after the lion sculptures on its balustrades. It looks out over the Hong Kong skyline and harbour, and the board recommends it for photographs at sunrise and at dusk. It is a few minutes' walk from the Peak Tram terminus and the Peak Galleria.

rows.name: Liu Man Shek Tong Ancestral Hall
rows.summary: Liu Man Shek Tong is the main ancestral hall of the Liu clan of Sheung Shui, built in the early years of the Yongzheng reign (1723–1735) and restored in the Qianlong reign (1736–1795). It is a three-hall, two-courtyard building decorated with plaster mouldings, wood carvings and murals, and from 1932 to 1974 it housed Fung Kai School. It was restored again in 1984 and 1994.

rows.name: Lo Pan Temple, Kennedy Town
rows.summary: A temple to Lo Pan, the master craftsman revered by the construction trade, first built in 1884 and rebuilt on the same site in 1928. It is decorated with murals, plaster mouldings, wood carvings and ridge ceramics made by the Junyu workshop of Shiwan, and its stepped gable walls are rare in Hong Kong. The local construction trade has long gathered here to honour Lo Pan on his birthday, and the temple was declared a monument in 2024.

rows.name: Lugard Road Lookout
rows.summary: Lugard Road Lookout is a viewpoint on Lugard Road, a shaded path that follows the hillside of Victoria Peak, with views over Hong Kong Island, Kowloon and the harbour. On clear days the hills of the New Territories can be seen as well. The Hong Kong Tourism Board suggests early morning or the time just before sunset for the light.

rows.name: Lui Seng Chun
rows.summary: Lui Seng Chun is a four-storey tong lau (a Hong Kong shophouse) built in 1931 for Lui Leung, a founder of the Kowloon Motor Bus Company, and declared a monument in 2022. The building mixes neo-classical style with Art Deco lines and has a curved front on a triangular corner site; the Lui family ran a Chinese medicine shop on the ground floor and lived above. It was given to the government in 2003 and has been a Chinese medicine and healthcare centre run by Hong Kong Baptist University since 2012.

rows.name: M+
rows.summary: M+ is a museum of twentieth- and twenty-first-century visual culture in the West Kowloon Cultural District, covering visual art, design and architecture, and moving image, with a focus on Hong Kong visual culture. It opened in November 2021 in a building by Herzog & de Meuron with TFP Farrells and Arup, which has 33 galleries and a roof garden with views of Victoria Harbour. The facade facing the harbour is a large LED screen that shows moving-image displays each night.

rows.name: MacPherson Playground
rows.summary: MacPherson Playground is an open-air public sports ground in Mong Kok, run by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department. It has a hard-surface football pitch that can be split into two five-a-side pitches, a basketball court, a spectator stand, a children's playground and fitness stations for older people.
