The Hong Kong Tourism Board describes it as a rare expansive public space in dense Mong Kok.

rows.name: MacPherson Stadium
rows.summary: MacPherson Stadium is an indoor multi-purpose venue on the edge of Mong Kok, run by the Hong Kong Playground Association. The original stadium opened in 1953 within the Queen Elizabeth II Youth Centre, and after redevelopment from 2009 the present indoor stadium opened in 2013. It has stage and sports facilities and is used for concerts and sports events.

rows.name: Madame Tussauds Hong Kong
rows.summary: Madame Tussauds Hong Kong is a wax museum inside the Peak Tower that opened in 2000. Its figures are grouped in themed zones, including Hong Kong Glamour, Music Icons, a Kung Fu Zone and a K-Wave Zone of Korean stars, and several zones let visitors pose or take part. It suits families and fans of celebrity culture.

rows.name: Main Building of St. Stephen's Girls' College
rows.name_zh: 圣士提反女子中学主楼
rows.summary: The main building of one of the first schools in Hong Kong devoted to educating girls, opened on Lyttelton Road in 1924 after the Prince of Wales laid the foundation stone in 1922. This four-storey classical building has four wings around a central school hall, a layout that resembles a traditional Chinese courtyard house. Its pitched roof of Chinese pan-and-roll tiles rests on timber trusses.

rows.name: Main Building, University of Hong Kong
rows.summary: The oldest structure on the University of Hong Kong campus, built between 1910 and 1912 with a donation from the Parsi businessman Sir Hormusjee Naorojee Mody. The three-storey red-brick building is classical in style, with granite Ionic columns, a central clock tower and a pair of turrets at each end of the main facade. It served as a temporary hospital in December 1941 and was badly damaged in the last stage of the Japanese occupation, and classes there resumed in October 1946.

rows.name: Man Lun Fung Ancestral Hall
rows.summary: The Man clan built this ancestral hall in Fan Tin Tsuen, San Tin, around the middle of the 17th century to honour Man Fat-po, also known as Lun-fung, the eighth-generation ancestor of the clan. It has three halls with two enclosed courtyards between them, and the ancestral tablets of the Mans are kept in the middle hall. In the past it also served as the office of the village patrol force and as a school for clansmen, and it was fully restored in 1987.

rows.name: Man Mo Temple Compound, Sheung Wan
rows.summary: Built between 1847 and 1862 by wealthy Chinese merchants, this compound on Hollywood Road has three blocks: Man Mo Temple, Lit Shing Kung and Kung Sor. The main temple honours Man Cheong, the god of literature, and Mo Tai, the god of martial arts, and is decorated with ceramic figurines, granite and wood carvings, plaster mouldings and murals. It is still a working temple, and the board of the Tung Wah Group of Hospitals gathers here each year for the Autumn Sacrificial Rites.

rows.name: Man Mo Temple, Tai Po
rows.summary: Built with donations from the Tsat Yeuk community and opened in 1892, this temple served as a meeting, arbitration and worship place for the market town of Tai Wo. Man Cheong, god of literature, and Mo Tai, god of martial arts, are enshrined on a carved timber altar in the rear hall. The two-hall grey-brick building has plaster mouldings on its ridges and facade, and a finely made wooden fascia board above the entrance.

rows.name: Maryknoll Convent School, Kowloon Tong
rows.summary: Built in 1937, the Main Building of Maryknoll Convent School is laid out like a medieval monastery or college, with cloisters around an open courtyard, pointed arches and a single tower on the facade. Its loose neo-Tudor style also borrows from Art Deco, Romanesque, Neo-Georgian and Gothic Revival architecture. The Maryknoll Sisters founded the school in 1925, the building served as a Japanese military hospital from 1942 to 1945, and the primary section still uses it today.

rows.name: Memorial Stone of Shing Mun Reservoir
rows.summary: A memorial stone of 1937 marking the completion of Shing Mun Reservoir, which took 14 years to build from 1923 and was the largest reservoir of the pre-war period supplying water to both sides of Victoria Harbour. The Antiquities and Monuments Office notes that it and the stone at Tai Tam Tuk Reservoir are the only two such stones for the largest pre-war reservoirs in the New Territories and on Hong Kong Island. It stands by the main dam in Shing Mun Country Park, where sections of the MacLehose and Wilson trails meet the reservoir.

rows.name: Monopoly Dreams
rows.summary: Monopoly Dreams is an indoor attraction on the third level of the Peak Galleria, themed around the board game and described by the tourism board as the world's first Monopoly-themed attraction. It has oversized game pieces, interactive and virtual games, a 4DX ride and a display of vintage Monopoly sets. It suits families who are already at the Peak.

rows.name: Nathan Road
rows.summary: Nathan Road is Kowloon's main thoroughfare, running north from Tsim Sha Tsui through Jordan, Yau Ma Tei and Mong Kok to Prince Edward. About 3.6 kilometres long, it is lined with shops, restaurants, malls and places of worship, and was once nicknamed the Golden Mile. It was named in 1909 after the governor Sir Matthew Nathan, and the Hong Kong Tourism Board presents it as a place to experience Kowloon's energy.

rows.name: Noah's Ark Hong Kong
rows.summary: Noah's Ark Hong Kong is a family theme park on Ma Wan, built around a full-size replica of the biblical ark. Visitors walk through the Ark Garden, where 67 pairs of life-size animal sculptures stand, then the Ark Expo with its 180-degree theatre and the Treasure House with 15 discovery galleries on subjects from science to music. There is also a children's play area, a ropes and zip-line course and a hotel on site, with the nature garden of Ma Wan Park close by.

rows.name: North and West Blocks of St. Joseph's College
rows.name_zh: 圣若瑟书院北座及西座
rows.pinyin: Shèng Ruòsè Shūyuàn Běizuò Jí Xīzuò
rows.summary: These are the only pre-war buildings on the campus of St Joseph's College, a school that the La Salle Brothers took over in 1875: the North Block of 1920 and the West Block of 1925. The four-storey North Block is flanked by two towers and has giant Ionic columns on the front facing Cotton Tree Drive, while the West Block is topped by a turret. Both stand within a working school.

rows.name: Ocean Park Hong Kong
rows.summary: Ocean Park is an amusement and animal theme park in Wong Chuk Hang, opened in 1977 and divided into two areas, the Waterfront and the Summit, which are linked by a cable car and the Ocean Express funicular. It combines rides with animal and marine exhibits, including the Grand Aquarium, penguins and giant pandas. It suits families and is large enough for a full day.

rows.name: Ocean Terminal Deck
rows.summary: Ocean Terminal Deck is a rooftop viewing deck on the Ocean Terminal extension of Harbour City on the Tsim Sha Tsui waterfront, designed by Foster + Partners. It gives a 270-degree view of Victoria Harbour, Hong Kong Island and Kowloon, with harbour-view restaurants, a lawn and an open-air event space. It is a place to watch the sunset and the evening skyline.

rows.name: Old Bank of China Building
rows.summary: Completed in the early 1950s on Des Voeux Road Central, the Bank of China Building mixes Chinese and Western architectural styles, with white granite cladding and deep red metal window frames. A pair of Chinese stone lions stand at the main entrance, behind which the central revolving door has a distinctly Western look. It has been a Grade I historic building since 2009, and appears in Wong Kar-wai's film Days of Being Wild (1990).

rows.name: Old District Office North
rows.summary: The Old District Office North was built around 1907 and was the first seat of civil administration in the New Territories after the area was leased to Britain; government business and land registration for the northern New Territories were handled here, and a magistrate's court sat in the building until 1961. It is a red-brick colonial building with open verandahs and brick arches along its east and west sides, and its antique fireplaces survive. Since 2002 it has housed the Law Ting Pong Scout Centre of the Scout Association of Hong Kong.

rows.name: Old House, Hoi Pa Village
rows.summary: A traditional Hakka village house built in 1904 by Yau Yuen-cheung (1865–1937), a scholar of Hoi Pa Village, from rammed earth, grey brick and timber, and declared a monument in 1986. It is a fine example of southern Chinese village architecture. The old village has been redeveloped as Tak Wah Park in the middle of Tsuen Wan, and the house stands in the park.

rows.name: Old House, Wong Uk Village
rows.summary: The only old building left of Wong Uk Village, this two-storey green-brick house was built around 1911 by Wong Tsing-wo, a 19th-generation descendant of the Wong clan. The clan, from Xingning in Guangdong, founded the village in the Qianlong reign, and it became a trading station on the route between Guangdong and Kowloon. Most of it was cleared when Sha Tin New Town was built on reclaimed land, and the house has fine mural paintings and traditional decoration.

rows.name: Old Lei Yue Mun Barracks (Blocks 7, 10 and 25)
rows.summary: Three buildings of the old Lei Yue Mun Barracks, one of the earliest British Army fortifications in Hong Kong, on the north-east corner of the island above the eastern approach to Victoria Harbour; all were declared monuments in 2016. Block 7 (1890–95) was built as officers' quarters in a Colonial Vernacular style with wide verandahs, Block 10 (1890–95, extended in 1935) as soldiers' quarters with arched, colonnaded verandahs, and Block 25 as the officers' mess, the last two in a simplified Classical style. The central area of the barracks became Lei Yue Mun Park and Holiday Village in 1988.

rows.name: Old Pathological Institute
rows.summary: A red-brick Edwardian building opened in 1906 as the first purpose-built public health and medical laboratory in Hong Kong, set up to help control plague and other infectious diseases. Its arcaded verandahs, balconies and double-layer Chinese tiled roof adapt Western design to the subtropical climate, and the parapet carries a Dutch gable with obelisk-shaped finials. Since 1996 it has housed the Hong Kong Museum of Medical Sciences, which covers the history of medicine in the city.

rows.name: Old Stanley Police Station
rows.summary: Built in 1859, the Old Stanley Police Station is the oldest surviving police station in Hong Kong, a two-storey building with colonnaded verandahs and a Classical look. It was the most southerly outpost on Hong Kong Island and was used by the Japanese Gendarmerie during the Japanese Occupation. The domed brick ceiling of the original gunroom and the fireplaces survive inside, and since the police left in 1974 the building has been let to tenants for various uses.

rows.name: Old Supreme Court Building
rows.summary: Opened in 1912 on reclaimed land and built on a foundation of hundreds of Chinese fir piles, this three-storey granite building is Neo-classical, with tall Ionic columns and a central pediment topped by a blindfolded statue of Justice as the Greek goddess Themis. It housed the Legislative Council chamber from 1985 to 2011 and has been home to the Court of Final Appeal since 2015. Only the exterior is declared a monument.

rows.name: Old Tai Po Police Station (Green Hub)
rows.summary: The Old Tai Po Police Station, built in 1899, was the first police station and police headquarters in the New Territories and is the oldest surviving police station there. Its three single-storey buildings, the main building, staff quarters and canteen block, keep their Dutch gables, ornamental window arches and fireplaces, with a guard house and octagonal well near the entrance and a brick incinerator on the lawn. It has been revitalised as the Green Hub, run by Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden, which offers a heritage display and heritage tours alongside sustainable-living programmes.

rows.name: Old Tsan Yuk Maternity Hospital
rows.summary: The red-brick main building of a hospital opened on Western Street in 1922 by the Chinese Public Dispensaries Committee to provide maternity care for Chinese women and train Chinese midwives. It has a granite portico at the main entrance and a spiral staircase inside. The hospital moved to new premises in 1955, and the building has been a community centre since 1961.

rows.name: Old Wan Chai Post Office
rows.summary: Built in 1912–13 and opened in 1915, this L-shaped building at the junction of Queen's Road East and Wan Chai Gap Road is the oldest surviving post office building in Hong Kong. It is a simple pitched-roof structure with gable ends and mouldings. Since 2024 it has been kNOw Carbon House, an environmental education centre about carbon neutrality that keeps some historic items from the old post office.

rows.name: Old Yau Ma Tei Police Station
rows.summary: The Old Yau Ma Tei Police Station was built in 1922 in Edwardian style and is one of Hong Kong's few surviving pre-war police stations. It is a Grade II historic building whose facade has appeared in many Hong Kong crime films, including Infernal Affairs. Part of it now holds a government-backed exhibition, Yau Ma Tei Police Station: A Cinematic Journey, with a retro cinema entrance, a re-created 1970s and 1980s detective office and open detention cells.

rows.name: PMQ
rows.summary: PMQ is a creative hub in SoHo, set in a Grade III historic building that was the Police Married Quarters and, before that, the site of Central School. More than 100 Hong Kong designers work from its studios and shops, and it runs workshops, design events and cultural activities. Traces of its past include old granite foundations from the school on display below ground, granite steps dating from 1889, and fifth-floor galleries on the history of Central School and a police family's home.

rows.name: Peking Road
rows.summary: Peking Road is a short street in Tsim Sha Tsui's commercial district linking Canton Road and Nathan Road, lined with shopping malls, hotels and restaurants. It was called Chater Road until 1909, when it was renamed to avoid confusion with another Chater Road on Hong Kong Island. Restaurants on the upper floors of some of the towers have views of Victoria Harbour.

rows.name: Po Lin Monastery
rows.summary: Po Lin Monastery, whose name means 'precious lotus', is a Buddhist monastery on the Ngong Ping plateau that monks established in 1906. Its main hall enshrines three large Buddha statues, and the Grand Hall of Ten Thousand Buddhas holds thousands of small gilded Buddha figures. A garden lies in the grounds, and the Wisdom Path, a walking trail of 38 wooden posts inscribed with the Heart Sutra, is about 0.5 km to the south-east.

rows.name: Prince's Terrace
rows.summary: Prince's Terrace is a quiet hillside lane in Central, running beside the Central–Mid-Levels Escalator among trees and a few cafés. At its end are granite steps, recognised as a Grade III historic site, that are the remains of Douglas Villas, a grand mansion from Hong Kong's early days of foreign trade. It suits a short, calm break from the busy streets below.

rows.name: Quarry Bay Market Footbridge
rows.summary: This white footbridge with rounded frames and red railings links Quarry Bay Market to the cooked food centre, and is an everyday passage for local residents. It stands among dense residential and commercial blocks on the east of Hong Kong Island, which makes it a good vantage point for photographs of the local cityscape. The area around it was used for fight scenes in the film Transformers: Age of Extinction (2014).

rows.name: Quarry Bay Park
rows.summary: Quarry Bay Park is a waterfront park between the Tai Koo Shing housing estate and Victoria Harbour, with sports grounds, a lookout tower with harbour views and a children's playground on an ocean theme. Phase One opened in 1994. Next door, the Fireboat Alexander Grantham Exhibition Gallery shows a fireboat that served from 1953 to 2002.

rows.name: Race Course Fire Memorial
rows.summary: Erected in 1922, this memorial remembers the more than 600 people of many nationalities who died in the fire at the Happy Valley racecourse on 26 February 1918. It rises in three terraces: two pavilions at the top, a central memorial arch below them and a pair of pagodas at the bottom, combining Western classical and traditional Chinese elements. It is the only memorial in Hong Kong dedicated to the victims of that fire.

rows.name: Residence of Ip Ting-sz, Lin Ma Hang
rows.summary: Built around 1908 and modelled on Sun Yat-sen's family home in Cuiheng village, Zhongshan, this two-storey grey-brick and timber house belonged to Ip Ting-sz (1879–1943), a tailor who set up a garment factory in Thailand and co-founded the Chinese Association there. The Antiquities and Monuments Office records that he was president of the Tong Meng Hui's Siam branch and gave funds to its revolutionary campaign, and that he returned to Lin Ma Hang in 1936. The house has a covered porch with a balcony, ceramic vase-shaped balusters and murals over the doors, mixing Chinese and Western features.

rows.name: Residence of Tang Pak Kau, Kam Tin
rows.summary: The house was probably built in the early twentieth century for Tang Pak Kau (1876–1950), a businessman and clan leader who helped develop education and medical services in Kam Tin, and who ran a private school for clan children inside it. It is a single-storey grey-brick building with a three-storey watchtower, blending Chinese and Western styles, and was declared a monument in 2024. It stands in Tsz Tong Tsuen, close to the walled village of Kat Hing Wai.

rows.name: Rock Carving at Big Wave Bay
rows.summary: This ancient rock carving on the rocky headland by Big Wave Bay shows geometric patterns with hints of animal and human figures. It was reported in 1970 and declared a monument in 1978. The Antiquities and Monuments Office suggests the carvings might have been meant to appease the sea and protect the seafarers who depended on it.

rows.name: Rock Carving at Lung Ha Wan
rows.summary: This rock carving is cut into a vertical, badly weathered boulder facing east, near Lung Ha Wan on the eastern side of the Clear Water Bay Peninsula. A group of hikers found it in 1978, and its geometric patterns include shapes that may resemble stylised animals or birds, although another school of thought holds that the marks are purely natural. It was declared a monument in 1983, which also leaves the way open for further study.

rows.name: Rock Carving at Shek Pik
rows.summary: The Rock Carving at Shek Pik shows geometric patterns of spiral squares and circles that closely resemble those on Bronze Age objects, and the Antiquities and Monuments Office dates it to about 3,000 years ago. Most of Hong Kong's ancient carvings overlook the sea, but this one stands about 300 m from the coast, where the sea inlet may once have reached. It lies near the Shek Pik Reservoir dam on south Lantau and was declared a monument in 1979.

rows.name: Rock Carving on Tung Lung Chau
rows.summary: This rock carving on the north-western side of Tung Lung Chau is the earliest rock carving recorded in its original place in Hong Kong, and at 1.8 by 2.4 metres the largest found in the territory. The 1819 gazetteer of Xin'an County already recorded the design as a dragon. It was declared a monument in 1979.

rows.name: Rock Carvings at Wong Chuk Hang
rows.summary: Three groups of spiral and meandering patterns, which look like stylised animal eyes, are carved into the rock beside a stream at Wong Chuk Hang. Unlike most rock carvings in Hong Kong, which are on the coast, these stand at least a kilometre from the sea, though they still overlook the water of the stream. They were declared monuments in 1984.

rows.name: Rock Carvings on Po Toi
rows.summary: These ancient rock carvings lie in the southern part of Po Toi, an island at Hong Kong's southern tip, and are estimated to be more than 3,000 years old. A rock fracture 70 cm wide divides them into two groups: lines resembling stylised fish and animals on the left, and interlocking spirals on the right. They were found in the 1960s and declared a monument in 1979.

rows.name: Rock Inscription at Joss House Bay
rows.summary: The inscription is cut into a rock at Joss House Bay, near the southern tip of the Clear Water Bay Peninsula, and is dated to 1274 in the Southern Song dynasty, which makes it the oldest dated inscription found in Hong Kong. It records a visit to the area by a salt administration officer and his friend, and gives the history of two temples, one on each side of the Fat Tong Mun channel. The stairs that lead down to the bay and its Tin Hau Temple pass the inscription.

rows.name: Russell Street
rows.summary: Russell Street is a busy shopping street in Causeway Bay, and its eastern section has been a pedestrian street since 2000. In the 1970s it was a neighbourhood of tenement buildings beside an open-air market and the Causeway Bay tram depot, and the depot site is now Times Square. Today it is lined with shops, cafés and street food, and it has been used as a film location.

rows.name: Salisbury Garden
rows.summary: Salisbury Garden is a public garden on the Tsim Sha Tsui waterfront between the Hong Kong Museum of Art and the Hong Kong Space Museum, with lawns, trees and contemporary art installations. Its Art Square opened in 2014, and the garden was renovated in 2017. It has open views across Victoria Harbour and sits close to the Star Ferry pier, the Cultural Centre and the Avenue of Stars.

rows.name: Sam Tung Uk Museum
rows.summary: Sam Tung Uk is a Hakka walled village built by the Chan clan in 1786 and restored in 1987 to open as a museum. Its symmetrical, chessboard-like layout has an entrance hall, a middle hall and the ancestral hall on the central axis, with dwellings enclosed by rows of houses on each side and at the back. The Hong Kong Intangible Cultural Heritage Centre is based here, with exhibitions on local festivals and traditional crafts.

rows.name: San Po Kong
rows.summary: San Po Kong is a largely industrial district in east Kowloon, south of Wong Tai Sin and north of the former Kai Tak Airport. Older factory buildings now stand alongside office towers, independent shops and long-established local eateries, and the Mikiki shopping mall opened in 2011 on the site of the old magistrates' courts. It is a place to wander through an everyday side of Hong Kong rather than to tick off a single sight.

rows.name: Sha Tin Marriage Registry
rows.summary: A government marriage registry on the ground floor of Sha Tin Town Hall, run by the Immigration Department, where couples give notice of marriage and marry by appointment. The Tourism Board lists it for its understated arched building and its setting beside Sha Tin Park and the Shing Mun River, a backdrop for strolls and couples' photographs. It also appears in the climax of the 2018 film Men on the Dragon.

rows.name: Sha Tin Racecourse
rows.summary: Opened in 1978, Sha Tin is the larger of Hong Kong's two racecourses, run by the Hong Kong Jockey Club, with a turf track and an all-weather dirt track watched from two grandstands. It hosts the Hong Kong International Races each December, and a tourist zone offers commentary for visitors from abroad. Racing takes place only on scheduled meeting days.

rows.name: Sheung Yiu Village
rows.summary: Sheung Yiu is a Hakka village built in the 19th century by the Wong clan, who came from Bao'an in Guangdong, on a raised platform inside Sai Kung Country Park. Its row of eight houses, drying terrace and watchtower over the entrance have been restored as the Sheung Yiu Folk Museum, furnished with farming tools and period furniture, and the village's lime kiln has also been restored for viewing. The village prospered by burning lime for mortar and fertiliser until modern bricks and cement undercut the trade.

rows.name: Signal Tower at Blackhead Point
rows.summary: The Signal Tower in Signal Hill Garden was built in 1907 by the Hong Kong Observatory to house a time-ball apparatus, whose copper ball was dropped at set times each day so that ships and the public could check the time. It is a red-brick building with carved granite details in a Classical Baroque design with Edwardian touches, and a storey was added in 1927 to make it easier to see from the harbour. The time-ball service ended in 1933, and the tower is now a landmark of the garden.

rows.name: Siu Sai Wan Promenade
rows.summary: Siu Sai Wan Promenade is a leafy waterfront park of 2.7 hectares on the eastern edge of Hong Kong Island, with a breezy promenade facing the South China Sea. It has a seven-a-side football pitch, outdoor fitness stations, a children's playground and a rest area. Small parks and rest spots such as the Leaping Dragon Pavilion lie close by along the Leaping Tiger Walk.

rows.name: St. John's Cathedral
rows.summary: Built in 1849, St John's Cathedral is the mother church of the Anglican Diocese of Hong Kong Island and the oldest surviving Western Christian church building in Hong Kong. It is a grey-brick and stone building in Gothic style, with a crenellated tower that recalls its role as a garrison church. An extension in 1873 gave it its cross shape.

rows.name: Stanley Main Street
rows.summary: Stanley Main Street runs along the waterfront in Stanley, a former fishing village on the south side of Hong Kong Island, and is also known as Bar Street. It has open-air cafés, pubs and restaurants serving Western and Asian food, with views over Stanley Bay. Stanley Market is around the corner, and the two are usually visited together.

rows.name: Stanley Market
rows.summary: Stanley Market is a street market of lanes and open-air stalls beside the Stanley waterfront, which grew out of the nearby village of Chek Chu. Stalls sell clothing, bags, toys, jewellery, souvenirs and Chinese arts and crafts, including personalised ink stamps and Chinese-style outfits. It is a traditional open-air market and a popular stop for souvenir shopping.

rows.name: Stone Circle at Fan Lau
rows.time_needed: Half a day, with the fort
rows.summary: The Stone Circle at Fan Lau is an oval setting of unhewn stones measuring 2.7 m by 1.7 m, laid out deliberately on the Fan Lau peninsula. The Antiquities and Monuments Office places it in the late Neolithic or early Bronze Age and says its purpose is unknown, possibly ritual. A signposted side path from the Fan Lau trail leads to it, close to Fan Lau Fort.

rows.name: Tai Fu Tai Mansion
rows.summary: Tai Fu Tai Mansion was built in 1865 as the home of Man Chung-luen of the Man clan of San Tin, who held the title of dafu, a senior official. It is a fine example of a scholar-gentry dwelling in southern China, a two-hall, three-bay house with side chambers, and the Antiquities and Monuments Office counts it among the most richly decorated historic buildings in Hong Kong. A full restoration was completed in 1988.

rows.name: Tai Kwun (Former Central Police Station Compound)
rows.summary: Tai Kwun is the everyday name for the former Central Police Station Compound on Hollywood Road, a group of historic buildings that also takes in the former Central Magistracy and Victoria Prison. Its dominant structures are the Barrack Block of 1864 and the Police Headquarters Block of 1919, and after restoration the compound opened to the public in 2018 as a centre for heritage and arts. Visitors can walk the courtyards, see the permanent heritage exhibitions in the former prison halls, join guided tours and visit the contemporary art galleries.

rows.name: Tai O Fishing Village
rows.summary: Tai O is a fishing village on the western side of Lantau Island, home to the Tanka boat people, where pang uk, houses on stilts, stand over the tidal creek and are linked by wooden bridges and boardwalks. Shops sell dried seafood and shrimp paste, and waterfront cafés and restaurants serve local snacks. A promenade walk of about 15 minutes along the shore passes the ferry pier, mangroves and Hung Shing Temple and ends at the old pier beside the former police station, now the Tai O Heritage Hotel.

rows.name: Tang Ancestral Hall, Ha Tsuen
rows.summary: Built in 1749–50 by the Tang clan of Ha Tsuen to honour their two founding ancestors, this is one of the few surviving local examples of a Qing vernacular hall with three halls and two courtyards. Honorary plaques in the middle hall record the clan's standing under the Qing. The compound also includes a guesthouse and Yau Kung School, and the hall is still used for the clan's religious and ceremonial events; it was fully restored in 2011.

rows.name: Tang Ancestral Hall, Ping Shan
rows.summary: The main ancestral hall of the Tang clan of Ping Shan, built by Tang Fung-shun in the Yuan dynasty, is among the finest three-hall, two-courtyard buildings in Hong Kong. Two drum platforms with granite and red sandstone columns front the hall, and a raised red sandstone path joins the first two halls. It is still used for ancestral worship and festivals, and stands on the Ping Shan Heritage Trail, which opened in 1993 as the first of its kind in Hong Kong.

rows.name: Tang Chi Ngong Building, University of Hong Kong
rows.summary: Built in 1929 with a donation from Tang Chi-ngong and opened in 1931, this building was designed to house the University of Hong Kong's School of Chinese. It is a symmetrical, three-storey Neo-classical block, with grooved plaster surfaces made to look like stone blocks and a band of Greek key fretwork between the ground and first floors. It now houses the Jao Tsung-I Petite Ecole, which displays the art and artefacts of the scholar and artist Jao Tsung-I.

rows.name: Tang Chung Ling Ancestral Hall
rows.summary: Tang Chung Ling Ancestral Hall is one of the largest ancestral halls in Hong Kong and the main hall of the Tang clan of Lung Yeuk Tau, dedicated to the founding ancestor Tang Chung-ling (1302–1387) and dating from around 1525. It has three halls and two spacious courtyards, decorated throughout with wood carvings, plaster mouldings, ceramic sculptures and murals, and the clan still uses it for festivals and meetings. It is one of the stops on the 2.6 km Lung Yeuk Tau Heritage Trail.

rows.name: Tang Kwong U Ancestral Hall
rows.summary: Tang Kwong U Ancestral Hall, also known as Loi Shing Tong, was built in 1701 in Shui Tau, Kam Tin, by Tang Tseung Luk to commemorate Tang Kwong-u, the 17th-generation ancestor of the Tang clan, and it was renovated in 1782. It is a Qing vernacular building of two halls and one courtyard, with plaster mouldings on the facade and carved woodwork inside. At one time it was converted into a shop and then a factory, before a full restoration in 1996.

rows.name: Tank Lane
rows.summary: Tank Lane in Sheung Wan takes its name from a drinking-water reservoir built for early residents, which was taken apart and made into a public lane once piped water arrived. Murals by a number of artists now cover its walls, and tall trees with intertwined roots grow from cracks in the old stone walls. The stairs on the lane appear in the film Rouge (1988).

rows.name: Tat Tak Communal Hall
rows.summary: Tat Tak Communal Hall, completed in 1857, is the only purpose-built communal hall left in Hong Kong, built as the assembly and worship place of a joint village alliance and as the management office of Ping Shan Market. It was started by Tang Fan-yau, a member of the local gentry, and side halls were added in 1866; the building is plain and functional, of grey brick on a granite base. According to the Antiquities and Monuments Office, it was probably one of the meeting places where the armed resistance to the British takeover of the New Territories in 1899 was organised.

rows.name: Temple Street Night Market
rows.summary: Temple Street Night Market is a street market in Jordan and Yau Ma Tei that fills with stalls in the evening. It sells clothing, bags, accessories, souvenirs and second-hand goods, and its open-air dai pai dong stalls serve local dishes such as claypot rice, fish balls and siu mai. Fortune tellers work along the street, and the Temple Street archway and the Tin Hau Temple at Yau Ma Tei are close by.

rows.name: The Bethanie
rows.summary: The Bethanie is a Neo-Gothic building completed in 1875 by the Paris Foreign Missions Society as a sanatorium where sick missionaries could recover before returning to their work in East Asia. It has a chapel, a sanatorium block and a service wing, with arched verandahs on all sides. Restored in 2006, it is now a campus of the Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts and includes the Bethanie Museum.

rows.name: The Cenotaph
rows.summary: Unveiled in 1923, the Cenotaph is the earliest memorial formally built in Hong Kong to the dead of the First World War, and an almost exact replica of the one on Whitehall in London. The years of the Second World War were added to its inscription later, and eight Chinese characters carved in the 1980s extend the dedication to all who died in the wars, especially in the defence of Hong Kong. Commemorative events are held here every year.

rows.name: The Center
rows.summary: The Center is a 346-metre steel-and-glass office tower at 99 Queen's Road Central, completed in 1998. By day its facade shows a pattern of triangular facets, and at night it is lit with rainbow-coloured neon lights. Companies and financial institutions occupy the building.

rows.name: The Helena May (Main Building)
rows.summary: Built in 1916 for an institute founded by Lady May, wife of the then Governor, to house single working women passing through Hong Kong, this Edwardian Classical Revival building has a U-shaped plan and three tiers of open verandahs on its Garden Road front. A segmental pediment decorated with floral motifs rises above the entrance porch, supported by columns with tasselled capitals. It still serves as a guesthouse and members' club for women.

rows.name: The Henderson
rows.summary: The Henderson is a 190-metre, 36-storey office tower in Central designed by Zaha Hadid Architects, with curved, flowing lines inspired by the bauhinia, Hong Kong's official flower. A three-metre Jeff Koons sculpture, Balloon Swan (Red), is the centrepiece of its interior. The footbridge outside Cheung Kong Park is a good place to photograph its curved outline against the traffic.

rows.name: The Mills
rows.summary: The Mills is the former Nan Fung Textiles cotton-spinning complex in Tsuen Wan, where operations ceased in 2008, and it reopened in 2018 as a mix of arts, shops and start-up space. Its CHAT (Centre for Heritage, Arts and Textile) holds exhibitions and programmes on the textile industry, and the Shopfloor has independent and artisanal shops. The conservation project received a 2019 UNESCO Asia-Pacific Award for New Design in Heritage Contexts.

rows.name: The Pavilion, Discovery Bay
rows.summary: The Pavilion, also called the White Chapel, is a 16 m tall glass building shaped like a triangular prism on the waterfront at Discovery Bay, within the Auberge Discovery Bay Hong Kong hotel. It is a popular wedding venue, and the Hong Kong Tourism Board names its triangular front door as the best spot to photograph the building's geometric form, with green hills and the sea behind.

rows.name: Tin Hau Temple, Causeway Bay
rows.summary: Tin Hau Temple was built by the Tai clan, who according to legend found a red stone shaped like an incense burner on the shore here and built a shrine for it that grew into the temple. The main hall has altars to Tin Hau, the goddess of the sea, to Judge Bao and to the God of Wealth, and the roof ridges are decorated with dragons and Shiwan ceramic figurines of scenes from Chinese opera. Among the Qing-dynasty relics inside is a bell cast in 1747.

rows.name: Tin Hau Temple, Joss House Bay
rows.summary: Known as Tai Miu, the 'great temple', this is one of the oldest and largest Tin Hau temples in Hong Kong, on the northern shore of Joss House Bay. Five buildings stand in a row, with a two-hall main building flanked by two side halls on each side, and rock inscriptions behind it link the temple to the Southern Song dynasty. Thousands of worshippers come on Tin Hau's birthday, on the 23rd day of the third lunar month, and it is one of the few Tin Hau temples still standing close to the sea.

rows.name: Tin Hau Temple, Lung Yeuk Tau
rows.summary: The main temple of Lung Yeuk Tau, a two-hall, three-bay building with a central courtyard and a facade of plaster mouldings and murals, standing between Tang Chung Ling Ancestral Hall and Lo Wai. Its oldest relics are two bells cast in 1695 and 1700 as offerings from the Tang clan, kept in the east chamber of the rear hall. It is a stop on the Lung Yeuk Tau Heritage Trail, a 2.6 km route through the area's walled villages and halls.

rows.name: Tin Hau Temple, Yau Ma Tei
rows.summary: The Tin Hau Temple compound in Yau Ma Tei was set up by the local boat people and land dwellers and is the largest surviving Tin Hau temple compound in Kowloon. The temple moved to its present site in 1876 and was completed in 1878, and four adjoining buildings were added between 1894 and 1920, as the compound served the community for arbitration and study as well as worship. It is a two-hall, three-bay building in Qing vernacular style around an open courtyard, with Shiwan ceramic figurines on the ridge of the entrance hall.

rows.name: Tong Lau Experience Room
rows.summary: The Tong Lau Experience Room is an exhibition on the first floor of 88 Staunton Street, a Grade II tenement building from 1951 that belongs to Central's 30 Houses community. Everyday items donated by former residents and an audio guide recreate daily life in the 1950s and 1960s. The hand-carved terrazzo and Shanghai plaster sign of the Po Pan Teahouse, which was on the ground floor in the 1970s, was uncovered during restoration.

rows.name: Tsing Fung Street
rows.summary: Tsing Fung Street in Tin Hau is a street of small restaurants, cafes, dessert shops and bars beneath a local footbridge. Korean barbecue, Japanese izakayas, cha chaan tengs and Sichuanese restaurants stand side by side, and the street turns from relaxed daytime cafes to busy restaurants and bars at night. The chase scene in the film Divergence (2005) was shot on the Tsing Fung Street Flyover.

rows.name: Tsing Ma Bridge
rows.summary: Tsing Ma Bridge is a suspension bridge linking Tsing Yi and Ma Wan on the road and rail route to Lantau and the airport. It is 2,160 metres long with a main span of 1,377 metres, and was once the world's longest suspension bridge to carry both road and rail traffic. Visitors heading to Lantau and the airport are likely to cross it by road or rail; to see it from outside, the Hong Kong Tourism Board suggests the Hilltop Lookout in Ma Wan Park.

rows.name: Tsing Yi Promenade
rows.summary: A 1.6 km waterfront walkway on the north-east coast of Tsing Yi, facing across Rambler Channel to Kwai Chung. To the south there are views of the Tsing Ma Bridge, the container port and the western end of Hong Kong Island. It is pleasant at sunrise and sunset, with locals jogging, cycling, practising tai chi and fishing along the shore.

rows.name: Tsui Sing Lau Pagoda
rows.summary: Tsui Sing Lau, the Pagoda of Gathering Stars, is the only ancient pagoda still standing in Hong Kong, built by the Tang clan of Ping Shan around the Hongwu reign (1368–1398), according to the clan's genealogy. The hexagonal grey-brick tower has three storeys and is about 13 metres high, although the Tangs say it once had seven storeys and lost the upper four, probably in typhoons. A statue of Fui Shing, the deity of success in examinations, stands on the upper floor.

rows.name: Tung Chung Battery
rows.summary: Tung Chung Battery is a small coastal battery on a hill slope in Tung Chung, recorded as built in 1817 to guard Tung Chung Bay from pirates. Only an L-shaped wall with a corner platform, probably a gun emplacement, survives; it was found under undergrowth in 1980 and has been partly restored. It is a quick stop that pairs with Tung Chung Fort, about 1 km to the south.

rows.name: Tung Chung Fort
rows.summary: Tung Chung Fort, called the Tung Chung Battalion City in the Qing dynasty, was the naval headquarters of the Right Battalion of Dapeng, and a carved granite slab above its entrance is dated 1832. Six old muzzle-loading cannons stand along the walls. After the Qing authorities left in 1898 the compound served as a police station and a school, and it now houses a Rural Committee office and an information centre.

rows.name: Tung Lin Kok Yuen
rows.summary: Tung Lin Kok Yuen is a Buddhist monastery in Happy Valley, founded in 1935 by Lady Clara Ho Tung and her husband Sir Robert Ho Tung. Its arrowhead-shaped plan was meant to suggest a ship carrying all beings to the other shore, and its Western structural frame is finished with Chinese flying eaves, brackets and glazed-tile roofs. It remains a working monastery that runs Buddhist courses and talks.

rows.name: Tung Lung Fort
rows.summary: Tung Lung Fort sits on the north-eastern tip of Tung Lung Chau, a small island off the southern end of the Clear Water Bay Peninsula, looking over the Fat Tong Mun channel. It was built during the Kangxi reign (1662–1722) to guard against pirates and is a walled rectangle of about 33.5 by 22.5 metres, with fifteen guardhouses and eight cannons in its day. The garrison was moved to Kowloon Fort in 1810, and the ruins were partly restored in 1979–82, when excavations inside recovered a large quantity of artefacts.

rows.name: Tung Wah Museum
rows.summary: Tung Wah Museum occupies the former main hall of Kwong Wah Hospital, which opened in 1911 as the first hospital in Kowloon and the New Territories. The hall was the only part kept when the hospital was rebuilt in 1958, and it was converted into a museum in 1970 to display relics and archives of the Tung Wah Group of Hospitals. The building mixes Chinese features, such as carved timber eaves and green glazed roof tiles, with Western bull's-eye and arched windows.

rows.name: Two International Finance Centre
rows.summary: Completed in 2003, Two International Finance Centre is the tallest building on Hong Kong Island and the second tallest in the city, rising from the harbour front in Central above Hong Kong MTR station and linked to the ifc mall, One ifc and a Four Seasons hotel. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority Information Centre on its 55th floor, with an exhibition area and a library, is open to visitors. The tower has appeared in films including Lara Croft: Tomb Raider – The Cradle of Life and The Dark Knight.

rows.name: T·PARK
rows.summary: T·PARK is a sludge treatment plant run by the Environmental Protection Department, where incineration cuts the volume of sewage sludge by 90 per cent and the recovered heat and power run the site. Visitors can take a guided tour, see the exhibition hall and the viewing windows onto the plant, and walk the 9,800 square metres of landscaped grounds, which include a water-bird sanctuary on Deep Bay. Three spa pools with sea views are heated by energy recovered from the incinerators.

rows.name: University Hall, University of Hong Kong
rows.summary: A castle-like building on a hill in Pok Fu Lam, built around 1861 by the Scottish businessman Douglas Lapraik as 'Douglas Castle' and later owned by the Paris Foreign Missions Society as 'Nazareth'. It blends Tudor, Gothic and Renaissance Revival styles, with colonnaded verandahs, Tudor arches, embattled parapets and corner towers. The University of Hong Kong bought it in 1954, and it has been a men's hall of residence since 1956.

rows.name: Urban Council Centenary Garden
rows.name_zh: 市政局百周年纪念花园
rows.summary: The Urban Council Centenary Garden is a small public park in Tsim Sha Tsui East, opened in 1983 to mark a hundred years of the Urban Council. It has a large circular fountain, walkways and shaded benches, and six Greek Revival granite columns saved from the former Kowloon railway station stand at the end of a second fountain. A waterfront promenade leads from the garden towards the Avenue of Stars.

rows.name: Victoria Park
rows.summary: Victoria Park opened in 1957 on reclaimed land where the Causeway Bay Typhoon Shelter once stood, and covers more than 190,000 square metres. It has a large central lawn, tennis courts, football pitches, a jogging path, a swimming pool and playgrounds, with a statue of Queen Victoria at the main entrance. Locals come for tai chi at sunrise, and the park hosts the Hong Kong Flower Show, Lunar New Year flower markets and Mid-Autumn Festival lantern displays.

rows.name: Wai Yip Pedestrian Bridge
rows.summary: The Wai Yip Pedestrian Bridge spans Kwun Tong Road beside Wai Yip Street in Kwun Tong. Its smooth, rounded shape recalls a train carriage, and its facade is white, blue and pink. It is best known as a romantic meeting place in the Hong Kong film Love in a Puff (2010).

rows.name: Wan Chai Ferry Pier
rows.summary: A harbourfront pier beside the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre, rebuilt in 2014, with a public observation deck looking across both sides of Victoria Harbour. Ferry services from Wan Chai have run since 1949, and the facade of the current pier carries a stone-wall tree pattern as a nod to local heritage. Star Ferry boats from here cross to Tsim Sha Tsui, and the deck is a place for harbour views and skyline photographs.

rows.name: Wan Chai Market
rows.summary: Wan Chai Market is the cluster of open-air stalls and shops around Tai Yuen Street, Cross Street and Wan Chai Road, selling fresh produce, seafood, meat, clothing and household goods. It gives a close look at everyday shopping in Hong Kong and has been used as a film location. It suits visitors who like to browse local markets.

rows.name: Water World, Ocean Park Hong Kong
rows.summary: Water World is a water park run by Ocean Park Hong Kong on the hillside at Tai Shue Wan, opened in September 2021 and separate from the main park. It is organised into five themed zones with indoor and outdoor slides, a river ride, a surf zone and a splash area for young children. It is built to operate in all weathers throughout the year and suits families and thrill-seekers.

rows.name: Wellington Street
rows.summary: Wellington Street runs through Central between Queen's Road Central and Wyndham Street, lined with a mix of old and new buildings, restaurants, bars and small shops. From the 1950s to the 1980s it was the centre of Hong Kong's movable-type printing trade, with more than 150 print shops, the last of which closed in 2019. Number 120, the former Wing Woo Grocery, is a pre-war tenement building preserved as a heritage site.

rows.name: West Kowloon Cultural District
rows.summary: The West Kowloon Cultural District is a large arts quarter on the Kowloon waterfront, planned by Foster and Partners and managed by the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority. Its venues include the M+ museum, the Hong Kong Palace Museum, the Xiqu Centre for Chinese opera and the Freespace performance venue. Open lawns, the Art Park and the waterfront promenade give views of the harbour skyline.

rows.name: West Kowloon Waterfront Promenade
rows.summary: The West Kowloon Waterfront Promenade runs along Victoria Harbour beside the West Kowloon Cultural District, with open lawns, landscaped gardens, small pavilions and cycle paths. It looks across the harbour to the Hong Kong Island skyline, with M+ and the Hong Kong Palace Museum behind it. It is also known for its sunset views.

rows.name: Western Market
rows.summary: Western Market is the surviving North Block of the old Western Market, built in 1906 in the Edwardian style, with white-banded 'bandaged' brickwork on its four corner towers. It is the oldest surviving market building in Hong Kong. Converted in 1991 into a centre of traditional trades, arts and crafts, it later became a neighbourhood shopping complex.

rows.name: Wong Tai Sin Temple
rows.summary: Wong Tai Sin Temple is a Taoist temple dedicated to Wong Tai Sin, a folk deity many worshippers ask for blessings and guidance, with shrines that also reflect Buddhist and Confucian traditions. Its buildings and courtyards follow the five elements of Chinese geomancy, with a Bronze Pavilion for metal, a Scripture Hall for wood, a fountain for water, the Yue Heung Pavilion for fire and an earth wall, and stalls in the grounds interpret kau cim fortune sticks. It is busiest around Lunar New Year, when worshippers queue overnight on New Year's Eve.

rows.name: Xiqu Centre
rows.summary: The Xiqu Centre in the West Kowloon Cultural District is a performance venue for Chinese opera (xiqu), especially Cantonese opera, and opened in January 2019. Its building is designed to evoke a glowing lantern behind a beaded curtain, and it has a Grand Theatre of more than 1,000 seats and a 200-seat Tea House Theatre. Guided tours in English, Cantonese or Mandarin cover the history of the building and the art form.

rows.name: Yan Tun Kong Study Hall
rows.summary: Yan Tun Kong Study Hall, also called Yin Yik Tong, is the most important building of the Tang clan in Hang Tau Tsuen, Ping Shan, which villagers say was built to commemorate three of their ancestors and which prepared young clansmen for the imperial civil service examinations. A plaque suggests it was renovated in 1870, and Tang descendants still gather here to worship their ancestors at the spring and autumn equinoxes. It keeps a finely carved ancestral altar and plaster mouldings on the roof ridges and facade, and is a stop on the Ping Shan Heritage Trail.

rows.name: Yau Ma Tei Market
rows.summary: Yau Ma Tei Market was built in 1957 and was once Kowloon's largest post-war market, a three-storey building with pink exterior walls. Outside, stalls with green tin roofs line Reclamation Street, selling fresh produce, pastries, flowers, dried goods and sundries. It is an everyday neighbourhood market rather than a single sight, and it has been used as a film location.

rows.name: Yee Wo Street Circular Footbridge
rows.summary: Built in the 1960s, this circular footbridge in Causeway Bay spans the junction of Yee Wo Street with Sugar Street and Pennington Street. It is about 300 metres around, one of the few circular bridges in Hong Kong, and links the surrounding buildings and shopping areas. From the curved walkway you look down on passing trams and across billboards and high-rise blocks, and the bridge has appeared in films and television dramas.

rows.name: Yeung Hau Temple, Ha Tsuen
rows.summary: A two-hall temple in Tung Tau Tsuen, probably built before 1811 by the Tang clan of the three Tung Tau villages in memory of Marquis Yang Liangjie, who gave his life protecting the last Southern Song emperors and is worshipped here as Yeung Hau. The front hall has red sandstone drum platforms and stone columns, and the whole building is decorated with woodcarvings and murals. An annex honours Wang Lairen, the Qing governor of Guangdong who petitioned for the end of the Evacuation Edict.

rows.name: Yeung Hau Temple, Tai O
rows.summary: Yeung Hau Temple in Tai O was probably built in 1699 or earlier, a date taken from an iron bell cast that year for the deity Hau Wong. Fishing families, fish merchants and Qing coastal soldiers patronised it, and it is closely tied to the Tai O Dragon Boat Water Parade, a festival on China's national intangible cultural heritage list since 2011. The grey-brick and granite temple has two halls with a covered courtyard between them, and Shiwan ceramic figurines decorate the roof ridge of the entrance hall.

rows.name: Yi Tai Study Hall
rows.summary: Yi Tai Study Hall in Shui Tau Village, Kam Tin, was built in the Daoguang reign (1821–1850) by 16 local scholar-gentry to house statues of Man Cheong, god of literature, and Kwan Tai, god of martial arts, which had been worshipped in a nearby pagoda. It became an important academy and later a primary school, which closed after the Second World War. The grey-brick and rammed-earth building has its main entrance on the side between the two halls, probably for feng shui reasons, and a forecourt paved with white stones.

rows.name: Yu Kiu Ancestral Hall
rows.summary: Yu Kiu Ancestral Hall was built between 1500 and 1520, in the Ming dynasty, by two brothers of the Tang clan, and it stands beside the Tang Ancestral Hall in Ping Shan. It has three halls and two internal courtyards, with the ancestral altar in the rear hall and a red sandstone door frame at the main entrance. From 1931 to 1961 it also housed Tat Tak Public School, and the latest major restoration was completed in 1995.

rows.name: Yuk Hui Temple (Pak Tai Temple), Wan Chai
rows.summary: Built by local residents of Wan Chai and completed in 1863, this temple is dedicated to Pak Tai, a deity associated with the stars of the north and the sea. The main building is a two-hall, three-bay Qing-style structure with an incense pavilion in the centre, which holds a Ming dynasty bronze statue of Pak Tai dated to 1603. Shiwan ceramic scenes from Chinese folk stories decorate the ridge and gable walls of the entrance hall.

rows.name: A-Ma Cultural Village
rows.summary: A temple complex on the Coloane hillside (Aldeia Cultural de A-Ma) that celebrates the legend of A-Ma, goddess of seafarers. It has a pavilion-style front gate, a carved marble altar, Tin Hau Palace, a dressing hall and bell and drum towers. A park lies beside it, and a hiking trail leads up to the statue of A-Ma on the hilltop.

rows.name: A-Ma Temple
rows.summary: A temple complex on the western slope of Barra Hill (Templo de A-Má), dedicated to A-Ma, goddess of seafarers, whose shrine here is older than the city of Macau. Its pavilions went up at different times: a gate pavilion, a memorial arch, the Prayer Hall of 1605, the Hall of Benevolence, which may date from about 1488, the Hall of Guanyin and a Buddhist pavilion. Rocks along the path uphill are engraved with poems about Macau's history and culture.

rows.name: Archaeological Pit Display Area, Rua de D. Belchior Carneiro
rows.summary: A display area at the northern foot of Mount Hill marking a circular shaft about 9.9 metres deep, cut into the bedrock on the east side of the former St Paul's College. Excavated in 2010–2012, it yielded pottery, porcelain and building materials of the late Ming and early Qing periods, including Kraak export porcelain made at kilns in Jingdezhen. Since protection works in 2025 the pit itself is covered over with soil and sand under a thin concrete layer.

rows.name: Arts Park
rows.summary: A landscaped strip of garden along Avenida da Amizade, opened in 1999 and running between Ho Yin Garden and Carlos d'Assumpção Park on the NAPE reclamation. It has flower beds, fountains and statuary. Roads now cut across the park after its rebuilding in 2006–07, so it works best as a short stop on the walk between the old town and the Cultural Centre.

rows.name: Banco Nacional Ultramarino Building
rows.summary: The Macau headquarters of Banco Nacional Ultramarino on Avenida de Almeida Ribeiro, first built in 1926 in a southern European style. When it was converted into a modern high-rise in 1997, the original façade and colonnades were kept. It is a good example of façade preservation in Macau.

rows.name: Barra Hill
rows.summary: The second-highest hill in Macau at 73.2 metres, covered in greenery at the south-western tip of the peninsula (Colina da Barra). It connects to Penha Hill to the east, with Praia Grande Lake to the south and the Inner Harbour to the west. The old São Tiago da Barra fortress, now a hotel, sits on its southern slope among other large buildings.

rows.name: Barra Square
rows.summary: The paved square (Largo do Pagode da Barra) in front of A-Ma Temple, facing the Inner Harbour. Its front section is laid in Portuguese mosaic pavement in ochre and charcoal, set in a wavy pattern that echoes the flow of the water nearby. The square is part of the Historic Centre of Macau.

rows.name: Blue House (Casa Azul), Estrada do Cemitério
rows.summary: A former one-storey private mansion built between 1941 and 1952 and enlarged in 1965 and 1985, whose outer walls were painted bright blue at the end of the 1980s. The building has a typical Portuguese look and has kept most of its original layout. Its blue walls have made it a visual landmark of the district.

rows.name: Border Gate (Portas do Cerco)
rows.summary: The Border Gate is a triumphal-arch portico built in 1870–71 at the northern end of the Macau Peninsula, at the site where the Chinese authorities had put up a gate house in 1574. Inscriptions on the arch record events in the site's history. The arch stands in Border Gate Square, which has fountains and planting and blue-tiled side walls carrying a poem by the Portuguese poet Camões.

rows.name: Bronze Statue of Xian Xinghai
rows.summary: A bronze statue of the composer Xian Xinghai, who was born in Macau, at the junction of Avenida Xian Xing Hai and Rua de Berlim in the Nam Van area. The tourism office describes him as a herald of modern Chinese music, and the Yellow River Cantata is one of his best-known works.

rows.name: Building at No. 1, Cathedral Square
rows.summary: The headquarters and offices of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Macau, beside the Cathedral on Largo da Sé. A plain façade is divided into five equal bays by twin pilasters, with Tuscan pilasters on the lower level and fluted Doric-style pilasters above. The walls have been repainted and the interior completely altered, but the façade keeps its original look.

rows.name: Building at No. 2, Company of Jesus Square
rows.name_zh: 耶稣会纪念广场2号房屋
rows.pinyin: Yēsūhuì Jìniàn Guǎngchǎng Èr Hào Fángwū
rows.summary: A neoclassical house of the second half of the 19th century (Casa no Largo da Companhia de Jesus, n.º 2), classified as a building of architectural interest. It faces the square below the Ruins of St Paul's, and academic research cited by the Cultural Affairs Bureau places it on the original site of the library of St Paul's College.

rows.name: Building at No. 2, Estrada Nova
rows.name_zh: 加思栏后新马路2号房屋
rows.pinyin: Jiāsīlán Hòu Xīn Mǎlù Èr Hào Fángwū
rows.summary: Known as the small green house for the colour of its outer wall, this building was designed in 1919 by the Portuguese architect Carlos Rebelo de Andrade as quarters for staff of the São Francisco Barracks. It is a good example of the Casa Portuguesa style, with two connected houses, a symmetrical façade on a coarse granite base with a front porch, and a double-tiled hip roof with ornaments resembling Chinese eaves at the ends of the ridge. It stands beside St Francis Fort and Barracks.

rows.name: Building at No. 30, Estrada da Vitória
rows.summary: A two-storey mansion set on a garden platform held up by a large stone wall, planned in 1924 and completed around 1930. Its style combines eclectic architecture with elements of Art Nouveau and the Portuguese House movement. It is now home to the Good Shepherd Sisters and, with the early 20th-century villas around it, keeps the character of Estrada da Vitória on the western slope of Guia Hill.

rows.name: Building at No. 55, Calçada da Vitória
rows.summary: A two-storey villa completed in about 1926–1928 as the Macau home of the overseas Chinese businessman Hee Cheong, founder of the President Hotel, later Hotel Central. It has a curved Baroque pediment bearing the year 1926, arcades on two sides and a polygonal turret, with Western ironwork and Chinese carved-wood details. It later passed through several owners to the Diocese of Macau.

rows.name: Building at No. 6, Avenida da República
rows.summary: This small house of the early 20th century blends styles: glazed ceramic tiles under the eaves, common in traditional Portuguese architecture, with classical columns and fan-shaped windows. The large arched window facing the avenue is divided vertically into three parts. The house has a sloping roof, a simply decorated entrance and pink walls with white lines.

rows.name: Building at No. 6, Calçada do Gaio
rows.summary: A three-storey villa completed in 1930 on the slope of Guia Hill, the only surviving villa of the first half of the 20th century on Calçada do Gaio. Its eclectic façade has Arabian-style decoration, with horseshoe arches above the balconies, slender pillars and tile and brick patterns. It is used as the headquarters of the Institute of European Studies of Macau.

rows.name: Building at No. 679, Avenida da Praia Grande
rows.summary: A three-storey house of the early 20th century that mixes Chinese and Western styles and is typical of the homes of wealthy Chinese merchants of its time. The Cultural Affairs Bureau records it as belonging to descendants of the Macau merchant Kou Ho Neng. It stands on Avenida da Praia Grande.

rows.name: Building at Nos. 14 and 16, Avenida de Horta e Costa
rows.name_zh: 高士德大马路14号、16号大楼
rows.summary: A two-storey eclectic building of 1930 with a ground-floor veranda on square pillars and an upper balcony on round columns with capitals. The balcony projects at the centre of the façade, and the railings and garden walls carry geometric decoration. It is used by the Macau Conservatory.

rows.name: Building at Nos. 24A–28A, Rua de Pedro Nolasco da Silva
rows.summary: A house built in 1925 that shows Macau's neoclassical style with some eclectic elements. It is classified as a building of architectural interest. It stands on Rua de Pedro Nolasco da Silva, east of the Cathedral.

rows.name: Buildings at Nos. 89–95G, Avenida do Conselheiro Ferreira de Almeida
rows.summary: A row of early 20th-century neoclassical houses and schools in the Tap Seac district, built on land drained from swamp in the late 19th century. Most are no longer homes: the Macau Central Library and the Archives of Macau, both in styles favoured by wealthy Macau families, stand in the row, together with Tap Seac Gallery, the House of Macau Literature and the Jao Tsung-I Academy. The buildings have been restored several times.

rows.name: CTT Staff Houses, Avenida do Coronel Mesquita
rows.name_zh: 美副将大马路28–30、34–36号及俾利喇街151–157号
rows.pinyin: Měifùjiàng Dàmǎlù 28–30, 34–36 Hào Jí Bǐlìlā Jiē 151–157 Hào
rows.summary: Four residential blocks of 1953–54 built by the post office (CTT) for senior staff at the corner of Avenida do Coronel Mesquita and Rua de Francisco Xavier Pereira, in the "Suave Portuguese" style of the period, with an arcaded ground-floor veranda, a porch veranda upstairs and a semicircular living room. Each block held two homes, eight in all. They belong to a group of public-servant housing along Avenida do Coronel Mesquita in Mong-Há.

rows.name: Calçada do Quartel, Taipa Village
rows.summary: A short sloping lane in Taipa Village lined with brightly painted buildings and covered in graffiti murals. It also holds small cafés, snack bars and cultural and creative shops, and is a popular spot for photographs.

rows.name: Camões Square
rows.summary: A small square at the northern edge of the old city, beside Luís de Camões Garden, Casa Garden and the Old Protestant Cemetery. Its Portuguese name, Praça de Luís de Camões, honours the poet, while the Chinese name means pigeon-nest square, after the white pigeons kept by a Portuguese merchant who lived nearby. It is a place where residents gather to relax, and one of the squares of the Historic Centre of Macau.

rows.name: Camões Square and the Old Streets, Taipa Village
rows.summary: A small square (Largo Camões) and three streets in the old village of Taipa, Rua dos Mercadores, Rua dos Negociantes and Rua do Meio, classified together as an ensemble. The area consists of the Pak Tai Temple, which stands on the square, and traditional buildings of the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

rows.name: Carmo Fair (Former Taipa Municipal Market)
rows.summary: The former Taipa municipal market (Antigo Mercado Municipal da Taipa), first built in 1879 and rebuilt in 1886, which fell out of use in the 1970s and was turned into a public square in the 2000s. A hip-roofed pavilion stands at its centre between arcades; the columns follow a Doric order, the roof is covered in Chinese tiles from Guangdong, and the wooden roof trusses are in a western style. A flea market is held in the square on Sundays.

rows.name: Carmo Square and Avenida da Praia, Taipa
rows.summary: The square in front of Our Lady of Carmel Church (Largo do Carmo) and the street below it, Avenida da Praia, where five 1921 Portuguese-style houses now form the Taipa Houses–Museum. The church, the houses and the buildings around them are in a southern European style, and the area is popular for sightseeing and wedding photographs.

rows.name: Casa Garden
rows.summary: A mansion of 1770 whose first known owner was a wealthy Portuguese merchant, later rented to the British East India Company, whose senior staff lived here. It now houses the Macau branch of the Orient Foundation, with a garden beside Camões Square (Praça de Luís de Camões). In the 1960s it served as a museum devoted to the Portuguese poet Luís de Camões.

rows.name: Cathedral Square
rows.summary: A small square (Largo da Sé) in front of Macau Cathedral, paved in black and white stone laid in religious patterns. Local people use it as a quiet place to sit, and it has a serene, religious atmosphere. It is one of the squares of the Historic Centre of Macau.

rows.name: Chapel of Our Lady of Penha
rows.summary: A neoclassical chapel with a steeple on top of Penha Hill (Colina da Penha), first founded in 1622 by the crew and passengers of a ship that had narrowly escaped capture by the Dutch. It was rebuilt in 1935 together with the neighbouring Bishop's Residence, which gave the 62.7-metre hill its other name, Bishop's Hill. Sailors once came here to pray before dangerous voyages, and the hill looks out over Praia Grande Bay.

rows.name: Chapel of St. Francis Xavier, Coloane
rows.summary: A small chapel of 1928 (Igreja de São Francisco Xavier) on Largo Eduardo Marques, with a cream-coloured façade, oval windows and a bell tower. It was rebuilt on the site of a nursery run by the Canossian Sisters in memory of the missionary St Francis Xavier, and for many years held a relic of the saint together with relics of Japanese and Vietnamese martyrs; his statue is still inside. In the fountain on the square in front stands a monument to a local victory over pirates in 1910.

rows.name: Chio Family Mansion
rows.summary: The Chio Family Mansion on Travessa da Porta was the home of a prominent family from Mong-Há village, who traced their descent to the Song imperial house. Its main building, put up by 1875 in the Lingnan style around three halls and two corridors, was later extended with four corner houses. It is the only surviving residence of the family in Macau.

rows.name: Cinematheque Passion
rows.summary: A small public cinema in a three-storey building on Travessa da Paixão, beside the Ruins of St Paul's, set up by the Cultural Affairs Bureau. The ground-floor screening room shows art-house and independent films, including themed seasons and films on their first release in Macau, and a reference room upstairs keeps Macau film materials, periodicals and books.

rows.name: Coloane Height Park and Statue of A-Ma
rows.name_zh: 路环山顶公园和妈祖像
rows.pinyin: Lùhuán Shāndǐng Gōngyuán Hé Māzǔ Xiàng
rows.summary: A hilltop park on Coloane Peak, about 170 metres high, reached by Estrada do Alto de Coloane, with a picnic area and the statue of A-Ma at the summit. The statue is 19.99 metres tall, a height that refers to the year 1999, and can be seen far out at sea. On the way up are an arboretum of more than 100 local and exotic tree species and the main access to the Coloane Trail.

rows.name: Coloane Hills and Country Walks
rows.summary: The hills of Coloane above 80 metres, classified as a site by the Cultural Affairs Bureau, which describes eight country walks with views over Coloane and the mouth of the Pearl River. Around 2,000 kinds of shrubs and plants grow along the paths. Coloane Peak, about 170 metres high, has a park and a statue of A-Ma.

rows.name: Coloane Library
rows.summary: A one-storey library (Biblioteca de Coloane) in a building of 1911 that began as a public primary school and became a public library in 1983. The front has a colonnade of six round columns with capitals under a pediment, in a southern European style. It stands on the waterfront road in Coloane Village.

rows.name: Coloane Pier
rows.summary: A former ferry pier on Coloane's west shore, with a covered Art Déco portico, plastered in light yellow, at the shore end of a trestle jetty; 'Coloane Pier' is lettered in Portuguese and Chinese on its front and rear. Ferries linked Coloane with Taipa and the Macau Peninsula until the road links of 1968 and 1974 reduced the service, and sailings stopped in the early 1980s. Today it is a waterfront spot at the edge of the village, where dried seafood is sold nearby.

rows.name: Coloane Village Murals
rows.summary: Street murals by local artists cover walls in Coloane Village, along Avenida de Cinco de Outubro, Rua do Caetano, Largo do Estaleiro and the Pátio do Galo. They take up the village's fishing past: fishermen coming home at sunset, the sea god Tam Kung as a child with a tiger or among shoals of fish, and large fish drawn in Portuguese tile patterns. Together they make a short photo walk through the old fishing village.

rows.name: Coloane Waterfront, Coloane Pier to Tam Kong Temple Square
rows.name_zh: 路环海旁（码头至谭公庙前地）
rows.pinyin: Lùhuán Hǎipáng (Mǎtóu Zhì Tángōng Miào Qiándì)
rows.summary: The waterfront road of Coloane Village, running along the bay from Coloane Pier to the square in front of Tam Kong Temple (Largo Tam Kong Miu). It is classified as a site for the historic buildings along it, which include the Chapel of St Francis Xavier, the Coloane Library and Tam Kong Temple, with Eduardo Marques Park and a children's playground on the way. It makes an easy walk through the old fishing village.

rows.name: Comendador Ho Yin Park
rows.summary: A green strip in the Nam Van district that runs from the rotunda with the Orient Arch on Avenida Rodrigo Rodrigues to Avenida da Amizade, between high-rise flats, offices and hotels. It has tree-shaded benches and tables for chess players, landscaped shrubs, bamboo groves, a playground and a small café. The Sculpture Park of the Chinese Ethnics is laid out inside it, and it adjoins Dr Carlos d'Assumpção Park.

rows.name: Commemorative Gallery of the Macau Basic Law
rows.summary: A museum beside the Macau Forum, opened in 2013, on the Basic Law of the Macau Special Administrative Region, the region's fundamental law. The tourism office lists exhibition areas on Macau's history, the "one country, two systems" policy, how the Basic Law was drafted and put into practice, and its relationship with the national Constitution, together with an interactive education area and a reference room. The gallery was reorganised and reopened in June 2025, and it is also used to teach young people about the Constitution and the Basic Law.

rows.name: Communications Museum
rows.summary: A museum run by the Macau Post and Telecommunications Bureau, opened in 2006. A postal and philately gallery covers the history of Macau's post with stamps and postal objects, and an interactive telecommunications gallery shows how communication techniques developed. Outdoor exhibits stand on a terrace next to D. Maria II Garden, close to the 1852 Fortress of Dona Maria II, which the tourism office describes as the only old fortress in Macau entered by a suspension bridge.

rows.name: Company of Jesus Square
rows.summary: A small square (Largo da Companhia de Jesus) at the foot of the staircase to the Ruins of St Paul's, named for the Jesuits who founded St Paul's College and paved with small stones. The buildings around it date from 1920–30, apart from two neoclassical ones of the 19th century. Mount Fortress and the Macau Museum stand on the hill to the east, and the Na Tcha Temple is close by to the north.

rows.name: Dom Pedro V Theatre
rows.summary: Built in 1860 as the first Western-style theatre in China, this neoclassical building has sage-green walls with white mouldings, dark green doors and shutters, and a terracotta roof. It once also housed a ballroom, a reading room and a billiard parlour, and its vestibule has an old crystal chandelier. The 276-seat hall remains a performing venue, and the theatre is part of the Historic Centre of Macau.

rows.name: Dr. Carlos d'Assumpção Park
rows.summary: A waterfront park in the Nam Van reclaimed area, opened in 1996 and named after the well-known Macanese Dr Carlos d'Assumpção. A Portuguese-pavement avenue lined with palms runs through lawns, arbours, ornamental ponds and fountains, past a children's playground. At its seaward end the park reaches the bronze Kun Iam statue on its island, and a promenade looks over the Outer Harbour, the bridges and Taipa.

rows.name: Dr. Sun Yat Sen Municipal Park
rows.summary: A large park at the northern end of the peninsula, laid out in 1987 on a former rubbish dump and named after Sun Yat-sen in 1990, when his statue was unveiled. It has flower gardens, an aviary, a Victorian-style greenhouse, a feng shui wood and a children's playground, with a 500-metre corridor linking most of its sights. High points give views across the canal towards Zhuhai.

rows.name: Eduardo Marques Square and Eanes Square, Coloane Village
rows.name_zh: 马忌士前地及恩尼斯总统前地
rows.pinyin: Mǎjìshì Qiándì Jí Ēnnísī Zǒngtǒng Qiándì
rows.summary: The centre of Coloane Village: Largo Eduardo Marques, a square paved with black-and-white wave-patterned cobbles in front of the Chapel of St Francis Xavier, with a fountain, a monument and arcades of Chinese and Portuguese restaurants. The classified group also includes Rua dos Negociantes, a traditional street of food and grocery shops, and Largo do Presidente António Ramalho Eanes, a small roundabout with flower beds, benches and a statue of Cupid, where several old lanes meet. Stalls in the area sell dried seafood, Portuguese egg tarts and other snacks.

rows.name: Exhibition Room of Master Lu Ban's Woodcraft Works
rows.name_zh: 鲁班先师木工艺陈列馆
rows.summary: A small museum in the Carpenters' Guildhall, a building of about 1840 on Rua de Camilo Pessanha that was one of Macau's earliest professional associations. Over 80 traditional tools, including saws, planes, drills and ink markers, are on show with an account of Lu Ban, the master carpenter, and how the tools were used. The altar hall displays a large version of the Lu Ban lock.

rows.name: Fire Services Bureau Building, Estrada de Coelho do Amaral
rows.summary: A two-storey fire station completed in 1923 and renovated in 1992, with thick yellow walls, arched doors and windows, brown shutters and three symmetrical gates for fire engines. Only the main façade survives from the original, as the interior has been completely rebuilt. The building houses the Fire Services Museum, opened in 1999 and reopened in December 2024 after its exhibition halls were renovated, which shows historic firefighting equipment.

rows.name: Flora Garden
rows.summary: A European-style garden at the foot of Guia Hill, once the grounds of an aristocratic mansion, with a stone gateway that was the old guardhouse. A straight avenue lined with palms and flowering shrubs leads to formal flowerbeds, and a stone path winds up past small waterfalls and viewpoints towards Guia Hill. A short cable car near the gate also climbs to the hill.

rows.name: Flower City Park
rows.summary: A walled garden in the middle of Taipa's high-rise residential district, laid out as a modern version of a classical Chinese garden, with lotus ponds, winding bridges and small pavilions. It also has a children's playground and an area for skating and scooters.

rows.name: Foc Tac Temple, Horta da Mitra
rows.summary: A Lingnan-style temple built in 1886 and renovated in 1986, where worshippers honour the Earth God, A-Ma, two gods of wealth and Tai Soi, the god of the year. The wall around its entrance patio is topped with green glazed balusters and floral ornaments of the kind seen on Macau's Western-style buildings. An inscription in both Chinese and Portuguese is the only one of its kind in a Macau temple.

rows.name: Foc Tac Temple, Rua do Almirante Sérgio
rows.summary: A neighbourhood temple built in 1868, rebuilt in 1871 and restored in 1914, set into a row of street arcades. It is the only temple in Macau integrated into such an arcade. The main altar is to the Earth God, with side altars to the Northern Emperor (Pak Tai) and A-Ma, and the walls hold many tablets, couplets and panels donated by local people.

rows.name: Foc Tac Temple, Rua do Patane
rows.summary: An Earth God temple on Rua do Patane, a street once known as Stone Wall Village. A tablet inside shows it was built no later than 1874, and the Cultural Affairs Bureau records it as the oldest building on the street. It sits in the Patane district north of the old centre.

rows.name: Foc Tac Temple, Rua do Teatro
rows.summary: A small temple to the Earth God, built before 1796 and renovated in 1881 and 1909. Its main altar honours the Earth God (Tou Tei Kung) and a side altar the Earth Goddess, a pairing the Cultural Affairs Bureau calls very rare in Macau. Unlike many Foc Tac shrines, which grew from open-air altars, it was planned from the start as a place of worship.

rows.name: Former Barra Slaughterhouse
rows.summary: The municipal slaughterhouse of the Macau Peninsula, a group of three buildings with eclectic façades on the side of Barra Hill, built in the 1880s and altered in 1916–17. It ceased to work as an abattoir in 1987, when the municipal slaughtering service moved to Ilha Verde. The buildings were later used as dormitories, offices and archives.

rows.name: Former Bela Vista Hotel
rows.summary: A three-storey, pale yellow neoclassical building of about 1870 on Penha Hill, with arcades, columns, railings and a pediment. It became a hotel in 1890, was renamed the Bela Vista Hotel in 1936, and closed in 1999. After restoration it became the official residence of the Portuguese consul-general for Macau and Hong Kong.

rows.name: Former Chong Sai Pharmacy
rows.summary: A shophouse on Rua das Estalagens (Antiga Farmácia Chong Sai), built before 1892, where Sun Yat-sen ran a clinic and the Chong Sai (Chinese-Western) Pharmacy from 1893, one of the first Western-style clinics run by Chinese doctors in Macau. The government bought and restored it, and it reopened in 2016 as an exhibition space. Displays cover archaeological finds, the restoration of the building, and Sun Yat-sen's links with Macau.

rows.name: Former Coloane Health Centre (Customs Station)
rows.summary: A single-storey Art Déco building of 1938–39 beside Coloane Pier, built as the Coloane Health Centre, later used by the marine police and now a Customs station (Posto Alfandegário). It has a symmetrical yellow façade with white decoration, a stepped parapet with geometric patterns and a large reinforced-concrete canopy around the building.

rows.name: Former Court Building
rows.summary: Built in 1951 as a shared office building for several government departments including the Court, this three-storey building was known as the Macau Civil Services Building. Its eclectic style shows in the stone steps and tall Ionic columns that mark its entrance. The Court of First Instance moved out in 2003.
