rows.name: Former Iec Long Firecracker Factory
rows.summary: The preserved site of a firecracker factory of about 25,000 square metres in the old village of Taipa, with a history of nearly a century. The Cultural Affairs Bureau describes it as the only well-preserved heritage site of Macau's firecracker industry; it keeps the original layout of the production buildings and has a 400-metre walkway, an exhibition hall and a shop selling cultural and creative products. Firecracker making was a mainstay of Taipa's economy, especially from the 1950s to the 1970s.

rows.name: Former Jardine Matheson Buildings
rows.summary: Two neighbouring houses on Rua da Praia do Bom Parto that belonged to the trading firm Jardine Matheson. One, built in the early 19th century, was first a residence and then the firm's Macau office; the other, built in 1868 as its commercial headquarters, has been part of the Ricci School since 1955. Their garden walls are linked and share a style, which suggests the two were planned as a group.

rows.name: Former Lok Kok Restaurant
rows.summary: A restaurant building of the 1940s at Rua de Cinco de Outubro 159, classified as a building of architectural interest. After the restaurant closed in 1990 the building fell into disrepair and collapsed, and it has since been rebuilt.

rows.name: Former Municipal Cattle Stable (Ox Warehouse)
rows.summary: The Former Municipal Cattle Stable was built in 1912 to quarantine and keep cattle and was rebuilt in 1924 with its layout and exterior largely unchanged. It is a pair of parallel bungalows with truss roofs, a mahogany roof and khaki walls in a Portuguese eclectic style, next to a simpler mid-20th-century section, now the municipal kennels, with Art Deco touches. After the stable moved out in 1987, part of the complex became a storehouse and part an exhibition venue, which the Cultural Affairs Bureau restored and lends to local arts groups for exhibitions.

rows.name: Former Opium House
rows.summary: Built in 1880 as a warehouse for storing opium, this building later served other purposes and is now a clinic run by the Tung Sin Tong Charitable Society. It has an arched corridor on the ground floor with a covered balcony above, a type of eclectic architecture common around the Inner Harbour. It stands on Praça de Ponte e Horta.

rows.name: Former Residence of Silva Mendes
rows.summary: Built in 1905, this was one of three stately private mansions on Guia Hill in its day. It belonged to Manuel da Silva Mendes, a noted Macau writer and art collector who donated part of his collection to the former Luís de Camões Museum. The mansion was later sold and put to other uses.

rows.name: Former St. Raphael Hospital (Portuguese Consulate-General)
rows.name_zh: 葡萄牙驻澳门及香港总领事馆
rows.pinyin: Pútáoyá Zhù Àomén Jí Xiānggǎng Zǒnglǐngshìguǎn
rows.summary: St. Raphael Hospital was founded in 1569 by Bishop Belchior Carneiro and run by the Holy House of Mercy, and the Chinese called it I Yan Miu, the Temple of Cures. The Cultural Affairs Bureau describes it as the first Western-style hospital in Asia and the place from which smallpox vaccination reached China. The present building dates from the last rebuilding in 1939 and houses the Consulate-General of Portugal.

rows.name: Former Tai Neng Chinese Pharmacy
rows.summary: A three-storey building of the early 20th century that blends Chinese and Western influences. Its most distinctive feature is the carved Chinese wooden windows on the first floor. The pharmacy that gave it its name has closed.

rows.name: Former Tarrafeiro Municipal Market
rows.summary: The Tarrafeiro Market was a fish market that existed before the 1870s, was rebuilt in 1907–09 and closed in 1928 because of poor sanitation. One of its eclectic-style gates survives at Travessa das Galinholas, an arched portico in three sections topped by a curved pediment. The lanes around it keep their old streetscape and show how Macau's early municipal markets were laid out.

rows.name: Fort Dona Maria II
rows.summary: Fort Dona Maria II (Fortaleza de D. Maria II) stands at the top of Ma Kau Seac Hill, 48.2 metres high, in the north-east of the Macau Peninsula. Built in 1852 to support Mong-Há Fort, it is an irregular hexagon entered across a movable bridge, with a vaulted corridor behind the gate; American aircraft bombed it on 16 January 1945. The grassy eastern slope of the hill is a recreation area with views towards the sea, and the park around the fort reopened in December 2023 after renovation.

rows.name: General Post Office Building
rows.summary: The General Post Office (Correios) on Avenida de Almeida Ribeiro, beside Senado Square, was built in 1925–29 to a neoclassical design by the Chinese architect Chan Kun Pui, on the site of the Tung Sin Tong charity's premises. The three-storey building has a bell tower that chimes the time with music. It is still a working post office, where visitors can buy stamps and postcards.

rows.name: General Ye Ting's Former Residence
rows.summary: General Ye Ting, a Chinese military commander, lived in this two-storey western-style house with his family in the 1930s and early 1940s. After later use as a student association office and a kindergarten, the house passed to the Cultural Affairs Bureau in 2011 and opened to the public on 28 May 2014. It is furnished with original pieces and holds displays of old photographs, with a bronze sculpture in the front yard.

rows.name: Grand Lisboa Palace Art Gallery
rows.summary: An art gallery inside the Grand Lisboa Palace resort in Cotai, run by the resort's operator, SJM Resorts. It stages regular exhibitions and special showcases, including projects by artists from other countries, and holds the Lisboa Collection, a gallery of works from the collections of SJM and STDM.

rows.name: Grande Praça at MGM Macau
rows.summary: The covered central atrium of MGM Macau, a casino resort on the NAPE waterfront that opened in 2007. It is designed in homage to old-world Europe and Macau's Portuguese heritage: the north wall is modelled on the façade of Estação Rossio, Lisbon's central railway station, and a domed glass ceiling lets daylight in. It sits inside a working resort, so it suits a short look rather than a long stay.

rows.name: Guia Fortress
rows.summary: A fortress (Fortaleza da Guia) built between 1622 and 1638 on the summit of Guia Hill, which together with Mount Fortress helped defend the city against the Dutch attack of 1622. Inside stand the Chapel of Our Lady of the Snows, whose frescoes were uncovered in 1996 and mix Western and Chinese motifs, and the 1865 Guia Lighthouse, the first modern lighthouse on China's south coast. The fortress and chapel can be visited; the lighthouse is not open to the public.

rows.name: Guia Hill
rows.summary: The largest green area on the Macau Peninsula (Colina da Guia), rising to about 90 metres and planted with pines about a century ago. A public park with paths covers its slopes, and Guia Fortress, its chapel and the lighthouse stand on the summit. The road that curves around the hill forms part of the Macau Grand Prix circuit.

rows.name: Handover Gifts Museum of Macau
rows.summary: A three-storey museum on Avenida Xian Xing Hai, next to the Macau Museum of Art, designed by the architect Vicente Bravo and opened in December 2004 to commemorate the handover of Macau at the end of 1999. The main gallery shows the gifts presented to Macau at the handover by the State Council, the provinces, municipalities and autonomous regions, and Hong Kong, together with an inscription for Macau by Jiang Zemin, the former president. A second gallery stages temporary exhibitions, and a third is used by the Education and Youth Development Bureau for youth education.

rows.name: Heritage Exhibition of a Traditional Pawnshop Business
rows.summary: A former pawnshop, Tak Seng On, opened in 1917 for the Macau merchant Kou Ho Neng and restored by the government as a museum of the pawnbroking trade. The building follows the pattern of Chinese pawnshops of the early 20th century, with a fortified tower behind the shop. A visit gives a view of how the pawn business worked in its heyday.

rows.name: Holy House of Mercy
rows.summary: The headquarters of the Santa Casa da Misericórdia, a charity founded in 1569 by Macau's first bishop, which set up the first Western-style clinic and hospital in the city. The neoclassical building on Senado Square dates from the mid 18th century and took its present form in 1905. A museum inside shows Catholic relics and sacred art from as early as the 16th century, including a manuscript of 1662 and the skull of its founder, Bishop Belchior Carneiro.

rows.name: Hong Kung Temple
rows.summary: A temple of 1860 in the old bazaar area, dedicated to Marshal Hong Gong and also to Hung Seng, the Buddha and Hua Tuo, god of medicine. Local legend tells of a wooden statue of Hong Gong that floated ashore here and was first given a shrine. The building shows southern Chinese architecture, with a courtyard uniting the main elements and coloured pottery figures on the roof.

rows.name: I Leng Temple, Taipa
rows.summary: A small temple built in 1900 and dedicated to I Leng, god of medicine, the deified form of an ancient physician renowned for his skill (Templo de I Leng). It has a front hall and a rear chamber separated by a courtyard, with the statue and altar in the rear chamber. The old sliding gate made of thick logs is a rare survival in Macau today.

rows.name: Ian Tak Tong Kong So (Lou Pan Temple)
rows.name_zh: 仁德堂公所（鲁班师傅庙）
rows.summary: A small temple to Lou Pan, patron god of carpenters, built by the carpenters' association in 1859 and enlarged in 1883. The temple has no courtyard between its entrance and the main hall. It is also known as the Ian Tak Tong Civil Office.

rows.name: Inner Harbour
rows.summary: The harbour on the western side of the peninsula (Porto Interior), with a coastline of about 3,500 metres and a half-ring-shaped embankment. The tourism office describes it as the first harbour to serve foreign merchant ships berthing at the North Bay. Its 34 piers, each named by number, handled cargo, river transport and fishing boats, and the waterfront traces the history of Macau's trade and of its fishing industry.

rows.name: Kou Ho Neng Mansion
rows.summary: A three-storey private house of 1916 built for the wealthy Macau merchant Kou Ho Neng, in Western style with a tower on each side, two levels of arcades in the centre and a pediment above the third floor. Inside, the layout follows Chinese style, in sharp contrast to the exterior. It is classified as a building of architectural interest.

rows.name: Kou Seng Pawnshop
rows.summary: A 19th-century pawnshop on Rua de S. Domingos whose fortified tower stands at the back of the shop. The business has since closed. It is classified as a building of architectural interest.

rows.name: Kun Iam Ecumenical Centre
rows.summary: A 20-metre bronze statue of Kun Iam (Guanyin), the Goddess of Mercy, stands on a lotus-shaped base on an artificial island in the Outer Harbour and was unveiled in 1999. Locals call it simply the Kun Iam statue. The domed base holds an ecumenical centre with information on Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism, and a shop selling publications of the Cultural Affairs Bureau.

rows.name: Kun Iam Temple, Coloane Village
rows.summary: A single-chamber temple to Kun Iam, goddess of mercy (Templo de Kun Iam), built around 1800 by local sea traders and rebuilt in 1839, on Travessa do Pagode in Coloane Village. It is one of the four temples of Coloane, with the Tin Hau, Tam Kong and Sam Seng temples, which are looked after by a local charity group. According to legend, Kun Iam often protected fishermen and seafarers so that they could return home safely.

rows.name: Kun Iam Temple, Estrada Nordeste, Taipa
rows.summary: A small temple of about 1871 on a hill above Estrada Nordeste da Taipa, placed to overlook the sea and the Macau Peninsula (Templo de Kun Iam). It has a front hall and a rear chamber, and the statue of Kun Iam, goddess of mercy, stands in a stone cave inside.

rows.name: Kun Iam Temple, Kun Iam Tchai
rows.summary: A temple to Kun Iam (Guanyin) built by a Chinese shepherd after 1821 and extended in 1867 to its present form; inside, worshippers also honour deities such as Loi Chou and Tao Mou. Two trees more than a century old stand in the courtyard. Linked to it on the right is the Seng Wong Temple of 1908, the only City God temple in Macau, which also honours the Qing viceroy Zhang Zhidong, who praised the villagers' defence force.

rows.name: Kun Iam Temple, Ká Hó
rows.summary: A single-chamber temple to Kun Iam, goddess of mercy (Templo de Kun Iam), built in 1881 and rebuilt in 1907, and the oldest building in Ká Hó Village. Three characters reading Kun Iam Miu are carved on a stone set above the doorway. Ká Hó is one of the only two Hakka villages left in Macau.

rows.name: Kun Iam Temple, Mong-Há
rows.summary: Kun Iam Temple (Templo de Pou Chai), dedicated to the Goddess of Mercy, is one of the three oldest temples in Macau and one of its largest, with a big entrance gate, roofs crowded with porcelain figures and richly decorated halls around open courtyards. Its present buildings date from 1627, with restorations in 1818 and 1858. In the terraced garden behind stands the stone table where China and the United States signed the Treaty of Wangxia on 3 July 1844, next to four intertwined banyan trees known as the Lovers Tree.

rows.name: Kun Iam Tong Temple, Taipa
rows.summary: A plain little temple built in 1902 on Rua Direita Carlos Eugénio (Templo de Kun Iam), with a statue of Kun Iam, goddess of mercy, inside. It stands in the old village close to the Carmo Fair.

rows.name: Lai Chi Vun Shipyards
rows.summary: A row of former boatyards (Estaleiros Navais de Lai Chi Vun) on the Coloane shore, built from the 1950s when shipbuilding was one of Macau's four main traditional industries. The yards closed one by one as the trade declined from the 1990s, and the last fishing boat was launched in 2005. Part of the site, units X-11 to X-15, opened to visitors in June 2023 as a cultural space with an exhibition on shipbuilding, a market, art activities and buskers' performances.

rows.name: Leal Senado Building
rows.summary: Macau's original city hall of 1784, still the seat of the municipal affairs bureau, on Senado Square, with a name (Loyal Senate) taken from a title given by the Portuguese king in 1654. The neoclassical building has a granite-columned entrance, blue-and-white tile panels by the main staircase and a courtyard garden at the back, with a council chamber, a small chapel and a carved library modelled on that of the Mafra Convent on the first floor. The IAM Gallery in the lobby shows art and cultural exhibitions when one is on, and the courtyard garden can be visited.

rows.name: Lilau Square
rows.summary: A small square around the Lilau spring (Largo do Lilau), once the main source of natural spring water in Macau and part of one of the first Portuguese residential quarters. A Portuguese saying holds that whoever drinks from Lilau never forgets Macau. The lanes around it have a Mediterranean feel, and the traditional Chinese compound known as the Mandarin's House stands alongside.

rows.name: Lin Fong Temple
rows.summary: One of the three oldest temples in Macau, with a spacious forecourt shaded by banyan trees, two stone flagpoles, stone lions at the entrance and a richly worked façade of clay relief. Halls in parallel bays honour Tin Hau, Kun Iam, Kuan Tai and other deities, and a courtyard has a lotus pond and an iron brazier. Chinese officials from Guangdong stayed here when they visited Macau, the imperial commissioner Lin Zexu met Portuguese officials here in 1839, and a memorial stone records the temple's construction in 1723.

rows.name: Lin Kai Temple
rows.summary: A Chinese temple (Templo de Lin Kai) in the Patane district, built in 1830 and rebuilt and enlarged between 1875 and 1908, which is why it is also called the New Lin Kai Temple. Its nine halls are dedicated to 15 deities; the main hall honours Va Kuong, the god who protects against fire, and other halls hold Kun Iam, Kuan Tai, goddesses of childbirth and the Monkey God. The façade has granite carvings and large lion statues on the roof, and the temple's festival for Va Kuong falls on the 28th day of the ninth lunar month.

rows.name: Lin Zexu Memorial Museum of Macau
rows.summary: A small museum next to Lin Fong Temple recording the visit to Macau on 3 September 1839 of the imperial commissioner Lin Zexu, who came during the dispute over the opium trade that led to the Opium War. It was completed in 1997 and shows photographs, documents and ship models from the period. A statue of Lin stands nearby.

rows.name: Lingnan Middle School Building (Former Vila Alegre)
rows.name_zh: 岭南中学大楼（原快乐别墅）
rows.summary: Built between 1917 and 1921 as the home of the Portuguese lawyer Francisco Xavier Anacleto da Silva, Vila Alegre was one of three grand residences on Guia Hill. The mansion has columns, wide balconies and an elegant staircase. It has been part of the Lingnan school since 1937.

rows.name: Lotus Square
rows.summary: A public square (Praça Flor de Lótus) whose centrepiece is Lotus Flower in Full Bloom, a gilded-bronze sculpture 6 metres high that the State Council presented in 1999 to mark the handover of Macau. The red granite base has three layers shaped like lotus leaves, standing for the Macau Peninsula, Taipa and Coloane. The Macau Forum and the Tourism Activities Centre stand beside it.

rows.name: Lou Kau Mansion
rows.summary: Lou Kau Mansion (Casa de Lou Kau), built around 1889, was the home of Lou Kau, a banker and businessman honoured by the King of Portugal in 1890. It is a two-storey grey-brick Chinese courtyard house in the Xiguan style, with western touches such as mother-of-pearl window panes, balustrades and perforated wooden ceilings like those in Macau's churches. Part of the Historic Centre of Macau, it stands near Senado Square and Cathedral Square.

rows.name: Lou Lim Ioc Garden
rows.summary: Lou Lim Ioc Garden (Jardim de Lou Lim Ioc) is a walled Chinese garden in the style of Suzhou, created by the merchant Lou Wa Sio and his son Lou Lim Iok, and opened to the public in 1974 after the government bought and restored it. Paths wind through bamboo groves and under moulded rockeries to a pond of golden carp and lotus, crossed by a nine-turn zigzag bridge. The main hall, Chun Chou Tong Pavilion, mixes Chinese and Western details and hosts exhibitions; Sun Yat-sen stayed there in May 1912, and the garden also holds the Macau Tea Culture House.

rows.name: Luís Gonzaga Gomes Luso-Chinese Secondary School Building
rows.summary: A modernist school building of 1939 on Avenida de Sidónio Pais, on land that was once part of Vasco da Gama Garden, laid out in 1898. It was the Pedro Nolasco da Silva Government Primary School, where Portuguese was taught as the official language, and since 1995 it has been part of the Luso-Chinese Luís Gonzaga Gomes Secondary School. The Cultural Affairs Bureau describes it as a local example of modernist architecture.

rows.name: Luís de Camões Garden and Old Protestant Cemetery
rows.name_zh: 白鸽巢公园及基督教坟场
rows.summary: A hillside public garden (Jardim de Luís de Camões) with benches shaded by banyan trees, a grotto sheltering a bronze bust of the Portuguese poet Luís de Camões, and a wooded hill where local people play Chinese chess, exercise and walk caged birds. Next to it lies the Old Protestant Cemetery, laid out in 1821, with the Morrison Chapel named after Robert Morrison, the first Protestant missionary in China. Graves include Morrison's and that of the British painter George Chinnery, alongside East India Company officials and other foreign residents.

rows.name: Macau Cathedral
rows.summary: The cathedral of the Macau diocese, first built around 1622 of earth and straw, rebuilt in 1844–1850 and given its present form in 1937. Its façade has pilasters and twin belfries and a plain Shanghai-plaster finish. A Latin inscription above the door dedicates it to the Nativity of the Virgin Mary, and the square in front is Largo da Sé.

rows.name: Macau Contemporary Art Center, Navy Yard No. 1
rows.name_zh: 澳门当代艺术中心·海事工房1号
rows.pinyin: Àomén Dāngdài Yìshù Zhōngxīn · Hǎishì Gōngfáng 1 Hào
rows.summary: A former mechanical room of the old D. Carlos I dock in the Barra district, where the government built and reconditioned ships. The tourism office lists it as a contemporary art centre for exhibitions and experimental performance art.

rows.name: Macau Cultural Centre
rows.summary: The Macau Cultural Centre (Centro Cultural de Macau) is a performing-arts complex by the architects Irene Ó and Bruno Soares on the reclaimed NAPE waterfront, opened in 1999. The Grand Auditorium seats 1,080 for opera, ballet, orchestral concerts and touring musicals, the Small Auditorium stages smaller productions and film screenings, and the Macau Museum of Art shares the complex. Annual events held here include the music festival and the Fringe festival.

rows.name: Macau Fisherman's Wharf
rows.summary: A themed waterfront complex (Doca dos Pescadores) of about 133,000 square metres on the outer harbour. The government tourism office describes it as the first cultural, themed and creative attraction in Macau's tourism industry, combining dining, shopping, entertainment, accommodation, and convention and exhibition space. It suits a relaxed outing or an evening meal by the water.

rows.name: Macau Giant Panda Pavilion and Pavilion of Rare Animals
rows.summary: A fan-shaped pavilion (Pavilhão do Panda Gigante de Macau) of about 3,000 square metres built into the hillside in Seac Pai Van Park, with indoor and outdoor areas for giant pandas and two viewing paths at different heights. The park's Pavilion of Rare Animals has indoor and outdoor areas for red pandas, with climbing perches and a regulated indoor temperature. A giant panda information centre in the park has exhibition rooms and video rooms.

rows.name: Macau Government Headquarters
rows.summary: A two-storey pink building of 1849 in Portuguese style, built as the Palácio do Cercal for a nobleman and used as the governor's office from 1884. It has a wing on each side and a winding corridor along the upper floor, and stands well back in a garden. On 19 December 1999 the last Portuguese governor lowered the Portuguese flag here at the start of the handover of administration to China, and it is now the headquarters of the Macau government.

rows.name: Macau Grand Prix Museum
rows.summary: The museum of the Macau Grand Prix (Museu do Grande Prémio) is run by the tourism office in the Tourism Activities Centre beside Lotus Square, and reopened in June 2021 after remodelling. Its four floors show Grand Prix cars and motorcycles from across the decades, with displays on the drivers, riders and teams who have raced on the street circuit since 1954. Some basement exhibition areas have been closed in stages for renovation since May 2026, so check what is open before going.

rows.name: Macau Monetary Authority Building (the White House)
rows.summary: A two-storey mansion of 1916–17 built for the lawyer Luís Nolasco da Silva, later a convent of the Little Sisters of the Precious Blood, and bought in 1998 by the Macau Monetary Authority for its headquarters offices. Broad balconies on the main rooms, a feature typical of the tropics before air conditioning, and its white-painted walls earned it the nickname the White House. It is classified as a building of architectural interest.

rows.name: Macau Mosque and Cemetery
rows.summary: Macau's only mosque (Mesquita de Macau), built in the early 1980s in the Mong-Há district, with a historic cemetery beside it. The cemetery is the resting place of several Parsis and Muslims of various origins, some of the graves more than a hundred years old. Together they record the Muslim presence in Macau.

rows.name: Macau Museum
rows.summary: The city's history and folk-culture museum (Museu de Macau) opened in 1998 inside Mount Fortress, with two of its three floors built beneath the fortress platform and the top floor in the former weather observatory. The first floor covers Macau's early history and the meeting of Chinese and Portuguese cultures, the second its folk arts, festivals and daily life, and the third the city today and how writers and artists have portrayed it.

rows.name: Macau Museum of Art
rows.summary: The Macau Museum of Art (Museu de Arte de Macau), opened in 1999 in the Macau Cultural Centre complex, has five floors and seven exhibition galleries. The fourth floor shows Chinese calligraphy, painting and Shiwan ceramics from Guangdong, the third floor has Western paintings and European prints of Macau's scenery, and the second and third floors stage changing exhibitions of Macau and international artists.

rows.name: Macau Science Center
rows.summary: A science museum on the NAPE waterfront (Centro de Ciência de Macau), designed by Pei Partnership Architects with Ieoh Ming Pei and completed in 2009. Its conical main building holds 13 permanent galleries of interactive exhibits, on subjects including astronomy, children's science, navigation, biodiversity, acoustics and smart technology. A planetarium with a dome screen and a convention centre complete the complex, and the building is a landmark of the waterfront.

rows.name: Macau Tea Culture House
rows.summary: A museum of tea inside Lou Lim Ioc Garden, opened in 2005 in a building that combines southern European features with a Chinese tiled roof and sits well with the garden's Suzhou-style landscape. Its exhibitions present the tea cultures of Macau, mainland China and the West, a fitting theme for a port that in the 17th century handled Chinese tea exports to the West.

rows.name: Macau Tower
rows.summary: A 338-metre tower (Torre de Macau) on the Sai Van waterfront, opened in December 2001, with an observation deck about 223 metres up that looks over Macau and much of the Pearl River Delta. Visitors can also walk around the outside of the tower on the Skywalk. The base has a convention and entertainment centre with a cinema and an outdoor plaza.

rows.name: Mandarin's House
rows.summary: The family home (Casa do Mandarim) of the reformist writer Zheng Guanying (1842–1921), dating from about 1869 and covering about 4,000 square metres beside Lilau Square. A gatehouse, courtyards and master's and servants' quarters stretch more than 120 metres along Barra Street, Chinese in style with western touches such as arched plasterwork over doors and mother-of-pearl window panes. The compound, part of the Historic Centre of Macau, also houses the Zheng Guanying Memorial Museum on his life and the history of the house.

rows.name: Maritime Museum
rows.summary: A museum in a building shaped like a sailing ship, beside A-Ma Temple on Barra Square (Largo do Pagode da Barra). The ground floor covers the fishing communities of Macau and South China with boats, tools, a replica fisherman's house and a Little A-Ma Theatre telling the goddess's legend; upper floors cover Chinese and Portuguese sea voyages, maritime technology and an aquarium gallery. Full-size boats, including a dragon boat, stand outside.

rows.name: Military Club Building
rows.summary: A one-storey neoclassical building of the early 1870s on Avenida da Praia Grande, the clubhouse of the Military Club that Portuguese officers founded in 1870. The pink façade has a Tuscan colonnade, a balustrade and a curved gable carrying the date 1870 and the words Clube Militar, and only the façade survives from the original after the rebuilding of 1994–95. The club still occupies the building, so most visitors see the exterior from the avenue.

rows.name: Mong-Ha Villas
rows.summary: A row of twelve two-storey Portuguese-style houses of 1950–51, built as rented homes for lower-ranking civil servants on Avenida do Coronel Mesquita and Estrada de Coelho do Amaral in Mong-Há. Each has a front garden, an arched porch and tiled eaves in the Suave Portuguese style, so that together they form a continuous façade. The Cultural Affairs Bureau has restored the houses on Avenida do Coronel Mesquita, and a selected operator now runs exhibitions, markets and community events there, with shops being added.

rows.name: Mong-Há Fort
rows.summary: Mong-Há Fort (Fortaleza de Mong-Há) crowns Mong-Há Hill, also called Lotus Hill, 60.7 metres high at the northern end of the Macau Peninsula. Begun in 1849 and finished in 1866 as a precaution against a Chinese attack, the walled fort covers about 650 square metres and had ten cannons able to reach the Border Gate. No longer in military use, the hill is now a municipal park of flowerbeds, grassy slopes and walkways, with good views over the north of the city.

rows.name: Montanha Russa Garden
rows.summary: A small hillside park laid out in a romantic style in the late 19th century in the north-east of the peninsula, between Mong-Há Hill and Dona Maria II Hill. A spiral path winds up to the top, which gives the park its Chinese name, and the hill holds tropical and European trees labelled in Latin and Chinese, secluded benches and a children's playground. It is a quiet retreat in a crowded part of the city.

rows.name: Moorish Barracks
rows.summary: Built in 1874 (Quartel dos Mouros) to house an Indian regiment from Goa that reinforced the Macau police, this neoclassical building adds Islamic and Mughal touches: a raised granite platform and four-metre-wide verandas with pointed arches. Designed by the engineer António Alexandrino de Melo, it has housed the harbour authority since 1905 and is now the headquarters of the Marine and Water Bureau. It is part of the Historic Centre of Macau, at the foot of Barra Hill.

rows.name: Moosa Houses
rows.summary: Two houses at 45 and 47 Rua Central (Casas Moosa), built before 1880 for the Moosa family, Muslim traders from India whose firm was founded in Macau in 1880. They are the only buildings on Rua Central that keep the look of the old two- and three-storey shophouses. Number 45 has Portuguese-style shuttered windows, while number 47 mixes mica windows, vase railings and Chinese wooden bracketing under the eaves.

rows.name: Morrison Chapel (Protestant Chapel)
rows.summary: A small whitewashed chapel in the Old Protestant Cemetery, renovated in 1922 and named after Robert Morrison, the missionary who translated the Bible into Chinese. Its stained-glass window shows an open Bible with Chinese characters, and plaques inside commemorate foreign residents of China. The cemetery behind it has more than 180 graves, mostly of British and American people, recalling the foreign trading and naval presence in Macau.

rows.name: Mount Fortress
rows.summary: The Jesuit-built fortress (Fortaleza do Monte) of 1617–1626 crowns Mount Hill above the Ruins of St Paul's. It was the city's main defence work, built to watch over the city in all directions, and helped hold off the Dutch attack of 1622. Its thick walls, 9 metres high and 3.7 metres wide at the base, have parapets for 32 cannon and now enclose a garden, the Macau Museum and a gallery in a former underground ammunition cellar that covers the history of Macau's fortresses.

rows.name: Mural at Rua Correia da Silva 51, Taipa
rows.name_zh: 告利雅施利华街51号壁画
rows.summary: A large mural by a local illustrator on the side walls of the staircase linking Calçada do Quartel and Rua Correia da Silva in Taipa Village. Called Lucky Tiger, it shows children in tiger costumes at play in bright cartoon colours, drawing on the Chinese tradition of the tiger as a symbol of good fortune and protection.

rows.name: Murals at Largo do Pagode da Barra
rows.summary: The Macau artists Vitorino Vong and Jing Daan Wai painted these murals based on the old scenery of the Inner Harbour and the A-Ma Temple area. They stand in the square in front of A-Ma Temple, known in Portuguese as Largo do Pagode da Barra. A second set by the same artists is on Travessa da Assunção.

rows.name: Murals at Rua do Sol 8–16, Taipa
rows.pinyin: Rìtóu Jiē Bā Zhì Shíliù Hào Bìhuà
rows.summary: Murals in Rua do Sol, a small alley beside Rua do Cunha in Taipa Village. A local illustrator painted Lucky Cat figures in bright red, in a paper-cutting style, on one side wall, inspired by the cats that live in the area. Another wall and a gate carry racing scenes with tracks, grandstands and motorcycles, a nod to the Macau Grand Prix.

rows.name: Murals at Travessa da Assunção
rows.summary: The Macau artists Vitorino Vong and Jing Daan Wai painted these murals on Travessa da Assunção, basing them on the old scenery of the Inner Harbour and the A-Ma Temple area. The same artists made a second set at Largo do Pagode da Barra. The Nam Kwong warehouse murals are close by on Rua do Almirante Sérgio.

rows.name: Murals at the Nam Kwong Warehouses
rows.summary: The Cultural Affairs Bureau and Nam Kwong Logistics had the local graffiti artists Lam Ka Hou and Anny paint 25 murals along the facade of the Nam Kwong warehouses on Rua do Almirante Sérgio. They are based on daily life in the Inner Harbour and show both old and new elements of the area, as well as the mix of Chinese and Western cultures there. The murals were made as part of a Deep Cultural Tour of the Inner Harbour area.

rows.name: Museum of Taipa and Coloane History
rows.summary: A museum (Museu da História da Taipa e Coloane) in the neoclassical building of the former Municipal Council of the Islands, which took on its role as a museum on 7 May 2006. The ground floor shows relics excavated on Coloane, the stone remains found in the basement of the old council building and displays on the villages, religions and culture of the two islands; the upper floor covers the former council, farming and handicrafts, the architecture of the islands and their recent development.

rows.name: Na Tcha Exhibition Room
rows.summary: A small exhibition room of about 70 square metres beside the Na Tcha Temple at the Ruins of St Paul's (Sala de Exposição de Na Tcha), opened in 2012 by the Cultural Affairs Bureau. It explains the legend of Na Tcha and the temple festival through objects such as the processional sedan chair, ceremonial umbrella, lion heads and festival firecrackers, and eight drawings by a local cartoonist. Na Tcha customs and beliefs of Macau were added to the national intangible heritage list in 2014, and the room also shows artefacts and building remains from nearby excavations.

rows.name: Na Tcha Temple, Calçada das Verdades
rows.summary: A small temple pavilion first built in the early Qing period and enlarged in 1898, standing on the slope of the Calçada das Verdades. It has no enclosed hall: six stone pillars carry the roof, and a granite niche, altar and incense burner are its main features. It is one of only two surviving temples to Na Tcha, a protector of children, in Macau, and the focus of the Na Tcha Festival on the 18th day of the fifth lunar month.

rows.name: Na Tcha Temple, Ruins of St. Paul's
rows.summary: A small Chinese temple built in 1888 and rebuilt in 1901, standing in the heart of the old Jesuit quarter right beside the Ruins of St Paul's. It honours Na Tcha, a teenage hero of Chinese folk stories who is worshipped as a protective god. A yearly procession in his honour starts from this temple.

rows.name: Nossa Senhora Village (Ká Hó Leprosarium and Our Lady of Sorrows Church)
rows.summary: A village founded in 1964 on the site of the Ká Hó Leprosarium (Vila de Nossa Senhora), the only leprosarium site left in Macau and the last in the city to close. Its main buildings are five single-storey houses of 1929–30 built in an arc along the shore and the Our Lady of Sorrows Church of 1966, a concrete building with a triangular façade, a roof carried on eight sets of angled beams and a crucifix by the Italian sculptor Francisco Messina. The church was the first in Macau to follow the interior reforms of the Second Vatican Council, with the altar in the middle of the hall and the seats fanned around it.

rows.name: Old City Wall Sections, S. Francisco, S. Januário and Penha
rows.name_zh: 城墙遗迹（加思栏马路、若宪马路、西望洋圣堂）
rows.pinyin: Chéngqiáng Yíjì (Jiāsīlán Mǎlù, Ruòxiàn Mǎlù, Xīwàngyáng Shèngtáng)
rows.summary: Three relatively well-preserved stretches of the old walls that once defended the Portuguese settlement, near Estrada de S. Francisco, near Estrada do Visconde de S. Januário and beside the Chapel of Our Lady of Penha. They are in addition to the section near the Ruins of St Paul's that forms part of the Historic Centre of Macau. The walls were an important part of the city's defences for a long period.

rows.name: Old City Walls (Calçada de S. Francisco Xavier)
rows.name_zh: 城墙遗迹（圣方济各斜巷）
rows.summary: A surviving segment of the city's old defences, built as early as 1569 beside the Ruins of St Paul's. It reflects the Portuguese habit of walling port settlements, also seen in Africa and India. The wall is built mainly of chunambo, a mixture of clay, soil, sand, rice straw, crushed rock and oyster shells packed in layers.

rows.name: Old Taipa Pier
rows.summary: The old ferry pier of Taipa (Ponte da Taipa), inaugurated in 1950 for the ferries linking the Macau Peninsula, Taipa and Coloane. It is an inverted-T structure with a symmetrical façade, a portico that once led onto a trestle jetty and parapets with house-shaped merlons like those of Pier No. 1 on the Macau Peninsula. Ferries stopped in the early 1980s, and the building now serves as a patrol station of the Customs Service.

rows.name: Our Lady of Carmel Church
rows.summary: Taipa's only Catholic church (Igreja de Nossa Senhora do Carmo), built in 1885 on a rise above Largo do Carmo, with a neoclassical façade and a belfry without a steeple. The hall holds more than two hundred worshippers, and angel statues beside the altar were added for the church's centenary. It overlooks Taipa Village and the restored 1920s houses on Avenida da Praia.

rows.name: Our Lady of Fátima Church
rows.summary: A modern Catholic church serving the northern district of the peninsula, rebuilt in the late 1960s. It stands in a quiet courtyard behind wrought-iron gates, with a large square bell tower and a broad staircase up to the nave. Inside, stained-glass panels line the side walls and the altar is a wooden crucifix against a red brick wall.

rows.name: Our Lady of Mercy Home for the Elderly
rows.summary: A care home run by the Holy House of Mercy, designed by the engineer Artur Rocha Schiappa Monteiro de Carvalho and inaugurated in 1925 as a shelter. Its eclectic façade has a three-part layout with a veranda, a balcony and Portuguese-style window shutters. The home was renovated in 1998 and reopened in 2000, keeping its original appearance.

rows.name: Painted Staircase at Escada do Coxo, Taipa
rows.summary: The steps of Escada do Coxo in Taipa Village have been painted with new artwork by two Macau artists, based on Portuguese elements. They make a quick photo stop close to Rua do Cunha.

rows.name: Painted Staircase at Travessa da Boa Vista, Taipa
rows.summary: The steps of Travessa da Boa Vista in Taipa Village have been painted with new artwork by two Macau artists, based on the scenery of the old village. They lie close to the Taipa Municipal Garden and Largo do Carmo.

rows.name: Pak Tai Temple, Taipa
rows.summary: A temple to Pak Tai, the Northern Emperor (Templo de Pak Tai), built around 1844 on Largo Camões and one of the larger temples on Taipa and Coloane. Inside, Pak Tai sits with his feet on a tortoise and a snake, and Kuan Tai, Lu Ban, Choi Bak and other deities are worshipped here too. It has three parallel halls and a worship pavilion for offerings, and Chinese opera is staged in a mat shed in front on the Feast of Pak Tai, the third day of the third lunar month.

rows.name: Pao Kong Temple and Temple of Divinity of Medicine
rows.summary: Pao Kong Temple on Rua da Figueira was built in 1889, when a plague struck Macau and residents brought a statue of Pao Kong, the God of Justice, from Foshan to protect them. It stands with three neighbouring temples: Nam San Temple (1895), which honours Zhong Kui, the god who drives out devils, and Loi Tsou Temple (1891) and I Leng Temple (1895). I Leng, the Temple of Divinity of Medicine, honours the sleeping Buddha and other gods and dates from a time when people prayed for the sick because medical care was limited.

rows.name: Parsee Cemetery
rows.summary: A burial ground opened in 1829 for the Parsee community, merchants who came originally from Gujarat in India and first reached Macau in the 1770s. Locals call it the White-Head Cemetery after the white turbans the Parsees wore. By the middle of the 19th century most of the community had moved on to Hong Kong.

rows.name: Patane Library
rows.summary: A public library in a row of seven arcade buildings of the 1930s along the Inner Harbour waterfront in Patane. The arcade form combines European and Southeast Asian features, and few such buildings remain in Macau. The library opened in December 2016 after the buildings were renovated, and it has reading areas, a children's section and an audiovisual collection.

rows.name: Patane Night Watch House
rows.summary: A small traditional Cantonese house on Rua da Palmeira in the old Patane quarter, once home to a night watchman and his family and the only night watch house left in Macau. It has single-storey rooms around a courtyard, a stone room and a water alley, with painted murals inside. Restored and opened in 2015, it now holds a small exhibition of photographs, objects and illustrations on the night-watch trade.

rows.name: Pier No. 1 (Barra Pier)
rows.summary: A government landing stage on Barra Square (Largo do Pagode da Barra), in front of A-Ma Temple, once known as the Royal Pier because governors and senior officials arrived and left Macau from it. The building is yellow-plastered concrete with a Moorish-style roofline of merlon-shaped parapets, and a granite staircase leads down to the water. The pier has been opened to the public as a display of historic local boats such as tugboats, sampans and dragon boats.

rows.name: Poly MGM Museum
rows.summary: A museum of nearly 2,000 square metres inside the MGM Macau resort on Avenida Dr Sun Yat Sen, opened in November 2024 by Poly Culture Group and MGM Macau. It stages changing exhibitions of Chinese art and cultural relics, using movable LED screens, flexible display panels and directional audio. Its first show was on the Maritime Silk Road.

rows.name: Ponte e Horta Square
rows.summary: A recreation square (Praça de Ponte e Horta) beside the Inner Harbour, named after Governor José Maria da Ponte e Horta, who governed from 1866 to 1868. In the Qing period it served as a pier for imported opium, and land reclamation in the late 19th century made it larger. Today it is a local recreation area, and the nearby lanes carry street art from festivals held there.

rows.name: Pooi Tou Middle School Building, Praia Grande
rows.name_zh: 培道中学大楼（南湾分校）
rows.summary: A neoclassical school building put up between 1910 and 1920 on Avenida da Praia Grande, with a fourth storey added at the end of the 1960s. It is the Praia Grande branch of Pooi Tou Middle School and is classified as a building of architectural interest.

rows.name: Pou Sun Pawnshop
rows.summary: A three-storey building (Casa de Penhores Pou Sun) at the corner of Rua Correia da Silva and Travessa da Felicidade in Taipa Village, rebuilt to the structure and design of the original pawnshop. Like other historic pawnshops in Macau, it stands on a street corner.

rows.name: Pou Tai Sin Un
rows.summary: Pou Tai Sin Un is a Buddhist temple on Taipa Island, described by the tourist office as one of the best-endowed and most picturesque temples in Macau. Its main hall holds a bronze Buddha statue 5.4 metres tall including its lotus throne and weighing about six tonnes. Besides the main hall there are further halls and a vegetarian restaurant.

rows.name: Praia Grande Bay Waterfront
rows.summary: A classified stretch of seafront running from the Macau–Taipa bridge round Praia Grande Bay to Praia do Bom Parto, taking in Avenida Doutor Mário Soares, Avenida da Praia Grande and Avenida da República. From the 19th century the Portuguese lined it with European-style buildings, with banyan trees along the shore, and film companies have used it as a backdrop. Land reclamation has since added two artificial lakes.

rows.name: Pui Ching Middle School Administrative Building (Former Lou Lim Ioc Residence)
rows.name_zh: 培正中学行政楼（原卢廉若私邸）
rows.pinyin: Péizhèng Zhōngxué Xíngzhènglóu (Yuán Lú Liánruò Sīdǐ)
rows.summary: This building was completed in the early 20th century as the private house of the Lou Lim Iok family, the creators of the neighbouring garden, and has been part of a school since 1938. Its eclectic design has façades influenced by European neoclassical architecture. It now serves as the administrative building of Pui Ching Middle School.

rows.name: Pátio de Chôn Sau
rows.summary: Pátio de Chôn Sau is a small alley on the old Macau Peninsula that used to be full of antique and nostalgic shops. Today it holds eateries, small shops and cultural-creative stores, with street graffiti and decorations hung overhead, and it has become a popular place for photographs. It suits a short wander north of Senado Square.

rows.name: Rainbow Houses and Murals
rows.pinyin: Cǎihóng Wū Jí Sān Fú Bìhuà
rows.summary: A group of two-storey buildings near Rua de Cinco de Outubro has been painted in bright colours under a government scheme to support local shops and bring visitors into the neighbourhood. Three murals nearby have different themes, among them the drunken dragon dance, an intangible cultural heritage of Macau, and Portuguese folk dance, reflecting the city's Chinese and Portuguese cultures. The photo spots link Rua de Cinco de Outubro with several old streets of the district.

rows.name: Red Market Building
rows.summary: A working municipal market on Avenida do Almirante Lacerda, opened in 1936 and named for its red bricks. The symmetrical brick building has a clock tower in the middle and a watchtower at each corner, and is a typical example of modern architecture of its time. Stalls inside sell seafood, meat and vegetables, and the market reopened on 30 May 2024 after two years of renovation.

rows.name: Rua da Felicidade and Beco da Felicidade
rows.summary: A short lane of two-storey Chinese shophouses with grey walls and sloping roofs, laid out on reclaimed marshland between 1862 and 1874 by wealthy Fujian merchants. It was once Macau's red-lantern district of brothels and opium dens, and after prostitution was banned it became a busy dining and trading street. Beco da Felicidade runs off it, and shops and restaurants now fill the ground floors.

rows.name: Rua de Cinco de Outubro
rows.summary: Rua de Cinco de Outubro is an old street on the Macau Peninsula, named after the Portuguese revolution of 5 October 1910 that ended the monarchy and founded the Republic. It keeps a nostalgic old-town atmosphere, with many shops and local restaurants worth a look. A group of painted houses and murals stands nearby.

rows.name: Rua do Cunha
rows.summary: A narrow pedestrian street in the heart of Taipa Village, made Macau's first pedestrian zone in 1983. It is lined with old restaurants serving traditional dishes and shops selling souvenir snacks such as almond biscuits, egg rolls, coconut flakes and peanut candy. It is named after Pedro Alexandrino da Cunha, a naval captain who became governor of Macau in 1850 and died of cholera 37 days after arriving.

rows.name: Rua dos Ervanários and Rua de Nossa Senhora do Amparo
rows.summary: These two old streets keep traditional shops selling incense, second-hand goods and antiques, alongside newer specialty coffee shops and cultural-creative stores. The Chinese name of the first street refers to the customs service that once handled Macau's foreign trade. Occasional events and cultural-creative flea markets are held in the area.

rows.name: Ruins of St. Paul's
rows.summary: The façade of the Church of Mater Dei (built 1602–1640 and destroyed by fire in 1835), known in Portuguese as the Ruínas de São Paulo, is all that remains standing, about 23 metres wide and 25.5 metres high and reached by a staircase. The carving combines a Western Baroque-Mannerist design with Oriental motifs: Jesuit saints, the Virgin Mary flanked by a seven-headed hydra and a Portuguese ship, Chinese lions and Chinese-character inscriptions. Archaeological remains of St Paul's College lie beside it, and a museum of sacred art and a crypt are built behind the façade.

rows.name: S. Francisco Garden
rows.summary: S. Francisco Garden is a small park beside Praia Grande, divided into two parts by Rua de Santa Clara. The lower part is level, with flowerbeds and footpaths through greenery, while the hillier upper part, built along the slope, has paths up to a children's playground. Low walls, columns, an arched entrance and a fountain give the park a European look, and a small round building near the top, once a museum honouring First World War soldiers, now houses a disability association.

rows.name: Sam Kai Vui Kun (Kuan Tai Temple)
rows.summary: A temple dating from the 18th century, with plaques recording a restoration in 1792. Its name means "three-streets meeting hall": merchants from Rua dos Mercadores, Rua das Estalagens and Rua dos Ervanários once met here, in the old Chinese bazaar quarter, and it later became purely a place of worship for Kuan Tai, the deity of loyalty and righteousness. Part of the Historic Centre of Macau, it stands beside the main square among largely Portuguese-style buildings.

rows.name: Sam Po Temple, Taipa
rows.summary: A fishermen's temple (Templo de Sam Po) first built in 1845 in the shape of a natural cave and rebuilt in 1864, dedicated to Sam Po, who is worshipped as the third sister of Tin Hau and is remembered for helping people to defeat pirates. A large rock sits inside the building, with a shrine carved into it. The front has painted decoration and carvings under the roof tiles, brown double doors and five halls in a row.

rows.name: Sam Seng Temple, Coloane Village
rows.summary: A small temple (Templo de Sam Seng) built in 1865 at the northern end of Coloane Village, dedicated to Kum Fa, a goddess who protects children, to Kun Iam and to Va Kuong, a fire god. It is a single chamber with an altar in the middle and, beside the entrance, a musical stone and a bell; it was rebuilt in 2002 after storm damage. Traditional iron-and-wood stilt houses stand along the shore nearby.

rows.name: Sam Seng Temple, Ká Hó
rows.summary: A village temple (Pagode de Sam Seng) built in 1883 on the site of a smaller Hung Shing temple, and named for the three gods enshrined in it: Hung Shing, Tam Kong and Kuan Tai. It has a porch and a main hall under two linked gabled roofs with no courtyard between them, which is unusual in Chinese temples, and coloured murals above the porch doorways. Ká Hó, together with Hac Sá, is one of the only two Hakka villages left in Macau.

rows.name: Sculpture Park of the Chinese Ethnics
rows.summary: An open-air display of 56 bronze sculptures of China's ethnic groups, set out roughly according to where each group lives in the country so that visitors can see their appearance, lifestyles and distribution. An exhibition centre shows pictures, videos and objects of the groups' ways of life. The park was set up on Taipa in 2009 and moved to Comendador Ho Yin Park in 2019.

rows.name: Seac Pai Van Park
rows.summary: A family park of about 198,000 square metres in the wooded hills of western Coloane (Parque de Seac Pai Van). Besides the panda and red panda pavilions it holds the Natural and Agrarian Museum, a large walk-in aviary, botanical gardens, children's playgrounds and paths for strolling.

rows.name: Seak Kam Tong Hang Toi Temple
rows.summary: A small temple of 1894 in the San Kio neighbourhood, unusual in China for worshipping Seak Kam Tong, the guardian stone that wards off evil, as its main deity, and once also a meeting hall for local residents. Only the entrance and the main hall survive, joined by a corridor round a small atrium, in brick and wood with stone lions at the door and carved auspicious motifs. The main hall holds a Seak Kam Tong statue of Jiang Ziya flanked by Kun Iam and the Tai Sui deities.

rows.name: Sin Fong Temple
rows.summary: Sin Fong Temple is a temple in the Mong-Há district that was already recorded in a survey of 1827. Its low halls and short eaves hold a main hall for General Vanguard, a deity of protection from disasters and danger, and a side hall for the Dragon King of the East Sea, linked to fishing and safety at sea. The oldest object inside is a hanging 'cloud plate' dated 1861.

rows.name: Sir Robert Ho Tung Library
rows.summary: A mansion built before 1894 as the home of Dona Carolina Cunha, bought in 1918 by the Hong Kong businessman Sir Robert Ho Tung as a retreat. His will left it to the Macau government as a public library, which has been open since 1958. The first floor holds a collection of old Chinese books, some going back to the Ming dynasty, and the building stands on St Augustine's Square (Largo de Santo Agostinho).

rows.name: St. Anthony's Church
rows.summary: One of the oldest churches in Macau, first built of bamboo and wood before 1560 on the site of the Jesuits' first headquarters in the city. It was rebuilt in 1875 and given a grainy Shanghai-plaster finish in 1930, and it has a neoclassical façade and a Baroque-influenced interior with an elaborate main altar. Its Chinese name, Fa Vong Tong, means Church of Flowers, a reference to the Portuguese weddings once held in the church.

rows.name: St. Augustine's Church
rows.summary: Part of the Historic Centre of Macau, St. Augustine's Church (Igreja de Santo Agostinho) was founded by Spanish Augustinians in 1591 and has had its present form since 1874. Its plain neoclassical facade contrasts with a richer interior of nave, high choir and sacristy. Local Chinese call it the Temple of the Long-whiskered Dragon, after the palm leaves once used to patch its roof, and the church organises an annual Way of the Cross procession, one of the most popular in the city.

rows.name: St. Augustine's Square
rows.summary: A cobbled square (Largo de Santo Agostinho) lined with classified buildings, among them St Augustine's Church, the Dom Pedro V Theatre, St Joseph's Seminary and the Sir Robert Ho Tung Library. The cobblestone pavement ties the area together and gives it the look of a traditional Portuguese streetscape. It is part of the Historic Centre of Macau.

rows.name: St. Dominic's Church
rows.summary: A church (Igreja de São Domingos) founded in 1587 by three Spanish Dominican priests who had come from Acapulco in Mexico; it was first built of wood, which gave it the Chinese name Pan Cheong Tong, 'Church of Wooden Planks'. It has a basilican plan with Baroque influences in its interior decoration, the Dominican insignia on the pediment of its façade, and a three-storey bell tower beside the sacristy that holds a small museum of sacred art. Our Lady of Fatima has been honoured here since 1929, and a procession leaves the church every year on 13 May.

rows.name: St. Francis Fort and Barracks
rows.summary: The fort stands by the old Praia Grande bay and dates from the 1720s, when it belonged to a Franciscan monastery and had six cannons able to reach as far as Taipa. Its oval wall, six metres high, is divided into upper and lower levels, and the two-storey building behind it, the St. Francis Barracks, is now the headquarters of Macau's Security Forces. The barracks lobby holds the Museum of the Macau Security Forces, which shows military equipment and the history of the Macau police.

rows.name: St. Francis Xavier Church, Mong-Há
rows.summary: Built in 1951, this small church is attached to an old people's home near Mong-Há Hill. Inside, it is simple and tranquil, with a black marble altar. Tall louvred shutters along the walls open onto courtyards and gardens.

rows.name: St. Joseph's Seminary and Church
rows.summary: The seminary (Seminário de São José) was founded by the Jesuits in 1728, and the church (Igreja de São José) beside it, built in 1758, is one of the rare examples of Baroque architecture in China. The church has a Greek-cross plan under a dome 12.5 metres across and 19 metres high, lit by two rows of 16 small windows, and a side altar holds a bone relic of St Francis Xavier. The three-storey seminary building, with a Chinese-style sloping roof and an F-shaped plan, is not open to the public.

rows.name: St. Lawrence's Church
rows.summary: A neoclassical church (Igreja de São Lourenço) first built by the Jesuits before 1560 and rebuilt in 1846 to a design by the Macanese architect Tomás D'Aquino. Before Praia Grande Bay was reclaimed it looked straight over the water, and sailors' families waited on its steps for ships to return, hence the Chinese name Feng Shun Tang, Hall of the Soothing Winds. Inside is a rare local set of stained-glass windows with biblical scenes.

rows.name: St. Lazarus' Church
rows.summary: A neoclassical church (Igreja de São Lázaro) in the old St Lazarus district, founded in the 16th century as a hospital chapel for lepers and one of the three oldest churches in Macau. The present building dates from the 1880s, with an asymmetrical façade, a pediment carrying a cross and an anchor, a belfry on the right and two aisles inside. The Cross of Hope from the original chapel stands in the forecourt, and the church has long been a centre of Macau's Chinese Catholic community.

rows.name: St. Lazarus' District
rows.summary: A quarter of narrow streets around Rua do Volong, Rua de São Roque and Rua de São Miguel, once the home of Macau's Chinese Catholics. In the late 19th century the government planned its streets and houses, and in recent years the roads have been repaved in stone and fitted with European-style street lamps. The classified area also includes the forecourt of the church of St Lazarus.

rows.name: St. Michael the Archangel Cemetery
rows.summary: Macau's old Catholic cemetery (Cemitério de São Miguel Arcanjo), completed in 1854 on a 19th-century plan, with a main entrance street leading to the Chapel of St Michael of 1875 and a network of lanes inside. It holds tombs and monuments in many styles from the 19th and 20th centuries, among them the poet Camilo Pessanha and Colonel Vicente Nicolau de Mesquita. Western and Chinese festivals and religious ceremonies are held here.

rows.name: St. Paul's College Walls, Pátio do Espinho
rows.name_zh: 圣保禄学院围墙遗迹（茨林围）
rows.summary: Sections of the rammed-earth wall that enclosed St Paul's College, the Jesuit college founded in 1594, together with excavated remains of its buildings. The longest surviving stretch, part of the north wall, is about 135 metres long and 3.4 to 4.4 metres high, running along the north side of Pátio do Espinho between houses. A further section of the south wall stands inside the neighbouring Matteo Ricci College.

rows.name: Stone with the Coat of Arms of Portugal, Lin Fong Temple
rows.name_zh: 刻有葡国徽号的石块（莲峰庙旁）
rows.pinyin: Kè Yǒu Pú Guó Huīhào De Shíkuài (Liánfēng Miào Páng)
rows.summary: A stone carved with the Portuguese coat of arms, a crown over a shield, and the date 22 August 1849, the day Governor João Maria Ferreira do Amaral was killed here. It was set up in his memory near the start of the road to the Border Gate, with its back to Lin Fong Temple and its face towards the Green Island (Ilha Verde) side.

rows.name: Stone with the Coat of Arms of Portugal, Rampa dos Cavaleiros
rows.name_zh: 刻有葡国徽号的石块（望厦马交石斜坡旁）
rows.pinyin: Kè Yǒu Pú Guó Huīhào De Shíkuài (Wàngxià Mǎjiāoshí Xiépō Páng)
rows.summary: A rock engraved in 1847 with the Portuguese royal coat of arms, a crown over a shield, and the inscription 'Rampa dos Cavaleiros 1847', meaning Slope of the Knights. It was set up beside the slope to celebrate the opening of new avenues in the Mong-Há area.

rows.name: Streets of the Old Christian Quarter
rows.name_zh: 龙嵩正街至妈阁斜巷街道
rows.pinyin: Lóngsōng Zhèngjiē Zhì Māgé Xiéxiàng Jiēdào
rows.summary: A route of old streets through the former Christian quarter, the Portuguese residential area where the first settlers lived after arriving in Macau. It runs between Rua Central, Rua de S. Lourenço, Rua do Padre António, Rua da Barra and Calçada da Barra. Many historic buildings remain along it, including St Lawrence's Church, St Joseph's Church and Seminary and the Lilau well.

rows.name: Sun Yat-sen Memorial House
rows.summary: A neo-Arabic villa that was the Macau home of Sun Yat-sen's family, including his first wife Lu Muzhen, who died here in 1952; it was rebuilt in 1931 after an explosion at the former governor's powder magazine damaged the original. Since 1958 it has been a memorial house presenting the life of Sun Yat-sen and his family, with documents on display and a bronze statue in the garden. The three-storey main building has a symmetrical façade with semicircular bays and foliage patterns on its columns, window frames and railings.

rows.name: São Tiago da Barra Fortress
rows.summary: A small fortress (Fortaleza de São Tiago da Barra) at the Barra tip of the peninsula, built in 1629 with 16 cannon on the site of a simpler 1622 fortification, to guard the water entrance to the Inner Harbour. Its commander was appointed directly by the King of Portugal, and a chapel to St James, patron saint of soldiers, was added within the walls in 1740. The fortress was converted into a hotel, the Pousada de São Tiago, in 1981, with the chapel preserved.

rows.name: Tai Wong Temple, Hac Sá
rows.summary: A small single-chamber temple (Templo de Tai Wong) in Hac Sá village, built before 1902 and dedicated to Tai Wong, whom local legend credits with protecting the residents. It is small even by Coloane standards. Hac Sá, together with Ká Hó, is one of the only two Hakka villages left in Macau.

rows.name: Taipa Fortress
rows.summary: A small hillside fort built in 1846 to defend against pirates, later a summer residence of the governor of Macau and, from 1975, the police station of the islands. It has small cannons at its entrance and around its walls, barracks with corridors facing the old shoreline, two sentry posts and a cylindrical building at the rear that was once an ammunition store. Today it is the headquarters of the Macau Scout Association, and the ground around it is laid out as a rest area.

rows.name: Taipa Grande Viewing Platform
rows.summary: A viewing platform on the slope of Taipa Grande hill with panoramic views over Taipa Village and the Cotai Strip. It can be reached by the Taipa Grande Hill inclined lift, which runs up the slope from Estrada Governador Nobre de Carvalho.

rows.name: Taipa Houses–Museum
rows.summary: A row of five green houses of 1921 on Avenida da Praia, once the homes of senior civil servants and Macanese families, restored as museums and opened to visitors in 1999. Since 2016 they have housed the Macanese Living Museum, an exhibitions gallery, the Creative Casa (a bookshop and gallery space), the Nostalgic House with changing exhibitions on the Macanese and the Cotai area, and a fifth house leased as a restaurant.

rows.name: Taipa Municipal Garden
rows.summary: A formal garden in European style on the hillside between Our Lady of Carmel Church and the Taipa Houses–Museum (Jardim Municipal da Taipa), completed in 1924. It has a vine-covered gazebo with fountains and stone benches, well-kept flower beds and paths winding up to a small belvedere. A zigzag walkway with low scalloped walls leads down to the old seafront.

rows.name: Tak Sang Pawnshop
rows.summary: A 19th-century pawnshop on Rua de Cinco de Outubro, typical of its time, with a fortified tower behind the shop in which valuables were stored. The business has since closed. It is classified as a building of architectural interest.

rows.name: Tam Kong Temple, Coloane Village
rows.summary: A temple to Tam Kong, a sea god who protects fishermen (Templo de Tam Kong), built in 1862 beside a square at the southern end of Coloane Village. It has three halls with a pavilion at either side, stone lions at the door and a wall painting of the tiger that follows the god in the legend, and it houses a model dragon boat made of whalebone, a gift from fishermen. Worshippers from Hong Kong and Macau come for the Tam Kong Festival on the eighth day of the fourth lunar month, when Cantonese opera is staged.

rows.name: Tap Seac Square
rows.summary: Tap Seac Square is a large public square on the site of the former Coronel Mesquita sports ground, which was opened early in the 20th century as a recreation ground outside the walls of the old Christian city and became known as the hockey pitch. The square was completed in 2007 and is surrounded by public buildings, including the Macau Central Library and the Archives of Macau. Tap Seac Gallery stands nearby.

rows.name: Temple of Kuan Tai and Tin Hau, Taipa
rows.summary: A small temple built between 1662 and 1723, also called Mou Tai Temple, with three chambers: the central hall to Kuan Tai, god of loyalty and bravery, a temple to Tin Hau on its right and a keeper's room on its left. The two shrines have separate entrances but are joined by a corridor, and couplets dated 1837 record the temple's history.

rows.name: The Spectacle and Art Collection, MGM Cotai
rows.name_zh: 美狮美高梅视博广场及艺术收藏
rows.pinyin: Měishī Měigāoméi Shìbó Guǎngchǎng jí Yìshù Shōucáng
rows.summary: The Spectacle is a glass-roofed atrium at the centre of the MGM Cotai resort, more than four storeys high and about as long as a football pitch, under a gridshell roof with no supporting columns, with 25 LED screens showing digital artworks and an indoor garden of more than 100,000 plants. Around it, more than 300 works from the resort's art collection are on show in the public areas, from Qing-dynasty carpets to contemporary Asian paintings, sculptures and large digital installations.

rows.name: Tin Hau Temple, Areia Preta
rows.summary: A temple to Tin Hau, worshipped as a protector of seafarers, that began in a natural cave on what was once an eastern bay of the peninsula; an inscription records its conversion into a temple in 1865. Stone pagodas and pavilions step up the hillside, with separate shrines to Tin Hau, Tei Mou, Kun Iam, Tai Soi and Mou Hau. It is the only surviving temple on the north-eastern side of the peninsula, and was restored in 1987.

rows.name: Tin Hau Temple, Coloane Village
rows.summary: A temple to Tin Hau (Templo de Tin Hau), goddess of seafarers, dated by an iron bell to at least 1763 and one of the four temples of Coloane village. It has an entrance hall and a main hall joined by a pavilion that once served as a public meeting place, and Kuan Tai, Lu Ban, Choi Bak and Hua Tuo are worshipped here as well as Tin Hau. A pair of stone lions stands outside, and an old hand-pulled fire engine is kept at the entrance.

rows.name: Tin Hau Temple, Taipa
rows.summary: Taipa's Tin Hau temple (Templo de Tin Hau, also called Tin Hau Kong), built before 1785, the date on its bell, and reconstructed in 1848. It once had three chambers, but only the central hall to Tin Hau remains. The goddess is venerated by Taipa's fishing and trading families.

rows.name: Tou Tei Temple, Patane
rows.summary: A group of temples set in a line along the foot of a hill in the Patane district, centred on Tou Tei, the Earth God, with shrines to Kun Iam, the Goddess of Mercy, and to the Buddha. The complex includes the Lei San Sheng Mu hall, the Soi Ut Temple (Kun Iam Grotto) and the I Leng Temple. A stone tablet of 1789 points to a foundation in the Qianlong reign, and the government began renovating the buildings in 1996 to recover their original appearance.

rows.name: Travessa da Paixão
rows.summary: A short pedestrian lane laid out in the 1920s beside the Ruins of St Paul's and named Travessa da Paixão in 1925. The Portuguese name implies passionate feeling and religious devotion, while the Chinese name, Love Lane, gives the lane a romantic reputation that has made it a favourite spot for wedding photographs and a location for films and television series. The matching houses at numbers 5 to 11 are decorated in red and pale yellow, and the neoclassical and modernist house at number 13 holds Cinematheque Passion.

rows.name: Travessa de S. Paulo
rows.summary: A short lane of houses near the Ruins of St Paul's, on land that once belonged to the St Paul's College complex, which included a clinic and a treasury. Most of those ancillary buildings were destroyed in the fire of 1835 that also destroyed the old Church of Mater Dei. The houses standing now are in a style similar to those of St Lazarus' District and are considered to be inspired by the Modern movement of the 1940s and 1950s.

rows.name: Tung Sin Tong Historical Archive Exhibition Hall
rows.name_zh: 同善堂历史档案陈列馆
rows.summary: The hall tells the story of the Tung Sin Tong Charitable Society, founded in 1892 and described by the tourism office as the first Chinese charitable organisation in Macau. The society began by giving food, clothing and medicine to the poor and now also runs nurseries, schools, an adult-education centre and medical clinics. The exhibits introduce the society and the people of Macau it has served.

rows.name: Vasco da Gama Garden
rows.summary: The garden was laid out in 1898 to mark 400 years since Vasco da Gama opened the sea route to India (Jardim de Vasco da Gama), and it was part of a long tree-lined avenue of the same name. At its centre a bronze bust of the navigator, set up in 1911, stands on a white marble plinth carrying an excerpt from the epic poem The Lusiads, with old cannons facing front and back. Renovations added a wave-shaped pond and a fountain around the bust.

rows.name: Victory Garden
rows.summary: The garden (Jardim da Vitória) opened in 1871 to mark the Portuguese victory over a Dutch attempt to take Macau in June 1622. At its centre stands an octagonal stone monument by the sculptor Rafael Bordalo Pinheiro, carrying the Portuguese emblem, laurel leaves and a cross, with an excerpt from Camões's Os Lusíadas on the pedestal. Stone terraces lead up from the avenue to this small park, which has flowerbeds, trees and benches.

rows.name: Xian Xinghai Memorial Museum
rows.summary: A museum in a two-storey 1950s villa with a garden, once post-office staff housing, that opened in November 2019 to honour the composer Xian Xinghai (1905–1945). He was born in Macau into a fishing family and wrote the Yellow River Cantata. The museum presents his life, his music and his ties to Macau.

rows.name: Youth Art Exhibition Pavilion
rows.summary: A two-storey building of 1925 on the south side of Tap Seac Square, built as the headquarters of the Caixa Escolar, a charity that supported pupils from poor families. Its yellow façade mixes classical and Moorish-style details with a tiled orange roof, and the Cultural Affairs Bureau describes it as the only classical building in Macau with such varied decorative art. It is now used for exhibitions of students' and young people's art and for performances.

rows.name: teamLab SuperNature Macau
rows.summary: A permanent digital art exhibition by the Tokyo art collective teamLab, in Hall F of the Cotai Expo at The Venetian Macau, open since June 2020. It fills a maze-like space of about 5,000 square metres under eight-metre ceilings with immersive, interactive artworks that visitors walk through.
